en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Beginning of the Text:
The Exposition of Grammar.
I pay homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One of infinite beauty, who has mastered the language of analysis,
and by whom eighty-four thousand divisions of the Dhamma— resplendent with infinite colors— shine throughout the world.
To him, the True Dhamma and the Saṅgha are a vessel of pure color.
Moggallāna, the one of great wisdom, a lion in the forest beyond the shore,
let out a roar of exposition like a river— a proclamation that pervades the forest beyond the shore of the Sugata’s teaching.
I shall illuminate its meaning, analyzing its various strata, having plunged into the treatises on grammar and the ninefold teaching of the Master. 1.
The Section on Sandhi.
The heap of consonants (saññārāsi) consists of the garu-consonant heap, vowel, semivowel, long, short, consonant, group, and the nasal stop (niggahīta).
1. The forty-three [consonants] beginning with *ka* (in many texts): *ka*. 2.
The forty-three syllables (*akkhara*) consisting of the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *bindu* (anusvāra) are called "phonemes" (*vaṇṇa*).
They are: *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *eta*, *e*, *ota*, *o*. *Ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*.
Ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ.
They are called *vaṇṇā* because they describe (*vaṇṇenti*) and reveal meaning; they are also called *akkharā*.

Because they are the form of name-designation (*nāmapaññatti*), they do not perish (*nakkharanti*)—that is, they do not undergo decay or destruction—and thus they are *akkharā*. For it is said in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (1.76): "Name and clan do not age."
2. Vowels (*sara*). [Kaccāyana 1.3.3]: *rūpa* 3; *nīti* 3.
Among those letters, the ten letters at the beginning are called vowels (*sara*). They are called *sara* because, having acquired their own form, they "shine" (*rājanti*) or "radiate" (*virocanti*).
3. Two by two, they are of the same class (*savaṇṇa*).
Among those vowels (*sara*), two pairs of vowels are called "homogeneous" (*savaṇṇa*).

[Namely: *a* and *ā* are the *avaṇṇa*; *i* and *ī* are the *ivaṇṇa*; *u* and *ū* are the *uvaṇṇa*; *e* and *eta* are the *etavaṇṇa*; *o* and *ota* are the *otavaṇṇa*. They are called "homogeneous" (*savaṇṇa*) because they have the same sound (*suti*). They are also called "identical in form" (*sarūpa*), because they have an identical form (*rūpa*) and the same sound (*suti*).
4. The preceding [vowel] is short. (Ka. 4; Rū. 4; Nī. 4.22)

Among pairs of similar vowels, whichever is the first is called "short" (*rassa*). They are called "short" because they are to be uttered in a short duration; the "short duration" is the time it takes for the eyelids to open and close once.

In that regard, the two [words] *eta* and *ota* are found in some instances when followed by a single-word conjunction (*ekapadasaṃyoga*). Examples: *eṭṭhi*, *seṭṭho*, *oṭṭho*, *sotthi*. Why "in a single-word conjunction"?
So that they do not become short when followed by a conjunction between words. For example: *Maṃ ce tvaṃ nikhaṇaṃ vane* (Jā. 2.22.5); *Putto tyāhaṃ mahārāja* (Jā. 1.1.7).

What is meant by "in some cases" (*kvaci*)? It is so that short vowels do not occur even when there is a conjunction of single consonants, provided they are followed by the finals of a class-consonant (*vagganta*) or by *y*, *r*, *l*, or *v*.
Examples: *enti*, *senti*, *eyya*, *bhāseyya*, *meṇḍo*, *soṇḍo*. 5. *Paro dīgho* (Aṭṭhakathā 5; Rūpasiddhi 5; Nyāsa 5).

When two similar vowels (*savaṇṇa*) occur, whichever comes after is called "long" (*dīgha*). They are called "long" because they are to be pronounced over a long duration (*kāla*); a long duration is twice the duration of short vowels.
6. The consonants are *ka* and so forth. (Ka. 6; Rū. 8; Nī. 6).

Among those phonemes, the phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with the nasal dot (*bindu*) are called consonants (*byañjana*). They are called "consonants" because they manifest meaning (*atthaṃ byañjayanti*). Furthermore, when pure, they consist of one-and-a-half morae (*mattikā*); when joined with a short vowel, they consist of two-and-a-quarter morae;
when joined with a long vowel, they consist of three-and-a-half morae. 7. There are five groups (*vaggā*) of five each. (Ka. 7; Rū. 9; Nī. 7).
Among those consonants, the five groups of five consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are called *vaggas* (classes).

The group of five beginning with *ka* is the *kavagga*; that beginning with *ca* is the *cavagga*; that beginning with *ṭa* is the *ṭavagga*; that beginning with *ta* is the *tavagga*; and that beginning with *pa* is the *pavagga*. It is established that the remaining [consonants] are non-classes (*avaggas*). In the *Vaṇṇuddesa*, they are called *vaggas* because they are connected to a class, which is a collection of consonants that share the same place of articulation (*ekaṭṭhānika*).
8. The *bindu* is the *niggahīta*. (Ka. 8; Rū. 10; Nī. 8)
A single consonant preceding a *bindu* (anusvāra) is called *niggahīta*. It is called *niggahīta* because it is grasped (*niggayha*) and uttered after having been held back.
The section on the collection of technical designations (*saññā*) is finished. Now follows the section on the usage of consonants (*byañjana*).
Place (*ṭhāna*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and effort (*payatana*) are explained at Rūpārūpa-vibhāga 2 (in the Piṭṭha), Niddesa 6 (in the Piṭṭha), and Sutta-aṅga 23.

There are six places: the place of the throat (*kaṇṭha-ṭhāna*), the place of the palate (*tālu-ṭhāna*), the place of the head (*muddha-ṭhāna*), the place of the teeth (*danta-ṭhāna*), the place of the lips (*oṭṭha-ṭhāna*), and the place of the nose (*nāsika-ṭhāna*).
Among these, for one speaking skillfully, that which is called "the axle" (*akkha*) is the place of the throat.
Where it is said "iccha," that is the location of the palate. Where it is said "raṭṭha," that is the location of the head.
Where it is said "sattha," that is the location of the teeth. Where it is called "puppha," that is the location of the lips. The region of the nose is the location of the nose.

In some places, however, the chest-location, the head-location, and the root-of-the-tongue-location are also mentioned. Therein, the "head-location" is indeed the same as the "palate-location. They say, moreover, that the "root-of-the-tongue-location" is common to all consonants.
The instrument (*karaṇa*) is fourfold: the root of the tongue, the base of the tongue, the tip of the tongue, and its own location.

The effort (*payatana*) is fourfold: closed (*saṃvuṭa*), open (*vivaṭa*), touched (*phuṭṭha*), and slightly touched (*īsaṃphuṭṭha*). In this context, the specific modes of the instruments—such as closing and so forth—in relation to their respective locations are termed "closed" and so on.
Among these, the gutturals (*avaṇṇa*), the *ka*-group consonants, and the letter *ha* arise through the mutual contact of the regions of the throat.
The *ivaṇṇa*, the *cavagga*, and the letter *y* are called "palate-born" (*tālujā*), as they arise as if through the contact of the middle of the tongue with the palate.
The *ṭavagga*, the letter *r*, and the letter *ḷ* are called "head-born" (*muddhajā*), as they arise through the contact of the tip of the tongue with the upper part of the interior of the mouth.
The *tavagga*, the letter *l*, and the letter *s* are "tooth-born" (*dantajā*), as they arise through the contact of the tip of the tongue with the upper row of teeth.
The vowel *u* produced by the contact of the two lips is called "lip-born" (*oṭṭhaja*). The *niggahīta* (anusvāra) is called "nose-born" (*nāsikaja*).

However, the five final consonants of each group (*varga*) are produced both in the nasal cavity and in their own respective places of articulation. The vowel *e* is born from the throat and the palate (*kaṇṭhatāluja*).

The vowel *o* is born from the throat and the lips (*kaṇṭhoṭṭhaja*). The vowel *va* is born from the teeth and the lips (*dantoṭṭhaja*). Furthermore, the vowels *i* and *u* are indeed produced in the throat as well. When...
When the letter *ha* is joined with the final consonants of the groups (*vagganta*)—namely *ya*, *ra*, or *la*—they call that *ura-ja*.
Examples are: *pañho*, *tuṇhi*, *nhāto*, *vimhito*, *gayhate*, *vulhate*, *avhānaṃ*.
The vowel *a* pronounced by constricting the throat is called *saṃvuṭa*. [The vowels] are produced by opening their respective places of articulation and instruments (*karaṇāni*).
The remaining vowels and the letter *ha* are called "open" (*vivaṭa*).

Those same [consonants] pronounced by making contact firmly are called "contacted" (*phuṭṭha*). Pronounced with slight contact, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are called "slightly contacted" (*īsaṃphuṭṭha*).
In that regard, first, when pronouncing the *pa*-group among the labials, firm contact between the two lips is required.
Why? Because the state of being closed (*phuṭṭha-payatanika*) characterizes *pavagga*. However, for those pronouncing *uvaṇṇa*, the opening of both lips is required.
Why? Because the state of being open (*vivaṭa-payatanika*) characterizes *uvaṇṇa*. This same method applies to all the remaining vowels.
In the *Cūḷanirutti*, however, it is stated that all short vowels are called "closed" (*saṃvuṭa*), and all long vowels are called "open" (*vivaṭa*).
Likewise, in the *Saddasāratthajālinī* and in certain Pali texts, this [latter view] is more appropriate.

Vowels joined with consonants from other positions do not abandon their own place of articulation (*ṭhāna*) or their mode of formation (*karaṇa*), even though they do abandon their point of effort (*payatana*). Therefore, when various sounds come together, one should also understand the specific combinations of their points of effort.
In that regard, if one says "suṇātu me": [The text continues: ...if... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
If one were to pronounce the letter *ṇa* by placing the tip of the tongue against the teeth, the *ṇa*-sound would become a dental sound.
And if one were to pronounce the letter *tu* by bringing the tip of the tongue to the head (the palate), the *tu*-sound would become a cerebral sound.

This being the case, there would be what is called a "defect in the syllables" (*akkharavipatti*). This same principle applies to the other sounds produced at the head and the teeth. Therefore, those who recite the ritual formulas (*kammavācā*)...
One should become thoroughly skilled in names, places, grammatical relations, and bases. Furthermore,
the loose (*sithila*), the tight (*dhanita*), the long (*dīgha*), the short (*rassa*), the heavy (*garu*), the light (*lahu*),
the nasalized (*niggahīta*), the released (*vimutta*), the connected (*sambandha*), and the fixed (*vavatthita*) should be observed in the suttas [of the *Nirutti*] numbered 9 through 21.
Those to be pronounced with a soft vocal effort—namely, the first, third, and fifth consonants of each group—are called "soft" (*sithila*).
Those to be pronounced with a stiff vocal effort—namely, the second and fourth consonants of each group—are called "hard" (*dhanita*). Long and short vowels have been explained previously.

Those that are long, preceded by a conjunct consonant, or followed by *niggahīta* (the nasal *m*), are called "heavy" (*garuka*). The remaining ones are called "light" (*lahuka*). This is according to the phonetic sound (*sadda*).
The wind, without exiting through the opening of the mouth, faces the nostrils; thus, when the mouth is kept closed, the consonant to be uttered is called *niggahīta*.
All consonants joined with that [nasal] are called *niggahīta*. The others are called *vimutta*.
That which is to be uttered by way of the euphonic combination (*padasandhi*) is called *sambandha*. [This concludes] the analysis of words (*padaccheda*).
Having performed what is to be done, it is called "determined.
The section on the usage of phonemes is finished.
The section on the perception of lightness.
Jho, lo, po, gho, go. 9.
*Iyuvaṇṇā iyuvaṇṇā* (in many instances) *jhalā nāmassante ka*. 58; Rūp 29; Nī 205.
The *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels at the end of a noun (*nāma*) that is not in the feminine gender are, respectively, designated as *jhal*.
10. *Pitthiyaṃ* (In the neuter): Rule 59; Rūp 182; Nī 206.
When a name is in the feminine gender, the vowels *i* and *u* are designated as *saññā*.
11. *Ghā* (The *gha*-suffix): Rule 60; Rūp 177; Nī 207.
*Gho*, *ā*: this is a two-word [sūtra]. In the feminine gender, the vowel *ā* bears the technical designation *gha*.
12. *Go syālapane ka* (Pāṇini 8.2.86): [The substitution of] *ka* occurs for the word *go* when used in addressing. Rūp. 71; Nī. 214.
In the case of address (*ālapana*), *ga* is considered a *saññā*.
The section on the group of light terms (*lahusaññā-rāsi*) is finished. The section on conventional terms (*saṅketa-rāsi*).
13. That which is a qualifier (*visesana*) [is subject] to that rule (*vidhi*). (Pāṇini 1.1.65; cf. 1.1.72; *vidhibbisesanantassa* in many manuscripts).
Whatever qualifier is seen in a sutta, the grammatical operation (*vidhi*) is to be understood as applying to it.
For example: *ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe*. [The forms] *narā*, *nare*. Here, *yonaṃ* is the qualifier, and *ṭāṭe* is the operation.
14. Regarding the seventh [case], the preceding vowel (*pubba-rū*). (Back page); Caṅkī 1.1.7; Pāṇini 1.1.66.
In the description of the locative case (*sattamī-niddesa*), it should be understood that the rule applies only to the preceding vowel.
“A vowel is elided before a vowel” (*saro lopo sare*). *Lokagga-apa-thera* 1.12.57.
15. On the fifth [case], it belongs to another. (Pāṇini 1.4.8; Pāṇini 1.4.67).
In the description of the fifth case, the rule should be understood as applying only to another [word].
"After *a*, for *yu* and *na*, there are *ṭā* and *ṭe*. Examples: *narā*, *nare*.
16. *Ādissa caṃ*. 1.1.9; Pāṇini 1.1.54.
When another [element] is being taught while visible, the grammatical operation (*vidhi*) is to be understood as applying to the initial sound (*ādivaṇṇa*).
"The letter *ra* is optionally counted [as the first]. Thirteen.
17. Regarding that which ends in the sixth case (chaṭṭhiyantassa):
A rule for that which ends in [a specific element] should be understood from the section on the sixth case (Chaṭṭhīniddesa). For example:
*rājassi nāmhi* (in the nominative singular), *rājinā* (in the instrumental singular).
18. A substitute (ādesa) having an *ṅ* as its indicatory letter (*anubandha*) should be understood to replace the final [phoneme] of that which is designated by the genitive case.
“*Gossāvaṅa*” [is an example]. [The result is] *gavassaṃ*.

19. That which has *ṭ* as its *anubandha* and that which consists of more than one syllable replace the whole [of the original]. (Aṭṭhasālinī 1.1.12; Pāṇini 1.1.55; Ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassa [in the plural]).

Both that substitute which has *ṭ* as its *anubandha* and that substitute which consists of more than one syllable should be understood to replace the entire collection of phonemes indicated by the genitive case.
First, regarding those with *ṭ* as their *anubandha*:
‘Imassānitthiyaṃ te’: *esu*.
In the case of multiple vowels:
‘animi nāmhi’. *Anena*, *iminā*.
20. *Ñakānubandhā ādyantā caṃ* (Pāṇini 1.1.46).

An affix (*āgama*) having *ñ* as its *anubandha* and an affix having *k* as its *anubandha* should be understood, respectively, as occurring at the beginning and at the end of that which is designated by the genitive case. Regarding an affix with *ñ* as its *anubandha*:
[example follows].
‘Brū-to tissa ñ’. It says [the following].
When there is a suffix beginning with *kā*: ‘Bhū-ssa vu-k’. *Babhūva*.
21. An augment having *m* as its *anubandha* follows after the final vowel of vowels. (Pāṇini 1.1.47).
An augment (*āgama*) that has *m* as its *anubandha* occurs after the final vowel among the vowels.
[Example: ‘*najjāyo svāma*’—the rivers flow. ‘*maṃ vā rudhādīnaṃ*’—he obstructs (*rundhati*). ‘*jara sadānamīma vā*’—he grows old (*jīrati*), he sinks (*sīdati*).
In this grammar, what is called "multiple vowels" (anekasara) exists only in nominal bases such as *nadī* and *purisa*, but not in verbal roots such as *gamu* and *paca*.
All verbal roots end in consonants; thus, there is no requirement for elision of the final element of a root.
Therefore, in the word *najjāyo*, the vowel *ī* is called "final vowel. From that, by the rule *najjāyo svāma*, [the suffix *ām* is applied].
There is the addition of the vowel *ā*. In the word *rundhati*, however, the vowel *u* is called the "final vowel" (*antasara*);
therefore, by the rule *maṃ vā rudhādīnaṃ*, there is the addition of the nasal dot (*bindu*). This is likewise the case in forms such as *jīrati* and *sīdati*.

In the Burmese manuscripts, however, the reading is *“mānubandho padānamantā paro”* (the *m* with its following consonant is added after the final of the words), which does not agree with the Sinhalese manuscripts.
22. Regarding prohibition (*vippaṭisedha*), Pāṇini 1.4.2; Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.16:
When there are two rules with the same scope that do not involve mutual prohibition, the subsequent rule generally finds its scope. For example, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*:

"Bhikkhus, there are these four things" (*cattāro ime bhikkhave dhammā*). Here, when the elision of the preceding word (*pubbalopa*) would apply, the elision of the subsequent word (*paralopa*) finds its scope.
23. *Saṅketa*: A suffix that is neither a constituent part [of a word] nor a phonetic marker (anubandha). Pāṇini 1.1.5.

Any phoneme (*vaṇṇa*) that is not a constituent part of an actual usage (*payoga*), but exists merely as a conventional symbol (*saṅketa*) within the grammatical rules (*sutta*), is called a suffix-marker (*anubandha*).
For example: *gossāva*. This indicates that when this word-form (*padarūpa*) is prescribed for the word *go* (cow), the suffix-marker does not enter into active usage.

24. By the term *vaṇṇapara* (followed by a vowel), those that share the same vowel (*savaṇṇa*) are also included. That which has a vowel as its subsequent element is called *vaṇṇapara*. When *avaṇṇa* is stated, both the long vowel *ā* and the short vowel *a* are understood; this is what is meant. The same applies to *ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa*. 25.
[The suffixes] *-ntu*, *-vantu*, *-mantu*, *-āvantu*, and *-tavantu* are related to [the corresponding forms] *-ntu*, *-vantu*, *-mantu*, *-āvantu*, and *-tavantu* (in many instances).
When *ntu* has been stated, the letter *n* belonging to the suffixes *vantu*, *mantu*, *āvantu*, and *tavantūnaṃ* is taken [as the subject].
“In the first [case], the *nto* of *nantūnaṃ* becomes *yo* before a vowel. Examples: *guṇavanto*, *satimanto*, *yāvanto*, *bhuttavanto*.
The section on conventional groups (*saṅketarāsi*) is concluded.
The Sandhividhāna:
Now the rules for euphonic combination (sandhi) are explained.

[They consist of: elision (lopa), lengthening (dīgho), shortening (rasso), vowel strengthening (vuddhi), substitution (ādeso), augmentation (āgamo), doubling (dvibhāvo), and transposition (vipallāso).
Loparāsi 26.
*Saro lopo sare ka* (Kaṇḍa 12; Rūpa 13; Nīti 30). That which is elided is called *lopa*.
When a vowel (*sara*) follows, a preceding vowel—whether similar (*sarūpa*) or dissimilar (*asarūpa*)—is subject to elision (*lopa*).
First, regarding similar vowels (*sarūpa*):
In *avaṇṇa*, *lokaggo* [is used] for *apathera* (Dhs 1102), *bhavāsavo* (Dhs 1102), and *avijjāsavo* (Vibh 949).
In *ivaṇṇa*, *munindo*, *munīrito*, *varavādīrito*, and *itthindriyaṃ* (Vibh 219) [are examples].
In a vowel, there is the *bahūpakāra* [sandhi] (Jātaka 1.22.588): *bahukā ūmi* becomes *bahūmi*; *sarabhuyā ūmi* becomes *sarabhūmi*;
*sarabhuyā udakaṃ* becomes *sarabhūdakaṃ*. In the case of dissimilar forms (*asarūpe*): *sotindriyaṃ* (Vibhaṅga 219); *kāmupādānaṃ*; *bhavesanā* (Dīghanikāya 3.305); *bhavogho* (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1156).

"Not two" (na dve vā): in certain instances, the elision of the preceding and following syllables does not occur, or it is optional.
"Vigilance is the deathless state" (Dhammapada 21); "Who shall discern this earth? (Dhammapada 44). In some instances:
"The ear-faculty" (Vibhaṅga 219), "the eye-faculty" (Vibhaṅga 219).

From here until the end of the section on compounds (*sandhikaṇḍa*), the words *kvaci* and *vā* occur everywhere in their appropriate places.

Therein, the word *kvaci* indicates various applications (*nānāpayoga*). The word *vā* indicates various forms within a single application (*ekapayoga*). This is a prohibition of elision (*lopanisedho*).
29. [The rule] for *parasara*.
In some instances, there is optionally the elision of a *sar* following a *niggahīta*.
(Pāṇini 8.3.19). Examples: *tvaṃsi* (Dhp 47); *jā. 2.22.764*; *candaṃva vimalaṃ suddhaṃ* (Dhp 413;
SN 642); *cakkaṃva vahato padaṃ* (Dhp 1); *halaṃdāni pakāsituṃ* (Mhv 8); *kinti vadeyyaṃ*.
"Cīvara," "patta," and "bhikkhunī"—thus is the group [of examples] for the elision of the initial vowel (saralopa). 30.

"It was given by the Lord of Men" (Jātaka 2.22.2161; *dinnaṃ* is read as *dinno* by the Lord of Men)—the analysis is *dinno āsī* ("it was given [and] was");
"there is a path" (Vibhaṅga 189)—*maggo atthi*; "it is declared the highest" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.47); [it refers to] the very mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).
And [in] *vibha.* 225: "The Saṅgha is like a mountain; the sound is like *cicciṭa*; 'yesterday's being' is *hiyyattanaṃ*;
'eating in the morning' is *pātarāsa*, [as in] 'instructed in the morning' (*pātamanusiṭṭho*); *Kakusandha Koṇāgamana*;
'the Elder, the best of speakers'—here there is a division between 'Kakusandha' and 'Elder'; the meaning is 'the doctrine of the Elder' (*theravāda*)."

It also occurs in the case of *animitte* according to the analysis in the Suttas. "You and the archer's son"—this is a great authority (*mahāpadesa*) regarding the grammatical condition (*paccaya*), this is a single unit, this is merely a distinction in expression, and so forth.
When a vowel follows, *avaṅ* replaces the final [sound] of the word *go*. (Ka. 22, 78; Rū. 28; Nī. 52, 229).
*Go* and *asso* [form] *gavāssaṃ*.
This also applies when the phonemes are analyzed according to the Sutta-vibhaṅga. Examples include *sagavacaṇḍo* (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.108) and *paragavacaṇḍo*.
Now, the rules for elision (*appa*) are stated.
According to the *Mahāvuttin*, the vowels *ava* and *ota* are substituted [for *pu*]:
*puthujjana*. One who has become manifold (*puthubhūta*) or one who is manifold (*puthu*) is a "worldling" (*puthujjana*). It is also seen as *puthunā* or *puthunī*.
*Apekkhiyāno* means "not looking back," with the sense of "having not looked back" (*apekkhitvā*). Thus: "rejoicing," "having fully awakened to that which is like a mirage," "do not..."
"Let the piśācas devour me; may you live for a hundred autumns. (1.2.9) "Day and night" means a divine hundred autumns; "human" means a hundred years—this is the sense.
"They follow from region to region" (Dīgha Nikāya 3.281); "they fly about from region to region"—the meaning is to each respective direction.
"Beyond a hundred," "beyond a thousand"; "one another" (*aññamaññaṃ*); "again and again" (*ponopuññaṃ*), that is, repeatedly (*punappunaṃ*).
Craving leads to renewed existence—or rather, "puno" is a single particle; "puno tassa mahe sīno," "puno pattaṃ gahetvāna," and "na ca dāni puno atthi.
There shall be no further meeting between me and you; I shall not see your face again in the future, nor in the form of the Deathless.
(Therīgāthā 2.2.235)

The substitution of *atta*, *utta*, and *etta* for *ivaṇṇa*—this should be understood by way of this method (*pariyāya*). The meaning is: "That category of meanings should be understood by this method.
One who comes once by nature is a *sakadāgāmī*; the state of a woman is *itthatta*; likewise, *evaṃ* is [the same as] *evaṃ + imaṃ*.
Cheda, you are our teacher, O Great Sage, you who know the meaning and the Dhamma.
[You are] one who has come from a noble lineage—
on the mother’s side (Dīgha Nikāya 1.303), on the father’s side, the maternal kin, the paternal kin, the maternal clan (Jātaka 2.19.118), and the paternal clan.
The wealth of your father, the wealth of your grandfather—will you obtain it? Will you be able to maintain yourselves?
How will you maintain yourselves? You desire to hear from us, monks;
indeed, there is nothing equal to us. Not by mixing with us... there is no way for us whatsoever.
"For there is no other way for us"—in these three instances, the particle *nu* has the sense of certainty (*ekamsatthe*). *Sosita* means both "dried up" and "boiled.
[According to] Pāṇini 1.1.94, *sotatta* means both "dried up" and "boiled"; [according to] the *Madhuratthavilāsinī* 1.157, it means "very cool" and "very heated.
*Jambonada* means "born of the Jambu River."
"O people, we shall dig up this earth—mountains and forests alike. (Dīgha Nikāya 2.2173) means "we shall dig them up.
"Whatever we do for Brahmā, that we shall give to you today" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.370); here [it refers to] winter and summer. (Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā).

pa. 286, regarding Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, there is conduct with those who are conscious and with the sons of those who are conscious. 1.106 – "Together with the sons of those who are conscious" means: *ossa uttaṃ* (the elision of *o* and the addition of *uttaṃ*).
"Pleasant, yet they did not bind themselves to that purpose" (Jātaka 1.6.7) means: by that speech, he did not bind himself to the purpose; he did not [commit himself].
The meaning is "one who obtains. *Avhāyantu su yuddhena jā* (Jātaka 2.22.871) means "let them call upon me with a challenge"; the sense is that he was calling out to him with words of provocation.
*Api nu hanukā santā jā* (Jātaka 1.1.146) means "are the jaws not entirely exhausted and fallen into suffering"?
Here, even a sandhi of modification (*vikārasandhi*) is included because it takes the form of a sandhi of substitution (*ādesasandhi*).
Thus ends the section on vowel substitutions (*sarādesa*).

From this point onward, the substitution of consonants belonging to the various classes (*vagga*) and non-classes (*avagga*) is demonstrated, beginning from the *ka*-class. 43. By means of the class-consonants (*vagga*) and the *la* sounds, those [substitutions] occur.

In the presence of a consonant belonging to the five groups (*pañcavagga*) or the labials (*la*), the *ya* sound of another word sometimes becomes those same [consonants] of the respective group or *la*, according to the sequence; that is to say, the *ya*-sound undergoes reversion to its original form (*pubbarūpa*).
One who acts with discernment is *nipaka*; the state of being *nipaka* is *nepakka*. That which is ripening is *vepakka*. That which is to be spoken is *vākka* or *vākya*.

That which is good in front is *pāmokkha*—in which case, when the reversion to the original form has occurred, the first letter of the second syllable becomes the first letter [of the preceding group].
The state of being fortunate is *sobhagga*; misfortune is *dobhagga*; that which is to be enjoyed is *bhogga*;

that which is to be yoked is *yogga*; the state of remorse is *kukkucca*; that which is to be spoken is *vācca*, as it is said (*vuccate*), "it is cooked" (*paccate*); the business of merchants is *vāṇijja*;
that which is to be eaten is *bhojja*; that which is to be yoked is *yojja*.
44. Regarding the rules for the substitution of *ca*-vaggas, *ba*, *ya*, and *ña* for *ta*-vaggas, *ra*, and *ṇa*: Kaccāyana 269, 41; Niddesa 104, 106, 119, 121–5.

When a *ya*-kāra follows—whether as a substitute (*ādesa*), a case-ending (*vibhatti*), or an affix (*paccaya*)—the *ta*-vaggas, *ra*, and *ṇa* optionally undergo substitutions by the *ca*-vaggas, *ba*, *ya*, and *ña*, respectively.

For example: *pokkharañño*, *pokkharaññā*, *pokkharaññaṃ*; *sāmaññaṃ* (the state of being a *samaṇa*), likewise *brahmaññaṃ*. These and others such as *kusalaṃ pārā* (Kaccāyana 411) are cited under the rule *yavā sare*.
The state of a wise person is *paṇḍiccaṃ*; the state of one who is peaceful is *saccaṃ*; the state of one who is such (as it is) is *taccchaṃ*. If it is thus—*yadi evaṃ*, *najjo*, *najjā*, *najjaṃ*.
The state of one who possesses happiness is *sohajjaṃ*. That which is to be spoken is *vajjaṃ*. He dwells having attained *jhānaṃ* (Dhs. 160);
[the forms] *upasampajjati*, *ajjhokāso*, *bojjhaṅgo*, *bojjhā*, or [the form] *bodhiyā*; that which is to be awakened to is *bujjhitabbaṃ*.
*Bojjhaṃ* (to be awakened), *bujjhati* (he awakens); *ponopuññaṃ* (a heap of merit); *thaññaṃ* (milk) produced from the breast (*thana*);
that which has its prior form in the *pavagga* (the *pa*-group):
*vappate* (is sown), *luppate* (is plucked), *abbhuggato* (risen up), *abbhokāso* (open space), *osabbhaṃ* (the state of being an ox, from *usabha*), and *labbhaṃ* (that which is to be obtained).

It is obtained (*labbhate*); it is beneficial (*hitaṃ*) in the village (*gāme*); it is a simile (*opammaṃ*); having come (*āgamma*), having approached (*upagamma*); that which is to be gone to is "gamya" (*gammiyateti gammo*);
likewise "damya" (*dammo*), "ramya" (*rammo*); it is gone to (*gamyate*), it is delighted in (*rammate*).
By this rule, "tavagga varaṇāna…," there is the substitution of *ya* for *ra*.
*Kayyate* means "it is made" (*kariyate*); *ayyo* means "noble one" (*ariyo*).
Regarding the phrase "*vaggalasehi te*": *lata* is the prior form of which [the following are derived]—*pallaṅko*, *vipallāso*, *kosallaṃ*, *pattakallaṃ*.
‘In *tavagga* and *varaṇa*, etc.’—that in which there is a rule (*vattaṃ*):
*puthabyā*, *puthabyaṃ*, *bhātu apaccaṃ*, *bhātabyo*, *korabyo*; that which exists in the sky (*dive*) is *dibbaṃ*, *dibyaṃ*.
‘With *vaggalasa*, they [are elided]’—of that which has a prior form (*pubbarūpaṃ*).
*Rahasi* means "in secret"; *somanassa*, *domanassa*, *sovacassa*, *dovacassa*—the augment *m* is inserted here due to the inclusion of the mind (*manogaṇattā*).

*Bhassam* means "that which is to be spoken" (*bhāsitabba*); *ādisitvā* (having pointed out), *uddisitvā* (having designated), *upavasitvā* (having fasted), *samphusitvā* (having touched)—[from these] one is pleased (*tussati*), displeased (*dussati*), or perishes (*nassati*), and so forth.
45. For *ta*, *tha*, *na*, and *la*, *ru* [is substituted]. (Back).
For those beginning with *tā*, substitutes beginning with *ṭā* optionally occur. Its *ṭattaṃ*—
*Paṭihaññati* (is struck back), *paṭaggi* (counter-fire), *paṭicchanno* (concealed), *paṭippanno* (engaged), *byāvaṭo* (occupied), *udāhaṭo* (uttered), *dukkaṭaṃ* (wrong-doing), and so forth.
Regarding the sense of *thassa ṭhattaṃ*:
the sense of oppression is *paṭi*; the sense of the conditioned is *paṭi*; "having made it a bone, one should listen" (*aṭṭhiṃkatvā suṇeyya*); the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), and so forth.
The change of *ṇ* to *l*:

"He leads to the village" (*gāmaṃ netīti*) becomes *gāmaṇi*; "He leads the army" (*senaṃ netīti*) becomes *senāṇi*. Also: *paṇidhi*, *paṇidhānaṃ*, *paṇihitaṃ*, *paṇāmo*, *pariṇāmo*, *oṇāmo*, *uṇṇāmo*, *karaṇīyaṃ*, *karaṇaṃ*, *ñāṇaṃ*, *tāṇaṃ*, *pamāṇaṃ*, *saraṇaṃ*, *gahaṇaṃ*, and so forth.
The change of *r* to *l*: [as follows].
*Paligho*, *palibodho*, *palipanno*, *pallaṅko*, *taluṇo taruṇo*, *kaluṇaṃ paridevayi jā*; *mahāsālo*, *aṭṭhasālinī*, *nayasālinī*, and so forth.
Now, the rule for the Great Substitution (*mahāvutti*) is stated:
"Whose [is] *khattam*?"—
He goes forth (*nikkhamati*), he has gone forth (*nikkhanta*), he is one who has renounced (*nekkhamo*); he performs the duties of a king, thus he is a *khatta*, or a doer (*kattā*).
And what is given—“One should be devoted to one’s own welfare” (Dhp 166).
And as for the effort:
one who gives a gift of flowers is a *pupphadāniya* or *pupphadānika*; one who dwells in the Sippali forest is a *sippalivaniya* or *sippalivanika*; a girl belonging to a maiden is a *kumārikā*.
The body of *Kha*—
Eḷamūga means one who is dull-witted. Regarding the word *ga*: it is called *loka* because it perishes (*lujjati*);

one who applies medicine is a physician (*bhisakka*); one who approaches families is a family-visitor (*kulūpaka*, *kulūpaga*); one who approaches milk is a milk-drinker (*khīrūpaka*, *khīrūpaga*); that which approaches the neck is a neck-halter (*gīvūpaka*, *gīvūpaga*).
His hand is like a lion’s—
due to his swiftness of movement he is a lion.
His head is like a parasol—
*Vinicchayo*, *acchariyaṃ*, *macchariyaṃ*. The meaning is that rays (*raṃsiyo*) "niccharanti," which is to say, they go forth (*nigacchanti*).

Regarding *chassa sattam*: there is the life of a thousand; *jā* [is the end of the verse]. 2.22.314—The analysis is *chāhaṃ assa*; thus it is *chāhaṃ-assa*, [which forms] the six sense bases (*saḷāyatanaṃ*).
Regarding *yassa dattaṃ*:

"He conquers the enemy army" (*parasenaṃ jināti*). By the rule *passe nadī-mahāvuttinā*, there is the elision of the vowel *a*; by the rule *rassa pararūpaṃ*, the short vowel is replaced by the subsequent form.
And as for *yat taṃ*—
“Niya” means that which is born depending [on something]; thus it is *niyo* or *niyako*, referring to one’s own son (*niyaṃ puttaṃ*).
The substitution of *ñ* for *n* occurs as follows: *paṇṇatti* becomes *paññatti*; *paṇṇāsaṃ* becomes *paññāsaṃ*; and *paṇṇavīsati* becomes *pañcavīsati*.
And "nattaṃ" means:
mere names are not known; without signs, purifications are not known. [This is] eightfold. 1.228 – The meaning is that they do not appear. Its agent—
Niyako means fixed.
And *tha* [is used in]:
*nitthiṇṇo*, *nittharaṇaṃ*, *netthāraṃ*.
And *nattaṃ*:
jino, pino, lino, paṭisallino, paḷino, malino, supino, pahīno, dhuno, puno, luno, āhunaṃ, pāhunaṃ.
From *dassa*, *ḍattaṃ*.
The burning of the corpse, the burning of the quarters, and the burning of the body. And as for the term *āḷahana*:
it is called *āḷahana* because they come and burn the corpse there; it is a cemetery (*susāna*).
And as for that very thing—the Sugata, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One—it gives forth (udati pasavati) from the heat (utu); thus it is "utu.
This is what is given of the Dhamma.
"Once, monks, on a certain occasion—I say this—*idha* (here) is a particle.
And what has been given?

'It is good to see the Noble Ones'—it is joined (*saṃhita*), arranged (*vihita*), covered (*pihita*), declared (*abhihita*), brought together (*sannihita*), directed (*paṇihita*); one has faith, one understands, one closes [the doors of the senses]."
The following is the explanation:
*Upaññāso* = *upanyāsa*; *ñāyo* = *nyāya*. It is called *ñāya* because the fruit always comes (*eti*) by means of it; *ñeyyaṃ* = *neyyaṃ*.
And as for *yattañca*:
Then there is his action, which is theft; it is dependent on the elders, thus it is "belonging to the elders" (*therādheyya*); it is the *pātimokkha*; suffering belongs to others (*parādheyyaka*).
Behold the result—its coming forth, its accomplishment, its being accomplished (*nipphanna*).
And [the word] *battañca*:
*sambahulaṃ* means *sampahulaṃ*; "even many being present, he does not support" (*na bharati*)—in the *Suttanipāta* (98) this is explained as "even being capable, he does not support.
*Bhassa* means *phattaṃ*.
"Endless and bringing fruit from every side" (Dīghanikāya 1.499).
"His bowl" (Ciram pavāsim, Dhammapada 219); "The elephant’s bursting temple-fluid" (Dhammapada 326).
Regarding the grammatical formations: *Dīghāvu* is *kumāro*; *mahāva* is *mahāva*. 459. *Dīghāyu* is *kumāro*. *Āyuṃ dhāreti* means "he bears life," hence *āvudhaṃ* is *āyudhaṃ*.

In the sense of "one who has life" (*āyu assa atthi*), the particle *āvuso* is used. *Kasāvo* is *kasāyo*; *kāsāvaṃ* is *kāsāyaṃ*. One who mows rice is *sālilāyako*; one who mows grass is *tiṇalāyako*.
Lassa rattaṃ:

"Nīlaṃ jalaṃ ettha" means "The blue water is here," thus it is the Nerañjarā; "jalaṃ gaṇhituṃ alaṃ" means "it is capable of holding water," thus it is the Arañjarā. "Sassataṃ pareti, ucchedaṃ pareti" means "it flows toward eternalism, it flows toward annihilation"—this is the meaning of *paleti*.
Vassa pattaṃ: [the leaf of the rain].
Pipāsati, pivāsati.
And *vatta*:
byākato, byatto, byañjanaṃ, sīlabbataṃ, nibbānaṃ, nibbutaṃ, dibbaṃ, dibbati, sibbati.

*kubbati*, *kubbanto*, *krubbati*, *krubbanto*; "a fool (*bāla*) should be restrained because he is not to be associated with"; "one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*)," "going forth" (*pabbajjā*), and so on.

Regarding *sassa chattaṃ*: it means "that which remains after being vomited" (*ucchiṭṭhaṃ-avasiṭṭhaṃ*). They also accept *sassa chattaṃ* in such passages as: "divine sounds resounded; rays of light resounded" (Vibhaṅga 730).
And regarding that:

“They hold up the bowl for one who has risen” (Mahāvagga 6.4). Here, however, in the phrase “one should rise and not be negligent,” the meaning of *uttiṭṭhati* is “standing with reference to [something]” (*uddissa tiṭṭhanaṃ*). It is said: “The Noble Ones stand with reference [to the Dhamma]; this is the invitation of the Noble Ones” (Jātaka 1.7.59).
Now, as for the word *ghattaṃ*:
*Nidāgho* means that which burns constantly (*niccaṃ dahati ettha*); it is very light (*laghu lahu*).
The substitution of *ḍa* for *la* results in *garuḍo* and *garuḷo*.
Thus ends the section on the substitution of phonemes.
Now the mixed substitutions will be stated. Regarding the word *ava*, it is said: *uttaṃ*.

*U-:* *Uddhammo*, *ubbinayo*, *uppatho*, *ummaggo*, *uññā* (disrespect), *avaññā* (contempt), *uññātaṃ* (disrespected), *avaññātaṃ* (contemned), *ujjhānasaññī* (one who perceives with reproach). *O-:* *Onaddho* (covered),
*okāso* (opportunity/space), *ovādo* (admonition), *olokanaṃ* (looking at), and so forth.
*Vassa* is derived from *uttaṃ*—the meaning is "it has been brought out. *Uposatha* means "fasting" (*upavasatha*), which is its established sense. *Nonītaṃ* means fresh butter (*navanītaṃ*).

*Nivatthakoca* means "one who wears armor" (*nivatthakavaca*). "What is your strength, O Great King?"—"Who indeed knows your chariot-circle?"—this is the meaning of *kvati*. "Who has seen you? [is the question].
Or "a son," or "a righteous monkey"—the break [in the verse] is: "Who indeed among Gotama’s disciples has gone? Where indeed have they gone? and so on, including "gold, fine gold," etc.
The derivation of *kussa* is:
it is formed from the root *krubbati*.
Its synonyms are:

*atrāja* (born from oneself), *putta* (son), *khetraja* (born of the field), *attaja* (self-born), *khettaja* (field-born), *gotrabhū* (lineage-become), *vatrabhū* (clan-become), *citraṃ* (variegated), *vicitraṃ* (diversified), *cittaṃ* (thought), *vicittaṃ* (manifold).
This mind is terrified (*utrastaṃ idaṃ cittaṃ*, Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.98); it has been terrified and has fled (*utrāsī palāyī*, Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249).
"And there will be a journey for me" (Ma. Ni. 1.23), and so forth. Regarding *dassadrattaṃ*:

that which has a pleasant outcome is "pleasant-resulting" (*sukhudrayaṃ*); "painful-resulting karma" (Ma. Ni. 2.109); "the earth is being split open" (*undriyyati*) (Saṃ. Ni. 1.158)—the meaning is "it breaks apart"; "one who betrays a friend" (*mittadrubbho*) [is] one who harms a friend (*mittaddubbho*).
The substitution of *dr* for *dd*:

*bhaddaṃ bhaddaṃ*, *asso bhadro* (Dhp 143), *sadā bhadrāni passati* (Dīp 2.153), *sabbe bhadrāni passantu* (Jāt 1.2.105), *bhadrāni bhadrāni yānāni yojetvā*. The substitution of *dr* for *ld*: *ludraṃ* (Dīp 2.43) [is] *luddaṃ*.
The substitution of *br* for *bb*: ...

*Brahāvanaṃ*, *brahantaṃ* (great forest), *vanappatiṃ* (tree); *brahmā*, *brāhmaṇo*—one who has cast out evil (*bāhitapāpa*) is called an *arahant* a *brāhmaṇa*; one born from Brahmā is called a *jātibrāhmaṇa*. *Va*: *vīnaṃ* (lute), *byattaṃ* (skilled)—*byaya* means destruction (*vayo-vināsa*);

*byāvaṭo* or *vāvaṭo* (engaged) in what should and should not be done; *byasanno* or *visanno* (sunk) in mud; *byamhito* or *vimhito* (astonished); *byamhaṃ* (palace)—the greatness of pride (*mānassa mhattaṃ*).
*Kkhassa cchattaṃ*: *Acchi* = *akkhi*; *sacchi* = *sakkhi*.

It is a particle used in the sense of "that which functions together with the eye" (*saha akkhinā vattati*), meaning "direct perception" (*paccakkha*). "I realize Nibbāna" (Mi. Pa. 5.3.12). *Macchikā* = *makkhikā*; *lacchī* = *lakkhī*, meaning "glory" (*sirī*).
According to the *Mahāvutti*, there is a contraction of syllables.
*Ācera* is *ācariya*; not raised by mother and father, born and living in a non-*ācera* family (Jā. 1.1.9); well-trained in the *ācera* (Jā. 1.7.82). *Brahmacera* is *brahmacariya*.
*Tiṇha* means sharp; *taṇhā* is *tasiṇā*. *Suṇhā* is *suṇisā*. *Abhiṇhaṃ* is *abhikkhaṇaṃ*.
*Paṇho* is *pubbaṇho*; in the *paṇha*, Mahosadha was executed (Jā. 1.15.324). *Surāmeraya* becomes *surāmereyyo*.
"Surā, mereyya, and drinks"—the person who indulges in these (DhA. 247). *Kammadhāraya* becomes *kammadhāreyya*;
*pāṭihīra*, *pāṭihera*, and *pāṭihāriya*; *acchera* and *acchariya*; *macchera*, *macchara*, and *macchariya*, and so forth.
There is also the increase of syllables (*akkharavaḍḍhi*).

*Ekacciyo* [is derived from] *ekacceyyo*, [and] *ekacco*; *mātiyo* [is derived from] *macco*; *kiccayaṃ* [is derived from] *kiccaṃ*; *paṇḍitiyaṃ* [is derived from] *paṇḍiccaṃ*; *suvāmi* [is derived from] *sāmi*; *suvāmini* [is derived from] *sāmini*;
*suvakehi* [is derived from] *puttehi*, [and] *sakehi* [is derived from] *puttehi*; *sattavo* [is derived from] *satto*; and you, O supreme being (*uttamasattavo*), are born.
(2.21.76) Likewise, *uttamasattavo jā*. (2.21.79), and so forth.
Thus ends the section on miscellaneous substitutes.
Now the substitute *bindu* (anusvāra) is illustrated. 46.
Within a class [of consonants], the final member of that class is substituted for *ka*. (Pāṇini 8.4.59; Rūpasiddhi 49; Nyāsa 138–9).
When followed by a consonant belonging to its own group (vagga), there is optionally a substitution of the final consonant of that same group for the *niggahīta*.
Examples: dīpaṅkaro, saṅkhāro, saṅgaho, sañcāro, sañjāto, saṇṭhitaṃ, attantapo, parantapo, amatandado, purindado, sandhi, sannidhi, sampatti, sambuddho, sambhavo, sambhāro.
In words such as *sambhinno* and *sammato*, [the suffix] is always present; in words such as *taṅkaro* and *taṃkaro*, it is not present.

In frequent repetition (*abhikkhaññe*)—as in *bhattaṃ pacati pacati* (he cooks rice repeatedly), *apuññaṃ pasavati pasavati* (he produces demerit repeatedly), *bhutvā bhutvā nippajjanti* (having eaten again and again they lie down), *paṭaṃ paṭaṃ karoti* (he makes cloth repeatedly), *paṭapaṭāyati*, *ekamekaṃ*, *ekamekāni*, and so forth—in these cases of distributive frequency (*vicchā*), there is elision of the case endings (*syādi*) of the preceding word. 56.
[Elision occurs] after *sabba* and other such words when expressing exchange (*vītihāre*).

*Atihāra* (carrying beyond) means carrying across; *vītihāra* is not carrying beyond, but rather the sense of mutual carrying within one another. When the sense of *vītihāra* is implied, the dual forms of all pronouns beginning with *sabba* occur, and there is the elision of the *syādi* suffixes of the preceding single [word].

These two persons are benefactors to one another, benefactors of each other; they see one another, they give to one another, they approach one another, [they have] wealth for one another, and they are dependent upon one another.
57. *Yāvatā-tāvaṃ* in cases of agitation (*sambhame*). [Pāṇini 8.1.12; Kaccāyana 6.3.14]. In many texts, it is given as *yāvabodhaṃ sambhame*.
That which has such a measure is *yāvaṃ*; that which has such a measure is *tāvaṃ*. Agitation (*sambhamo*) is repeated wandering or occurrence.
It is agitation when various means are indicated by hurried vocal application; it is simply called repetition (*āmeḍita*).
When there is agitation (*sambhama*), one employs as many words as are necessary for that meaning to be understood;
the sense is that it may be uttered twice, thrice, or more than that. There is also a reading *yathābodhaṃ sambhameti*, which has the same meaning.
[Agitation occurs] in fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, and excitement.
The wise person should employ reduplication (āmreḍita) in cases of laughter, sorrow, and confidence.
Among these, for fear—as in:
"A snake! A snake! or "A thief! A thief!"—it is used.
In anger:
"Pierce, pierce! Strike, strike!
In praise: [the same].
Excellent, excellent!
Turite— go, go!
In curiosity—
“Come, come!”—
the celestial nymphs—
"Aho! The Buddha! Aho! The Buddha!
"Come forward, Vāseṭṭhas! Come forward, Vāseṭṭhas! (Dīgha Nikāya 2.210)
Sokena – "Where is my only son? Where is my only son? (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.120).
With confidence –
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! (M.N. 2.106), and so forth. Three times he uttered this inspired utterance: “Homage to that Blessed One” (M.N. 2.357), and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the clusters of two words and sentences. The section on the clusters of euphonic combinations (*sandhi*) involving two elements is completed.
The Junction of Perversions (Vipallāsasaṇḍhi):
Now the junction of perversions is explained.
A perversion is the reversal of the sequence of words and syllables.
58. The perversion of laughter (*hassa-vipallāsa*).
This refers to that in which another person undergoes a perversion regarding what precedes and follows laughter;
they burn, cling, bind themselves, are carried away, suffer, and are deluded.
In the case of *vātveva*: it is gathered (*saṅgaṇhiyati*); having thus gathered, having gathered; having ascended, having ascended; having plunged, having plunged. Having overcome, having overcome.
59. *Ve vā rū*. 40 (in the *Piṭṭha*).
When *vam* follows, there is optionally a substitution of *ha* for *sa*.
"Much afflicted, much afflicted; many people bathe here indeed. (9) = "Many people bathe here.
This is called the rule for the Great Substitution (*mahāvuttividhāna*).
It is the transposition of *ya*, *rā*, and *na*.
"A hut is being built for me on the far shore. (Jā. 2.17.54) — he spoke these words; he attended upon his teacher; "I revere you, noble lady, with a mind full of faith" (Jā.
2.17.54). [The doubling of a consonant:
"In hell they were boiled in cauldrons" (Jā. 2.22.60); "They asked me for horses" (Jā. 2.22.1863). They recited these verses.
There is also a perversion regarding the streams:
“*Haññayyevāpi koci naṃ jā*” (Even if someone should kill him). “*Haññeyya*” (He might be killed) refers to persistence; the meaning is:

having gone to what is not a root-foundation, without going to a root-foundation. The same applies elsewhere. Having caused an opening to be made, [as in] *Pārā* 389, having made it signless, [he established] faith.
"One who does not eat" means one who eats uninvited (*asaddhabhoji*); "having seen that the footprint has not been stepped over" (Jātaka 1.1.20)—the meaning is "not having seen it stepped over.
There is also a transposition of words—as in Jātaka 1.15.268:
"But with the acquisition of a new robe, the Nāga maiden moved with the group"—the established reading is "she moved with the group of Nāga maidens."
Thus ends the section on the heap of perversions (vipallāsa-rāsi). 60. *Bahulam* (often). Pāṇini 3.3.113; 1.1.130.

The rule for euphonic combination (*sandhi-vidhāna*) is said to be "often" (*bahulam*), meaning it occurs in the majority of cases. This is a governing rule (*adhikāra-sutta*) that extends to the end of the book.

It operates in all instances where it is appropriate. By this, both the exclusion of what is undesired and the inclusion of what is desired have been established for all rules concerning the word *sabba*.
Thus ends the section on euphonic combination (*sandhi*) in the Moggallāna-dīpanī, known as the Elucidation of Etymology.
2. The Section on Names:
The Collection of Case Endings.
Now, the application of the case endings beginning with *si* (nominative) according to gender is elucidated.
*Liṅga*, *nāma*, and *pāṭipadika* are one in meaning. This is the name for the natural form of a substance’s designation, such as "man" and so forth.
For that [form], having reached its division by way of the seven case-endings (*vibhatti*), becomes in some instances a distinct form, in some an indistinct form, and in some a medium form;
thus, because it is endowed with these three kinds of gender-forms (*liṅgarūpa*), it is called *liṅga*.

That very [word] occurs transforming itself in accordance with the gender of the sound (*sadda*) in some cases, and in accordance with the gender of the meaning (*attha*) in others; therefore, it is called a *nāma* (noun).

That same [word], when made into a "separate word" (*visuṃ bhūtaṃ padaṃ*) by means of roots (*dhātu*), suffixes (*paccaya*), case-endings (*vibhatti*), and words that express the meaning of the sound (*saddapadatthaka*), is called a *pāṭipadika* (inflected noun).
Among these, a root-word (*dhātupada*) is such as *brū*, *bhū*, *hū*, and so forth.
The class of conditional suffixes (*paccayapada*) consists of *ṇa*, *tabba*, *anīya*, and so forth.
The class of case endings (*vibhattipada*) consists of *si*, *yo*, *aṃ*, *yo*, *ti*, *anti*, and so forth.
The class of words expressing the meaning of nouns (*saddapadatthakapadāni*) consists of *rājassa*, *sakhassa*, *pumassa*, and so forth. And herein, [the examples] such as *rājassa*...
In the *Saddasutta*, words have sounds as their referents (*saddapadatthaka*), whereas in actual usage (*payoga*), they have meanings as their referents (*atthapadatthaka*).
However, the words for roots (*dhātu*), suffixes (*paccaya*), and case-endings (*vibhatti*) always have sounds as their referents; they are found only within the *Saddasutta* and not in actual usage.
This is the distinction between the two.
If this is so, how does the arising of case endings occur for *yadievaṃ*, *bhussa*, *brussa*, *bhūto*, *hūto*, *ṇe*, *tabbe*, *simhi*, *timhi*, and so forth?
These are indeed imitation words (*anukaraṇapada*), like *atthi* and *karoti*;
therefore, both these and words such as *rājassa* are included here by virtue of their status as imitation markers (*anukaraṇaliṅga*), and not because they possess an absolute gender.
Having established this, they said: "The base (dhātu), the suffix (paccaya), and that which possesses meaning (atthavant) while excluding the case-endings (vibhatti) constitute gender (liṅga).

In this context, "possessing meaning" refers to that which has a semantic referent (atthapadatthaka); it excludes those whose referents are merely phonetic forms (saddapadatthaka), such as *rājassa* and so forth.

By this, when a semantic referent exists, they establish the absolute gender-status even for secondary derivatives (taddhita), compounds (samāsa), and words formed with primary suffixes (kitaka). For these [phonetic forms] do not possess the function of being designated by the name "gender."
There are also those words which are worthy of being qualifiers (*visesana*) of a noun;
here, prepositions (*upasagga*), indeclinable particles (*nipāta*), and words ending in *tvā* and so forth are included under the category of qualifying nouns. 61.

From a noun, when referring to two, two, or many [objects], the following suffixes are applied: *si*, *yo*, *aṃ*, *yo*, *nā*, *hi*, *sa*, *naṃ*, *smā*, *hi*, *sanaṃ*, *smiṃ*, *su*, and *ka*. (Kaccāyana 55; Rūpasiddhi 63; Nyāsa 200)

The case endings (*vibhatti*)—namely *si*, *smā*, *smiṃ*, and so forth—are those that occur after a noun (*nāma*) in both the singular and the plural. They are called "case endings" (*vibhatti*) because they divide (*vibhajanti*);

that is to say, they divide each individual base-noun-word (*pakati-nāmapada*) by way of various formal distinctions, by way of the various meanings such as agent, object, and so on, and by way of the numerical distinctions of singularity and plurality. *Si* and *lo* are called the nominative (*paṭhamā*), and so forth.
*Smim* and *su* are called the locative case (*sattamī*). Among each pair [of cases], the former is called the singular (*ekavacana*), meaning "a word occurring in reference to a single object.
Each subsequent one is called the plural (*anekavacana*), meaning "a word occurring in reference to many objects.
Its other names are the plural (*bahuvacana*) and the manifold (*puthuvacana*). All of this is established by this sutta.
62. First Case (Nominative) alone: Ka. 284; Rū. 65; Nī. 577; Caṃ. 2.1.93; Pā. 2.3.46.
The first case ending occurs after a noun when it expresses the meaning of gender alone, without regard for external meanings such as the agent or the object. For example:
*ayaṃ mama puriso* (this man is mine), *ime mama purisā* (these men are mine).
63. Addressing (Āmantane). Ka. 285; Rū. 70; Nī. 578; Caṃ. 2.1.94; Pā. 2.3.47.
"Addressing" (āmantana) is said to mean "speaking to" (ālapana). In the domain of addressing, the nominative case ending occurs after a noun when it functions merely as a marker of gender. Examples:
*Bho purisa* (O man), *bhonto purisā* (O men).
64. The second case ending is used for the object. (Ka. 297; Rū. 76, 284; Nī. 580; Caṃ. 2.1.43; Pā. 1.4.49–51).
The second case ending occurs after a noun in the sense of the object. For example:
*purisaṃ passati* (he sees the man), *purise passanti* (they see the men).
65. The third case ending (*tatiyā*) is used for the agent (*kattā*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). (Ka. 286, 288; Rū. 83; Nī. 591, 594; Caṃ. 2.1.62, 63; Pā. 2.3.18).
After a noun, the third case ending occurs to denote both the agent and the instrument.

For example: *purisena kataṃ* (done by a man), *purisehi kataṃ* (done by men); *purisena kulaṃ sobhati* (the family shines because of the man), *purisehi kulaṃ sobhati* (the family shines because of the men).
66. The fourth case ending occurs in the sense of the recipient (sampadāna). Ka. 293; Rū. 85, 301; Nī. 605; Caṃ. 2.1.73; Pā. 2.3.13.
After a noun, the fourth case suffix is used in the sense of the recipient. For example:
*purisassa deti* (he gives to the man), *purisānaṃ deti* (he gives to the men).
67. Regarding the ablative case (*pañcamī*) when expressing a limit (*avadhi*): Ka. 295; Rū. 89, 307; Nī. 607; Caṇḍa. 2.1.81; Pāṇini 2.3.28; 1.4.24. The term *pañcamy-avadhismiṃ* (in many texts).
A limit (*avadhi*) is called the *apādāna* (ablative relation). The fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-vibhatti*) occurs after a noun in the sense of a limit.
Examples: *purisasmā apeti*, *purisehi apeti*. (He departs from the man.)
68. The sixth case (chaṭṭhī) is used in the sense of relationship (sambandha). Rule 30; Rūpasiddhi 92, 315; Nyāsa 609; Cāndra 2.1.95; Pāṇini 2.3.50.
The sixth case ending occurs after a noun when the sense is that of a relationship. For example:
*purisassa dhanaṃ* (the wealth of the man), *purisānaṃ dhanaṃ* (the wealth of the men).
69. The seventh case (locative) occurs in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*). (Ka. 312; Rū. 94, 319; Nī. 630; Caṃ. 2.1.88; Pā. 2.3.36; 1.3.45).
The seventh case ending occurs after a noun in the sense of a locus. Examples:
*purisasmim tiṭṭhati* (he stands on a man), *purisesu tiṭṭhati* (he stands among men).
The section on case endings (*vibhatti*) is completed.
Section 70: The Section on Feminine Suffixes (*itthipaccaya-rāsi*). *Itthiyam atvā ka.* (Pāṇini 4.1.4) [Referenced sources: Ka. 237; Rū. 176; Nī. 466; Caṃ. 2.3.15; Pā. 4.1.4.
*Itthiyaṃ ato ā* is the word division. The suffix *āp* occurs after a noun ending in *a* when expressing the feminine gender.
This is obligatory after certain terms for designations (*saññā-sadda*) that do not have a corresponding masculine form—namely:
*kaññā*, *paññā*, *saññā*, *nāvā*, *sālā*, *taṇhā*, *icchā*, *bhikkhā*, *sikkhā*, *gīvā*, *jivhā*, *vīsā*, *tiṃsā*, *cattālīsā*, *paññāsā*, and so forth.
It must always be formed from all nouns, whether they are masculine, as well as from those ending in the suffixes *-tabba*, *-nīya*, and *-ta*—for example:
*sabbā*, *katarā*, *katamā*, *anubhavitabbā*, *anubhavanīyā*, *gatā*, *jātā*, *bhūtā*, *hūtā*, and so forth.
However, with other [suffixes], it is not constant.

*Kalyāṇā*, *kalyāṇī*, *sundarā*, *sundarī*, *sobhaṇā*, *sobhaṇī*, *kumbhakārā*, *kumbhakārī*, *kumbhakārinī*, *atthakāmā*, *atthakāmī*, *atthakāminī*, *paribbājikā*, *paribbājikinī*, *ekākā*, *ekākinī*, *dīpanā*, *dīpanī*, and so forth.

According to the analysis of the sūtras, the suffix *āp* occurs after [words ending in] *mātu*, *dhītu*, and so on, when forming a compound. Examples include *Nandamātā*, *Uttaramātā*, *Devadhītā*, *Rājadhītā*, and *assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā*. And so forth.
And here, the meaning of “in the case of a woman” (*itthiyam*) is that either the mere sound or the mere meaning should be made manifest as the female state (*itthibhāva*).
This being so, it is established that the feminine suffixes (*itthipaccaya*), like *syādi*, are merely indicators (*jotaka*) and not denoters (*vācaka*).
71. From *nadī* and so forth, the suffix *ṅī* [is applied]. (Kaccāyana 238; Rūpasiddhi 187; Niddesa 467; Vīmam̐saka [Bahūsu] 238).

The suffix *ṅī* occurs after words beginning with *nadī* when denoting the feminine. The *ṅ* is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) for the purpose of specification in the rule: “In the case of words ending in *ṅ*, *n*, or *t*, the final vowel may optionally become *ī* before the suffix *ṅī*.
Examples: *nadī*, *mahī*, *itthī*, *kumārī*, *taruṇī*, *vāseṭṭhī*, *gotamī*, *kaccānī*, *kaccāyanī*, *māṇavī*.

*Sāmaṇerī*, *nāvikī*, *pañcamī*, *chaṭṭhī*, *catuddasī*, *pañcadasī*, *sahassī*, *dasasahassī*, *satasahassī*, *kumbhakārī*, *mālakārī*, *cakkhukaraṇī*, *ñāṇakaraṇī*, *dhammadīpanī*, and so forth. 72.
For words ending in *-nt*, when followed by the suffix *-ṅī*, the *-t* optionally becomes *-k*. (Aṭṭhakathā 239, 241; Rūpasiddhi 190, 191; Nyāsa 468, 471).
The suffixes *nta* and *ntūnaṃ* become *to* before the feminine suffix *ṅīm*.
Examples: *gacchatī*, *gacchantī*; *satī*, *santī*; *bhavissatī*, *bhavissantī*; *guṇavatī*, *guṇavantī*; *satimatī*, *satimantī*;
*sabbāvatī*, *sabbāvantī*; *yāvatī*, *yāvantī*; *tāvatī*, *tāvantī*; *bhuttavatī*, *bhuttavantī*.
73. Goto vā ka. 238; rū. 187; nī. 467.
After the word *go*, the suffix *vī* optionally occurs in the feminine.
*Gāvī*.
What does it mean? The canonical text reads: *gokāṇā pariyantacārinī* ("a blind cow wandering near the boundary").
In this context, *kāṇā* means "blind. 74. *Yakkhādīhinī ca* (Ka. 238, 240; Rū. 287, 193; Nī. 467, 469; *yakkhāditvinī ca* [in many manuscripts]).
From words beginning with *yakkha* and others ending in *-a*, the feminine suffixes *-ī* and *-inī* also occur.
Yakkhī, yakkhinī, nāgī, nāginī, mahiṃsī, mahiṃsinī, migī, miginī, sīhī, sīhinī, dīpī, dīpinī, byagghī, byagghinī, kākī, kākinī, kapotī, kapotinī, mānusī, mānusinī, and so forth. 75.
From *ārāmika* and others, [the suffix] *ka*. (Ka. 240; Rū. 193; Nī. 469).
The suffix *inī* occurs after words ending in short *a*, such as *ārāmika*, when forming feminine nouns.
“Ārāmikinī, antarāyikinī, nāvikinī, olumbikinī, paṃsukūlikinī, paribbājikinī, rājinī, ekākinī,” and so forth. Regarding the feminine suffix (*saññā*):
“mānusinī” or “mānusā,” except for the excellence of being human (*mānusī*).
76. *Gharaṇy-ādayo* (ka. 240; ru. 193; nī. 469).
Feminine nouns ending in the suffix *-nī* such as *gharaṇī*, etc., are formed.
In *gharaṇī*, *vetraṇī*, and *pokkharaṇī*, the *n* is replaced by *ṇ*. In *ācariṇī*, there is elision of the *i*, or it may remain as *ācariyā*.
77. *Ānī* is used for the wife of *mātula* and others. (Ka. 98; Rū. 189; Nī. 261).
The suffix *ānī* is added after words ending in short *a*, such as *mātula*, to denote the wife.
*Mātula* is the brother of one's mother; his wife is *mātulānī*. Likewise: *varuṇānī*, *gahapatānī*, *ācariyānī*, *khattiyānī*.
Due to the governing influence of the term "frequently" (*bahulā*), the words *khattiyī* and *khattiyā* [are formed]. 78. *Nī*:
The suffix *nī* occurs after feminine bases ending in *yu*, *iva*, and *uva*.
Chattapāṇinī, daṇḍapāṇinī, daṇḍinī, chattinī, hatthinī, mālinī, māyāvinī, medhāvinī, piyapasaṃsinī, brahmacārinī,
bhayadassāvinī, atthakāminī, hitacārinī, bhikkhunī, khattiyabandhunī,
paṭunī, paracittavidunī, mattaññunī, atthaññunī, dhammaññunī, and so forth.

79. *Timhāññatthe* (Moggallāna 31). In a compound whose referent is another (*aññapadattha-samāsa*), the suffix *nī* is applied in the feminine after a word ending in the third case-affix (*tipaccaya*).
Examples include: *ahiṃsāratinī*, *dhammaratinī*, *vacchagiddhinī*, *puttagiddhinī*, *muṭṭhassatinī*, *micchādiṭṭhinī*, *sammādiṭṭhinī*, *attaguttinī*, and so forth.
What is meant by "elsewhere"? Delight in the Dhamma is *dhammarati*.
80. Regarding "yuvā":
[the form] *yuvato* becomes *itthiyaṃ*.
*Yuvati*.
And here, by the analysis of the sutta, there is either *vīsa* or *tiṃsato pi*. [The forms are] *vīsati*, *vīsaṃ*, *tiṃsati*, *tiṃsaṃ*.
81. *Upamā saṃhita sahita saññata saha sapha vāmalakkhaṇāditūrutvū caṃ*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.69, 70; *tūrutū* occurs in many texts).
The word *ūru* is derived from the root *ūr*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *-a*.

In a compound where another word serves as the referent (*aññapadattha-samāsa*), the word *ūru* becomes *ū* when used in the feminine sense, provided it is preceded by a word such as a simile (*upama*).
One whose thighs (*ūrū*) are like the trunk of an elephant (*nāga-nāsā*) is called *nāga-nās-ūrū*. One whose thighs are closely joined (*saṃhita*) is called *saṃhitorū*.
One whose thighs are joined and bound together is *sahitorū*; one whose thighs are restrained and not restless is *saññatorū*.
Because it functions together with the thigh (*ūru*) by means of the thigh, it is *sahoru*; "sapha" refers to a hoof;

because they are like hoofs due to their close contact, one whose thighs are thus is *saphorū*; one whose thighs are beautiful and lovely is *vāmorū*; one whose thighs are endowed with auspicious marks is *lakkhaṇorū*.
By the analysis of the suttas, the form *brahmabandhū* is established. And [in the examples]:
“If she of the radiant light, whose thighs are like an elephant’s trunk, should look at me” (Jā. 2.20.14); “You stand alone, O lady with well-knit thighs” (Jā. 1.16.297);
“The maiden Mahāmāyā, of beautiful appearance, with restrained thighs” (Jā. 2.17.109); and “O lady with lovely thighs” (vāmorū).

The following Pāli phrases are found: “*Saja maṃ, bhaddeti*” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.348), “*Kāraṇaṃ nappajānāmi, sammattolakkhaṇūruyā ti*” (Dīgha Nikāya 2.348), and “*Gārayhassaṃ brahmabandhuyā ti*” (Jātaka 2.22.2109).
Therein, “*saja*” means “embrace,” and “*gārayhassan*” means “I would become blameworthy.”
And here, those ending in the *tāp* suffix are exclusively feminine by their very nature (*sabhāva-itthilinga*), such as: *lahutā*, *mudutā*, *gāmatā*, *janatā*, *devatā*, and so forth.
Likewise, those ending in the *tip* suffix: *gati*, *mati*, *ratti*, *sati*, *tuṭṭhi*, *diṭṭhi*, *iddhi*, *siddhi*, and so forth; likewise:
*yāgu*, *dhātu*, *dhenu*, *kaṇḍu*, *kacchu*, *mātu*, *dhītu*, *duhitu*, and so forth; and *jambū*, *vadhū*.
Examples include *camū*, *sutanū*, *sarabū*, and so forth. In the Pali scriptures, however, they apply the suffix *-ū* even to words such as *sutanū* and *sarabū*.

Among these, all those that possess the feminine gender are always designated with the technical term *itthi* by the rule “*ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā pitthiyaṃ*,” and they are always designated with the technical term *gha* by the rule “*ākāro ca ghā*.
The section on the group of feminine suffixes is concluded.
The Feminine Gender Group Ending in Vowels:

The feminine gender ending in vowels is sixfold: ending in *ā*, ending in *i*, ending in *ī*, ending in *u*, ending in *ū*, and ending in *o*. Therein, from the word *kaññā* (maiden), the nominative case occurs in the sense of the mere object.
82. *Gasīnaṃ ka* (Pāṇini 7.1.15). *Rū.* 74; *Nī.* 447.
The elision of *g* occurs when a suffix whose rule (*vidhi*) has not been obtained by any other sutta; this is the elision of *s* (*silopa*).
"A maiden stands" (*kaññā tiṭṭhati*). 83.
After *jantu*, *hetu*, *īgha*, and *pe*, there is optionally *ka*. (Kaccāyana 118; Rūpasiddhi 146; Nyāsa 293).

Jantu: In the case of words ending in *ī*, *u*, or *ū* (whether masculine, feminine, or neuter), as well as those designated as *gha* and those containing the vowels *i* or *u*, the elision (*lopa*) of the case endings (*yonaṃ*) may optionally occur.
Examples: *kaññā tiṭṭhanti* or *kaññāyo tiṭṭhanti*.
The nominative case is used in the sense of address; by the rule "in addressing [one who is] like a cow," the designation *ga* is applied.

84. Regarding the substitution of *e* for *gha* after words beginning with *gha*, *brahma*, etc.: Rule 114, 193; Verse 122, 178; Commentary 288; [the group] beginning with *gha* and *brahma* (*bahusu*). When *ā* follows, there is elision of the preceding vowel; for example, "pucchāma kattāra anomapañña" (we ask the author of peerless wisdom), where it is seen in the *Jātaka* as "kattāraṃ anomapaññaṃ" (the author of peerless wisdom).
