"Merit has been performed by you; merit has been performed by us; merit has been performed by us.
To what extent [does this apply]? "It has been relinquished by you; it has been relinquished by us.
Only when there is an ablative case (*apādāna*)? "And strength was bestowed upon the monks; indeed, not a small amount of merit has been performed by you. (Pāṭha 7.12)
Is it only when [the words] are in the ablative case? For example: "You go; we go.
Is it only when [the words] are in the same case? For example: "Devadatta stands in the village; you stand in the city.
Is it only when [the words] have case endings? For example: "The Dhamma is worthy of those like you."

In place of the words *tumha* and *amha*, when followed by the particle *nā* or the suffix *sesu*, these forms become *te* or *me*, respectively, along with their case endings (*savibhattīnaṃ*). For example:
*kataṃ te puññaṃ* (merit was done by you), *kataṃ tayā puññaṃ* (merit was done by you); *kataṃ me puññaṃ* (merit was done by me), *kataṃ mayā puññaṃ* (merit was done by me); *dinnaṃ te*.

"the cloth," "the cloth was given to you," "the cloth was given to me," "the cloth was given to my [self]," "this kingdom is yours," "this kingdom is your [kingdom]," "this kingdom is mine," "this kingdom is my [kingdom].
268. *Anvādese caṃ*. Pāṇini 8.1.23.
In the place of the *anvādesa* (subsequent reference), the substitutes *vo*, *no*, *te*, and *me* always take the place of the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* when they are repeated. For example:
"The village is your possession, and the city is also your possession. The same applies to the remaining cases. 269.
[The rule] "with *sa-* preceding" or "with *saṃ-* preceding" (*sapubbā paṭhamantā vā saṃpubbā paṭhamantā vā*)—Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.21; Pāṇini 8.1.26.

That which has a preceding word (*pubbapada*) is called *sapubba*. After the first case-ending form of a word that is *sapubba*, the substitutes *vo*, *no*, *te*, and *me* optionally take the place of the words *tumha* and *amha* when they follow with their respective case-endings, even in the sense of subsequent reference (*anvādesa*).
For example: *gāme paṭo tumhākaṃ, atho nagare kambalaṃ vo*; or *atho nagare kambalaṃ tumhākaṃ vā*. The same applies to the remaining cases. 270.
[The substitution does not occur] when there is conjunction with *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *eva*, or *caṃ*. (Kaccāyana 6.3.22; Pāṇini 8.1.24)
When used in conjunction with the particles *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *aha*, or *eva*, the substitutions *vo*, *no*, *te*, and *me* for *tumhākam* and *amhākam* do not occur. For example:
*gāmo tava ca mama ca pariggaho* (the village is the possession of both you and me), or *gāmo tava vā mama vā pariggaho* (the village is the possession of either you or me), and so forth.
Why specify "in conjunction with *ca* and the others"? [Consider: *gāmo ca te pariggaho, nagarañca me pariggaho* (the village is your possession, and the city is my possession).
271. In the sense of seeing (*dassana*), [the term] *ālocana* [is used]; see *caṃ. 6.3.23*; *pā. 8.1.25*. *Ālocanaṃ* means looking at (*olokanaṃ*).
When another sense of seeing than "looking at" is employed, the substitutions *tumhaṃ*, *amhaṃ*, *vo*, *no*, *te*, and *me* do not occur. For example:
*gāmo tumhe uddissa āgato* (the village has come for you), *gāmo amhe uddissa āgato* (the village has come for us). Here, "the village" refers to the great multitude of people living in the village.
What is meant by "not being considered" (*anālocanā*)? For example: *gāmo vo passati* ("the village sees you"), *gāmo no passati* ("the village sees us").

272. Regarding the rule: *āmantanapubbaṃ asantaṃ va* ("a preceding word that is a vocative is treated as if it were non-existent"; cf. *caṃ*. 6.3.24; *pā*. 8.1.72). A preceding word that has become a vocative is as if it did not exist; it does not count toward the number of words [in the compound].
Devadatta! This is your property. 273.
*Na sāmaññavacanamekatthe caṃ*. (Pāṇini 8.1.73).
When there is a word standing in apposition, the preceding vocative word, which expresses a general term, does not exist as if it were non-existent; it is counted as a single word.
"O young brahmin, matted-hair ascetic! That is your property.
What is the purpose of the term "common designation"? "O young brahmin, Devadatta!
That is your property. Why "in the same sense"? "Devadatta! Yaññadatta! That is your property."
274. *Bahūsu vā* (Caṅgavātupāṭha 6.3.26; Pāṇini 8.1.74).

When there is a word of address expressing a general sense that applies to many persons, it may, when followed by a word of identical meaning (*ekattha*), become as if it were not present. For example:
*brāhmaṇā guṇavanto vo pariggaho*, "O virtuous brahmins, you are my retinue"; *brāhmaṇā guṇavanto tumhākaṃ pariggaho*, "O virtuous brahmins, you are your own retinue."
The section on all the initial groups is concluded.
Now, the section on the case-suffixes and other suffixes is explained. First, the case-suffixes are indicated.
Because they indicate the sense of a case-ending (*vibhatti*), the suffixes situated in the place of a case-ending are called "case-suffixes" (*vibhattipaccaya*).
275. *To* [is used] after the fifth case (*pañcamī*); [Pāṇini 5.4.45]; [Kaccāyana 248]; [Rūpasiddhi 260]; [Niruttidīpanī 493]; [Candaviveka 4.3.6]; [Pāṇini 5.4.45].
The suffix *to* occurs in the sense of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*).
After *toma*, the long vowel becomes short: after *kañña*, *ratti*, *itthi*, and *dhenu*.

According to the *Mahāvutti*, after *toma* there is the suffix *-tta*: after *mātāpitaro*, *mātā*, *pitā*, *vadhū*, *purisa*, *muni*, *daṇḍa*, *bhikkhu*, *satthar*, *kattar*, *gotrabhu*, *sabba*, *ya*, and *ta*.
"Ima, eta, kiṃ—do not make these sounds. 276.
*Itotettokuto* (from *ito*, *etto*, *kuto*) [is used] in the sense of "from here," "from there," and "from where" (*bahūsu*). Pāṇini 5.3.8; Pāṇini 7.2.104.
The words *ito*, *ato*, *etto*, and *kuto* are indeclinables (*nipāta*) formed with the suffix *to*.
*Imamhā* means "from this" (*ito*), or "by this" (*etasmā*); *imehi* means "by these" (*etehehi*). *Ita* means "from here" (*etto*). *Kasmā* means "from what" (*kehīti vā kuto*).
Furthermore, having seen the explanatory phrases such as *imamhā* and *imehi*, the original gender (*pakatiliṅga*) should be understood.

By this rule, the substitution of *it* occurs for *ima*, the substitution of *at* and *et* for *eta*, the doubling of the vowel following *esa* by the rule "after *esara*, there is doubling," and the substitution of *ku* for the word *kiṃ*.
This same method applies to the remaining prefixes (*nipātana*).
277. *Abhyādīhi pā.* (Pāṇini 5.3.9). By means of *abhi* and the others, the suffix *ta* is applied;
furthermore, because of the restatement [of the rule], it is established that this occurs even when not in the sense of the ablative case (*apañcamyatthe*).
"Towards the village" means facing the village.
"Around the village" means on all sides of the village.
"On both sides of the village" means on both flanks of the village.
Behind, below, above. 278.
*Ādyādīhi caṃ* (Pāṇini 5.4.44): after words such as *ādi*, the suffix *to* is used even when it does not express the sense of the ablative case (*apañcamyatthe*).

The locative case is frequently seen in the sense of "in" (locative) in such instances as *ādito*, *majjhato*, *purato*, *passato*, *piṭṭhito*, *orato*, *parato*, *pacchato*, *puratthimato*, *dakkhiṇato*, and so forth.
Likewise, it is used in the sense of the instrumental (*tatiyattha*) in such examples as *rūpaṃ attato samanupassati* (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.44) and *pañcakkhandhe aniccato vipassati*.
Furthermore, in such cases as *yatonidānaṃ* (Sutta Nipāta 275), *yatvādhikaraṇaṃ*, and *yatodakaṃ tadādittam* (Jātaka 1.9.58), they maintain that it expresses the ablative (*paṭhamattha*).
In phrases such as "Come here, Balāka, come from here; my friend is a fierce crow," the suffix *ito* expresses the sense of the accusative case (*dutiyatthe*).
In phrases such as "The sound from afar, no fault is seen from afar," the suffix *parato* expresses the sense of the genitive case (*chaṭṭhyatthe*).
279. From *sabbā* onwards, the suffix *tra* is used in the sense of the locative case (*sattamyā*). (Kaccāyana 249; Rūpasiddhi 266; Niddesa 494; Caṅkī 4.1.10; Pāṇini 5.3.10).
After all pronouns (sabbanāma) whose names begin with *sabb-*, the forms *tra* and *ttha* occur in the sense of the locative case.

Thus: *sabbasmiṃ* or *sabbesu* becomes *sabbatra* or *sabbattha*; likewise *sabbassaṃ* or *sabbāsu* becomes *sabbatra* or *sabbattha*. Similarly: *kataratra*, *katarattha*, *aññatra*, *aññattha*, and so forth;
as well as *yatra*, *yattha*, *tatra*, *tattha*.
280. *Kattha*, *ettha*, *kuttra*, *atra*, *tva*, *iha*, *idha*: these words are formed with the suffixes *tha*, *tra*, *va*, *ha*, and *dha* in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*).

In the sense of "in what" or "in which," one forms *kattha*, *kuttra*, and *kva*. The form *kuvaṃ* is also established, as seen in the Pāli: "Where is the maker of the being? Where has the being arisen? (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.171); and "Where shall I eat? Where shall I drink? (Pāli). *Kattha*, *ettha*, *kuttra*, *atra*, *tva*, *iha*, and *idha*—these words are derived from the bases *ka*, *eta*, *ku*, *a*, *tu*, *iha*, and *idha*, respectively, and are completed by adding the suffixes *tha*, *tra*, *va*, *ha*, and *dha* to express the meaning of the locative case.

Examples: *kattha* = *kasmiṃ* or *kesu* ("where"); *kuttra* = *kuttra*; *kva* = *kva*; *kuvaṃ* is also established, as in the canonical text: "Where is the maker of the being? Where has the being arisen? (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.171); and "Where shall I eat? Where shall I drink? (Pāli).
*Etasmiṃ etesu* means "in this" or "in these"; *ettha*, *atra*, *imasmiṃ*, and *imesu* mean "here.
281. *Dhi* optionally [replaces] all [locative endings]. (Ka. 250; Rū. 268; Nī. 502).
After the word *sabba*, the suffix *dhi* optionally occurs in the sense of the locative case.
Homage to you, O Buddha, O Hero! You are completely liberated in every respect.
(Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.90.282; Khuddakapāṭha 255; Rūpasiddhi 275; Niddesa 504).
For the particle *hiṃ* occurs in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*).
Yahiṃ. 283.
Tā hañca ka. 253; rū. 273; nī. 501. From that [ablative case], the suffix *hiṃ* occurs in the sense of the locative (*sattamī*), as well as *ha*.
*Tahiṃ* and *tahaṃ*. It is also seen in the sense of repetition:
“looking here and there, he goes. 284. Regarding *kiṃ*: *kukaṃ* and *kaṃ* [are substitutes].
From *kiṃ*, in the sense of the locative case, *hiṃ* is added, and it becomes *taṃ*. For *kiṃ*, *kuttaṃ* and *kattaṃ* are also [substitutes].

"Where does he go? Where does he go? Where, O only son? Where, O only son? (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.63). In the words *kuhiñci* and *kuhiñcanaṃ*, the two particles *ci* and *cana* are established as indeclinables (*nipātanta*).
Thus ends the section on the locative case (*sāmaññasattamī*) ending in *-anta*.
Now, the locative case ending in a temporal term (*kālasattamī*) is discussed.
285. *Sabbekaññayatehi kāledā* (Pāṇini 5.3.17). The suffix *dā* is applied after the words *sabba*, *eka*, *añña*, *ya*, and *ta* when expressing time.
Thus: at all times—*sabbadā*; at one time—*ekadā*; at another time—*aññadā*; at whatever time—*yadā*; at that time—*tadā*.
286. *Kadā*, *kadāci*, *kadāpi*, *dā*, *adhunā*, *idāni*: Ka. 257–8–9; Rū. 276–8–9; Nī. 505–6–7.
These suffixes ending in *-dā*, *-dhunā*, and *-dāni* are established in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*) as time:
*kadā* means at what time; *kadāci* and *kadāpi* mean at some time; *sadā* means at all times; *adhunā* means at this time; and *idāni* means now.
287. *Ajja-sajju-parajje-tarahi-kara-hā* (Ka. 259; Rū. 279, 423; Nī. 507).
These suffixes—*ajja*, *sajju*, *parajje*, *tarahi*, *kara*, and *hā*—are also formed with the temporal sense.
"In this time" (*imasmiṃ kāle*) means "on this day" (*imasmiṃ divase*).

*Samāne kāle*: when it is the same time; *sajju*, meaning "immediately" (*samāne*). For it is said: "An evil deed that has been committed does not bear fruit immediately, like fresh milk" (Dhp 71). He sent it *sajjukaṃ*—here *sajju* means "on that very day.
*Aparajju*: at another time; the meaning is "on the following day.
*Imasmiṃ kāle*: at this time; *etarahi*. *Kismiṃ kāle*: at what time? *Kutoci*: from somewhere; *kvaci*: anywhere; *katthaci*: somewhere; *kuhiñci*: anywhere; *kadāci*: at some time.
Furthermore, the particle *ci* occurs as the suffixes in *karahaci*, as well as in *yato kutoci*, *yattha katthaci*, and *yadā kadāci*.
The particles *cana* occur in *kiñcanaṃ*, *kuhiñcanaṃ*, and *kudācanaṃ*.
The section on the various case-suffixes is concluded.
The Section on Indeclinables:
The Collection of Prepositional Words.
Now, the indeclinable words are being elucidated.

The six kinds of indeclinable words (*abyayapada*) are: the prepositional word (*upasaggapada*), the particle word (*nipātapada*), the word with case-suffixes and affixes (*vibhattipaccayantapada*), the indeclinable compound word (*abyayībhāvasamāsapada*), the indeclinable derivative word (*abyayataddhitapada*), and the word with *tvā*-type affixes (*tvādipaccayantapada*).

"Decay" (*byaya*) means change; those which do not undergo any change of form through various genders, case-endings, or numbers are called "indeclinables" (*abyayā*), and they are also called "innumerable" (*asaṅkhyā*).

In this context, there is no further arising of case endings (*vibhatti*) from a word that already possesses a case ending. Regarding the *abyayībhāva* compound, the rule for case endings will be stated in the section on compounds (*samāsakaṇḍa*); therefore, setting aside those two, the remaining four [types of indeclinables] are discussed here.
288. *Asaṅkhyehi sabbāsaṃ caṃ.* (Pāṇini 2.4.82).
After words that are not numerals (*asaṅkhya*), there is the elision (*lopa*) of all case endings as appropriate; after certain words, there is the elision of the nominative case.
There is elision (*lopa*): by certain words, there is elision of the second case; ... [and so on] ... by some, of the seventh; by some, of two; by some, of three; ... [and so on] ...
by some, of seven—this is what is meant.

In that regard, with the vocative particles such as *āvuso*, *bho*, *bhante*, etc., and with words such as *atthi*, *natthi*, *sakkā*, *labbhā*, *siyā*, *siyuṃ*, *sādhu*, *tuṇhī*, etc., there is elision of the first case.
The second case is used with words such as *ciraṃ*, *cirassaṃ*, *niccaṃ*, *satataṃ*, *abhiṇhaṃ*, *abhikkhaṇaṃ*, and *muhuttaṃ* when they signify uninterrupted connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
The third case is used with words such as *yathā*, *tathā*, *sabbathā*, *sabbaso*, *musā*, and *micchā*.
The fourth case is used with words such as *kātuṃ* and *kātave*.
The fifth case ending is elided after words such as *samantā*, *samantato*, *dīghaso*, and *oraso*.
The seventh case ending is elided after words such as *pure*, *purā*, *pacchā*, *uddhaṃ*, *upari*, *adho*, *heṭṭhā*, *antarā*, *anto*, *raho*, *āvi*, *hiyyo*, and *suve*.
After the word *namo*, the first case ending is elided, as in the example: *“namo te buddha vīra’tthū”*; and the second case ending is elided, as in the example: *“namo karohi nāgassā”*.

From the word *sayam*, [the elision of case endings] occurs as follows: in the phrase "The granary breaks by itself" (*kusūlo sayameva bhijjate*), there is elision of the nominative; in the phrase "Pleasure and pain are self-made" (*sayaṃ kataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ*; Dīgha Nikāya 3.191, 193), there is elision of the instrumental, and so forth. Thus, the appropriate distinctions should be understood according to the context.
Therefore, they maintain that with the words *iti* and *evaṃ*, there is elision of the seven cases according to the requirements of usage.
With prefixes (*upasagga*) as well, there is elision of the respective cases according to the sense.
In the *Rūpasiddhi*, however, it is stated at Rū. 131 (back): "By means of those [prefixes], only the singular number of the first case occurs.

In that context, prefixes (*upasagga*) are so called because they approach the verbal roots and gender-terms (*dhātuliṅga*), and by doing so, they produce various modifications of their meaning and fashion them. For they sometimes make that meaning distinct.

In such instances as "he knows," "he understands," "he perceives," "he despises," "he cognizes," "he fully comprehends," "virtuous," "immoral," "handsome," "ugly," "a good king," and "a bad king," [the root *jñā*] is used. In some cases,
it is analyzed by dividing it into various forms for that purpose, as in "he goes," "he comes," "he rises," and "he descends."
In some cases, setting aside that primary meaning, they apply those words to a sense that is either opposed to it or something other than it.
Among these, examples of the sense opposed to it are:
*jeti*, *parājeti*, *omuñcati*, *paṭimuñcati*, *gilati*, *uggilati*, *nimmujjati*, *ummujjati*, *dhammo*, *addhammo*, and so forth.
In other instances— such as *dadāti*, *ādadāti*, *dadhāti*, *vidheti*, *pidheti*, *nidheti*, *sandhiyati*, *saddahati*, *abhidhāti*, and so forth—

the suffixes follow that meaning. However, in some cases, for the sake of the euphony of the word, they follow that meaning after having been modified, such as *vijjati*, *saṃvijjati*, *labhati*, *paṭilabhati*, and so forth.
Those twenty [prefixes] are: *ā*, *u*, *o*, *du*, *ni*, *vi*, *su*, *saṃ*, *ati*, *adhi*, *anu*, *apa*, *api*, *abhi*, *ava*, *upa*, *pati*, *parā*, *pari*.

However, in the *Kaccāyana* [grammar], since the sound *os-* is merely a variant of *ava-*, it is not included there and instead the sound *ni-* is taken; here, however, since the sound *nī-* is merely a long vowel of *ni-*, it is not included here and instead the sound *os-* is taken.
Among those, *pa-*—

In the sense of manner: *paññā* (wisdom). In the sense of beginning an action: *vippakataṃ* (half-done). In the sense of exertion: *paṇītaṃ* (excellent). In the sense of mastery: *pabhū* (lord). In the sense of inclusion:

*pakkhittaṃ* (placed within), as in *passāso* (inhalation). In the sense of separation: *pavāso* (departure). In the sense of devotion: *pācariyo* (teacher). In the sense of succession: *putto*, *paputto*, *nattā*, *panattā* (son, grandson, great-grandson).

In the sense of intensity: *pavaḍḍho* (increased greatly). In the sense of origin: *pabhavati* (arises). In the sense of satiety: *pahutaṃ annaṃ* (abundant food). In the sense of being undisturbed: *pasanno* (serene).
In the *Paṭṭhāna*, it means "aspiration.

As a prefix (*ā*): In the sense of facing toward: *āgacchati* (he comes). In the sense of ascending: *ārohati* (he climbs). In the sense of a boundary: "The field extends as far as the mountains" (*āpabbatā khettaṃ*). In the sense of pervasion: "Up to the Brahma-world" (*ābrahmalokā*).
Fame (*kittisaddo*). Attainment (*pattiyaṃ*). Desire (*icchāyaṃ*). Embracing (*parissajane*). Undertaking of a new work (*ādikamme*).
Taking up (*gahaṇe*). A dwelling (*nivāse*). Proximity (*samīpe*). Addressing (*avhāne*). *Ā*—

*Ugga* [is used] in the sense of rising: *uggate uggacchati*. In the sense of exertion: *uddhaṃkamme uṭṭhāti*. In the sense of preeminence: *padhāne uttaro*. In the sense of separation: *viyoge upavāso*. In the sense of arising: *sambhave ubbhūto*. In the sense of obtaining an object: *atthalābhe rūpassa uppādo*. In the sense of capability: *sattiyaṃ ussahati gantuṃ*.

In the sense of enumeration: *sarūpakhyāne uddeso*. *O:* In the sense of inclusion: *antobhāve ocarako*, *orodho*. In the sense of downward action: *adhokamme okkhitto*. In the sense of restraint: *niggahe ovādo*. In the sense of interval and place: *antare dese ca okāso*. In the sense of manifestation: *pātubhāve opapātiko*. In whatever meanings the word *ava* occurs, the word *o* also occurs in those same meanings.

Du—In the sense of "not beautiful": *duggandha* (bad smell). In the sense of "absence": *dubbhikkha* (famine), *dussīla* (immoral), *duppañña* (unwise). In the sense of "blameworthy": *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). In the sense of "lack of prosperity": *dusassa* (bad harvest). In the sense of "difficulty": *dukkara* (hard to do). In the sense of "ugly": *dubbaṇṇa* (ill-favored), *dummukha* (ill-faced). Ni—

*Nissesa* in the sense of remainderlessness; *niyyāna* in the sense of having gone out; *niddhāraṇa* in the sense of extracting; *nikhāta* in the sense of being driven inside; *nimmakkhika* in the sense of absence of flies;
*nivāreti* in the sense of prohibition; *nibbāna* in the sense of having departed; *nimmita* in the sense of manifestation; *vinicchaya* in the sense of determination;
*niddesa* in the sense of analysis; *nidassana* in the sense of illustration; *nisāmeti* in the sense of attending to; *niṭṭhita* in the sense of conclusion; *nipuṇo* in the sense of skillful.

Vi—in *visese*, it means "one sees with insight"; in *vividhe*, it means "variegated"; in *viruddhe*, it means "dispute"; in *vigate*, it means "stainless"; in *viyoge*, it means "dissociated"; in *virūpe*, it means "remorse. Su—

*Sobhaṇe* means a good destination (*suggati*). *Sundare* means well-minded (*sumano*). *Sammāsaddatthe* means one who has gone rightly (*sugato*). *Samiddhiyaṃ* means an abundant harvest (*subhikkhaṃ*). *Sukhatthe* means easy to do (*sukaro*). *Saṃ*: *Samodhāne* means a junction (*sandhi*).

*Sammā*, in the sense of evenness, refers to concentration (*samādhi*) and its associated factors (*sampayutto*). *Samantabhāve* means scattered all around (*saṃkiṇṇo*). *Saṅgate* means a meeting (*samāgamo*).
In brief, this is a summary: *sāratto* [is used] in the sense of intensity; *saṃvāso* and *sambhogo* in the sense of association;
*samaggho* in the sense of worthlessness; *sambhavo* in the sense of origin; *sammukhaṃ* in the sense of facing toward; *saṅgayhati* in the sense of inclusion; *saṃvuto* in the sense of covering;
*sandhāvati* and *saṃsarati* in the sense of repeated action; and *sampanno* in the sense of accomplishment.

*Ati*: In the sense of surpassing—*atirocati* (shines beyond); in the sense of transgression—*accayo*, *atīto* (past); in the sense of having passed—*atikkante*, *accantaṃ* (extremely); in the sense of excellence—*atikusalo* (very skillful); in the sense of intensity—*atikodho* (excessive anger). In the sense of bringing inside—having brought a bed or a chair inside (*atiharitvā*), one places it. *Adhi*:

In the sense of "superiority": *adhisīlaṃ* (higher morality). In the sense of "lordship": *adhipati*, as in "the Pañcālas [are subject] to King Brahmadatta. In the sense of "being above": *adhiseti* (he lies upon).
In the sense of "overpowering": *adhibhūto* (overpowered). In the sense of "studying": *ajjheti*, as in "he studies the grammar (*byākaraṇaṃ adhīte*). In the sense of "determination":

*navakammaṃ adhiṭṭhāti* (he determines the new construction), *cīvaraṃ adhiṭṭhāti* (he determines the robe), *iddhivikubbanaṃ adhiṭṭhāti* (he determines the transformation by supernormal power). In the sense of "resolute conviction": *adhimuccati*.
He attains the mass of enjoyment in its acquisition; he attains the Deathless. *Anu*:

in the sense of "gone after," as in *anugata* (followed); in the sense of "not cut off," as in *anusaya* (latent tendency); in the sense of the word "behind," as in *anurathaṃ* (behind the chariot); in the sense of "repetition," as in *anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ* (every half-month).

*Anusaṃvaccharaṃ*: every year. In the sense of suitability: *anurūpaṃ*. In the sense of being younger: *anubuddho*, *anuthero*. The remainder will be explained in the section on case-roles (*kārakakaṇḍa*).

*Apa-*: In the sense of having departed: *apagate*, *apeti*, *apāyo*. In the sense of reproach: *apagabbho*, *apasaddo*. In the sense of exclusion: *apasālāya āyanti* (they come from outside the hall). In the sense of honoring: *vuḍḍha-mapacāyanti* (they honor the elders). In the sense of offending: *aparajjhati*.
*Api*—in the sense of possibility: one might split even a mountain; one might pierce even Mount Meru. In the sense of expectation: this phenomenon (*dhamma*) is also indeterminate.
In the sense of conjunction: thus indeed the Worthy One (*arahaṃ*); it burns the outer skin, it burns the inner skin, it burns the flesh.
Even in reproach we are "wise" (paṇḍitaka). Even in questioning, venerable sir, you have received alms; do you wish to hear? *Abhi*: toward (*abhimukhe*), advanced (*abhikkanto*).

*Abhiññā*: distinguished (*visiṭṭhe*). *Abhidhamma*: superior (*adhike*). *Abhirūhati*: climbs up (*uddhaṃkamme*). *Abhijāto*: born into a noble family (*kule*). *Abhirūpo*: handsome (*sāruppe*). *Abhivādeti*: salutes (*vandane*). The remainder he will explain in the section on verbal derivatives (*kārakakaṇḍe*).

Ava—In the sense of "below": *avakkhitto* (cast down). In the sense of "separation": *avakokilaṃ vanaṃ* (the forest devoid of cuckoos). In the sense of "contempt": *avajānāti* (he despises). In the sense of "knowing": *avagacchati* (he understands). In the sense of "purity": *vodāyati*, *vodānaṃ* (it becomes pure, purity). In the sense of "certainty": *avadhāraṇaṃ* (determination). In the sense of "place": *avakāso* (space). In the sense of "stealing": *avahāro* (theft). Upa—

In the sense of approaching: he sits near (*upanisīdati*). In the sense of vicinity: a suburb (*upanagaraṃ*). In the sense of rebirth: he is reborn in the heavenly world (*saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati*). In the sense of similarity:

a comparison (*upamāṇaṃ*) and the object compared (*upameyyaṃ*). In the sense of excess: a *doṇa* measure exceeding a *khāri*. In the sense of being above: ordained (*upasampanno*), accumulation (*upacayo*).

In the sense of fasting: the fast (*upavāso*). In the sense of censuring: he reviles another (*paraṃ upavadati*). In the sense of perception: a foundation (*upadhā*), an affliction (*upasaggo*). In the sense of a prior action: an undertaking (*upakkamo*).

*Upahāra*: offering; it stands near the Buddha as an act of worship (*pūjā*). In the sense of being grasped, it is *paccupaṭṭhāna* (manifestation). In the sense of intensity, it is *upādāna* (clinging), *upāyāsa* (despair), and *upanissaya* (decisive support).
*Pati-*...
In the sense of going toward: *paṭigata*. In the sense of reverse order: *paṭiloma*. In the sense of an opponent: *paṭipuggala*.

In the sense of prohibition: *paṭisedha*. In the sense of turning back: *paṭikkamati*. In the sense of similarity: *paṭirūpaka*. In the sense of counteracting a disease: *paṭikāra*. In the sense of taking up: *paṭiggaṇhāti*.
In the sense of awakening: *paṭivedha*. In the sense of depending upon: *paṭicca*. The remainder will be explained in the section on grammatical cases (*kārakakaṇḍa*).

*Parā*: in the sense of decline, it is *parābhava* (ruin); in the sense of defeat, it is *parājita* (defeated); in the sense of a destination, it is *parāyana* (refuge); in the sense of exertion, it is *parakkama* (prowess); in the sense of touching, it is *parāmasana* (misapprehension).
*Pari*—
In the sense of being all-encompassing: it is surrounded, encircled, and equipped as an accessory. In the sense of delimitation:

one fully understands that which is to be fully understood. In the sense of avoidance: one shuns; it is an exclusion. In the sense of embracing: one embraces closely. In the sense of wearing: one puts on a garment. In the sense of honoring:
it is service. In the sense of eating: one serves food. In the sense of overcoming: one treats with contempt. In the sense of censuring: one reviles.
The remainder will be explained in the Section on Verbal Roots (*Kārakakaṇḍa*).
Furthermore, the prefix *ni-* occurs in the senses of "removal," "obstruction," and so forth, as in *nīharaṇa* (removal), *nīvaraṇa* (obstruction), and the like.
Thus ends the collection of prefixes.

The Collection of Indeclinable Words (*Nipātapadarāsi*): They are called *nipātas* because they fall (*patanti*) into the path of speech always in a single form. It is also said that they are called *nipātas* because they fall at the beginning, middle, or end of words.
Furthermore, particles (*asatvavācaka*) such as "and" (*ca*) and others are known as *nipātas*. These, moreover, are of two kinds: those joined with case-endings (*vibhatti*) and those not so joined.
Among those, the particles (cādayo) joined with case-endings have already been shown previously. Those not so joined are called "unjoined" (ayutta).
They, moreover, have hundreds of various divisions and should be learned from the Nighaṇṭu treatises. This concludes the section on indeclinables, secondary suffixes, and groups of words.

Those ending in indeclinable (*abyaya*) or secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffixes are as follows: *yathā*, *tathā*, *ekadhā*, *ekajjhaṃ*, *sabbaso*, *kathaṃ*, *itthaṃ*, and so forth. When these [suffixes] occur, there is elision of the third case ending (*tatiyālopa*).
The group of words ending in suffixes such as *tvā*:
those ending in suffixes such as *tvā* are as follows: *katvā*, *katvāna*, *kātuna*, *kātuṃ*, *kātave*, *dakkhitāye*, *hetuye*, *ādāya*.
[Examples include: *upādāya*, *viceyya*, *vineyya*, *sakkacca*, *āhacca*, *upasampajja*, *samecca*, *avecca*, *paṭicca*, *aticca*, *āgamma*, *ārabbha*, and so forth.

Among these, when [the suffixes] *tvā* and *tvānanta* are present, there is elision of the first case ending (*paṭhamālopa*). When [the suffixes] *tuṃ*, *tave*, *tāye*, and *tuye* are present as verbal suffixes (*paccayanta*), there is elision of the fourth case ending (*catutthīlopa*).
The roots (*dhātu*) are both conditions and prefixes and particles;
they possess manifold meanings within the domain of the knowledge of the analytical sciences (*paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa*).
Thus ends the *Moggallānadīpanī*, titled the Elucidation of Etymology.
The Section on Names is finished.
3. The Section on Agents.
The First Set of Case Endings.
Now, the distinctions in meaning of the noun case-endings (nāmavibhatti) are stated.
In what sense is the nominative (paṭhamā) used?
289. *Paṭhamatthamatte caṃ* (Pāṇini 2.3.46). [The nominative is used] in the sense of mere nominative function.
The first case ending occurs after a noun (*nāman*) in the sense of its mere denotation (*abhidheyyamatta*). Examples:
*rukkho* (tree), *mālā* (garland), *dhanaṃ* (wealth).

Here, by the word "mere" (*matta*), the meanings of the case endings such as the agent (*kartr*) and the object (*kamma*) are excluded. Therefore, "mere meaning" (*atthamatta*) refers specifically to the meaning of the gender (*liṅga*).

In that context, when [a word] has not been uttered, its meaning remains unknown to the listener; this is called "hidden meaning" (*līnattha*). That which makes known—that is, awakens—the understanding of that hidden meaning is a "sign" (*liṅga*), namely, the uttered word.

Furthermore, that is twofold: the base sign (*pakatiliṅga*) and the derived sign (*nipphannaliṅga*). Among these, the base sign—devoid of case-endings—is intended here as "sign," because case-endings occupy distinct positions of division.

It is a "sign" (*liṅga*) because it is a "limb" (*aṅga*) of that which is "hidden" (*līna*). Here, "hidden" means unmanifest, and "limb" means a part. In terms of meaning, "sign" (*liṅga*), "name" (*nāma*), and "nominal base" (*pāṭipadika*) are one and the same.

The meaning of a grammatical gender (*liṅga*) is twofold: the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*) and the conventional meaning (*paññatti-attha*). Likewise, there is the qualifying meaning (*visesana-attha*) and the qualified meaning (*visesya-attha*).
Among these, the "qualifying meaning" refers to its own specific sense; it is said to be the particularized meaning fixed to each respective word.
That very [meaning] exists because of the initial emergence of the word for that respective object and because of the continued application of the word over a long period of time.

It is called "the meaning of the sign" (*nimittattha*) because it is the cause for being bound [to a specific referent]. It is sevenfold, by way of genus (*suti*), birth (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), substance (*dabba*), action (*kriyā*), name (*nāma*), and relation (*sambandha*).
What is called "the qualified meaning" (*visesyattha*) is the general meaning (*sāmaññattha*); that is to say, it is the common meaning shared by many signs. That very same [meaning]...

That which arises through connection with various causes is called "the derivative meaning" (*naimittika-attha*); it is fivefold, according to birth (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), substance (*davva*), action (*kriyā*), and name (*nāma*).
For example: *go*, *sukko*, *daṇḍī*, *pācako*, *tisso*.

Among these, when the word *go* expresses mere birth—as in "the birth of a cow" (*go-jāti*)—then the suffix (*sutī*) is the qualifier. When it expresses a substance—as in "the cow goes" (*go gacchati*)—then both the suffix and the birth are qualifiers.
When the word *sukka* expresses a mere quality, as in "the quality white," then the genus (*suti*) is the qualifier.
When it expresses a specific quality, as in "the white of the cow," then both the genus and the quality are qualifiers.
When it expresses a substance possessing a quality, as in "the white cow," then the genus, the quality, the specific quality, and the relation are all qualifiers.
When the word *daṇḍī* expresses merely the genus—as in "the genus 'staff-bearer'"—then both the audible form (*suti*) and the substance (*dabba*) are qualifiers.
When it expresses a substance possessing [a genus]—as in "the man with a staff"—then the audible form, the substance, the genus, and the relation are all qualifiers.
When the word *pācaka* expresses merely the genus—as in "the genus 'cook'"—then both the audible form and the action (*kriyā*) are qualifiers.

When one says, "a man who cooks," referring to a substance that produces an action, then the hearing (*suti*), the action (*kriyā*), the genus (*jāti*), and the relationship between the action and its factor (*kriyākārakasambandha*) are the qualifiers (*visesana*).

When the word *Tissa* expresses a mere name, as in "the one named Tissa," then the hearing is the qualifier. When it refers to a substance possessing a name, as in "the monk Tissa," then the hearing, the genus of the name (*nāmajāti*), and the relationship are the qualifiers.
In every instance where it is said "whatever he says," that should be understood as both a quality (*dhamma*) and a substance (*davva*).
Furthermore, here "hearing" (*suti*) is of the very nature of sound; it belongs exclusively to the category of sound.
And it has been stated in the *Ñāsa* that "every sound first denotes a being. Therefore, in all places where there is hearing, only beings are appropriately present.
"Existence" (*satta*) refers to the fact that each respective object exists in the world even as a mere conventional designation (*vohāramatta*).
When one hears a particular word, knowledge first recognizes the mere existence of that respective object;

thereafter, in the case of a word for "birth," it recognizes birth, and in the case of a word for "quality," it recognizes quality—and so on for everything that must be stated. [The same applies to] gender (*liṅga*), etc.
Number and measures are also included under the category of qualifiers (*visesana*).
Among these, "gender" (*liṅga*) refers to those characteristics, signs, marks, and modes of appearance said in the Abhidhamma to belong to women and men,
as well as those characteristics, signs, marks, and modes of appearance belonging to neuters that are established even without being explicitly stated, and those [found] among words.
Furthermore, among meanings, clear, unclear, and intermediate forms are discerned; all of this is called *liṅga* (gender).

Thus, the meaning of the grammatical gender (*saddaliṅga*) previously mentioned is twofold, according to the qualifier (*visesana*) and the qualified (*viseyya*). That [meaning] is threefold: with gender (*saliṅga*), with number (*sasaṅkhyo*), and with measure (*saparimāṇo*).
Among these, what is "with gender"? For example: *saññā*, *phasso*, *cittaṃ*; *kaññā*, *puriso*, *kulaṃ*; *mālā*, *rukkho*, *dhanaṃ*.
How is it "with number" (sasaṅkhya)? For example: one, two, three, many, and so forth.
How is it "with measure" (saparimāṇa)? For example: a span, a cubit, a doṇa, an āḷhaka, and so forth.
Furthermore, the meaning of gender (liṅgattha) is twofold: pure (suddha) and associated (saṃsaṭṭha). Therein, that which is devoid of association with action and the like is pure.
It is sixfold: by name, by gender, by number, by measure, by the sense of a prefix (upasagga), and by the sense of a particle (nipāta).
Here, "pāṭipadika" refers to [words] such as *atthi*, *sakkā*, and *labbhā*.
Furthermore, suffixes such as *tuna*, *tvāna*, *tvā*, *tave*, *tuṃ*, and *khattuṃ* are also included among the particles (*nipāta*).
Association (*saṃsaṭṭha*) is twofold: that which is expressed by a compound (*vutta-saṃsaṭṭha*) and that which is not expressed by a compound (*avutta-saṃsaṭṭha*).

Therein, association expressed by a compound is fourfold in brief: that expressed by a nominal compound (*samāsa*), by a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), by a verb (*ākhyāta*), and by a primary derivative (*kita*).

Therein, that expressed by a nominal compound is sevenfold according to the connection with the six grammatical cases (*kāraka*), or eightfold when including the abstract state (*bhāva*); likewise is that expressed by a secondary derivative. That expressed by a verb—
It is threefold by way of agent (*kattu*), object (*kamma*), and state (*bhāva*). When expressed with the *ki* suffix, it is sixfold; by way of state, it is sevenfold.
All of these—whether pure or conjoined with what has been stated—are the domain of the first case (*nominative*).

Those not conjoined with what has been stated are also manifold, such as conjoined with the agent, conjoined with the object, and so forth; these belong to the second case (*accusative*) and the others.

Thus ends the section on "the object" (*visaya*). And here, since a bare word (*sadda*) cannot be employed without a case-ending (*vibhatti*), the nominative case (*paṭhamā*) is employed in the sixfold pure and the fourfold mixed [compounds] solely for the purpose of making them fit for usage, not for the purpose of indicating meaning.
However, because actions (*kamma*) and so forth, when not expressed by any denotative word, cannot be understood without case-endings, [the other cases are employed].

The second case (accusative) and others are also employed for the purpose of indicating meaning (*atthajotanattha*) in relation to the object (*kamma*) and so forth. Therefore, in the phrase "in mere meaning" (*atthamatte*), the locative case here refers to the mere object (*visayamatte*) that delimits another location.
However, in rules such as "the second case for the object" (*kamme dutiyā*), the locative refers to the purpose (*payojana*) to be accomplished.
Thus, the difference between these two uses of the locative case should be understood.
290. Addressing (āmantane): Ka. 285; Rū. 70; Nī. 578; Caṃ. 2.1.94; Pā. 2.3.47; āmantane (in many cases).
Addressing is the act of bringing a thing already established toward oneself by means of its name or a particle.
In addressing, the nominative case is used for the mere sense of the object. And here, what is called an "addressing word" is dependent upon a verb.
It does not exist; therefore, it does not receive the designation of "agent.
That [addressing] is, moreover, twofold, according to whether it is respectful or disrespectful: "Come, friend! Come, Jetā!

Likewise, according to whether it is with life or without life: "Speak, O man! Speak, O conch-shell! Speak, O conch-shell! (Dīgha Nikāya 2.426); "Arise, O large stone! Arise, O large stone! (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.358).
Likewise, by way of direct perception and non-perception: "O man, where is my only son? Where is my only son? (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.63; Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā 1.2).
Likewise, by way of restriction and non-restriction: "O man, it is wonderful indeed, O man! It is marvelous indeed! (Dīgha Nikāya 2.192).
"For here, being possessed of perception... and so forth (Dīgha Nikāya 2.192). This is called addressing; how much more so [the others].
It is indeed already established, not something to be enjoined; for people do not address one who has not yet attained the status of a king or the status of a monk by saying, "O King! or "O Monk!
The first section on case endings is concluded.
The Second Case Group. In what sense is the second case used? 291.
The second case is used for the object (kamma). Ka. 297; Rū. 284; Nī. 580; Caṃ. 2.1.43; Pā. 1.4.49–51.

The second case ending occurs in the sense of "action" (*kamma*). That which is performed is "action"; it is threefold: productive action (*nibbattikamma*), transformative action (*vikatikamma*), and attaining action (*pattikamma*).
Among these, what is productive action? For example: one possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*) creates the form of an elephant; a king builds a city; a mother gives birth to a son;
a seed produces a tree; karma produces its result (*vipāka*); and nutriment produces strength.
A person performs merit, performs evil; the Buddha taught the Dhamma, laid down the Vinaya;
a bhikkhu arouses jhāna, arouses the Path, and so forth.
What is the action of transformation (*vikatikamma*)? As in: he builds a house, makes a chariot, makes a pot, weaves cloth, [cooks] rice.

"He cooks," "he cooks the meal," "he turns wood into charcoal," "he fashions gold into a bracelet," "he burns down a house," "he cuts down a tree," "he breaks down a wall," "he reaps the crops," "he kills a living being," "he eats a meal," and so forth. What is the *pattikamma* (action by attainment)?
"He goes to a village," "he enters a house," "he climbs a tree," "he crosses a river," "he sees the sun," "he hears the Dhamma," "he pays homage to and attends upon the Buddha," and so forth.
It is twofold: natural action (*pakatikamma*) and modified action (*vikatikamma*). One makes gold into a bracelet; one makes wood into charcoal.
One sees a man standing; one sees a man walking. One sees a bhikkhu who is mindful, clearly comprehending, advancing, retreating, looking forward, looking aside, bending, or stretching.
In this context, "a man, O monk" is the natural object (*pakatikamma*), while "standing," "mindful," and so forth are the modified objects (*vikatikammāni*).

There are two kinds: the root-object (*dhātukamma*) and the causal object (*kāritakamma*). For example: "He goes to the village" (*gāmaṃ gacchati*) and "He causes the man to go to the village" (*purisaṃ gāmaṃ gameti*).
Furthermore, the root-object of roots that take two objects is twofold: the primary object (*padhānakamma*) and the secondary object (*appadhānakamma*). [As in: "The goat-herd..."
He leads a goat to the village; a man carries a burden to the village, he brings it; he drags a branch to the village;
he milks a cow for milk; he asks a brahmin for a blanket; he begs food from a brahmin; they pen the cows in the fold;
he asks the Blessed One a question; he plucks fruits from a tree; [he teaches] the Dhamma to a pupil.
The Blessed One said this to the bhikkhus; thus it is stated [in the Udāna] at 23 (slightly different). "He instructs his pupil in the Dhamma," and so forth.

Herein, the "principal object" (*padhānakamma*)—such as "the goat" or "the milk"—is so called because it is more desired by the agent for its own apprehension. The "non-principal object" (*appadhānakamma*)—such as "the village" or "the cow"—is so called because it is less so desired.
Among these, the principal object is called the "fixed object" (*kathinakamma*), meaning that its status as an object is stable. The non-principal object...

"Indeterminate case" (*akathinaka-kamma*) means a case that is unstable. For it is sometimes the recipient (*sampadāna*), sometimes the source (*apādāna*), sometimes the possessor (*sāmi*), and sometimes the location (*okāsa*). For example:

*so maṃ dakāya neti* (he leads me for water), *gāvito khīraṃ dohati* (he milks milk from the cow), *gāviyā khīraṃ dohahi* (may you milk milk from the cow), *gāviyaṃ khīraṃ dohati* (he milks milk from the cow), and so forth.
"Kamme dutiyā" (the accusative case is used for the object) continues [from the previous rule].

292. For verbs meaning "to go," "to know," "to eat," and those meaning "sound," as well as intransitive verbs (*akammaka*), when they are employed [as transitive], the suffix *ka* is added [to form causatives].
This is a sutta prescribing an obligatory rule (*nicca-vidhi*). It applies to verbs meaning "to go," "to know," "to eat," "sound," and intransitive verbs.

The second case ending occurs after causative (*payojaka*) roots such as *bhajj* (to fry) when the object is expressed. Here, the "causative object" (*payojakakamma*) is called the "object caused to act" (*kāritakamma*).

Examples: *A puruṣa causes another puruṣa to go to the village.* (*puriso purisaṃ gāmaṃ gamayati*) *A master causes a goat-herd to lead a goat to the village.* (*sāmiko ajapālaṃ ajaṃ gāmaṃ nayāpeti*) *A teacher causes a student to understand the Dhamma.* (*ācariyo sissaṃ dhammaṃ bodheti*) *A man causes a man to eat food.* (*puriso purisaṃ bhattaṃ bhojeti*) *A teacher causes a student to recite the Dhamma.* (*ācariyo sissaṃ dhammaṃ pāṭheti*)
A man makes another man lie down, sit, or stand up; a man makes another man roast grain, pound it, or winnow it.
What is the meaning of "by these"?
A man has rice cooked by means of another man.

And here, regarding the application of the third case (*tatiyā*) for the purpose of going and so forth, it has been stated in the *Rūpasiddhi* (p. 141), in the *Saddanīti*, and in the commentary on Sutta 148.

In the *Saddanīti*, even in the usage of the third case, they maintain that it expresses only the object (*kamma*). In the *Ñāsā* and other works, they maintain that it expresses the sense of the absolutive (*katv-attha*).

But when a second instigator prompts the first instigator, then the first is called the "prompted" (*payojja*). Regarding that, it is stated in the *Vutti*: "The third case ending [is used] for that [prompted one]. One causes another to complete a hut that was begun by oneself: *pārā*. (363. 293).
From *harā* and so on, optionally the second case ending occurs in the sense of the prompted object. (Ka. 300; Rū. 286; Nī. 587; Caṃ. 2.1.45; Pā. 1.4.53).
For the verbs beginning with *harati*, the second case ending is optionally employed in the sense of the prompted object (*payojja-kamma*).
A husband causes a man to carry a burden by means of another man, or causes a man to swallow food by means of another man,
or causes a man to perform work by means of another man; a king shows himself as himself by means of a man,
or has a man pay homage to the Buddha by means of another man.
194. Regarding *khād*-roots and others: Ka. 300; Rū. 286; Nī. 587; Caṃ. 2.1.47; Pā. 1.4.57.
When *khād* and other such roots are employed with respect to the object (*kamma*), the second case ending does not occur. For example:

*sāmiko purisena khajjaṃ khādāpeti* (the master causes the man to eat the food); *ada bhakkhane* (the root *ad* in the sense of eating); *bhattaṃ ādeti* (he eats the meal); *sāmiko dāsena purisaṃ...* (the master [causes] the man by means of the slave...).
He causes to call out, he causes to make a sound, he cries out, he makes a noise. And here, “he causes to make a sound” (*saddāyāpeti*) means he causes a sound to be produced;
this is a denominative root (*nāmadhātu*).
*Kanda* and *nada* also have the meaning of sound alone. 295. *Vahissāniyantuke ka.* (Kaccāyana 300; Rūpasiddhi 286; Nyāsa 587; Cāndra 2.1.48; Pāṇini 1.4.52)
*Vahissā* is an indication of the verbal root *vah*, where the vowel *i* serves as a marker.

One who directs or employs [another] is a *niyantā* (director); that which has no director is *aniyantuka* (self-directed). That which has no need for another director, but proceeds by itself having understood [the way], is called *aniyantuka*.
When the object of the root *vah* is such a self-directed entity, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not occur.
The master causes the burden to be carried by the slave.
What is the purpose of the term *aniyantuka*? [It is used when one says: "He causes the burden to be carried by oxen.
296. *Bhakkhissā-hiṃsāyaṃ ka*. (Kaccāyana 300; Rūpasiddhi 286; Niddesa 587; Cāndra 2.1.49; Pāṇini 1.4.5).

Causing one who desires to eat to eat is not called *hiṃsā* (harming); causing one who does not desire to eat to eat is called *hiṃsā*. When the object (*kamma*) of the verbal root *bhakkha* (to eat) is used in the sense of non-harming (*ahiṃsā*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is not employed.
Example: *Sāmiko purisena modake bhakkhāpeti* (The master has the man eat sweetmeats).

In this context, when there is a connection with prefixes that express specific types of actions such as "sending forth," the accusative case is used in the sense of the object (*kammattha*). The Third Case Group: In what sense is the third case used? 305.
The third case is used for the agent and the instrument (kattukaraṇesu). Ka. 286, 288; Rū. 291, 293; Nī. 591, 594; Caṃ. 2.1.62–3; Pā. 2.3.18.
The third case ending occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattari*) and the instrument (*karaṇe*). "Agent" (*kattā*) and "doer" (*kāraka*) are one in meaning;

for "he does, thus he is an agent" (*karotīti kattā*) and "he does, thus he is a doer" (*karotīti kārako*). Therefore, when both "agent" (*kattā*) and "doer" (*kāraka*) are mentioned, by virtue of these two synonymous terms, it is understood that he performs this very action exclusively, he performs it as a master, and he performs it with himself as the primary focus.
Furthermore, it is held that action (*kriyā*) is the activity of the agent alone and not of others;

moreover, while others are called "factors" (*kāraka*) because they assist the agent in accomplishing the action, they are likewise understood as "non-factors" (*akāraka*) because they do not so assist.
In this context, the agent (*kattā*) is threefold: the self-agent (*sayaṃkattā*), the instigating agent (*payojakakattā*), and the object-agent (*kammakattā*).
In this context, one who performs the action oneself is called the "self-agent" (*sayaṃkattā*), as in: "A man performs the work.
One who instigates another is called the "instigating agent" (*payojakakattā*), as in: "A man causes a slave to perform the work.
The term "agent of the action" (*kammakattā*) is also used for the instigating agent, as in: "A man causes the work to be done by a slave," or [the work of] the slave.

And one who, depending on an action performed by another, is designated as the agent—whether because the act is easy to perform, or because he does not wish to assume the status of agent, or because of ignorance, or because he wishes to deceive—is called the "agent of the action" (kammakattā). For example:
"The granary breaks itself," or "The jar breaks itself. Furthermore, whether the act be easy or difficult, [it remains so].
That agent who stands first in a sentence where the object (*kamma*) is itself the form of the action (*rūpa-kriyā*) is called the "object-agent" (*kammakatta*).

It is an "object-agent" because it is the object by way of its verbal form (*sadda-rūpa*) and the agent by way of its referential meaning (*attha-rūpa*); for example: *kusūlo bhijjati* (the granary breaks), *ghaṭo bhijjati* (the jar breaks), *paccati munino bhattaṃ* (the sage's meal is cooked), *thokaṃ thokaṃ ghare ghare* (little by little, in every house), and so forth.
And here, the meaning of a word is twofold: the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) and the conceptual sense (*paññattattha*). Among these, the ultimate sense exists exclusively as a reality.

The meaning is as follows: Sound indeed functions in dependence upon the speaker’s intention; and there is no such thing as a sound that, while being uttered, does not indicate its meaning.
Furthermore, when the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) exists, there is no such thing as it failing to produce in the listener an awareness whose object is that meaning.
Thus, even though an object is considered non-existent [in an ultimate sense], it is nonetheless existent as the objective domain for both sound and cognition. Otherwise, [it would follow that]...
The intention is this: when one hears the word ‘the son of a barren woman,’ the mind would not function with that object as its domain;

furthermore, an object that exists by way of being the referent for both sound and cognition becomes manifold when there is a difference in sounds and a difference in cognitions—it is, as it were, existing separately and individually.
