The Fifth Case (Pañcamīvibhatti).
In what sense is the fifth case used? 312.
*Pañcamy-āvadhismiṃ* (The fifth case is used in the sense of a limit). Ka. 295; Rū. 307; Nī. 607; Caṃ. 2.1.81; Pā. 2.3.28; 1.4.24.

That from which a word-meaning is delimited (*avadhiyati*) or defined (*vavatthiyati*) is called a limit (*avadhi*); the fifth case ending occurs in relation to that. Furthermore, this is termed the ablative (*apādāna*).

It is called the ablative because, having set something aside from this, one takes up or grasps something else. That [ablative] is threefold: the expressed domain (*niddiṭṭhavisaya*), the extracted domain (*uppāṭavisaya*), and the inferable domain (*anumeyyavisaya*).

Among these, that in which a specific action constituting the ablative domain is expressed in its own form is the expressed domain. For example: "The sages depart from the village" (*gāmā apenti munayo*); "The king has gone out from the city" (*nagarā niggato rājā*).
However, that in which a remainder of the text must be supplied by way of insertion is the domain of *uppāda* (supplying). For example:
"The lightning flashes from the clouds; he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness" (*Mahāvagga* 30).
For here, the word "having gone out" (*nikkhamitvā*) must be supplied.

But when that [object] is neither explicitly stated nor can it be supplied by ellipsis, yet is nevertheless to be understood through inference from the sense, that is the domain of the inferable (anumeyya).
For example: "The people of Mathurā are more handsome than those of Pāṭaliputta";
"Virtue alone is better than learning" (Dhp 284); "There is nothing superior to me" (Sn 550); "I am the foremost in the world; I am the eldest" (Sn 550).

"I am the best in the world," "I am the foremost in the world," and so forth (M.N. 3.207). Since a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) cannot be established without an action (*kriyā*), an act of exaltation must be inferred here.
In this way, even in cases such as the connection with distance (*dūrayoga*) that lack a finite verb, the inference of an inseparably concomitant action (*avinābhāvikriyā*) should be understood.
Furthermore, it is twofold by way of being movable and immovable.
What is movable? For example: a man falls from a galloping horse; two rams, having fought, retreat from one another.
And in this case, if it were movable, how could there be a limit? For a limit is characterized by its absolute nature (*accuti-lakkhaṇa*).
It is said: two rams move according to their own respective actions; they do not become a limit for one another’s action.
Thus, there is no contradiction here with the characteristic of a limit (*avadhi*).
How is it "non-limiting" (*acala*)? "The sages depart from the village; the king has gone out from the city."
Furthermore, there are two types: that preceded by physical contact and that preceded by mental contact. "The sages depart from the village;
fear arises for the thieves. And here, even when one says, "How far is the village from here?
That is the southern direction," or "In the ninety-first aeon from here" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.4), etc., it should be understood as being preceded by mental contact.
“The mother does not fear her son, nor does the son fear his mother; being afraid out of fear, you do not speak”—this is the Pāḷi at Ja.
2.21.138. “There is fear for you from this” (attha te ito bhayam) at Ma. Ni. 2.350; “there is no fear for you from this” (natthi te ito bhayam);

“fear from that which is secure” (yato khemam tato bhayam) at Ja. 1.9.58; “he fears thieves” (corā bhāyati), “frightened by thieves” (corā bhīto). And [with] the genitive: “he fears the thief” (corassa bhāyati), “of the thief” (corassa).
[He was] terrified. And the second [verse]: “How could one not fear the next world? Thus one should not fear the next world.
You fear me, ascetic Sunīta Sūciloma; I do not fear you, Sunīta Sūciloma.
One does not fear that which ought to be feared; I do not fear the serpent, nor do wild beasts terrify me. (Jā 2.22.307) (Cf. Jā 2.22.835).

The Pāli words are seen there. In that context: “*Bhoginam*” refers to a serpent (*nāga*). “*Corā tasati*” means he trembles in fear of thieves; or, “*corassa vā sabbe tasanti*” means all tremble before the thief.
“*Daṇḍassa dha.*” [refers to] fear of punishment (Dhammapada 129). “*Pāpato ottappati*” means he is afraid of evil; he feels disgust, shame, or is ashamed because of evil.
Whatever craft, knowledge, or Dhamma one receives, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used for that teacher, as in “from the preceptor” (*upajjhāyā*).
“He studies,” “the preceptor learns the craft,” “I received eighty-two [thousand verses] from the Buddha, two thousand from the bhikkhus.
Regarding the eighty-four thousand teachings that have been handed down as the Theras’ verses:

when one hears [them], the fifth and sixth cases are used—such as “having heard from him,” “having heard from this one,” or “having heard from whomsoever one might understand the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One. (Dhp 392)
The ablative case (pañcamī) is used for that from which one obtains: one obtains from the Saṅgha, one obtains from a group.
The ablative case is used for that from which one is defeated, from which something originates, or from which something is born:
"The followers of other sects are defeated by the Buddha. However, in the Pāḷi, when there is a connection with defeat, the ablative is obtained by way of ellipsis; in that case...
But in that battle, the gods were victorious and the asuras were defeated. Here, there is an elliptical remainder of the text:
"the gods were defeated. [The passage continues: "We have been conquered by Ambakā. The five great rivers originate from the Himālayas:
this is the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, which has its source in the Himālayas" (Ap. Thera 1.1.255). Fear of thieves...
Fear arises from desire (Dhp. 215); fear born of birth arises from clinging (Jā. 1.1.36; 1.2.13; 1.9.56, 57, 59).
Whatever fear, enmity, affliction, or calamity arises, all that arises from the fool, not from the wise man;
sorrow arises from desire (Dhp. 214). A son well-born on both sides...
Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā 1.311: "Born from the chest" (*urasmā jāto*) or "born on the chest" (*ure jāto*); a robe might arise from the Saṅgha, from a group, from relatives or friends;
Pārājika 500 (slightly different). The fifth case is used in connection with "other than" (*aññattha*);
"other than that," "beyond that"; Mahāvagga 346; "at a later time than that"; Pārājika 195.
Furthermore, regarding the application of prefixes (*upasagga*):
313. *Apaparīhi vajjane* (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī 272; Rūpasiddhi 309; Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā 558, 568; Cūḷanirutti 2.1.82; Pāṇini 1.4.88; 2.3.10).
When used in the sense of exclusion (*vajjana*), the fifth case ending occurs in connection with *apa* and *pari*.
"The rain falls from off the mountain" means the rain falls from beyond the mountain; "the rain falls all around the mountain" means it falls from every side.
"Merchants come from outside the hall" or "merchants come from within the hall"—the meaning is that they come having avoided the mountain-hall (*pabbata-sāla*).

However, in the *Kaccāyana* [grammar], the reading "the rain falls from above the mountain" (*uparipabbatā*) is the ancient reading, which is consistent with the form *paripabbatā*. Furthermore, in the sense of "above," only the locative case is seen.
—“In that upper mountain” (ma. ni. 3.216; jā. 1.8.16), “in the upper palace” (dī. ni. 2.408), “in the upper chamber,” “in the upper chamber-cottage” (pāci. 130).
Here, “upper mountain” (*uparipabbata*) means on top of the mountain. 314. Regarding *paṭinidhi* (substitute) and *paṭidāna* (giving back):
*Paṭinidhi* means the setting up of a counterpart; *paṭidāna* means the giving of a counter-gift. When used in connection with these, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) occurs. For example:
*buddhasmā pati sāriputto dhammaṃ deseti* (Sāriputta teaches the Dhamma as a counterpart to the Buddha); *telasmā pati ghataṃ deti* (he gives a vessel of ghee as a counter-gift for the oil).
315. *Rite* takes the second case ending (*dutiyā*). [Kaccāyana 272; Rūpasiddhi 309; Nyāsa 558, 568; Candra 2.1.84; Pāṇini 2.3.29]
When used with the word *rite*, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) occurs, as does the second case ending (*dutiyā*).
For example: *rite saddhammā* (apart from the true Dhamma), *rite saddhammaṃ*. 316.
With the words *vinā* and *aññatra*, the third case ending (*tatiyā*) also [occurs]. (Ka. 272; Rū. 309; Nī. 558, 568; Caṃ. 2.1.85; Pā. 2.3.32; ‘vināññatra tatiyā ca’ [found in many texts]).
In connection with the words *vinā* (“without”) and *aññatra* (“except”), when used with a word other than *vajjaṃ* (“fault”), the fifth, second, and third cases occur.
*Vinā saddhammā*, *vinā saddhammaṃ*, *vinā saddhammena*; *aññatra saddhammā*, *aññatra saddhammaṃ*, *aññatra saddhammena*.
317. *Puthunānāhi ca* (Ka. 272; Rū. 309; Nī. 558, 568; Caṃ. 2.1.86; Pā. 2.3.32; ‘puthanānāhi ca’ [in many recensions]).

When *puthu* (separate) and *nānā* (various) are used with the sense of separation (*vajjana*), the fifth case ending occurs; the third case endings also occur when used in conjunction (*yoga*). Examples include:
*puthageva janasmā* (separate from people), *puthageva janena* (separate from people); *nānā saddhammā* (various true Dhammas), *nānā saddhammena* (with various true Dhammas);

and *piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo vinābhāvo* (separation and absence from those who are dear and pleasing) [Dīgha Nikāya 2.183; Cūḷavagga 437]. Also: “Those bhikkhus had gone forth from various families.”
In this context, however, the word *nāna* has the sense of "diversity" (*nānāppakāra*), not the sense of "exclusion" (*vajjana*). Here, "exclusion" means the sense of separation or non-mixture.
With the words *ā* and *yāva*, when used in the senses of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*), both the fifth case (*pañcamī*) and the second case (*dutiyā*) are employed.

Among these, that which is related to the action as its boundary is called the "limit" (*maryādā*). How so? For example: *ā pabbatā khettaṃ tiṭṭhati* or *ā pabbataṃ*; *yāva pabbatā khettaṃ tiṭṭhati* or *yāva pabbataṃ*. In these cases, setting aside the action connected to that limit, it functions [as a marker]. Thus, the field stands up to the mountain, or as far as the mountain.
That which encompasses and pervades the action connected to it is *abhividhi* (inclusive extension). How so?
"The fame of the Blessed One has spread up to the peak of existence (*ābhavagga*)," or "up to the peak of existence" means from existence up to the peak of existence;

"they flow from the Dhamma up to the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhū*)"—thus they are called *āsava*s (taints); "as far as the peak of existence, up to the peak of existence," meaning the sound has spread as far as the Brahma-world.
The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used with *ārabbhe* and *sahatthe*. "From the time that I, sister, was born into the noble birth" (MNI 2.351);
the meaning is "from which point onward. "Since I remember myself, since I have attained discernment" (JĀ 2.22.307).
"From which point onward," "from which time forth."
*Sahatthe* (in the sense of "together with"): *Saha sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭilābhā*, *saha parinibbānā* (Dīgha Nikāya 2.220), *saha dassanuppādā*.

In the passage, “Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.20), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇe*).
In the phrase “*sahatthā dānaṃ deti, sahatthā paṭiggaṇhātī*” (he gives with his own hand, he receives with his own hand), the instrumental case (*karaṇe*) is used.

In expressions such as “*ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ*” (from this day forth for as long as life lasts; Dīgha Nikāya 1.250) and “*tadagge kho vāseṭṭha*” (from that time on, Vāseṭṭha; Dīgha Nikāya 3.130), the locative case (*sattamī*) is used in the sense of “starting from” (*ārabbhe*). In expressions such as “*yatvādhikaraṇaṃ*” (wherein it has its basis;

Dīgha Nikāya 1.213), “*yatonidānaṃ*” (having its source in which; Sutta Nipāta 275), and “*tatonidānaṃ*” (having its source in that; Majjhima Nikāya 1.238), when a sentence is intended, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of cause (*hetvatthe*); when a compound is intended, the ablative is used in the mere sense of the object (*atthamatte*).
The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used for words expressing the duration of time occurring between two agents or two actions, as in:

*luddako pakkhasmā migaṃ vijjhati* (the hunter shoots the deer after [a certain interval] from [the first shot]), and *kosā kuñjaraṃ vijjhati* (he shoots the elephant from [after] the sheath). Here, the hunter does not shoot the deer again within the same wing-interval after having shot it once;
rather, he shoots again when the wing-interval is complete. In this context, the word *pakka* refers to the interval between two instances of shooting.
It expresses time; since both piercing actions are accomplished together with the agents, it is said to be "among the agents" (*kārakānaṃ majjhe*).
However, in the *Vutti*, it is stated: "Having eaten today, Devadatta will eat in two days" (*dvihē bhuñjissati*); "He will eat in two days" (*dvihā bhuñjissati*);

"The archer here pierces the target through the shield" (*atraṭṭho'yam issāso kose lakkhaṃ vijjhati*); "The archer pierces the target from the shield" (*kosā lakkhaṃ vijjhati*)—thus [it is used]. (Moga 79) In this way...
A complete sentence has also been stated by way of the locative case. In the Canon, there is the reading: “There is no offense if she completes it within six years;
there is no offense if she completes it in more than six years” (Pārājika 564). There is also the reading “six years.
This is in connection with the sense of protection.
When a thing is desired as that which is protected (*gutta*), or when it is desired from that which it is protected, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used:

*yavehi gāvo rakkhati vāreti* (he protects or wards off the cows from the barley); *taṇḍule kāke rakkhati vāreti* (he protects or wards off the crows from the rice); *taṃ maṃ puññā nivāresi* (that merit warded me off [from evil]);
*pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye* (one should ward off the mind from evil) (DhP 116); *na naṃ jāti nivāreti* (neither birth wards him off), nor does misfortune or reproach (SvN).
141 (na ne). May they receive protection from the king or from thieves.
In the sense of conjunction with disappearance (*antaradhāna*):
when one desires the non-seeing of someone, the fifth case is used; for example, "the pupil disappears from the preceptor" (*upajjhāyā antaradhāyati sissō*), meaning he hides.
This is the meaning. However, in the Pāḷi, when disappearance from someone is intended, the genitive case alone is used—as in:
“I shall disappear from the ascetic Gotama; I shall disappear from the ascetic Gotama. The Pāḷi reads: “I was not able to disappear.
The meaning of “I shall disappear” (*antaradhāyissāmi*) is: “I shall place myself in a location that has vanished from sight, beyond the range of vision.”
"I shall hide myself"—this is what is meant.
In whatever place one disappears, only the locative case is seen there; for example:

"The eye will disappear from the world very quickly" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.224, though the context differs), "having disappeared in Jeta’s Grove," or "having disappeared in the Brahma-world," or "in Maddakucchi."

“Having vanished, he vanished right there,” and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.1). Regarding the phrase “having vanished in front of the Blessed One,” here too the particle *to* has the sense of the locative case.
The canonical text reads: “Sakka vanished in the presence of King Nimi.
In the phrase “having vanished in the Dhajata Grove,” this means having made himself invisible to others in the Jeta Grove, [placing himself] beyond the range of sight of others.

The meaning is "having made. However, in expressions such as “darkness disappears,” “light disappears,” “the true Dhamma disappears,” and “the Dispensation disappears,” the genitive and locative cases should be understood according to their respective applicability.
In the construction with words denoting distance—
"How far is the village from here? Is it far from negligence? (Sni 156), "and indeed far from negligence" (Sni 157). [The term] *gāmato* means not far from the village.
"Those foolish men are far (*ārakā*) from this Dhamma and Vinaya; the Blessed One is far from them";
because he is far from the defilements (*kilesa*), he is an *Arahat*. "He is far from the destruction of the taints" (Dhp 253). This applies to the second, third, and sixth [cases].
And [it means] far from this Dhamma and Vinaya, or by means of this Dhamma and Vinaya; purity is far from those of dull intellect.
Regarding the sense of distance:
"They pay homage from afar" (Dūratova namassanti); "The Blessed One saw him coming from afar" (Addasā kho bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ). What indeed...?
"Stay far away; therefore we stay far away. Regarding the second and third [examples]:
"He has come from a distant village," "he has come by means of a distant village," or "he has come from a distant village"—this is the meaning; or [it means] "by means of a distant village.
In connection with the sense of proximity—
"Near villages," "close villages," "proximate villages. [The forms] in the second, third, and sixth cases are: *antikaṃ gāmaṃ*, *antikaṃ gāmena*, *antikaṃ gāmassa*.
Regarding the expression of the measure of time or distance:
"From here, Sāṅkāśya is four *yojanas* from Mathurā; Sāvatthī is forty-five *yojanas* from Rājagaha."

"In the ninety-first aeon from now" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.4), "in the thirty-first aeon from now" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.4), "seven days from now," "after the lapse of three months from now, I shall attain final nibbāna" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.168; Udāna 51), and so forth.
[The particle *ito* is used] in the sense of measure:
The Middle Country is one *yojana* in length and breadth, and nine hundred *yojanas* in circumference;

or, in terms of its perimeter, it is nine spans long from east to west. "One *yojana* in length, one *yojana* in breadth, one *yojana* in height—a heap of mustard seeds," and so forth. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.129) etc.
The ablative case (pañcamī) is also used when there is the elision of *tvā*.
Here, "elision of *tvā*" means that in an incomplete sentence, there is the absence of a word ending in *tvā* which would have been present in a complete sentence;

and whatever word serves as the object (*kamma*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) when the *tvā*-ending word is present, that same word becomes the limit (*avadhi*) when the *tvā*-ending word is absent. In that case, the ablative is used, as in *pāsādā vā pāsādaṃ*.

"He would transfer" (saṅkameyya) [from Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.132], or "he would transfer from the back of one elephant to the back of another elephant" (hatthikkhandhā vā hatthikkhandhaṃ saṅkameyya) [Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.132], and so forth.
And here, the complete sentence is either: "having first ascended one palace, he would transfer to another palace," or "having first sat down in one palace, he would transfer to another palace."
It should be understood thus: “One might go from darkness to darkness, or from gloom to gloom” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.132).
Likewise, he wanders from kingdom to kingdom, from village to village, from forest to forest;
he goes from monastery to monastery, from cell to cell, and from existence to existence.
"From family to family he goes," and so forth. Likewise, one asks about the Vinaya from the Vinaya, asks about the Abhidhamma from the Abhidhamma;
one speaks about the Vinaya from the Vinaya, speaks about the Abhidhamma from the Abhidhamma.
Here too, having first asked about one statement of the Vinaya, or having stood upon one statement of the Vinaya, [one asks] another statement of the Vinaya.
"Pucchatī" (he asks) should be understood as a complete sentence. However, in the *Vutti*, it is stated: "Having ascended the palace, he looks out; from the palace, he looks out;
having entered the seat, he looks out; from the seat, he looks out.

When used in connection with the sense of direction (*disattha*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is employed for the sense of direction: "From here, that is the eastern direction" (Dī. ni. 3.278); "from here, that is the southern [direction]."

"Directions": *Dīgha Nikāya* 3.278; from above Avīci, upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the hair at the crown of the head: *Dīgha Nikāya* 2.377; *Majjhima Nikāya* 1.110. Regarding the meaning of "direction":
to the east of the village, to the south of the village, above the mountain, below the palace, to the front (east), etc.

The ablative case is used in the sense of "from" (dakkhiṇato), "where there is safety, from there comes danger" (Jā. 1.9.58); in the sense of "whencever" (yato yato), as in "whenever one contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates" (DhA.

374), and so forth. It is also used in connection with words such as *pubba* ("before"): "even before my full enlightenment" (AN 3.104); "prior to this," "prior to that"; "beyond this, the bordering countries" (Mahāvagga 259); "before that," "after that," "further than that" (Pārāyaṇa 499), and so forth.
The fifth and sixth case endings occur in the sense of analysis (*vibhattattha*).

"Analysis" (*vibhatti*) means, even before [the word is] distinct, the separation of the meaning of that which has become distinct from something else by means of some superior or inferior portion; for example:

"The people of Māthura are more handsome than those of Pāṭaliputta," or "There is none more excellent, more refined, or more distinguished than him," or "Self-restraint is better than that. (Dhp. 322), or "Of the ninety-six... (*channavutīnaṃ*).
Of all religious sects, this discipline of the Sugata is the most excellent. In the world with its devas, the Teacher is unsurpassed.
"I am the eldest in the world," "I am the best in the world"—thus [it is said].
Those called wise are inferior to Sāriputta, or at most equal to him; there is none superior to him.
"Or less than [the required amount] is not permitted," and so forth.
In the sense of abstaining: "Abstention (ārati), refraining (virati) from evil" (Khu.pā. 5.8); "Refraining from the taking of life" (Khu.pā. 2.1), and so forth.
In the sense of purity:
"Pure from things that provoke lust," and so forth.
In the sense of liberation, both the ablative and the instrumental cases are used: "He is fully liberated from birth, from aging, from death, from sorrow, and from lamentation."
"He who is liberated from sufferings, mental distresses, and despair, him I call one who has escaped from suffering" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.29);
"They are released from the bonds of Māra" (Dhammapada 37); "They are not released from death," and so forth—in all such cases, the sense of a limit (avadhi) should be understood.
In the sense of a cause (hetu):...
For what reason, by what cause, why indeed do the young ones not die in your family?
(1.10.92) [Variant: *miyare*]. Therefore, monks, [you should practice]... (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.157). The second, third, and sixth [verses], "What is the reason?
(*kiṃkāraṇaṃ*)... (Jātaka Aṭṭhakathā 6.22, Ummagga-jātaka commentary). "On account of which" (*yatvādhikaraṇaṃ*)... (Dīgha Nikāya 1.213); "from which source" (*yatonidānaṃ*)... (Sutta Nipāta 275).
"Because of that" (*tatonidānaṃ*) [is used] at Ma. Ni. 1.238; "for what reason" (*kena kāraṇena*) at Jā. Aṭṭha. 4.20 in the *Mātaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā*; and "for what cause" (*taṃ kissahetu*) at Ma. Ni.
1.2, as in "For what do you weary yourselves? (*kissa tumhe kilamatha*). In the sense of analysis (*vivecanattha*), it is used in conjunction with: [yoga].
"Secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states" (Dīgha Nikāya 1.226). "Secluded from evil states.

Regarding the sense of separation (*bandhana-tyāga-yoga*): [this is explained] in the *Pañcamī-ṇa* section of the *Kaccāyana-vyākaraṇa* (296); *Rūpasiddhi* (314); *Niruttidīpanī* (608); *Candavutti* (2.1.69); and *Pāṇini-sūtra* (2.3.24).
When the cause (*hetu*) is implied, the fifth case ending optionally occurs.
A man is bound by truth, or [bound] with truth.
(319) *Guṇe ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.25).

A cause that has become internal is called a "quality" (*guṇa*); even what is not a quality is here called a "quality," and the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) may optionally occur after it. For example:
*jaḷattā bandho naro* (the man is bound because of his dullness), or *jaḷattena* (by means of his dullness). The meaning is: he is bound solely by his own foolishness. [Other examples include:

*paññāya bandhanā mutto* (released from the bond of wisdom), *vācāya marati* (he dies because of speech), *vācāya muccati* (he is released because of speech), *vācāya piyo hoti* (he is dear because of speech), *vācāya desso* (he is hated because of speech), and *issariyā janaṃ* (people [are subdued] by power).
The king protects [them] by means of his sovereignty, or they praise him for his virtue (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.6). Or, because they exist and then cease to be, they are impermanent;

because they are oppressed by arising and passing away, they are suffering. With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations (udāna 2); with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness (udāna 2).
Due to the lack of knowledge and non-penetration of the Four Noble Truths, beings wander for a long time through the cycle of existence.
*Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā* 2.186 (*visadisaṃ*) and so forth.
The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is also used in the sense of "from where" (*kuto*), as in: "From where are you? or "I am from Pāṭaliputta.

The ablative is also used in the sense of "a little" (*thoka*) when it does not refer to a substance (*asattvavacana*). A substance (*satva*) is called *dabba*; thus, [the forms] *thokā muccati* or *thokena muccati* [are examples].
"It is merely a release" is what is meant; as it is said in the *Mahāvaṃsa* (1.48): "Crossing the river, he was carried away by the mind.
Here, one is released by a small thing or from a small thing; one is released with difficulty or from difficulty:
"A beloved son is obtained with difficulty" (Jā. 2.22.353); "We have been released from suffering with difficulty, O Mahosadha" (Jā. 2.22.700).

What is an example of an expression used for that which is not a sentient being (*asattvavacana*)? “The Sage’s meal is cooked little by little in every house,” from the *Theragāthā* (248; *kule kule*).
In such cases as “Gradually, the wise man, little by little, moment by moment” (*Dhammapada* 239), the accusative case is used as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is also used even when there is no agent, because of the having been done, accumulated, increased, or expanded of that karma by the Tathāgata.

"He has feet well-planted" (Dīghanikāya 3.201). Here, they say that "non-agent" (*akattarī*) refers to a causal indicator (*ñāpakahetu*) that is not the agent. In the *Ñāsa*, however, it is stated: "'Non-agent' includes the sense of cause.
For where the notion of an agent arises, it is possible to say that very thing is not the agent. By this, the generative cause (*janakahetu*) which resembles the agent is called "non-agent."
It illuminates [the meaning of] "name" (nāma), as well as [the phrase] "because of having performed the deed," and so forth, as the generative cause (*janakahetu*).
In connection with the sense of "more than" (*bhiyyattha*): "He who here does not consider cold and heat to be more than grass" (Dīgha Nikāya 3.253); "Gladness is more than pleasure."
"There is nothing found greater than patience" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.287); "There is nothing found greater than truth" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.250); "There is nothing found greater than me.

Regarding the section on the sixth case ending:
in what sense is the sixth case used?
320. The sixth case ending is used for the genitive relation (chaṭṭhī sambandhe). [Kaccāyana 301; Rūpasiddhi 315; Nyāsa 609; Candra 2.1.95; Pāṇini 2.3.50].

The state of dependence of two related things by some manner is called "relation" (sambandha). When a relation is to be expressed, the sixth case ending occurs for the related thing that serves as the qualifier.

Regarding this, it is stated that the relation arising from the action and the factor of action (kriyākāraka) is caused by the relationship between "this" and "that" (assedambhāva). In that context, there are two...
Relatives perform their respective actions for one another;
seeing this, for one who understands that "these are mutually related," the relationship itself becomes known by virtue of the conjunction of two agents and two actions.
Thus, the relationship is born from action and agent, because it serves as the cause for the cognition that arises in the form: "this belongs to that."
And [it is] caused by the state of being a horse and a donkey.

Therein, relation (*sambandha*) is threefold: the relation of possession (*sāmisa-sambandha*), the relation of difference (*nānātta-sambandha*), and the relation of action and agent (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*).

Therein, "possessor" (*sāmī*) is a name for anything that possesses a qualifier; therefore, the connection of the referent of the qualified term with its respective qualifier is called the relation of possession.

Thus, it is of many kinds according to the distinctions among the meanings of the qualified terms (*visesya-pada*). Among these, "his mother," "his father," and so forth, are called relationships of procreation (*janaka-sambandha*).
"Her son," "her daughter," and so forth, are called relationships of birth (*jañña-sambandha*).
The relationship of kinship (*kulasambandha*) refers to such things as "his brother" or "his sister.
The relationship of ownership (*āmisa-sambandha*) refers to such things as "Sakka, lord of the gods" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.248).
The relationship of possession (*saṃ-sambandha*) refers to such things as "I have abundant wealth, O Sakka" (Jātaka 1.15.72) or "the bowl and robe of a bhikkhu."
"Near the mango grove," "in the very presence of Nibbāna"—these and others are examples of what is called a relationship of proximity (*samīpa-sambandha*).
"A heap of gold," "a multitude of monks"—these and others are examples of what is called a relationship of collection (*samūha-sambandha*).
"The head of a man," "the branch of a tree"—these and others are examples of what is called a relationship of constituent part (*avayava-sambandha*). (Jātaka 1.4.81)
The relationship of transformation (*vikārasambandha*) refers to such things as a vessel for gold, a cauldron for what has not been obtained, and groats for grain that has been lost.
The relationship of effect (*kāriyasambandha*) refers to such things as a sprout from a barley seed, sound from a cloud, fragrance from flowers, juice from fruits, and smoke from fire.

The relationship of state (*avatthāsambandha*) refers to such things as the birth of the aggregates (*khandhā*), the aging of the aggregates, and the dissolution of the aggregates (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.1).

The color of gold, the color of the Tathāgata that does not fade (Dīgha Nikāya 8.1.304), the fame and renown of the Buddha, "there is no hundredth part of a sesame seed" (Jātaka 1.1.113), and "a handful of sesame seeds"—these and others are called relations of quality (*guṇasambandha*).
The lifting of a foot, the bending of a hand, the going or standing of elements (*dhātu*)—these and others are called relations of action (*kriyāsambandha*).
The abode of the Four Great Kings and so forth are called relations of location (*ṭhānasambandha*). By such methods as these, there is a relation of substance (*sāmisambandha*).
It has many thousands of subdivisions, yet because it lacks a connection with an action (*kriyā*), it is not called a "doer" (*kāraka*).
If this is so, does it not follow that the statement "the lifting of the foot," and so forth, is a connection with an action? It is said in reply:

the phrase "because it lacks a connection with an action" was spoken with reference to the absence of a connection in the sense of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*); however, there is a connection with an action that is already established (*siddha*).
It is said that the connection of action occurs through intentional implication (*sandhāya*).

However, in the case of a connection of diversity (*nānātta-sambandha*), the genitive case is used for various meanings. In this regard, after the suffixes *ṇī* and *āvī*, the genitive is invariably used for the object (*kamma*):

for example, "one who attains meditation" (*jhānassa lābhī*), "one who attains robes" (*cīvarassa lābhī*), "one who attains wealth" (*dhanassa lābhī*), or "one who sees the danger" (*ādīnavassa dassāvī*). There is [this rule].
One who sees forms, one who sees the even and the uneven, one who sees the forms of the stars,
and one who sees the moon and the sun.
When the suffixes *tu*, *aka*, *ana*, and *ṇa* are employed, the genitive case is used in some instances to express the object.

First, regarding the *tupacca* suffix: examples include “*tassa bhavanti vattāro*” (M. i. 2.173), “*sahasā kammassa kattāro*” (M. i. 1.203), “*bhinnānaṃ sandhātā*” (D. i. 9, 164), and “*sahitānaṃ vā anuppadātā*” (D. i. 9, 164), and so forth. What is the purpose of the word “*kvaci*” (in some cases)?
[It is to show: “*gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā*” (A. iv. 7.37), “*gādhaṃ kattā ovasitā*” (A. ii. 4.107).
"A timely discourse on the Dhamma was spoken by you; you remember having spoken such words; you rejoiced in the merit of others;
you awakened to the great Truths. (192) And so forth. In the case of the *aka* suffix:
"There is no doer of karma, nor is there an experiencer of its result" (Visuddhi 2.689); "one who does not deceive the world" (Dīgha Nikāya 1.9), and so forth. What is the meaning of "in some cases"?
For example: "the ruler of the great earth," "one who does not harm people," "one who makes a mat," "one who slaughters cattle," and so forth. [This applies] in the absence of the *an* prefix.

"The non-doing of evil is happiness" (Dhammapada 61), "the lifting up of a burden," "the grasping of the hand," "the touching of the hand," "the touching of a certain limb" (Pārājika 270), and so forth. What is the meaning of "in some instances"?
For example: "for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One" (Udāna 23), and so forth. [This applies] when the suffix *ṇa* is present.

It is wonderful that a washerman has the dyeing of clothes, a cowherd the milking of cows, or one of little merit the gaining of gains; likewise, the grasping of a hand or the receiving of a bowl, and so forth. Even with the suffix *tvā*, the genitive case is occasionally used for the object:

*nissāya* in the sense of "depending on" those who are shameless (*alajjīnaṃ nissāya*), "I shall go depending on the Venerable One" (*āyasmato nissāya vacchāmi*), or "the sensitive matter derived from the four great elements" (*catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo*; Dhs. 596–599 [upādāya]), and so forth.

However, when used in conjunction with the suffixes *-tu*, *-tavant*, *-tāvī*, and those ending in *-māna*, the second case (*dutiyā*) alone is employed for the object (*kamma*): *sukhakāmo vihāraṃ kato* (one desiring happiness built a monastery), *gāmaṃ gato* (he went to the village), *odanaṃ bhuttavā bhuttāvī* (having eaten rice, he is one who has eaten), *kammaṃ kurumāno* (performing work), *kammaṃ karonto* (doing work), and so forth.
In some instances, the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) is also seen: *dhammassa gutto medhāvī* (the wise man is a guardian of the Dhamma) [Dhp 257], and so forth.
For the verbal roots *sara*, *isu*, *cinta*, *isa*, and *daya*, the sixth case is optionally used for the object: *mātussa sarati* or *mātaraṃ sarati* (he remembers his mother).
He remembers his father, he remembers his father; you will not remember sovereignty, O King (Jā. 2.22.1721).
No one at all remembers them, for it is by the condition of karma that beings [act] (Pā. 7.2). He does not remember the limit of the offense, nor does he remember the limit of the night (Cūḷava.
157). He desires a son for his son, or he thinks of a mother for his mother, for the elder...
The meaning is: he entreats the elder, or he gives oil, or he protects.

In the case of the verbal root *kṛ*, which expresses the sense of "preparing," the sixth case (genitive) is used for the object, as in: *udakassa paṭikaroti* or *udakaṃ paṭikaroti*; *kaṇḍassa paṭikaroti* or *kaṇḍaṃ paṭikaroti*, and so forth.

When the suffix *-ta* is added, the sixth case is optionally used for the agent of roots expressing "honoring" and other such meanings, as in: *rañño sammato* or *raññā sammato*; *gāmassa...* [and so forth].
Whether honored by a village, or respected by a king, or revered by a king, or esteemed by a king (Dīgha Nikāya 1.303);
likewise, the Dhamma-element of the Buddhas is well-penetrated, and the Deathless has been partaken by those who have partaken of mindfulness directed to the body (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.603).
The Deathless has been missed by those for whom mindfulness directed to the body [is not cultivated].
Regarding the *viruddha* (contrary) [usage] at Aṭṭhasālinī 1.603:

even in the case of the three suffixes (*tipaccaya*), the genitive may sometimes be used for the agent (*kattari*), as in "the beautiful nature of Kaccāyana" (*sobhaṇā kaccāyanassa pakati*) or "by Kaccāyana" (*kaccāyanena*); or "the beautiful nature of Buddhaghosa" (*sobhaṇā buddhaghosassa pakati*) or "by Buddhaghosa" (*buddhaghosena*), and so forth.

Furthermore, the genitive is used for the instrument (*karaṇe*) in the sense of honoring (*pūjana*) and filling (*pūraṇa*), as in "he honors the Buddha with flowers" (*pupphassa buddhaṃ pūjeti*) or "with flowers" (*pupphena*).
One offers fire with a ladle (*ghata*), or [offers] with a ladle; having filled a bowl with water, or [filled] with various kinds of impurity (Dīghanikāya 2.377);

"The fool is filled with evil" (Dhammapada 121), "The wise man is filled with merit" (Dhammapada 121), or "filled with grain, or mung beans, or black gram," and so forth. Or it is the third case: "the lotus pond named Khemā."
It stands full of swans (*puṇṇā haṃsehi tiṭṭhati*).
However, in the case of connection with illness (*rujādiyoga*), the fourth case ending alone is used for the recipient (*sampadāna*):

"it must be complained against, it must be wailed, it must be cried out against the yakkha generals" (*yakkhasenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ vikkanditabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ*; Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā 3.283 [is dissimilar]), "Devadatta is ill," "he gives cloth to the washerman," and so forth.

In the case of words such as *bhaya* (fear), the genitive is frequently used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). For example: "Why indeed am I afraid of that pleasure? (*kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi*);
"All tremble at punishment, all fear death" (*sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno*, Dhp 129); "Frightened of the four venomous snakes" (*bhīto catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ*, Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.238);

“Shame regarding false speech” (musāvādassa ottapaṃ), Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.184, and so forth. In that context, “ottapaṃ” means being ashamed.
Likewise, “I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world,” Majjhima Nikāya 3.207, and so forth.
In the cases of *kusala*, *kovida*, and *pasāda*, the sixth case (genitive) is used in the sense of a support (*ādhāra*): “skilled in dancing and singing,” Jātaka 2.22.94; “skilled [in it].”
“You are [the master] of the major and minor parts of the chariot,” *Majjhima Nikāya* 2.87; “O dear one, know [these] ministers, wise and skilled in matters of state,” *Jātaka* 1.17.13;
“men skilled in the Dhamma,” *Jātaka* 1.1.37; “skilled in what is the path and what is not the path”; there is also the expression, “some are skilled in psychic powers.
There are *yakkhas* who have faith in the Buddha, *Dīgha Nikāya* 3.276 (variant reading); [faith] in the Dhamma.
"Faithful, faithful toward the Saṅgha, faithful toward the Buddha, faithful toward the Dhamma, or faithful toward the Saṅgha. Likewise:
"I am a master of the knowledge of others' minds, O Great Sage"; "I am a master of jhāna," and so forth. 321.
The sixth case ending occurs in the sense of cause (*hetu*), according to *Rū* 163, *Piṭṭha*; *Nī* 650; *Caṃ* 2.1.71; and *Pā* 2.3.26.
When joined with words having the sense of "cause" (*hetu*), the sixth case ending occurs in the sense of cause.

For what reason? (e.g., *taṃ kissa hetu* [Majjhima Nikāya 1.2]; *caṃ. 2.1.96*; *pā. 2.3.72*). Examples include: *aṅgavarassa hetu*, *udarassa hetu*, and *udarassa kāraṇā* (Pārājika 228), and so forth.
Alternatively, when used in the sense of "equality," the third case ending occurs (Nīti 638).
When used in connection with the sense of "equal" (*tulya*), the sixth case ending occurs, or optionally the third.
For example: *tulyo pitu pitarā vā* (equal to the father), *sadiso pitu pitarā vā* (similar to the father).

Thus ends the section on the relationship of diversity (*nānāttasambandha*). The so-called "relationship between action and factor" (*kriyākārakasambandha*) refers to the mutual expectancy among the factors of action (*kāraka*) by way of the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) and that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in relation to the action (*kriyā*).
Inseparable connection (avinābhāvitā) is what is meant; for indeed, no "agent" (kāraka) can be established without an "action" (kriyā), nor can an "action" be established without an "agent.
However, that [connection] does not fall within the scope of the genitive case.
The section on the genitive case endings is concluded.
The Heap of the Seventh Case: In what sense is the seventh case used? 323.
*Sattamyādhāre ka* (Pāṇini 2.3.36). [Referenced in: Rūp 313; Nī 630; Caṃ 2.1.88; Pā 1.3.45.

*Ādhāra*, *okāsa*, and *adhikaraṇa* are one in meaning; the locative case is used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāratthe*). That which intensely supports (*bhuso dhāreti*) an action together with its agent or object is a locus (*ādhāra*).

For example: "The man sits on the mat" (*kaṭe nisīdati puriso*), "He cooks rice in the pot" (*thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati*). Therein, the mat supports the act of sitting residing in the man who is the agent, and the pot supports the act of cooking residing in the rice which is the object.
This [locus] is fourfold: the pervasive locus (*byāpikādhāra*), the contiguous locus (*opasilesikādhāra*), the proximate locus (*sāmīpikādhāra*), and the metaphorical locus (*vesayikādhāra*).
In this context, that which remains pervading the entire or a portion of the receptacle is called "pervasive" (*byāpika*).
For example: oil remains in sesame seeds; juice remains in sugarcane; milk remains in water; and ghee remains in curds.
That which remains either by clinging to the receptacle or by merely being established within it—[is called "adherent"].
It is "that which is supported" (*opasilesika*). How so? Rice-scum remains in a mortar; water remains in jars; a monk sits on a seat;
a king lies upon a couch.

Furthermore, even when a thing that is the recipient (*ādheyya*) has not yet become its physical locus (*avatthubhūta*), it is designated as the "locus" (*ādhāra*) for the purpose of indicating that its existence is dependent upon that [recipient].
That is called "proximate" (sāmīpika). For example: "A sound stands on the Ganges," or "The Blessed One dwells in Sāvatthī" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.1).
Furthermore, that which is spoken of as a locus because, in the absence of the self, the thing to be contained would be unable to accomplish its action elsewhere;
and that which is spoken of as a locus for the purpose of indicating that the thing to be contained does not face toward anything other [than itself].
It is expressed thus; this is called "the manner of a courtesan. How so? "Birds fly in the sky, humans walk upon the earth, fish move in the water;
he worships the Blessed One at his feet, falls at his feet and weeps, the mind delights in evil" (Dhammapada 116);
"I have faith in the Buddha’s teaching" (Dhammapada 368).
324. *Nimitta* (The Locative Case on the Cause). [Ka. 310; Rū. 324; Nī. 641; Caṃ. 2.1.89; Pā. 2.3.36] That by which they mark or recognize is called a *nimitta* (cause/sign);
this is the name for a cause of recognition that exists either prior to or simultaneously with the object. In that *nimitta*, the locative case (*sattamī*) occurs. Examples include:

"The leopard is killed for its skins" (*dīpi cammesu haññate*); "The elephant is killed for its tusks" (*kuñjaro dantesu haññate*); "An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) in the case of lying" (*musāvāde pācittiyaṃ*); "An offense of expiation in the case of abusive speech" (*omasavāde pācittiyaṃ*), and so forth.
325. *Yambhāvo bhāvalakkhaṇaṃ* (Ka. 313; Rū. 327; Nī. 644; Caṃ. 2.1.90; Pā. 2.3.37; ‘yabbhāvo’ in many manuscripts). Whatever state that exists is *yambhāvo*;
it is called a *lakkhaṇaṃ* because by means of it something is characterized. A *bhāvalakkhaṇaṃ* is a characteristic of another state.
When whatever state serves as the characteristic of another state, the locative case (*sattamī*) is used for that state when it is understood, though the genitive (*chaṭṭhī*) is also seen.
Not long after Sāriputta had departed, the brahmin passed away... "While you dwell heedful, your harem will also dwell heedfully" (cf. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.129). "When this exists, that comes to be;

In some instances, the nominative case is also frequently seen: "While going, that Bhāradvāja saw the immortal seer" (Jātaka 2.22.2007: *addassa*). "While being sacrificed, the great king saw [him] on the mountain between the Sīda [rivers]" (Jātaka 2.22.566), and so forth.

Likewise: "It rains for him out of season, and it does not rain for him in season" (Ja 1.2.88; 1.8.48). "A hundred thousand aeons from now, the Leader appeared" (Ap Thera 2.54.28), and so forth.
326. The sixth case ending is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). (Kacc 305; Rūp 323; Nī 633; Cāndra 2.1.91; Pāṇini 2.3.38).

"Disregard" is a designation for the simultaneous occurrence of two characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and the actions characterized (*lakkhitabba-kiriyā*). When a characteristic state of disregard is implied, both the seventh and the sixth case endings are employed.

Here, the locative case of diversity (*nānāttasattamī*) is expressed.

The locative case in the sense of the object (*kamma*) is seen in: "They pay homage among the bhikkhus" (Pārājika 517); "Having kissed the son on the head"; "Having seized the man by various arms" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.63), and so forth.

Alternatively, in expressions such as “on the head” (*muddhani*) or “on the arms” (*bāhūsu*), the locative case denotes the locus (*ādhāra*) itself. How so? For example: “He cuts the tree at the root” (*rukkhaṃ mūle chindati*), “He cuts the tree at the trunk” (*rukkhaṃ khandhe chindati*), “He strikes the man on the head” (*purisaṃ sīse paharati*), “He worships the Blessed One at his feet” (*bhagavantaṃ pādesu vandati*).

The locative is also used for the instrument (*karaṇa*): “They wander for alms with their hands” (*hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti*), “They wander for alms with their bowls” (*pattesu piṇḍāya caranti*), “They go on the paths” (*pathesu gacchanti*), “May he also instruct me” (*so pi maṃ anusāseyya*), “I accept it upon my head” (*sampaṭicchāmi matthake*). The locative is also used for the recipient (*sampadāna*):
“When given to the Saṅgha, it is of great fruit” (*saṅghe dinne mahapphalaṃ*), “Gotamī, you should give to the Saṅgha” (*saṅghe gotamī dadeyyāsi*), “When given to the Saṅgha... (*saṅghe dinne*).
"I myself shall be honored" (Ma. Ni. 3.376). "Having discerned, a gift should be given; where it is given, it is of great fruit" (Pe. Va. 329).
Furthermore, in these cases, the locative case expressing the object (*visaya-sattamī*) is also appropriate.
There is also the locative case expressing the ablative (*apādāna*), as in: "They protect the elephants in the *gadali* trees," and so forth.

In the case of the *sāmi*, *issara*, and other [terms] used in conjunction [with a noun], the sixth and seventh cases occur: *gunnaṃ sāmi* (the owner of the cows), *gosu sāmi*; *gunnaṃ issaro* (the lord of the cows), *gosu issaro*;
*gunnaṃ adhipati* (the master of the cows), *gosu adhipati*; *gunnaṃ dāyādo* (the heir of the cows), *gosu dāyādo*; *gunnaṃ sakkhi* (the witness of the cows), *gosu sakkhi*;
*gunnaṃ patibhū* (the surety of the cows), *gosu patibhū*; *gunnaṃ pasuto* (the one devoted to the cows), *gosu pasuto*; [or] *āyutto kaṭakaraṇassa* (appointed for the making of a mat).

Regarding "appointed for the making of a mat," among these relations, the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) is used for the [direct] relation, while the seventh case (*sattamī*) is used for the object-domain (*visaya*) and the locus (*ādhāra*).

In "faithful in knowledge" and "striving for knowledge," the seventh case is used for the object-domain and the locus. In "faithful by means of knowledge" and "striving by means of knowledge," the third case (*tatiyā*) is used for the instrument (*karaṇa*).
328. When the seventh case is used in the sense of "in addition to" (*adhikye*), Kaccāyana-vutti 314; Rūpasiddhi 328; Niddesa 645; Cāndra-vyākaraṇa 2.1.60; Pāṇini 2.3.9; 1.4.87.
When the sense is that of "excess," the seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *upa*. For example:

*upakhāriyaṃ doṇo* (a *doṇa* measure is in excess of a *khārī*), *upanikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ* (a *kahāpaṇa* coin is in excess of a *nikkha*). What is meant is: "a *khārī* exceeds a *doṇa*" and "a *nikkha* exceeds a *kahāpaṇa*. 329.
[The suffix] *caṃ* is added when expressing lordship (*sāmitta*) or possession (*edhitā*). (Aṭṭhakathā 2.1.61; Pāṇini 2.3.9; 1.4.97).
When joined with *adhi* in the sense of lordship (*sāmibhāva*), the seventh case ending occurs after a noun stem.
For example: *adhi brahmadatte pañcālā*, *adhi pañcālesu brahmadatto*, *adhi devesu buddho*.
Regarding these, they explain that in the phrase *adhi brahmadatte pañcālā*, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Pañcāla are under the sovereignty of Brahmadatta; thus, "Pañcāla" refers to the people.

Or, the plural number [is used] for the names of countries (*janapada*); the meaning is that sometimes King Brahmadatta is the lord over the King of Kāsi, and sometimes Brahmadatta is the lord over the King of Pañcāla.

When joined with words expressing cause (hetvattha), all case endings occur after all pronouns.

The Section on Compounds (Samāsakaṇḍa)
Now, the formation of a single conceptual unity (*ekatthībhāva*) among words ending in case-suffixes that have been properly joined is being discussed.
Here, "single conceptual unity" refers to a compound (*samāsa*). That compound is sixfold: *abyayībhāva*, *tappurisa*, *kammadhāraya*, *digu*, *bahubbīhi*, and *dvanda*.
First, the *abyayībhāva* compound.
Therein, the *abyayībhāva* compound is explained first. "Byaya" means change; that which has no change (*byaya*) is "abyaya. Because it exists as something unchanging, it is called *abyayībhāva*.
The meaning is that it exists without undergoing any morphological change (*rūpavikāra*) across various genders, case endings (*vibhatti*), and numbers.
What is intended is that it generally proceeds with a single form even through all genders, case endings, and numbers.

The term *abyaya* (indeclinable) applies specifically to prefixes (*upasagga*) and particles (*nipāta*). However, this [compound] base itself is not inherently an indeclinable; it becomes an indeclinable by virtue of having a single referent (*ekatthata*) with numerals (*asaṅkhyā*). Thus, because even that which is not an indeclinable becomes an indeclinable, it is called *abyayībhāva*. 331.
When [words] beginning with *si* [the locative case ending] are combined with [words] beginning with *si*, there is a single referent (*ekattha*). (Ka. 316; Rū. 331; Nī. 675; Caṃ. 2.2.1; Pā. 2.1.4.)

This is the governing rule (*adhikārasutta*). A *syādi* word is a word ending in a *syādi* suffix; by the phrase "by a *syādi* [word]," it means by a word ending in a *syādi* suffix. That which has a single meaning is *ekattha*; the meaning is that a *syādi* word becomes *ekattha* (having a single meaning) together with a *syādi* word.

And here, by the mention of "*syādi*," all nominal words (*nāmikapada*)—including prefixes (*upasagga*) and particles (*nipāta*)—as well as those that resemble nouns (*nāmapaṭirūpaka*), are included, while words ending in *tyādi* suffixes are excluded.
Among these, those called "resembling nouns" are such as *yevāvanakadhammā* and so forth. Likewise, [it includes] those having the nature of technical terms (*saññā-sadda*).

In examples such as *pattāni* (“bowls”), *atthipaccayo* (“presence-condition”), *natthipaccayo* (“absence-condition”), *atthikhīrā brāhmaṇī* (“a Brahmin woman who has milk”), *aññāsikoṇḍañño* (“Koṇḍañña who knows another”), and *makkhaligosālo* (“Makkhali Gosāla”),
the words *atthi* and so forth [function as the governing term].

By the phrase “having a single meaning” (*ekattha*), it is stated that even in a *dvanda* compound, there is a state of having a single meaning for the constituent members by virtue of their having a single agent, a single object, and so forth.

332. *Asaṅkhyam* [is used] in the senses of case-ending (*vibhatti*), perfection (*sampatti*), proximity (*samīpa*), totality (*sākalya*), absence (*abhāva*), sequence (*yathāpacchā*), and simultaneity (*yugapad*). (Kacc 319; Rūp 330; Nī 696; Cāndra 2.2.2; Pāṇini 2.1.6).

The term *asaṅkhya* is called both a prepositional word (*upasaggapada*) and an indeclinable word (*nipātapada*). Both of these are called *asaṅkhya* because they are devoid of morphological change (*rūpavikāra*) in dependence upon the numbers one (*ekatta*) and many (*bahutta*).
It is used in the sense of a case-ending, in the sense of perfection, in the sense of proximity, and so forth.
The indeclinable termed *asaṅkhyam* (innumerable), which occurs in the senses of totality, absence,

"according as," "afterwards," and "simultaneously," becomes identical in meaning with another nominal word when combined with it. This compound is called both “*asaṅkhyo*” and “*abyayībhāvo*” by virtue of its etymological derivation (*anvatthavasena*).
Regarding the sense of the case endings (*vibhattiatthe*) first: *adhitthi*. Here, [the base] *adhi* is present; by the rule "of all [prefixes] except *asaṅkhyā*," there is elision (*lopa*).
From the feminine suffix *su*, the phrase becomes *adhi-itthīsu*. And when explaining its meaning, because it is a compulsory compound (*niccasamāsa*), it is expressed by another word.
A compound (*viggaha*) should be formed as "a discourse occurring regarding women," or "the path of speech occurring regarding women," or "speech occurring regarding women.

From that, by means of the preceding sutta, there is the designation of "single meaning" (*ekattha-saññā*); by this [present] sutta, the designation of "innumerable single meanings" (*asaṅkhyekattha-saññā*) is also effected.
Once the designation of single meaning has been established, the meaning of the case-endings (*vibhatti*) employed for the sake of the sentence-meaning [is understood].
When [a word] is expressed by a single-meaning compound (*ekatthapada*), then the case endings (*vibhatti*) are said to have their meaning already expressed (*vuttattha*).
Now, because those whose meanings are already expressed do not require further application, he states the rule for their elision (*lopa*). 333.
*Ekatthatāyaṃ* (In the state of having a single meaning). *Ka.* 316; *Rū.* 331; *Nī.* 675; *Caṃ.* 2.1.39; *Pā.* 2.4.71; 1.2.45, 46.

Those things which have a single meaning are "ekaatthāni. Here, by the word *attha* (meaning/object), one should understand specifically the primary object (*padhānattha*) that is to be predicated in relation to other words as the agent, the object, and so forth.

For instance, in the expression "king’s son" (*rājaputta*), it is only the meaning of the word *putta* (son) that is thus predicated, not the meaning of the word *rāja* (king). And every verbal expression consists precisely of such objects to be predicated.
It is established, and not otherwise, because the term ‘rājaputto’ (prince) is the name for the referent of the word *putta* alone, and not for the referent of the word *rāja*.
Therefore, only one primary referent, that of the word *putta*, constitutes the meaning of those two words, and not the referent of the word *rāja*.
The state of having a single referent is *ekatthatā*; thus it is said: “the state of being of a single referent” (*ekatthībhāvo*).
It exists. That [compound] is threefold: a *samāsa*, a *taddhita*, and that which ends in a verbal root (*dhātu*) or an affix (*paccaya*).

In this threefold [category], there is the elision of all case-endings (*syādi-vibhatti*) whose meanings have already been expressed by the state of having a single referent (*ekatthatā*); by this rule, the elision of the suffix *su* occurs. However, because of the governing principle of "generally" (*bahulādhikāra*), a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*) is also seen.

By the rule "That which is called *asaṅkhyā*, having a single referent, is neuter," the word *adhitthi* is assigned the status of a neuter noun; from that, the generation of the *syādi* (case-endings) follows.
335. *Syādīsu rasso* (Ka. 342; Rū. 337; Nī. 734; Caṃ. 2.2.84; Pā. 1.2.47). [In the case of] the *syādi* [endings], [the final vowel becomes] short.
"Before the neuter singular [ending], there is a short vowel in the case-endings beginning with *si*. By this rule, the long vowel *ī* becomes short.
336. *Pubbasāmādito ka*. (Kaṭantavibhaṅga 343; Rūpasiddhi 338; Niddesa 375; Cāndra 2.1.40; Pāṇini 1.1.41).
That which begins with *pubba* and *āma* is called a compound where the meaning of the first member (*pubbapada*) is predominant, namely an *asaṅkhyasamāsa*; from that, all subsequent [rules apply].
There is elision of the case endings (*vibhatti*); and by the word "etc. (*ādi*) here, the nominative case (*paṭhamāvibhatti*) is also included.
Alternatively, the term *amādi* refers to the *tappurisa* compound; that which precedes it is called the *asaṅkhyasamāsa*.

Thus, when an *asaṅkhya* compound consisting of a single meaning stands prior to the [terminations] beginning with *am*, there is elision of all subsequent case endings. By this rule, there is elision of all case endings from the word *adhitthi*.

*Adhitthi tiṭṭhati*: the meaning is that the discourse occurring among women stands. *Adhitthi tiṭṭhanti*: the meaning is that the discourses occurring among women stand. This same method applies to the remaining cases, the remaining words, and the remaining genders.
Thus, in all genders, all cases, and all numbers, it stands in one and the same form; therefore—
This compound is called an *abyayībhāva* because it is devoid of modification of form (*rūpavikāra*).

And here, the "meaning of a case ending" (*vibhatyattha*) refers to the bare meaning of the case endings, as in "adhitthi," "bahigāmaṃ," "uparigaṅgaṃ," and so forth, which are devoid of specific meanings such as "presence" (*sampatti*) and the like.
However, in the analytical statement (*viggaha*), [the words] are "kathā" and "pavattā."
Phrases such as these, understood through the power of compounding (*samāsa*), are called *atthapada*; they are also referred to as *atthapadāni* with the prefix *adhi*.
Thus, we have *adhikumāri*, *adhivadhu*, *adhijambu*, and so forth.

Regarding the meaning "a phenomenon (*dhamma*) that occurs within oneself" or "that which causes occurrence," when the case endings (*vibhatti*) are elided, the word *adhiatta* is treated as neuter; from that, the suffixes beginning with *si* (*syādi*) arise. Then, when the elision of the *syādi* suffixes applies according to the rule "from the preceding [word] ending in a vowel" (*pubbasmāmādito*)—
337. Not after the fifth case-ending. (Ka. 341; Rū. 336; Nī. 733; Caṃ. 2.1.41; Pā. 2.4.83; Mu. 4.3.374).
After a word ending in *a* that does not denote a number, there is no elision of any case-ending; instead, the suffix *am* is substituted for all case-endings except the fifth.
Example: *ajjhattaṃ dhammo jāyati*, *ajjhattaṃ dhammā jāyanti*; *ajjhattaṃ dhammaṃ passati*, *ajjhattaṃ dhamme passanti*.
What is meant by *apañcamiyā*? [Examples are: *ajjhattā apeti*, *ajjhattehi apeti*. 338.
*Vā tatiyāsattamīnaṃ ka.* (Kaccāyana-vutti 336; Nyāsa 733; Candra 2.1.42; Pāṇini 2.4.84; Moggallāna 4.3.375).
After a word ending in *a* that does not denote a number or a single entity, the suffix *aṃ* optionally occurs in place of the third and seventh case endings.
It functions internally by way of a phenomenon, or [it functions] internally; it functions internally by way of phenomena, or [it functions] internally;
it gives to an internal phenomenon, or it gives to internal phenomena; it departs from an internal phenomenon, or it departs from internal phenomena;
it belongs to an internal phenomenon, or it belongs to internal phenomena; internally...
“He abides in phenomena internally” means he abides in internal phenomena or among internal things.

Here, the meaning should be understood as “internal phenomenon” (*ajjhattaṃ dhammo*) meaning a phenomenon that has become internal, and “internal phenomena” (*ajjhattaṃ dhammā*) meaning phenomena that have become internal, and so forth.
Even when it is said that [the mind] “occurs with reference to the self” (*attānaṃ adhikicca pavatto*) or “occurs having made the self its object,” [it refers to the self].
The state of being a basis is indeed established. Thus, *adhicitta* (higher mind) refers to that which occurs individually within oneself, or to those occurrences that are individual (*paccatta*).

And here, there is a reading in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā* (350) and the *Saṃyutta-nikāya-aṭṭhakathā* (2.2.32): "Having focused inwardly, one emerges inwardly; having focused outwardly, one emerges inwardly. Therefore...

On the fifth [day], it should be understood that there is a limited occurrence of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*). There is a reading in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Tikamātikā (Dhs. Tikamātikā) stating, "internal states, external states";
therefore, an alternative formulation is also available for the first and subsequent [categories].
In the sense of attainment—
“Perfectly endowed with Brahma, together with Brahma”—here, “Veda” is called “Brahma. And in this context, by the rule *sahassa sakatthassā*, there is the substitution of *sa* for the word *saha*;
“subhikkhaṃ” means the abundance of alms (*bhikkhānaṃ samiddhi*), where the shortening of the neuter form is effected by the rule *syādīsu rasso*.

In the sense of proximity: *nagarassa samīpaṃ* is *upanagaraṃ* (near the city); *kumbhassa samīpaṃ* is *upakumbhaṃ* (near the jar); *maṇikāya samīpaṃ* is *upamaṇikaṃ* (near the water-pot); *vadhuyā samīpaṃ* is *upavadhu* (near the bride); *gunnaṃ samīpaṃ* is *upagu* (near the cattle)—wherein, by the rule "gossū," *ossa* becomes *utta*.
In the sense of totality:
The meaning is that he swallows the entire thing together with the grass, the whole site together with the grass; this is a substitution (*sādeso*) for the word *saha*.
Regarding the absence (*abhāve*): the absence of flies is "flyless" (*nimmakkhikaṃ*); the absence of distress is "distress-free" (*niddarathaṃ*); the absence of alms is...
The prefix *du-* also has the sense of "absence" or "non-existence. For example: *dussīlo*, *duppañño*.

Furthermore, in the grammatical treatises (*saddabyākaraṇa*), explanations of meaning such as "perfectly sublime" (*sampannaṃ brahma*) are merely for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of the word.
However, in the discourses (*suttanta*), one should understand the appropriate denotative meaning of these terms and provide an explanation of the meaning accordingly.
Regarding the meaning of the word *yathā*:
"suitable" (*yogga*) means appropriate to the intrinsic nature of form; "individual" (*paccatta*) means occurring in dependence upon each respective self;
"fortnightly" (*anvaḍḍhamāsa*) means following every half-month; "house-to-house" (*anughara*) means following from house to house; "yearly" (*anuvassa*) means [following] year after year.
Following along year by year (*anugataṃ anuvassaṃ*); according to seniority, in successive order from the eldest to the next eldest (*jeṭṭhānaṃ anupubbaṃ anujeṭṭhaṃ*);

in accordance with one’s capability, as far as one’s strength permits (*sattiyā anurūpaṃ yathāsatti*, *balassa anurūpaṃ yathābalaṃ*); in accordance with the sequence, step by step (*kamassa anurūpaṃ yathākkamaṃ*). Thus [it is] according to enumeration (*yathāsaṅkhyaṃ*) and according to what is obtained (*yathālābhaṃ*).
Against the current of the stream, upstream (*sotassa paṭilomaṃ paṭisotaṃ*), against the wind (*paṭivātaṃ*), and against the sound (*paṭisaddaṃ*).
In the case of *pacchāpadatthe*:
"Behind the chariot" means *anurathaṃ* (following the chariot).
The meaning of "foot" (*pada*) here is equivalent to "yoke" (*yuga*); thus, *yugapadattha* is a name for two co-existent meanings. In that context, by the fruit of the thunderbolt...

*Sacakka* means a wheel that moves together with [something else]. They also say that for Vāsudeva, the *cakrāyudha* (discus-weapon) moves as a pair along with the *gadāyudha* (mace-weapon). According to the *Moggallāna-vutti*, place *sacakka* in the sense of "simultaneously":
*sacakkaṃ* means "hold simultaneously with the discus" (*mugdhabodhavutti*). O Viṣṇu! Hold the mace simultaneously, at one and the same time, together with the discus.

Regarding the word *yathā* when not used in the sense of equality: *ka.* 319; *rū.* 330; *nī.* 696; *caṃ.* 2.2.3; *pā.* 2.1.7.

When the word *yathā* occurs in a sense other than equality, it becomes one in meaning with the case endings beginning with *si* (the nominative). In the *Moggallāna*, its usage in other senses has been demonstrated.

According to capacity (*yathāsatti*), according to strength (*yathābala*), according to sequence (*yathākkama*), whichever elders there may be, according to seniority (*yathāvuḍḍha*), or in the order of seniority for those who are elders.
What is not equal (*natulya*)? For example: "As Devadatta, so Yaññadatta. 340.
*Yāva* [is used] in the sense of limitation (*avadhāraṇe*). (Kacc 319; Rūp 330; Nīruttippakaraṇa 696; Candra-vyākaraṇa 2.2.4; Pāṇini 2.1.8).

*Avadhāraṇa* is said to mean delimitation (*paricchindana*). The word *yāva*, when occurring in the sense of delimitation, becomes synonymous with *syādi* [the suffixes *sya*, etc., i.e., the genitive].

*Yattako attho vattatīti yāvadatthaṃ*: "as much as the purpose extends" is *yāvadatthaṃ*; here, the augment *d* is inserted. *Yattako jīvo vattatīti yāvajīvaṃ*: "as long as life extends" is *yāvajīvaṃ*. *Yattakaṃ āyu vattatīti yāvatāyukaṃ*: "as long as the lifespan extends" is *yāvatāyukaṃ*. Here, the letters *t* and *k* are augments. 341.

*Parāpābahitiropurepacchā vā pañcamyā ka.* (Kaccāyana 319; Rūpasiddhi 330; Niddesa 696; Cāndra 2.2.7; Pāṇini 2.1.12, 13; 'payyapā... in many manuscripts). [This rule prescribes the suffix *ka* after words such as *para*, *apa*, *bahi*, *iti*, *ro*, *pure*, and *pacchā* when used with the fifth case ending.]
The words *pari*, *apa*, *ādi*, and so forth, optionally become co-referential (*ekattha*) with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) along with a form such as *si* (the nominative singular).
For example: *pabbatato pari samantā vassati devo paripabbataṃ paripabbatā vā*; the meaning is "the god rains all around the mountain" or "having excluded the mountain.
Similarly, *pabbatato bahiddhā apapabbataṃ apapabbatā vā*; [and] "outside of Pāṭaliputta."
*Vassī* means "rain"; *āpāṭaliputtaṃ* or *āpāṭaliputtā* [means "as far as Pāṭaliputta"]. *Ākumārehi* [means] "the fame of Kaccāyana extends even to children," thus it is *ākumāraṃ* or *ākumārā*.
"The fame of the Blessed One extends up to the peak of existence" (*ābhavagga*), thus it is *ābhavaggaṃ* or *ābhavaggā*.

"The going for refuge extends to the very limit of life" (*āpāṇakoṭiyā*), thus it is *āpāṇakoṭikaṃ*; this is the suffix *-ka*. *Bahigāmaṃ* [means] "outside the village," [from] *bahigāmaṃ* or *bahigāmā*.
Or likewise outside the city, outside the cave; from a mountain, across [to] another mountain, or from one mountain [to] another;
likewise across a rampart, across a wall. And here, “across” (tiro) refers to the far side. Before the meal, prior to the meal, or from before the meal (purebhattaṃ, purebhattā);
before dawn, prior to dawn, or from before dawn (purāruṇaṃ, purāruṇā); after the meal, subsequent to the meal, or from after the meal (pacchābhattaṃ, pacchābhattā).
The word *anu*, when used in the sense of proximity (*samīpa*) or extension (*āyāma*), optionally forms a compound with words ending in the locative case (*syādi*) to express a single meaning.

Examples: *vanassa samīpaṃ anuvanaṃ* (near the forest), *asani anuvanaṃ gatā* (the thunderbolt went along the forest); *gaṅgaṃ anuyātā anugaṅgaṃ* (having gone along the Ganges), [referring to] Bārāṇasī.

343. *Ora*, *pari*, *paṭi*, *pāre*, *majjhe*, *heṭṭhā*, *uddha*, *adhonto* [take] the sixth case (*chaṭṭhiyā*) [and form a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix]. (Ka. 319; Rū. 330; Nī. 696; Caṃ. 2.2.11; Pā. 2.1.18; ‘orepari…’ [in many texts]).
Words beginning with *ora* optionally become one in meaning (*ekattha*) with a word ending in the sixth case, such as those beginning with *si*.
Here, in the words *ora*, *pāre*, and *majjhe*, the vowel *e* is substituted by the rule *tadaminādīni*; thus: *gaṅgāya oraṃ* becomes *oregaṅgaṃ*.
From one peak to the next higher peak. Likewise, from the upper palace to the upper palace, from the upper bedchamber to the upper bedchamber, from the upper mountain to the upper mountain;

against the current, upstream. Likewise, with the wind at the back, across the Yamunā from this bank to that bank, in the middle of the Gaṅgā from one side to the other, below the palace to the lower palace, to the lower bedchamber, above the Gaṅgā from this side to the other side.
*Adhogangam* means "downstream from the Ganges"; *antopāsādam* means "inside the palace. Likewise, *antogāmam*, *antonagaram*, and *antovassam*.
Why [is the word] *anta-* used? [Examples include:
*gangāoram* ("the bank of the Ganges") and *majjhesamuddasmiṃ* ("in the middle of the ocean"), etc. 344. *Tiṭṭhagvādīni* (Ka. 319; Rū. 330; Nī. 697; Caṃ. 2.2.10; Pā. 2.1.17).
Words such as *tiṭṭhagu* and others are established in the sense of an indeclinable compound (*asaṅkhyekattha*).
The time during which cows stand is *tiṭṭhagu*; the time during which cows carry [loads] is *vahagu*.
By the rule "of *go*, *ossu*," the *o* is changed to *u*. The time when barley will come in the future is *āyatiyavo*; the time when barley is in the threshing floor is *khaleyavaṃ*.
In the first member [of the compound], there is the elision of the case-ending (*vibhattialopa*). "At the time when the barley has been reaped" is *lunayavaṃ*;
here, "reaped" (*lunā*) means having been caused to be reaped (*lāvitā*), as in *luyamānayavaṃ* ("at the time when the barley is being reaped"), and so forth.

Likewise, "at the time when bathing occurs in the morning" is *pātanahānaṃ*. Similarly, *sāyanahānaṃ* ("bathing in the evening"). "The time for performing work in the morning" is *pāto kammakaraṇakālo*.
*Yasmiṃ pāto kālo*: that in which it is morning time. Likewise, *sāyakālaṃ*. *Pāto vassati megho yasmiṃ*: that in which the cloud rains in the morning;
thus, *pātameghaṃ*. Likewise, *sāyameghaṃ*. *Pāto gantabbo maggo yasmiṃ*: that in which the path is to be traveled in the morning; thus, *pātamaggaṃ*. Likewise, *sāyamaggaṃ*, and so forth.

By the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), the word *pāta-* becomes *pāta-*. And here, compounds such as *tiṭṭhagu* and others are formed in the sense of a different referent (*aññapadattha*) by way of their analytical meaning (*viggaha*).
They appear as if they were established [words], yet there is no modification of their form according to the gender and other properties of another word;
therefore, because they are indeclinable (abyaya-rūpa), they are included here. All of this is called an "innumerable compound" (asaṅkhyasamāsa-pada) and is exclusively neuter;
it ends only in a short vowel. Furthermore, from a stem ending in *a*, the suffix *am* frequently occurs for all case endings, while elision (*lopa*) occurs after stems ending in *i*, *u*, or *ū*.
The abyayībhāva compound is finished.
The tappurisa compound:
Dative tappurisa.
Now, the *amādi-samāsa* (compound beginning with *am*) is discussed; it is also called *tappurisa*. A person (*puriso*) [belonging] to that [thing denoted by the first member] is a *tappurisa*;
because this compound is similar to the word *tappurisa*, it is called *tappurisa*.
For just as the word *tappurisa* itself, having abandoned the meaning of the qualifying term (*visesana-pada*), remains in the sense of the qualified term (*visesya-pada*), so too does this compound.

A word ending in a *syādi* suffix that is joined with a case ending beginning with *am* becomes a single meaning when combined with another word ending in a *syādi* suffix having the nominative case (*paṭhamanta*).
This compound is called both an "amādi-compound" and a "tappurisa-compound" according to its literal sense (*anvattha-vasena*). By this—

Having assigned the technical designation *ekattha* (single-meaning) to a compound consisting of an initial member (*amādi*) followed by another word, there is the elision of the case endings of the expressed meanings;
thereafter, the case suffixes beginning with *si* (the nominative) arise after the single-meaning word.
Furthermore, that compound is a *tappurisa*: a second-case *tappurisa*, a third-case *tappurisa*, a fourth-case *tappurisa*, or a fifth-case *tappurisa*.

The tappurisa compound is sixfold: the genitive tappurisa and the locative tappurisa. Each of these is further twofold, being either a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*) or a non-permanent compound (*aniccasamāsa*), and either a compound with elision (*luttasamāsa*) or a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*).
Among these, the accusative tappurisa occurs when words expressing the agent are followed by such terms as *gata*, *nissita*, *atīta*, *atikkanta*, *patta*, *āpanna*, and so forth.

"Gone to a village" means having gone to a village (*gāmagato*) or one who has gone to a village (*gāmaṃ gato*). Likewise, "gone to the forest" (*araññagato*), "gone to the ground" (*bhūmigato*), and "dependent on a king" (*rājanissito*).
Likewise, "dependent on the meaning" (*atthanissito*), "dependent on the Dhamma" (*dhammanissito*). "Transcended existence" (*bhavātīto*) means one who has transcended existence.

Likewise, "transcended fear" (*bhayātīto*), "transcended time" (*kālātīto*), "transcended the moment" (*khaṇātīto*), "exceeded the measure" (*pamāṇātikkanto*), and "attained happiness" (*sukhappatto*).

Thus, one who has encountered suffering is "one who has entered the stream" (*sotāpanna*). Likewise, one who has attained cessation is "one who has entered the path of the journey" (*addhānamaggappaṭipanna*);
one who has climbed a tree is "one who has climbed a tree" (*rukkhārūḷha*); one who has climbed a chariot is "one who has climbed a chariot" (*rathārūḷha*);
and one who has crossed the flood is "one who has crossed the flood" (*oghātīṇṇa*) or "one who has crossed the flood" (*oghantiṇṇa*), and so forth.

However, with *kitanta* compounds formed by means of verbal roots (*kamma-upapada*), there is always a fixed compound (*nicca-samāsa*). For example: one who makes a pot is a "pot-maker" (*kumbhakāra*);
a "chariot-maker" (*rathakāra*); one who takes a bowl is a "bowl-taker" (*pattaggāha*); one who desires welfare is a "welfare-desirer" (*atthakāma*); a "dharma-desirer" (*dhammakāma*);

one who upholds the discipline is a "discipline-bearer" (*vinayadhara*); a "dharma-bearer" (*dhammadhara*); one who lives the holy life through virtue is a "holy-liver" (*brahmacārī*); [one who has reached] the further shore of existence...

One who goes by means of virtue is "one who has gone to the further shore of existence" (*bhavapāragū*). One who knows all is "omniscient" (*sabbaññū*), as in "knower of meaning" (*atthaññū*) and "knower of the Dhamma" (*dhammaññū*), and so forth.

Due to the governing rule of abundance (*bahulādhikārattā*), there is no compound formation when followed by the suffixes *ta*, *tavantu*, *tāvī*, *anta*, *māna*, *tuna*, *tvāna*, *tvā*, *tuṃ*, and *tave*. For example:
*vassaṃ vuttho* (one who has spent the rains retreat), *odanaṃ bhutto* (one who has eaten rice), *odanaṃ bhuttavā* (having eaten rice), *odanaṃ bhuttāvī* (having eaten rice).
*suṇanto dhammaṃ*, *suṇamāno dhammaṃ*, *sotuṃ dhammaṃ*, *sutvā dhammaṃ*, *sutvā dhammaṃ*, *sotuṃ dhammaṃ*, *sotave dhammaṃ*.
Thus ends the second type of tappurisa compound.

The Third Tatpurusa Compound: A third tatpurusa compound occurs when the first member is one of the following: (1) among words expressing an object (*kamma-vācaka*) ending in the past participle suffix *-ita*; (2) among words such as *sampanna*, *sahagata*, etc.; (3) among words such as *pubba*, *sadisa*, *sama*, *ūna*, *kalaha*, *nipuṇa*, *missaka*, *sakhila*, etc., where the second member has a sense of deficiency;
and (4) when followed by other words. For example: *buddhena bhāsito* = *buddha-bhāsito*. Likewise: *buddha-desito*, *buddha-paññatto*, *buddha-rakkhito*.
Praised by the Teacher is *satthuvaṇṇita*; censured by the wise is *viññugarahita*; disapproved of by the wise is *viññupasattha*.
Made by Īśvara is *issarakata*; made by oneself is *sayaṃkata*; made by others is *paraṃkata* (with the addition of the suffix *-bindu*).
Brought by parrots is *sukāhaṭa*; killed by the king is *rājahata*; afflicted by disease is *rogapīḷita*; burnt by fire is *aggidaḍḍha*.
One bitten by a snake is "snake-bitten"; one pierced by an arrow is "arrow-pierced"; one overcome and subdued by desire is "overcome by desire. One endowed with virtue is "virtuous.
Likewise: accompanied by pleasure; associated with knowledge; association with friends; union with the beloved;
separation from the beloved; blind from birth is "born-blind"; deficient in qualities; increased in qualities; [the compound] consisting of four parts.

A formal act to be performed by the Saṅgha is one to be performed by a quorum of four; likewise, there are those to be performed by a quorum of five. *Kākapeyyā* means "drinkable by crows," as in the case of a river.

In compounds consisting of single syllables, there is always a compound when the following word begins with a consonant: for example, "one who goes on his belly" is *uraga* (a snake), and "one who drinks with its feet" is *pādapa* (a tree), and so forth.
In some cases, there is elision of the middle member: rice mixed with molasses is *guḷodana*; likewise, *khīrodana* (rice with milk). Similarly, [there is] "yoked with a horse."
A chariot with horses is an *assaratha*. Likewise, a chariot with thoroughbreds is an *ājaññaratha*; consciousness associated with the path is *maggacitta*;
the island known by the Jambu tree is *Jambudīpa*; ten plus one is eleven, and so forth. Regarding words such as *pubba* (first):
"first of the month" is *māsapubba*; "equal to the mother" is *mātusadisa*. Likewise, *mātusama* (equal to the mother), *pitusama* (equal to the father).
