Twenty minus one is nineteen; deficient in virtue is "vicious"; a quarrel with a sword is a "sword-quarrel"; skillful in speech is "eloquent in speech.
Likewise, mixed with what is only for the time being; harsh in speech; like the Teacher, "resembling the Teacher";
having need of merit is "one seeking merit"; desiring merit is "one desirous of merit. Likewise, one seeking a superior state, one seeking something of great value.
"Superior by virtue" (*guṇena adhiko*), "one superior in virtue" (*guṇādhiko*), and so forth.

Due to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikārā*), in some cases there is no compound: for example, "cut with an axe" (*pharasunā chinnaṃ*), "to be abandoned by crows" (*kākehi pātabbā*), "states to be abandoned by seeing" (*dassanena pahātabbā dhammā*), "states to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanāya pahātabbā dhammā*), and so forth.
Thus ends the third-case tappurisa compound.
The Fourth Tatpurusa Compound:

A fourth tatpurusa compound occurs when [the first member] stands in the sense of the fourth case (dative), or when it stands before words such as *attha* (purpose/benefit), *hita* (beneficial), or *deyya* (to be given).
For example: *kathinassa dussaṃ* = *kathinadussaṃ*, meaning "cloth brought for the sake of the kaṭhina. Likewise, *kathinacīvaraṃ*.
"Kathināya dussaṃ" (cloth for the kaṭhina) and "kathināya cīvaraṃ" (robe for the kaṭhina) are both appropriate; the meaning is "for the purpose of the kaṭhina-spreading.

"Cīvarāya dussaṃ" is "cīvaradussaṃ" (cloth for a robe). Likewise, "cīvaramūlaṃ" and "cīvaramūlyaṃ" (the price/value of a robe). "Saṅghassa ābhaṭaṃ bhattaṃ" is "saṅghabhattaṃ" (food brought for the Saṅgha), or food prepared for the sake of the Saṅgha is "saṅghabhattaṃ.
Similarly, there are "āgantukabhattaṃ" (food for guests), "gamikabhattaṃ" (food for those departing), and "gilānabhattaṃ" (food for the sick).
The welfare of the Saṅgha is *saṅghattha*; the benefit of the world is *lokahita*; what is to be given to the Buddha is *buddhadeyya*;
homage to the Buddha is *buddhappaṇāma*. Thus, the praise of the Buddha, the service to the Buddha, and that which is in accordance with the Sutta is *suttānuloma*.
Likewise, that which conforms to the Sutta, is favorable to the Sutta, and is consistent with the Sutta; and that which is worthy of the occasion is *ṭhānāraha*.
“Worthy of a king” means fit for a king. Likewise, “fit for a king,” “to be given by a king. “Desires to do” means one who wishes to do;

likewise, one who wishes to go, one who wishes to speak, one who wishes to see, or one who wishes to hear. In this context, because the suffix *tum* is not a numeral, the rule “after numerals, [the case ending] of all [words]” applies, whereby there is always the elision of the fourth case ending (*catutthī*).
Once the compound is formed, there is also always the elision of the *niggahīta*. [Thus: “of the Saṅgha.”
In such expressions as “it should be given,” “to give to the Saṅgha,” and so forth, there is no compound.
Thus ends the fourth-case tappurisa.
Now, the fifth-case tappurisa.
The *pañcamī-tappurisa* compound occurs with other words in the sense of departing (*apagamana*), fear (*bhaya*), abstention (*virati*), release (*mocanā*), and so forth.
For example: "one who has departed from sexual intercourse" is *methunāpeta*; "one who has gone away from envy" is *palāsāpagata*; "one who has gone out from the city" is *nagaraniggata*;
"one who has returned from alms-round" is *piṇḍapātappaṭikkanta*. Likewise, [there is] *gāmanikkhanta* ("one who has departed from the village").

"Fallen from a tree" (*rukkhapatita*); "fallen from the teaching" (*sāsanacuta*) means one who has lapsed from the dispensation; "emergence from an offense" (*āpattivuṭṭhāna*); "risen above water" (*udakuggata*) means emerged from water;

"escaped from existence" (*bhavanissaṭa*) means escaped from becoming; "escaped from the inclusion within the aggregates" (*khandhasaṅgahanissaṭa*) means escaped from being comprised within the aggregates;
"frightened of a thief" (*corabhīta*) means afraid of a thief; "timid of evil" (*pāpabhīruka*) means one who fears evil because of his virtue; "disgusted by evil."
"By virtue" means one who loathes evil; "disgusted with the round of existence" means one who has become weary of the cycle of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*);
"abstinence from bodily misconduct" means refraining from bodily misconduct. Likewise for abstinence from verbal misconduct. "Released from bondage" means freed from bonds.
Thus it is "release from bondage. "Arising from karma" means produced by karma. Thus it is "born of karma," "originated from karma."
Born of karma, he is the foremost in the world, the world-foremost (*lokagga*). Thus he is the eldest in the world, the supreme in the world;
the eldest of all, the all-eldest (*sabbajeṭṭha*); the youngest of all, the all-youngest (*sabbakaniṭṭha*). Likewise, he is the lowest of all, the last of all;
superior among the superior, thus "superior-superior" (*ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭha*); inferior among the inferior, thus "inferior-inferior" (*omakomaka*).
In some cases, there is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*): born from a mother is *mātuja*. Likewise, *pituja*, *kammaja*, *cittaja*, *utuja*, and so forth.
Thus ends the genitive tappurisa compound.
Now, the genitive tappurisa [compound].
The son of a king is a *rājaputta*. Likewise: a king’s man (*rājapurisa*); a disciple of the Buddha (*buddhasāvaka*);
the sound of the ocean (*samuddaghosa*); a heap of grain is a *dhaññarāsi*; a bowl made of clay is a *mattikāpatto*, where the genitive case indicates a relationship of transformation;
the meaning is "a bowl consisting of clay. Similarly: a golden basin (*suvaṇṇakaṭāha*); a golden vessel (*suvaṇṇabhājana*); a dish for drinking water is a *pānīyathālaka*.
In the middle of a compound, *ī* and *ū* are frequently shortened: *daṇḍino kulaṃ* becomes *daṇḍikulaṃ*;
*hatthipadaṃ*, *itthirūpaṃ*, *nadikūlaṃ*, *naditīraṃ*, *bhikkhunīnaṃ saṅgho* becomes *bhikkhunisaṅgho*, *jambuyā sākhā* becomes *jambusākhā*, and so forth.

There is no compound with words ending in the suffixes *-anta*, *-māna*, nor with words having the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇiya*), completion (*pūraṇa*), abstract state (*bhāva*), or satiety (*suhitattha*); for example: *mamaṃ anukubbanto*.
"Following my example, among cows, the black ones possess the highest quality of milk. However, when the sixth case ending is analyzed separately, it occurs as follows:
"The best of men is the supreme man (naruttama), the most excellent man (naraseṭṭha), the foremost man (naravara); the best of groups is the supreme group (gaṇuttama);
the best of bipeds is the supreme biped (dvipaduttama)," and so forth. Also: "the fifth disciple among disciples," "the third part of an eon (kappa)," "of a fortnight (pakkha)."
The eighth [case]: the whiteness of cloth, the lightness of form, the malleability of form, the wieldiness of form.

In some instances there is lightness of body, lightness of mind, the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha, the perfect nature of the Dhamma, the satisfaction of the fruits, the satiety of the fruits, the contentment of the fruits;
here the sixth case is used in the sense of the instrument.
In the expression “The soldier is the king’s son, [the son] of Devadatta,” the compound *rājaputta* (“king’s son”) does not occur because there is no mutual expectation (*aññamaññānapekkhattā*).
In the expression “Devadatta’s black teeth,” the compound *devadattakaṇhadantā* does not occur because of dependence on another (*aññasāpekkhattā*).
Nevertheless, even when there is dependence on another, a compound always occurs for words that inherently expect a correlative, just as in a sentence.
Because the relationship [of dependence] is understood even in a compound (*samāsa*). And it has been said:
"Even though there is expectancy (*sāpekkhatta*), a compound occurs because it is expressive" (Ka. 328; Rū. 352; Nī. 691), as in *devadattagurukulaṃ*, *rājadāsīputto*, *devadāsīputto*, and so forth.
In that context, the analysis (*viggaha*) is: *devadattassa guru* is *devadattaguru*; his family (*kula*) is *devadattagurukulaṃ*.
“Guru’s family” is *gurukula*; they also say that “Devadatta’s guru’s family” is *devadattagurukula*.
In the expression “the son of King Bimbisāra of Magadha,” because it depends on another [word], the form *bimbisāraputta* does not occur;
rather, in the sense of “the king’s cow, horse, and man,” the form *rājagavassapurisā* occurs due to the elision of the first member (*pubbapada*) from a *dvanda* compound.
Because the connection is understood with each member individually even in a *dvanda* compound; likewise, it applies to the word following the *dvanda*:
"charioteer of men and gods" (*narānañ ca devānañ ca sārathi*, *naradevasārathi*).
Thus is the genitive *tappurisa*.

In a genitive tappurisa compound, "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*) means perception regarding form. And here, because grammatical factors (*kāraka*) are characterized by accomplishing an action, their connection occurs only with verbal expressions;
therefore, when a compound is formed with a subsequent word that does not denote an action, [the following applies].

In the middle, a corresponding verb is understood, as in “a chariot yoked with a horse” (*assaratha*), which means “a chariot [yoked] by a horse,” or “perception regarding forms” (*rūpe saññā*), which means “perception arisen in regard to forms.
“Consciousness in the eye” is “eye-consciousness” (*cakkhuviññāṇa*); “delighting in the Dhamma” is “one who delights in the Dhamma” (*dhammarata*).

Likewise, “delight in the Dhamma” (*dhammaruci*), “reverence for the Dhamma” (*dhammagārava*), and “an inclination toward giving” is “inclination for giving” (*dānajjhāsaya*). Likewise, “resoluteness upon giving” (*dānādhimutti*).
*Vaṭṭe bhayam* is *vaṭṭabhayaṃ*, meaning the suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). A pig in a village is a *gāmasūkaro*; a wild buffalo; a fish in the ocean.
A rogue among women is an *itthidhutto*, one who is addicted to women.

In compounds where the second member is a *kita-anta* (ending in *-ka*), there is always a compound (according to Pāṇini 2.2.18). One who wanders in the forest is a *vanacaro*; one who dwells in the realm of sense-desire is a *kāmāvacaro*. In the womb...

One who lies in a womb is a *kucchisaya*; one who lies in a womb is a *gabbhasaya*. One who stands on dry land is a *thalaṭṭha*; likewise, a *jalaṭṭha* (one standing in water) and a *pabbataṭṭha* (one standing on a mountain).

That which is born in mud is a *paṅkaja*. In this same way, there are terms such as *atrāja* (born of the womb) and *khetraja* (born of the field), and so forth. Here, however, it is not [the case that] "nī" [applies]; for example:

moderation in eating (*bhojane mattaññutā*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties (*indriyesu guttadvāro*), sitting on a seat (*āsane nisinno*), and that which is to be sat upon in a seat (*āsane nisīditabbaṃ*).
Thus ends the seventh section on the tappurisa compound.
Regarding elided tappurisas,
there is in some instances a reversal [of the order of members] according to the Mahāvuttisutta on tappurisa compounds.

"Upstream of the Ganges," "downstream of the river," "within the monastery," "within meditative attainment," "the king of swans, a royal swan, or a swan-king," "half of a month, a half-month," "half of a kahāpaṇa, a half-kahāpaṇa," "half a month," "half of the night, a half-night.
Likewise: "the first part of the night," "the latter part of the night," "one's own part. "The front portion of the body."
*pubbakāyo* (former body), *parakāyo* (other body), *ahassa pubbo* (the morning of the day), *pubbaṇho*, *majjhaṇho*, *sāyanho*, *pubbediṭṭho* (previously seen), *diṭṭhapubbo* (formerly seen),
"the Elder has seen the Tathāgata," "the Tathāgata has been seen by the Elder," and so forth.
Thus ends the elided tappurisa compound.
The Non-elided Tatpurusa:
Now the non-elided tatpurusa compounds are being explained.
Dīpaṅkara, Pabhaṅkara, Amataṇḍada, Purindada, Vessantara, Attantapa, Parantapa, Raṇañjaha.
*Jutindharo*, *vijjāndharo*, a phenomenon to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena pahātabba-dhammo*), born from that, born from this, born from here,
appearance as fear (*bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ*), karma performed (*kaṭattā-kammaṃ*), matter produced by karma (*kaṭattā-rūpaṃ*), the word for another (*parassa-padaṃ*), the word for oneself (*attanopadaṃ*),

the lord of the gods (*devānamindo*), Tissa, beloved of the gods (*devānaṃ-piya-tisso*), the elder Gavampati, past abodes (*pubbenivāso*), beautiful in the middle (*majjhe-kalyāṇaṃ*), form at a distance (*dūre-rūpaṃ*).
Proximity-form (*santikerūpa*), remote cause (*dūrenidāna*), proximate cause (*santikenidāna*), pupil (*antevāsika*), son of Janasuta (*janesuto*), sexual misconduct (*kāmesumicchācāra*),
and so forth— see Kaṇḍa 327, Rūpasiddhi 351, Niddesa 686.
Thus ends the non-elided *tappurisa* compound.
And this entire *amāditappurisa* compound denotes its referent and takes the gender of the subsequent word.
The *amāditappurisa* is finished.
[Now begins] the *kammadhāraya* compound.
Now, the first type of tappurisa compound, known as *kammadhāraya*, is explained.
It is called *kammadhāraya* because it "bears two things like an action" (*kamma*).
Just as an action bears a twofold nature—both the act itself and its purpose—for when there is an action, those two are possible; likewise, this compound bears two meanings for a single referent.
"Names are maintained when this compound exists, because two names that indicate a single meaning can occur"—this is from Ka.
Furthermore, "that which is to be done" is *kamma*; "that which is to be maintained" is *dhāriya*. Since it is both *kamma* and *dhāriya*, it is a *kammadhāriya* (descriptive compound).
Whatever beneficial action there may be, because it resembles the term *kammadhāraya*, this entire compound is called a *kammadhāraya* by way of applying the suffix *-issa*.
For just as the word *kammadhāraya* bears two names for a single meaning, so too does this compound.
That very [compound] is characterized as a *tappurisa* by the definition of a *tappurisa*, which consists in the predominance of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*).

Because it is joined [with another word], it is called a *tappurisa*. The occurrence of two words—which possess distinct bases for their application—in a single referent through the relationship of qualifier (*visesana*) and qualified (*visesitabba*), is known as *tulyādhikaraṇa* (co-referentiality).
Because it is joined with that characteristic of co-referentiality, it is called a *tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa* (co-referential compound).
And that very same [compound] is also [called] a *visesanapada* (qualifier-word), because it illuminates a specific quality (*guṇavisesa*).
It is also called a *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (attributive compound). In that *viśeṣaṇasamāsa*: 346.
*Viśeṣaṇam ekatthena ka.* (Pāṇini 2.1.57; Kaccāyana 2.2.18; Rūpasiddhi 339; Nyāsa 702;

Cāndra 2.2.18) A word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) which functions as an attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) enters into a state of unity (*ekattha*) with a word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) which functions as the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
And here, *visesanaṃ* (qualification) is that by which a substance (*dabbaṃ*) is distinguished or made specific. That which has one meaning is *ekatthaṃ* (having one meaning);
"one" (*eko*) means identical, and "meaning" (*attho*) refers to the denoted object or the causal object.
That very [object] is also called the "locus" (*adhikaraṇaṃ*) in the sense of being the basis for two operative causes. And of those operative causes...

When there is a state of being determined (*adhiṭṭhānatte*), the state of being determined also holds for the words themselves; thus, "having a single meaning" (*ekattha*) means having a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), which is what is meant by "having a common locus" (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
By that "single meaning," [the compound is formed]. The phrase "it becomes a single meaning" (*ekatthaṃ hoti*) means it has become a single-meaning unit (*ekatthībhūta*).

And that compound is of nine kinds: that which has a qualifier as the first member (*visesanapubbapada*), that which has a qualifier as the final member (*visesanuttarapada*), that which has qualifiers as both members (*visesanobhayapada*), and that which has a comparison as the final member (*upamānuttarapada*).

[These are: those preceded by a term of esteem (*sambhāvanā*), those preceded by a term of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), those preceded by the particle *na*, those preceded by the particle *ku*, and those preceded by *pa*.
Among these, what is an example of one preceded by a qualifying attribute (*visesanapubbapada*)? "A Great Man" (*mahāpuriso*), "a great river" (*mahānadī*), "great fear" (*mahabbhayaṃ*).
And here: "That army appeared great" (Jātaka 2.22.771); "The kingdom of Bārāṇasī is indeed great" (Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā 1.1, commentary on the Mahāsīlava Jātaka).
The Pāli text is seen. Therefore, even in a compound, the word *mahā* is appropriate as an indeclinable (*nipāta*) form in all three genders.
Thus: *mahā ca so puriso ca* = *mahāpuriso*; *mahā ca sā nadī ca* = *mahānadī*;
*mahā ca taṃ bhayañca* = *mahabbhayaṃ*, with the doubling of the consonant in the conjunction and the shortening of the vowel. To show the sentence using the synonym *mahanta* for the word *mahā*:
It is appropriate [to analyze them as follows]: "a great man" is a *mahāpurisa*, "a great river" is a *mahānadī*, and "great fear" is *mahabbhaya*.
Furthermore, it is appropriate to demonstrate them by completing the compounds with the word *ca* ("and"): "he is both great and a man" thus he is a *mahāpurisa*;
"it is both great and a river" thus it is a *mahānadī*; "it is both great and that fear" thus it is *mahabbhaya*.
Alternatively, the word *mahanta* becomes *mahā*. According to the rule “*ṭa ntantūnaṃ*,” when a following word begins with a suffix, the entire *nta* is replaced by *atta*;
furthermore, by the general rule (*mahāvutti*), the vowel is lengthened.
Here, the two particles *ca* indicate the distinctness of meaning within each of the two words. By the word *taṃ*, even though there is a distinctness of meaning within its own scope—
The term *sakatthāna* indicates the unity of the material object that constitutes the subject of the grammatical derivation (*adhikaraṇa*).
In this system of grammar, there is no separate function for the formulation of word-forms;

rather, once the meaning and phonetic analysis of each established word are understood by observing the specific rules of the sūtras and the corresponding analytical statements (*viggaha-vākya*) presented therein, the function of formulating word-forms is thereby accomplished.
One who exists and is a good person (*sappurisa*) is a "good person," like a white elephant, a blue lotus, or red sandalwood.
Even when the gender markers differ, words may have the same meaning; for example: *vinaya* (the discipline) and that which is the *pariyatti* (the teaching/text) together form *vinayapariyatti*;
*vinaya* (the discipline) and that which is the *piṭaka* (basket) together form *vinayapiṭaka*; and *avijjā* (ignorance) and that which is the *paccaya* (condition) together form *avijjāpaccaya*.

Ignorance and that which is an obscuration is "the obscuration of ignorance" (*avijjānīvaraṇa*). Likewise, womanhood and that which is a jewel is "the woman-jewel" (*itthiratana*); virtue and that which is a quality is "the quality of virtue" (*sīlaguṇa*);
virtue and that which is a foundation is "the foundation of virtue" (*sīlapatiṭṭhā*), and so forth.
Similarly, twenty and those who are men are "twenty men" (*vīsatipurisa*); a hundred and those who are men are "a hundred men" (*satapurisa*).

"Formations (*saṅkhārā*) and they are the condition (*paccayo*)" thus it is "conditioned by formations" (*saṅkhārapaccayo*); "the Aṅgas and they are the country (*janapada*)" thus it is "the country of Aṅga" (*aṅgajanapada*);
"Magadha and it is the kingdom (*raṭṭha*)" thus it is "the kingdom of Magadha" (*magadharaṭṭha*). Likewise, "the kingdom of Kāsi," and so forth.
Here, the suffix *rū* does not occur [in these cases], as in: Puṇṇa Mantāṇīputta, Citta the householder, Sakka the king of gods, Brahmā Sahampati, and so forth.
In some cases there is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*), such as *kaṇhasappo* (black snake) and *lohitamālaṃ* (red garland), and so forth.

What is an example of a compound with a qualifying word as the final member (*visesanuttarapada*)? For instance: *Sāriputtatthero* (the Elder Sāriputta), *Buddhaghosācariyo* (the Teacher Buddhaghosa), or *Ācariyaguttilo* (the Teacher Guttila); *Mahosadhapaṇḍito* (the Wise Mahosadha); *purisuttamo* (the supreme person), *purisavaro* (the excellent person), *purisaviseso* (the distinguished person), and so forth.

What is an example of a compound with a qualifying word as both members (*visesanobhayapada*)? For instance: that which was cut and has grown back is *chinnaparūḷhaṃ*; that which is cold and hot is... [sītuṇhaṃ].
"Cold and heat" [is a compound]; "lame and humpbacked" is *khañjakhujjo*. Likewise, "blind and deaf" is *andhabadhiro*; "done and not done" is *katākataṃ*;
"with holes and without holes" is *chiddāvachiddaṃ*; "cut and split" is *chinnabhinnaṃ*; "sprinkled and well-smeared" is *sittasammaṭṭhaṃ*.

The state of being real (*santa*) is "truth" (*sacca*); "suffering" in the sense of insecurity and "truth" in the sense of being non-erroneous is "the truth of suffering" (*dukkhasaccaṃ*), and so forth.

What is the category of the simile as the first member of the compound (*upamānuttarapada*)? For example: "like a lion" is *sīho viya*, thus he is a lion; and since he is both a sage (*muni*) and a lion, he is the "Sage-Lion" (*munisīha*). In the same way:

the "Bull among Sages" (*munipuṅgava*), the "Naga of a Buddha" (*buddhanāga*), the "Sun of a Buddha" (*buddhādicca*); "like a ray" is *raṃsi viya*, thus it is a ray; and since it is both the True Dharma (*saddhamma*) and a ray, it is the "Ray of the True Dharma" (*saddhammaraṃsi*). Likewise:
the "Ocean of Discipline" (*vinayasāgara*), the "Lotus of a Recluse" (*samaṇapaduma*), the "White Lotus of a Recluse" (*samaṇapuṇḍarīka*), and so forth.
What is an example of a compound with *sambhāvanā* as the prior member? "Being a cause and being a condition, it is a 'cause-condition' (*hetupaccaya*).

Likewise: "object-condition" (*ārammaṇapaccaya*); "become a human," "become a deity"; "reckoned as a phenomenon" (*dhamma*), thus "reckoned as a phenomenon" (*dhammasaṅkhāta*), "regarded as a phenomenon" (*dhammasammata*), "perceived as a phenomenon" (*dhammasaññita*), "characterized as a phenomenon" (*dhammalakkhita*);
"the word reckoned as 'thus'," thus "the word 'thus'" (*evasadda*). Likewise: "the word 'and'" (*casadda*), "the word 'or'" (*vāsadda*), "become noble" (*ariyabhūta*).
The Saṅgha is the Noble Saṅgha. Likewise for "Buddha-muni," "Pacceka-muni," and so forth.
Herein, "appreciation" (sambhāvanā) means praising by strengthening the general meaning of the subsequent word-component while indicating its specific nature;
the intention is that it does not merely indicate a quality. The Teachers, however, say: "Dhamma-intellection is 'dhammabuddhi. Likewise, 'dhamma-perception,' 'anicca-perception'..."
“Perception of elements,” “perception of mother,” “the state of perceiving a living being,” and “the view of self”—these and others are also cited here.

However, these are appropriate as examples of *paṭhamātappurisa* compounds with elided particles (*itilutta*), similar to the phrase “gone to, approached, or entered as a refuge” (*saraṇaṃ iti gato upagato saraṇaṅgato*);
thus [state] Rūpasiddhi 343 and Netti-ppakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā 702.

What is an example where the first member of the compound is a restrictive term (*avadhāraṇa*)? “Virtue alone is wealth, not gems, gold, and so forth” is *guṇadhana* (wealth of virtue). Likewise, *saddhādhana* (wealth of faith), *sīladhana* (wealth of virtue);

“the eye alone is the door, not the village gates and so forth” is *cakkhudvāra* (eye-door). Likewise, *cakkhuvatthu* (eye-base), *cakkhundriya* (eye-faculty), *cakkhāyatana* (eye-sphere), *cakkhudhātu* (eye-element);
“the aggregates alone are the burdens” is *khandhabhāra* (burden of the aggregates). And here, if in the sense of that which is to be borne...
"Burdens" (bhāra) may indeed exist; the five aggregates alone are what are called "burdens," not the burden of the head, the burden of the shoulder, and so forth.

For the aggregates are perpetual burdens, whereas the others are merely temporary and are rooted in the aggregates. Thus, the restrictive statement that "the aggregates alone are the burdens" is employed for the purpose of emphasizing their preeminence, not for the purpose of absolutely denying the status of being a burden to the burden of the head and so on.
Thus it is in all cases: ignorance alone is the stain, not the stain on bronze and so forth, hence "the stain of ignorance" (*avijjāmala*);

ignorance alone is the taint, not honey-taint and so forth, hence "the taint of ignorance" (*avijjāsava*). Likewise: the dart of craving (*taṇhāsalla*), the sword of wisdom (*paññāsattha*), the light of wisdom (*paññāloka*), the lamp of wisdom (*paññāpajjota*), the fire of lust (*rāgaggi*), the fire of hatred (*dosaggi*), the fire of delusion (*mohaggi*), and so on.
But the Teachers [say]: "It is like wealth, thus it is 'wealth' (*dhana*); faith alone is the wealth of the Noble Ones..."
They construe it thus: "Faith is the wealth; 'weapon' means like a weapon; wisdom itself is the weapon, thus 'wisdom-weapon'.
If this were so, the purpose of expressing excellence would not be achieved (Rūp 343; Nī 702, 347).
According to the rule *na-nipāta-pubba-pade na u* (Kacc 326; Rūp 341; Nī 707), [the *u* of *satthu* is not elided].

The suffix *ñā* is for the purpose of negation and the exclusion of other meanings. The word *naū*—ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*)—becomes a single syntactical unit (*ekattha*) with another word ending in a case-suffix.
By applying the technical designation *kattha* to *nañ* through this [rule], [the following applies]: **348. Ṭa naussa ka.** (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.65; Rūpasiddhi 344; Nyāsa 717; Candra-vyākaraṇa 2.2.20;

Pāṇini 2.2.6) "When the word *nau* follows as the second member of a compound (*uttarapada*), the letter *ṭa* is the suffix *anubandha* of the *a* [substituted] for the *na* of *naū*. Thus, the *na* is replaced by *a*.
“Neither a brahmin nor a non-brahmin. Here one might ask: is this a negation of what exists, or of what does not exist?
What of it? If it were a negation of what exists, then all those who are considered brahmins in the world would have to be called non-brahmins.
Therefore, [the Blessed One said]: “The people here are not brahmins; the people there are not brahmins,” and so forth.
A prohibition of a brahmin who exists in the world cannot be logically maintained without a restriction such as "this" (desa) and so forth;
yet, if it is a prohibition of one who does not exist in the world, then what is the purpose of prohibiting that which is non-existent, since the very object to be prohibited is itself non-existent?

It is said in reply: this is a prohibition by means of applying the designation [“brahmin”] to things similar to a brahmin and so forth. For instance, in the case of a non-brahmin who resembles a brahmin—
In some cases, the perception of "brahmin" becomes established, and in accordance with that perception, the conventional designation "brahmin" occurs in reference to that person.
This [sutta] is a negation of such a conventional designation of "brahmin" applied to one who is not a brahmin. How so?
In the world, among foolish people, a false conventional designation occurs precisely through the power of false perception, such as "form is the self," "feeling is the self," and so forth; for them—
In order to demonstrate that [notion] as a false state of being, a negation is applied: "Form is non-self, feeling is non-self" (Mahāva.

20), and so forth. By this much, it is established that even for the pure word *brāhmaṇa*, there is the possibility of its application to a sense similar to that [of the original], and it is established that the letter *na* is merely an indicator of that meaning.
And this being the case, [there arises] what is termed the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member [of the compound].
The characteristic of a *tappurisa* compound is not contradicted here; therefore, "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇo*) means one who resembles a Brahmin.
This same method applies to the senses of "other than that," "opposed to that," and "absence of that.
Among these, regarding the sense of "other than that":

Conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena: this is the dyad-matrix of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. And here, "unconditioned" means not conditioned; the meaning is that they are phenomena other than conditioned phenomena.
Its opposite—“unwholesome” (akusala)—means a phenomenon that is the antithesis of the wholesome (kusala).
In the absence of that—“neither having done nor not having done”; the meaning is that one is completely freed by means of doing.
There are two kinds of negation: absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and relative negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*).
In this context, *pasajjapaṭisedho* (prohibitive negation) is so called because it prohibits by attaching itself after having projected a meaning connected with its own [negating] term;

the negative particle (*na*) indicates the mere absence of that [projected meaning], which is to say, it is a negation of the mere action. Examples include: *akatvā*, *akātuṃ*, *akaronto*, *na karoti*, *na kātabbaṃ*, and so forth.

When, instead of remaining at the mere act of projecting, one seizes a portion of the surrounding area such as something similar to that [action] and negates the intended meaning in its absence—this is [the other type of negation].

*Payirudāsa* means "one who throws away" or "one who abandons"; it indicates something similar to that, meaning a negation of the substance (*dabbanirodha*). For example: *abrāhmaṇo* ("one who is not a brahmin"), and so forth.
Likewise, *asamaṇo*, *asakyaputtiyo*, *amitto*, and *mittadhammavidhuro*—this is the meaning.
349. *Ana sare ka*. (Kaccāyana 334; Rūpasiddhi 345; Niddesa 718; Cāndra 5.2.119; Pāṇini 6.3.105).
There is no success for one whose mind is wavering. One who is not noble is a non-noble;
the meaning is that he is turned away from the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. There is no dwelling, no non-dwelling; there is no lord, no non-lord.
There is no calamity, no non-calamity—“calamity” means a misfortune; there is no suitable means, no non-means; there is no wave, no non-wave; there is no suitable search.
"Improper seeking," "not appropriate," "opportunity," "non-opportunity," "not having transgressed," "not having exceeded," "without taking," "without looking," and so forth.
Due to the governing rule of frequent occurrence (*bahulādhikāra*), a compound is formed even with words that do not have a [grammatically] connected meaning (e.g., *ka* 336; *rū* 347; *nī* 689).
Furthermore, "that which is not to be sung again" is *apunageyyā*, [meaning] a verse (*gāthā*). "Not looking up at the moon" is *acandamullokikāni*, [meaning] faces. "Not seeing the sun" is... [etc.]
"Without seeing the sun," O princesses, means "not eating while there is faith" because of her virtue; thus, *asaddhabhojī*. Likewise, *alavaṇabhojī* (one who eats without salt).
"Not desiring welfare" means they do not wish for benefit; thus, *anatthakāmā*. Likewise, *ahitakāmā* (desiring harm). "Without having made an opportunity" means without having created an opening;
thus, *anokāsaṃkāretvā*. Likewise, *animittaṃkatvā* (without making a sign). "Going to the very root" means going to the fundamental source; thus, *amūlamūlaṃgantvā*, and so forth.
“*Punagāyitabba* means ‘to be sung again’; *apunageyya* means ‘not to be sung again. *Atthakāmā* means ‘desiring welfare’;

*anatthakāmā* means ‘not desiring welfare. Alternatively, that which is not welfare (*attha*) is non-welfare (*anattha*); those who desire non-welfare are ‘those desiring non-welfare’ (*anatthakāmā*).
When the sentence is construed in this way, the compounds are grammatically correct. However, the teachers [explain]: “Those who do not desire welfare, but rather non-welfare itself...”
“They desire what is not beneficial, thus they are ‘anatthakāmā’; they do not desire welfare but desire only harm, thus they are ‘ahitakāmā’;
they do not desire comfort but desire only discomfort, thus they are ‘aphāsukāmā’”—so they explained. This is a term consisting of two intended meanings (*dvādhippāyapada*).

Because it is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*) with the prefix *kun-* as the first member, the analysis is made with a different word: a small river is a *kunnadī*, a small pond is a *kusombha*, and a small forest is a *kuvana*.
When a word beginning with *sa* follows as the second member of a compound, the particle *ku-* becomes *kada* when it refers to the meaning of that second member.
*Kucchitaṃ annaṃ* = *kadannaṃ* (wretched food); *kucchitaṃ asanaṃ* = *kadasanaṃ* (wretched eating); *kucchito ariyo* = *kadariyo* (a wretched noble one, i.e., a miser).
What is excluded [by the particle *kiṃ*]? Bad sons, bad wives, bad slaves.
What is excluded in the sense of "superior" (*uttara*)? One who has a contemptible lip is a *kuoṭṭha*. 351.
Regarding the sense of "suitable" (*kāppa*), see Kaccāyana 336; Rūpasiddhi 347; Niddesa 720.
When the word *kum* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) and denotes a small quantity (*appattha*) of the thing expressed by that subsequent member, it optionally becomes *kā*.
For example: *appaṃ lavaṇaṃ* becomes *kālavaṇaṃ*; likewise, *kāpupphaṃ*.

Furthermore, compounds preceded by *pā-* are always fixed compounds (*niccasamāsa*): *pakaṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ* (excellent speech) becomes *pāvacanaṃ*, with the lengthening of the vowel; [likewise] *pakaṭṭhaṃ*...
Having offered, it is *nītaṃ*; having offered, it is *paṇītaṃ*. Having become preeminent, it is *dhānaṃ*; having become preeminent, it is *padhānaṃ*.
Likewise, *paṭṭhānaṃ*. Various thoughts are *vividhā mati*; lack of certainty is *vimati*. A superior deity is *adhidevo*; a doctrine that is excessive or distinguished is *abhidhammo*.
A beautiful fragrance is *sugandho*; a foul-smelling odor is *duggandho*. That which is beautifully done is *sukataṃ*; that which is badly done is *dukkataṃ*.
The opposite path is a wrong path (*uppatha*). Likewise, there are terms such as *ummagga* (wrong way), *uddhamma* (contrary to the Dhamma), and *ubbinaya* (contrary to the Vinaya).
This *kammadhāraya* compound is also expressive of its own meaning and takes the gender of the subsequent member.
The *kammadhāraya* compound is concluded.
The *Digu-samāsa*:
Now, the first type of *tappurisa* compound, known as *digu*, is explained.
Two cows is a *digu*; because it has a numeral as its prior member and possesses both neuter gender and singular number—being similar to the word *digu* itself—all such compounds are called *digu*.

In a compound expressing a collective sense (*samāhāra-ekattha*), a compound preceded by a numeral becomes neuter. Since the singular number is already established by the very term "collective" (*samāhāra*), [only the gender needs to be specified].

For example, *dve gāvo* (two cows) becomes *digu*; by the rule *gossū*, the *o* is changed to *u*, resulting in *dvigu*. Similarly, *tayo lokā* (three worlds) becomes *tilokaṃ*. [In the phrase] *tayo lokā ñāṇasmiṃ*...
"Triloka" means brought together and combined; "triloka" is the collection of the three worlds, or those three worlds themselves.

In this same way: *tibhava* (the three existences), *tipurisa* (the three persons), *timala* (the three stains), *tiratana* (the three jewels), and *tisso saññāyo* (the three perceptions)—in these cases, according to the rule "there is shortening in *si*, etc.," there is shortening [of the final vowel].
*Cattāro pathā* is *catuppatha*; *cattāri saccāni* is *catusacca*.
"Four directions" (*catasso disā*) becomes "the four directions" (*catuddisaṃ*).
In this same way, there are *pañcasikkhāpadaṃ*, *saḷāyatanaṃ*, *sattāhaṃ*, *aṭṭhapadaṃ*, *navalokuttaraṃ*, *dasasikkhāpadaṃ*, *satayojanaṃ*, *sahassayojanaṃ*, and so forth.
In this collective digu compound, everything is exclusively neuter, has a short final vowel, and is in the singular number.

In the case of non-compound *digu* (numeral compounds), according to Rūp 350, Nī 703, it is as follows: *eko puggalo* becomes *ekapuggalo*; *tayo bhavā* becomes *tibhavā*; *catasso disā* becomes *catuddisā*, and so forth.
However, in the place of numbers, according to Ka 392, Rūp 418, and Nī 831, *dve satāni* becomes *dvisataṃ*. Likewise:
*tisataṃ*, *catusataṃ*, *pañcasataṃ*, *chasataṃ*, *sattasataṃ*, *aṭṭhasataṃ*, *navasataṃ*, *dasasataṃ*, *dvisahassaṃ*.
Three thousand, four thousand, five thousand, ten thousand.

Two hundred thousand is "two-hundred-thousand. Likewise, one may say "three hundred thousand, four hundred thousand, five hundred thousand," or "two hundreds, two hundreds, three hundreds, three hundreds, four hundreds, four hundreds, two thousands."
The two pairs of words and phrases should be understood as follows: “two thousand,” “three thousand,” “three thousand,” “two hundred thousand,” and “two hundred thousand.
The same applies even to the term *satasahassa* (hundred thousand). Here it might be asked:

“Is not a *digu* compound only that which has a numeral as its first member, and in these cases, every word is a numeral? [The answer is: In a *digu* compound, the preceding member must indeed be a numeral; however, the subsequent member may be either a numeral or something else.
The *digusamāsa* (compound of direction) is finished.
Now the *bahubbīhisamāsa* (relative compound) is explained.
That place in which there are many rice-fields is a *bahubbīhi*; such a village, region, or province, because it resembles the word *bahubbīhi* itself, is called a *bahubbīhi* compound.

For just as the word *bahubbīhi* stands for the meanings of other words—such as "village," "region," or "province"—transcending the meaning of the compound itself, so too does this [type of] compound.
For a bahubbīhi compound has as its primary meaning another word (aññapadattha).
In brief, it is of two kinds: that which conveys the quality of that [other word] (tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa) and that which does not convey the quality of that [other word] (atagguṇasaṃviññāṇa).
In this context, "quality" (guṇa) refers to the subordinate meaning of the words in the compound; because it serves as an adjective for the other word's meaning, it is subordinate.
The word *tagguṇa* means "the quality (*guṇa*) of that (*tassa*) other referent (*aññapadattha*). That which is to be known (*viññātabba*) is "cognizable" (*viññāṇa*);
it refers to the other referent. When the other referent is not abandoned—that is, when the other referent is cognized together with its quality—it is called *tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*.
That which is not *tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa* is *ata-gguṇasaṃviññāṇa*, wherein the meaning of the compound is present either as a subordinate part (*avayavabhāvena*) or [as a whole].
Or, by virtue of its state of being subordinate, it is included within another word; that is what is known as *tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*.
How so? For example: "a man with a severed hand," "he gives alms-food to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha," "he has come with his sons and wife," and "prefixes such as *pa-* and *adhi-*."
And here, the phrase “he gives a meal to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha” means that he gives a meal both to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and to the Buddha who is the head;
it means he gives a meal to the Buddha who has become the leader.

The phrase “he has come with his sons and wife” means that the sons and wife have come, and the man has also come. Regarding the statement “the prefixes are the letters beginning with *pa*,” the letter *pa-*...

"Upasaggo" means "the prefixes beginning with *para* and so forth are called *upasaggas*. Thus, the state of being subject to modification by the meaning of another word (*aññapadattha*) along with the meaning of the compound word (*samāsapadattha*) is what is meant by "being capable of such construction.

How is there non-perception of its own quality (*atagguṇasaṃviññāṇo*)? For example: "The king, having given a bribe, gives a gift," or "He plows fields such as mountains," and so forth. In these cases, however, the meaning of the compound word is not subject to modification; rather, it is the meaning of the other word alone that is subject to modification.

The first type, the *paṭhamābahubbīhi* (plural compounds with the nominative case), is sevenfold: *paṭhamābahubbīhi*, *dutiyābahubbīhi*, *tatiyābahubbīhi*, *catutthībahubbīhi*, *pañcamībahubbīhi*, *chaṭṭhībahubbīhi*, and *sattamībahubbīhi*.

Among these, the *paṭhamābahubbīhi* is fivefold by way of having a preceding word (*pubbapada*) such as *saha* (with), having a preceding word that is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), having both members as numerals (*saṅkhyobhayapada*), expressing the meaning of an intermediate direction (*disantarāḷattha*), and characterized by reciprocal exchange (*byatihāra*).
In this regard—353. *Vānekamaññatthe* (Ka. 328; Rū. 352; Nī. 708):
A word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) that is not singular may optionally become singular in meaning when it is in apposition with another word.

“Accompanied by applied thought” (*savitakka*) means that which exists together with applied thought; or rather, it is “accompanied by applied thought” because it proceeds along with applied thought—this refers to concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, in this expression “accompanied by applied thought,” the external referent (*aññapadattha*), which constitutes the meaning of the first case ending, is established through the power of the sentence.
For indeed, a sentence devoid of action and agent is not possible. By this sutta, the word *saha* [is explained].
There is a state of identity (ekatthībhāva) between the words of the *vitakka* [compound] and the other word-meaning designated as "concentration" (*samādhi*).

And when there is this state of identity, all the meanings of the other words and their case-endings (*vibhatti*) standing within the sentence are said to be expressed by the compound through that single unified meaning;

thus, the other words and the case-endings are said to have their meanings already expressed (*vuttattha*), and because those whose meanings have been expressed are devoid of further meaning (*attharahita*).
There is no need for further grammatical operation; therefore, by the rule "ekatthatāyaṃ," there is the elision of the case endings.

Likewise, in all compounds, by the Mahāvutti-sutta, there is the elision of other words such as *ya*, *ta*, *eta*, *ima*, *iti*, *eva*, *iva*, *viya*, *ca*, *vā*, and so forth, which appear in the original sentence;
and when the case endings have been elided, [the forms of] compound words ending in vowels or consonants [are established].

The natural state [of the word] is itself; however, here, by the rule "the word *saha* has the sense of emptiness," the presence of the word *saha* is indicated, from which the case endings (*syādi*) arise:
*savitakko samādhi*, *savitakkā samādhayo*, *savitakkā paññā*, *savitakkā paññāyo*, *savitakkaṃ jhānaṃ*, *savitakkāni jhānāni*, and so forth, according to all genders, case endings, and numbers.
Having joined [the parts], the accomplishment of the method (payogasiddhi) should be understood.
What is an example where the preceding word is a comparison (upamānapubbapada)? Because his body is equal in measure to a fathom (vyāma), he is "round like a banyan tree" (nigrodhaparimaṇḍala);
or, he who is round like a banyan tree is "one who is round like a banyan tree" (nigrodhaparimaṇḍala)—such as a prince or a conch-shell.
Like a white conch shell, he is "white as a conch" (*saṅkhapaṇḍaro*); like a crow at dawn, he is "crow-dawn" (*kākasūro*);

because he causes sentient beings to obtain the eye of wisdom, he has become their eye, thus he is "become-eye" (*cakkhubhūto*); because he causes them to obtain the supramundane Dhamma, he has become their Dhamma, thus he is "become-Dhamma" (*dhammabhūto*);
because of his constant benevolence of heart, he has become like Brahmā, thus he is "become-Brahmā" (*brahmabhūto*); [and] blind...
"Having become like [something], they go; having become blind," and so forth.
What is a numeral as both members [of a compound]? "Two or three bowls" (*dvittippattā*);
here, the word *vā* itself is called a "different word" (*aññapada*), and their meaning, being indefinite, is called the "meaning of a different word. "Two days or three days" (*dvīhatīhaṃ*).
Six or five times by way of speech is "six-or-five-voiced" (*chappañcavācā*). Likewise for seven or eight months, one or two *yojanas*, and so forth.
How is the meaning of "intermediate direction" (*disantarāla*) [expressed]? That which is the intermediate space between the south and the east is "southeast" (*dakkhiṇapubbā*).
Likewise, "northeast" (*pubbuttarā*), "northwest" (*pacchimuttarā*), and "southwest" (*aparadakkhiṇā*); according to the great rule, there is shortening of the first member of the compound. South.
And since it is both "eastern" (*pubbā*) and "that" (*sā*), the *kammadhāraya* compound "southeast" (*dakkhiṇapubbā*) and so forth is also appropriate.
Regarding the definition of reciprocal exchange (byatihāra) at Ka. 328; Rū. 352; Nī. 708–354:
therein, having seized [the opponent] with that [weapon] and struck him, the form is identical in battle.

Taking a word ending in the seventh case (locative) or the third case (instrumental) that has the same form as a word ending in a *syādi* suffix, and having struck with it in battle, there is optionally a single meaning (*ekattha*) in relation to another word (*aññapadatthe*).
355. *Ṅi vītihāre ka*. 404; *rū*. 370:

When a reciprocal action (*kriyābyatihāre*) is implied within the scope of another word (*aññapadatthavisaye*), the suffix *ip* with *ṅ* as its *anubandha* occurs at the end of the word; here, the vowel *i* is short.
356. Ṅi smiṃ ca ka. 403; rū. 354.
When the suffix *vip* follows, the final vowel of the preceding word becomes long (*ātta*) when a following word begins with a consonant (*ka*). For example:

"Having seized each other by the hair, this battle proceeds" is *kesākesi*; "Having struck each other with sticks, this battle proceeds" is *daṇḍādaṇḍi*. Likewise, *muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi* (hand-to-hand) and *musalāmusali* (club-to-club).
Thus ends the first type of bahubbīhi compound.
Regarding the second type of bahubbīhi:

"The ascetics have come to this monastic park (saṅghārāma); that [monastic park] is the 'ascetic-arrived' (āgatasamaṇa) monastic park. Furthermore, in this context, the meaning of a compound word is twofold: the expressed meaning (vāccattha) and the denoted meaning (abhidheyyattha).

In this context, the "power of action" (kamma-satti) consisting of the state to be attained by the ascetics belonging to the monastic park (saṅghārāma) is called the "expressed meaning" (vāccattha). The monastic park, which possesses that power, is called the "denoted meaning" (abhidheyyattha).
Therein, the word "ascetic" (samaṇa), when it occurs [in the compound], expresses only the expressed meaning directly, not the denoted meaning.

What is meant is that upon hearing the phrase "an ascetic who has arrived," one understands merely the state to be attained by the ascetics, but does not understand the substance of the monastic park itself.

Therefore, its denoted meaning is expressed by another word, "saṅghārāma"; however, because the expressed meaning has already been stated directly by that [word], there is no need to state it again, and thus there is no function for the second case ending (accusative) to perform in expressing it.
Consequently, the occurrence of the second case ending is impossible in the word *saṅghārāma*; rather, the first case ending (nominative) applies to the mere sense of gender.
Thus it proceeds; furthermore, when there is a connection with another word, all case endings proceed from that [base] in such ways as:
"He sees the monastery and the arrived ascetic," "The village shines with the monastery and the arrived ascetic," and "He honors the monastery and the arrived ascetic.
This same method should be applied to all expressive words.

"Āgatasamaṇā Sāvatthī" means "Sāvatthī where recluses have arrived"; "āgatasamaṇaṃ Jetavanaṃ" means "Jetavana where recluses have arrived"; or alternatively, "āgatasamaṇo" refers to the monastery itself, meaning "where recluses have come.
"Ārūḷhavānaro" refers to the tree, meaning "the tree which monkeys have climbed. "Sampattagāmiko" refers to the village, meaning "the village which villagers have reached.
In the same way, there are compounds such as "paviṭṭhagāmiko" (the village entered).
Thus ends the second type of bahubbīhi compound.
Regarding the third type of bahubbīhi:

one by whom the sense-faculties (indriya) have been conquered is "one who has conquered the faculties" (jitindriya), namely, a recluse (samaṇa). One by whom the Dhamma of the Four Truths has been seen is "one who has seen the Dhamma" (diṭṭhadhamma).
Thus, one by whom the Dhamma has been attained, the Dhamma known, and the Dhamma fathomed;

one by whom the functions of the four paths have been performed is "one who has done what was to be done" (*kata-kicca*). When used in the plural, those by whom the duties have been performed are "those who have done what was to be done," namely, the Arahants. One by whom wealth has been acquired through the Dhamma is "a person who has acquired wealth by the Dhamma.
Likewise, there is "one who has acquired wealth by what is not the Dhamma" (*adhammādhigata-bhoga*). Thus [the suffix] is used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).

In the case of the instrumental [case], however, [a compound] such as *chinnarukkho* ("one by whom a tree has been cut")—meaning "a tree that has been cut by someone"—and *pharasu* ("an axe"), etc., are examples.
Thus ends the instrumental bahubbīhi compounds.
Now, the dative bahubbīhi compounds.
One to whom a tax has been given by a king is "one to whom tax has been given" (*dinnasunko*); one to whom food has been brought is "one to whom food has been brought" (*upanītabhojano*).
One who has no measure is "immeasurable" (*atulo*)—the change of the letter *na* to *ṭa* occurs according to the rule "ṭa nañssā.
One who has no counterpart is "without a counterpart" (*appaṭipuggalo*). One who has no virtue is "immoral" (*dussīlo*). One who has no wisdom of rebirth-linking is "unwise" (*duppañño*).
In the sutta “ghassantassāppadhānassa,” the vowel *ā* of the word *ghasañña* is shortened. One who has no virtue (*sīla*) is *nissīlo*;
one who has no wisdom (*paññā*) is *nippanno* or *apañño*. One whose face is deformed is *dummukho*. Similarly, *dummano* and *dubbaṇṇo*.
One for whom there is no superior or higher [person] is *anuttaro*; by the sutta “*ana sare*,” the *na* becomes *ana*.
In this context, what is called a "bahubbīhi compound with an external referent" (bāhiratthabahubbīhi) is as follows: one who has attained final nibbāna seven days ago is "seven-day-parinibbuta";
one who has attained final nibbāna not long ago is "not-long-ago-parinibbuta"; one who has been born for a month is "month-born" (māsajāta); one who has been born for two months is "two-month-born";
a king who has been consecrated for one month is "one-month-consecrated"; and one who has been dead for one day is "one-day-dead."
Thus, "one for whom it has been concealed for two days," "for three days," or "for one day" is *ekāhappaṭicchannā*.
Likewise, there is the offense of *dvīhappaṭicchannā*. "One who has gone a league" is *yojanagato*; likewise, *dviyojanagato*, and so forth.
Thus, these are genitive *bahubbīhi* compounds.
The fifth-case *bahubbīhi* compounds:

"People have departed from this village" is *niggatajano*; "the blackness has departed from it" is *apagatakāḷako*, as in *paṭo* (a cloth); "the cloth is free from blackness" is *apagatakāḷakaṃ vatthaṃ*. "That from which consciousness has departed" is *apetaviññāṇaṃ*, as in *matasarīraṃ* (a dead body), and so forth.
Thus ends the fifth-case *bahubbīhi*.
The sixth type of *bahubbīhi* compound:

"one whose hand is cut" (*chinnahattha*) is [analyzed as] "he whose hand is cut" (*yassa hattho chinno so*); "one in whom desire has arisen" (*jātachanda*) is [analyzed as] "desire has arisen in him" (*yassa chando jāto*);

"one in whom joy and gladness have arisen" (*sañjātapītisomanassa*) is [analyzed as] "joy and gladness have arisen in him" (*yassa pītisomanassaṃ sañjātaṃ*). These are examples of the sixth type of *bahubbīhi*.
"One whose virtue is pure" is *visuddhasīlo*; he is one purified in virtue (*sīlavisuddho*). "One whose body is great" is *mahākāyo*.
Here, it is called a compound with a preceding term of comparison (*upamānapubbapada*): "one whose complexion is like that of gold" is *suvaṇṇavaṇṇo*;
"one whose voice is like that of Brahmā" is *brahmassaro*; "one whose gait is like that of an elephant" is *nāgagati*. Likewise, *sīhagati* [is explained].
“Nāgavikkama” means the stride of an elephant; “sīhahanu” means one whose jaw is like that of a lion;
“eṇijaṅgha” means one whose shanks are like those of an antelope; “usabhakkhandha” means one whose shoulders are like those of a bull, and so forth.
“Rūpa” refers to intrinsic nature (sabhāva); thus, “yathārūpa” means having such a nature as this. Likewise for “tathārūpa” and “evaṃrūpa.”
*Assa* means "of such a kind"; there is an elision of the *bindu*. *Evamādi* means "having such as its beginning.
Similarly, *iccādi*, *iccevamādi*, and *itthannāmo*—meaning "one whose name is such"—and *evaṃnāmo*. *Kinnāmo* means "one whose name is of what kind?
In the expression *konāmo*, the word *kiṃ* becomes *ko* according to the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*).

"What is its origin? means "having what as its origin" (*kiṃsamudaya*). "What is its birth? means "of what kind of birth" (*kiṃjātiko*). "What is its source? means "having what as its source" (*kiṃnidāno*).
"How many years old is it? means "of how many years" (*kativasso*). "What is its purpose? means "a statement having what as its purpose" (*kimatthaṃ vacanaṃ*).
By the *Mahāvutti* rule, the word *kiṃ* becomes *kvattha* [when combined with *attha*]. "Having what kind of purpose" means "having such a purpose" (*yadattho*). "Such a one" means *tādiso*.

*Tad-attho* means "having that as its purpose. *Etadattho* means "the Vinaya which has such a purpose as this"; [this is] the Vinaya. *Etadatthā* refers to the discourse on the Vinaya (*vinayakathā*).
*Etadatthaṃ* refers to the application of the ear (*sotāvadhāna*), and so forth.
Thus ends the section on genitive *bahubbīhi* compounds.
A country in which crops are abundant is "sampannasassa"; a country in which alms-food is easily obtained is "subhikkha";
a country in which alms-food is difficult to obtain is "dubbhikkha"; and a country in which there are many villages is [described as] "bahugāma."
*Bahugāmo* (a village with many [people]). Likewise, *bahujano* (many people), *gāmo* (village). That forest in which there is no village-field is *agāmakaṃ* (without a village);

[the suffix] *-ka* occurs at the end of a compound. *Samanusso* (with humans) is that village in which humans exist; *amanusso* (without humans) is that village in which humans do not exist, and so forth.
Thus ends the seventh type of bahubbīhi compound.
Regarding the bahubbīhi with different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa-bahubbīhi*):

it is called "with different substrata" when [the members] do not share a common locus. For example: *ekarattivāso*, meaning "one whose dwelling is for a single night," where [the members] are joined together...
"Living together with people" is *samānavāsa* (co-resident). "Possessing both sets of sexual characteristics arising from both [karmic] actions" is *ubhatobyañjana*;
this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*). Likewise, "having a dark spot on the throat" is *kaṇṭhekāḷa*;
"having hair on the chest" is *urasiloma*; "one who has a bowl in his hand" is *pattahattha*. Similarly, *asihattha* (sword-in-hand) and *daṇḍahattha* (staff-in-hand).
One who has an umbrella in the hand is *chattapāṇi*. Likewise, *satthapāṇi*, *daṇḍapāṇi*, and *vajirapāṇi*. One whose inclination (*ajjhāsaya*) is toward giving is *dānajjhāsayo*;
one who is intent upon giving is *dānādhimuttiko*. One who has devotion (*bhatti*) toward the Buddhas is *buddhabhattiko*; one who has reverence (*gārava*) for the Buddhas is *buddhagāravo*;
"reverence for the Dhamma" (*dhammagāravo*), and so forth.
Regarding the three-word *bahubbīhi*:

that which is called a three-word *bahubbīhi* is as follows: those by whom prosperity has been attained through exertion are "those who have attained prosperity through exertion" (*parakkamādhigatasampadā*);

those by whom wealth has been attained through righteousness are "those who have attained wealth through righteousness" (*dhammādhigatabhogā*); he by whom the hand has been withdrawn from the bowl is "one who has withdrawn his hand from the bowl" (*oṇītapattapāṇi*).
"Having a body like the forepart of a lion" is *sīhapubbaddhakāyo*; "a forest in which there are many (*matta*) elephants (*bahumātaṅga*)" is *mattabahumātaṅgaṃ*, and so forth.
The *bahubbīhi* compound is concluded.
The *Dvandva* Compound:
Now the *dvanda-samāsa* is illustrated.

Two and two words are *dvandas*, or two and two meanings are *dvandas*; by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is the substitution of the term *dvanda* for the two occurrences of the word "two. Because it resembles the word *dvanda*, this entire compound is called *dvanda*.
Alternatively, *dvanda* is that wherein two members (*avayava*) are joined (*andiyanti*) or bound together; it is a name for a pair (*yugaḷa*), as in the example:
"I bow my head to the pair of feet of the Lord of Sages. Here, however, both a pair of words and a pair of meanings are intended, for a *dvanda* is primarily characterized by its dual referents.

Here it might be asked: "If the *dvanda* compound has both members as its primary referents (*padattha*), then how can the characteristic of 'unification of meaning' (*ekatthībhāva*) exist in a *dvanda*?

It is replied: because the objects to be predicated (*vidheyyattha*) are non-distinct. For when reaching the path of expression, the objects to be predicated—such as the agent, the state of being, or the object—become the absolute primary referents of the words, since they constitute the principal factors for the perfection of the expression and the sentence.
And that meaning which is subject to grammatical rule remains undivided even in a *dvanda* compound.

For instance, in such cases as “Sāriputta and Moggallāna go” (*sāriputtamoggallānā gacchanti*) or “He sees Sāriputta and Moggallāna” (*sāriputtamoggallāne passati*), two referents, having become the objects of a single case ending, attain oneness through their state of having a single agent, a single object, and so forth;
in the same way, this occurs in a *dvanda* compound involving two, three, or many words.
The characteristic of becoming a single referent (*ekatthībhāva*) is indeed obtained. 357. [In the sense of] "or" (*ca*): Rule 329; Example 357; Commentary 709.
Several words ending in case-suffixes may become a single referent in the sense of the word *ca*.
In this context, there are four meanings of the word *ca*: conjunction (*samuccaya*), addition (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itarītarayoga*), and aggregate (*samāhāra*).
Among these, what is conjunction? For example: "He gives robes, almsfood, and lodgings. What is addition? For example:
"He gives a gift and he guards his virtue. These two meanings of *ca* are found only in copulative compounds (*dvanda*).
They say that in a compound (samāsa) or a copulative (dvanda), there is no mutual dependence between the words.

This is appropriate in the sense of "conjunction" (anvācaya), because [the members] depend on different actions; however, in the sense of "aggregation" (samuccaya), it is indeed appropriate to construe it in two ways, as in:
"he gives robes, almsfood, and lodgings," or "he gives robes, almsfood, and lodgings. Thus he is a recipient.
This is because it is seen in the Pāḷi at Ma. Ni. 1.65: "of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Alternatively, the particle *vā* (or) is not excluded from a dvanda compound, as it is seen in the Pāḷi at Dī.

Ni. 1.10: "the wearing of garlands, scents, and unguents, and the use of ornaments and finery. However, this would be more appropriate [if understood] as follows: the sense of the word *ca* (and) is a single action, distinguished by its relation to various actions.

Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is twofold: *anvācaya* (cumulative) and [simple] conjunction; and each of these is further twofold, according to the distinction between that which emphasizes the individual members and that which emphasizes the aggregate:

namely, *itarītarayoga* (mutual connection) and *samāhāra* (aggregation). Among these, because *itarītarayoga* emphasizes the individual members, the plural number alone is appropriate in all case endings.
In a dvanda compound, the more distinguished term is placed first. For example:
*sāriputto ca moggallāno ca* becomes *sāriputtamoggallānā*, *sāriputtamoggallāne*, *sāriputtamoggallānehi*, and so forth. Likewise:
*samaṇabrāhmaṇā*, *brāhmaṇagahapatikā*, *khattiyabrāhmaṇā*, *devamanussā*, *candimasūriyā*.
Among words with many syllables, a word with few syllables sometimes comes first: *gāmanigamā*, *gāmajanapadā*, and so forth.
Sometimes words ending in *i* or *u* vowels come first: *aggidhūmā* (fire and smoke), *rattidivā* (night and day), *dhātuliṅgāni* (elements and genders).
Among words ending in *a* vowels, a word beginning with a vowel comes first: *atthadhammā* (meaning and dharma), or *dhammatthā*, and so forth.
And this rule is generally applicable to dvanda compounds consisting of two-word members, but it does not apply to those consisting of many-word members.
Regarding the collective (samāhāra) dvanda: 358. "In a collective compound, the neuter gender [is used]. Kaccāyana 322; Rūpasiddhi 359; Nyāsa 700.
In a collective compound (*samāhāra*), a single-meaning word is neuter; however, its singular number is established by the very term "collective.

Furthermore, this collective compound is invariably found in *dvanda* compounds consisting of parts of living beings and the like, while it is optional in *dvanda* compounds consisting of trees, grass, and so forth.
Therein, first, regarding the pairs of bodily parts that are not movable:
*cakkhu* (eye) and *sota* (ear) make *cakkhusota*; *mukha* (mouth) and *nāsikā* (nose) make *mukhanāsika*, with the shortening according to the rule “*syādīsu rasso*” [Pāṇini 6.1.65];
*hanu* (jaw) and *gīvā* (neck) make *hanugīva*. Likewise, *kaṇṇanāsaṃ* (ear-nose); and *chavi* (skin), *maṃsa* (flesh), and *lohita* (blood).
Skin, flesh, and blood; name and form is *nāmarūpa*; aging and death is *jarāmaraṇa*.

Due to the predominance of usage, the form of the distributive compound (*vikappa*) is also seen in some cases, such as "hands and feet" (*hatthapāda*) or "hands or feet" (*hatthapādā*), and so forth.
In the case of a pair of musical instruments:

"Dancing, singing, and instrumental music" (*naccagītavāditaṃ*): thus, *sammatāḷaṃ*; "well" (*samma*) refers to a bronze cymbal, and "cymbal" (*tāḷa*) refers to a hand-clap; "conch, drum, and kettledrum" (*saṅkhapaṇavaḍiṇḍimaṃ*) refers to the conch, the drum, and the kettledrum, and so forth.
In the case of a dyad of implements: "plow and sickle" (*phālapācanaṃ*), "yoke and plow" (*yuganaṅgalaṃ*), and so forth.

In the case of a compound of military parts (*senaṅgadvanda*): elephants and horses are *hatthiassaṃ*. Likewise, chariots and infantry are *rathapattikaṃ*; sword and shield are *asicammaṃ*. "Shield" (*camma*) refers to a wooden board for protection against arrows; bow and quiver are *dhanukalāpaṃ*, and so forth.
In the case of a compound of small creatures (*khuddakapāṇadvanda*):
*Ḍaṃsa* (mosquito) and *makasa* (gnat) form *ḍaṃsamakasaṃ*. Likewise, *kunthakipillikaṃ*, *kīṭapaṭaṅgaṃ*, and so forth. In the case of a permanent enmity (*niccavera*), in a dvanda compound:

*ahi* (snake) and *nakula* (mongoose) form *ahinakulaṃ*; *biḷāra* (cat) and *mūsikā* (mouse) form *biḷāramūsikaṃ*, with shortening of the vowel. *Kākolūkaṃ* (crow and owl), *sappamaṇḍūkaṃ* (snake and frog), *nāgasupaṇṇaṃ* (serpent and garuḍa), and so forth.
In the case of a copulative compound (sabhāga-dvanda):
virtue and wisdom are "virtue-and-wisdom" (sīlapaññāṇaṃ); serenity and insight are "serenity-and-insight" (samathavipassanaṃ);
true knowledge and conduct are "true-knowledge-and-conduct" (vijjācaraṇaṃ). Likewise for mindfulness and clear comprehension, moral shame and moral dread, and restlessness and remorse.
“Lethargy and drowsiness,” and so forth.
Regarding various contradictory pairs:
“wholesome and unwholesome,” “blameworthy and blameless,” “dark and bright,” “inferior and superior,” “wise and foolish,” and so forth.
In the case of a dvanda compound involving a single enumeration:
*dīgha* and *majjhima* form *dīghamajjhima*; likewise, *aṅguttara*, *saṃyuttaka*, *khandhaka*, *vibhaṅga*, and so forth.
In the case of a dvanda compound involving numerical measurement:
The group of one and two, the group of two and three, the group of three and four, the group of four and five, and so forth.
Regarding the pair of the two types of outcaste cooks:

the sheep-slaughterer and the pig-slaughterer form the compound *orabbhikasūkarikaṃ*. Likewise: the fowler and the cowherd (*sākuṇikamāgavikaṃ*); the scavenger and the outcaste cook (*sapākacaṇḍālaṃ*); the basket-maker and the cartwright (*venarathakāraṃ*); the scavenger and the corpse-burner (*pukkusachavaḍāhakaṃ*), and so forth.
In a compound of dissimilar genders—
such as *itthipumaṃ* (woman and man), *dāsidāsaṃ* (female and male slave), and so forth.
In a compound of directions—
"Pubba" (eastern) and "apara" (western) form "pubbāparaṃ. Likewise, "dakkhiṇuttaraṃ," "pubbadakkhiṇaṃ," "pubbuttaraṃ," "aparadakkhiṇaṃ," and "aparuttaraṃ.

In the case of a compound of two rivers—such as "Gaṅgāyamunaṃ" or "Mahisarabhu"—there is shortening of the long vowels at the end due to the neuter gender throughout, and it takes the singular ending in all seven cases.

Thus ends the section on the compound of constant conjunction (*niccasamāhāra*). Regarding the compounds of specific types of grass obtained through optional application (*vikappa*), as stated at Ka. 323; Rū. 360; Nī. 701:
in the case of a dual compound of specific grasses—*usīrāni ca bīraṇāni ca* becomes *usīrabīraṇaṃ*, or *usīrabīraṇā*; likewise, *muñjapabbajaṃ*, *muñjapabbajā*, *kāsakusaṃ*, *kāsakusā*.
Regarding the praise of specific trees:
*khadiro ca palāso ca* is *khadirapalāsaṃ*; [in the plural] *khadirapalāsā*. *Dhavo ca assakaṇṇo ca* is *dhavassakaṇṇaṃ*;
[in the plural] *dhavassakaṇṇā*. *Pilakkhanigrodhaṃ*, [in the plural] *pilakkhanigrodhā*. *Assatthakapītanaṃ* is *kapitthanaṃ*.
(In some cases): *assatthakapītanā*, *sākasālaṃ*, *sākasālā*.
In compounds of different types of animals:
*gajā ca gavajā ca* = *gajagavajaṃ*, *gajagavajā*; *gomahisaṃ*, *gomahisā*; *eṇeyyavarāhaṃ*, *eṇeyyavarāhā*.
Goat and sheep; goats and sheep; cock and pig; cocks and pigs; elephant, cow, horse, and mule;

elephants, cows, horses, and mules. In the case of a compound of specific types of birds: swan and wild goose; swans and wild geese; kāraṇḍava and ruddy goose; kāraṇḍavas and ruddy geese; crane and heron; cranes and herons.

In the case of a dual compound of wealth (*dhanadvanda*): *hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ*, *hiraññasuvaṇṇā*; *maṇi ca saṅkho ca muttā ca veḷuriyañca* becomes *maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyaṃ*, *maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyā*; *jātarūparajataṃ*, *jātarūparajatā*.
In the case of a dual compound of grain (*dhaññadvanda*):...
Rice and barley, rice and barley; sesame and mung beans, sesame and mung beans; peas and horse gram, peas and horse gram.
In the case of a dvanda compound of condiments:
fish and meat, fish and meat; vegetables and soup, vegetables and soup; bovine and buffalo, bovine and buffalo; antelope and wild boar, antelope and wild boar; deer and peacock, deer and peacock.
In the case of country names (*janapada*):
*Kāsikosalaṃ*, *kāsikosalā*; *Vajjimallaṃ*, *vajjimallā*; *Cetavaṃsaṃ*, *cetavaṃsā*; *Majjhañca Sūrasenañca* becomes *majjhasūrasenaṃ*, *majjhasūrasenā*; *Kurupañcālaṃ*, *kurupañcālā*.
This is the section on optional compounds and aggregations.
The *dvanda* compound is concluded.
Regarding specific rules:
now, the specific rules for the six types of compounds—both those previously mentioned and those not yet mentioned—are being stated.

Neuter singular, shortening of the middle vowel in a compound, extension of the masculine state, *ka* at the end of a compound, *a* at the end of a compound, various substitutions (*nānādesa*), indeclinable (*abyaya*), and numeral (*saṅkhyā*).
Regarding the neuter singular group:

therein, every *abyayībhāva* compound is exclusively neuter gender; the *digu* compound that has become a collective (*samāhāra*) and neuter *dvanda* compounds are also [neuter], as are the singular number.
359. In some instances, there is neuter gender and singularity in the sixth-case compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*). This rule applies only to *chāyā* and *sabhā*.
For example: *salabhānaṃ chāyā* becomes *salabhacchāyaṃ*;
*sabhacchāyaṃ* (in the root text). [References: Ka. 327; Rū. 351; Nī. 704; Caṃ. 2.2.69–73; Pā. 2.4.22–25.]

Likewise, *sakaṭacchāyaṃ* (the shadow of a cart) and *gharacchāyaṃ* (the shadow of a house). Here, there is no [shortening] for *rukkhacchāyā* (the shadow of a tree) or *pabbatacchāyā* (the shadow of a mountain).

Regarding the word *sabhā*, this rule applies only to the assemblies of non-human beings (*amanussa*); thus, the assembly of the Brahmas is *brahmasabhaṃ*. Likewise, *devasabhaṃ*, *indasabhaṃ*, *yakkhasabhaṃ*, and *rakkhasasataṃ*.
It does not apply to the assemblies of human beings; thus, *khattiyasabhā* (an assembly of nobles), *rājasabhā* (a royal assembly), and so forth.
What is the meaning of "kvaci"? [The answer is: "rājaparisā" (the king's assembly).
Thus ends the section on neuter singular compounds.
Now follows the section on the vowels of other compounds.

By the rule “*syādīsu rasso*,” there is shortening of the vowel in *abyayībhāva*, *samāhāra-dvigu*, certain *dvanda*s, and some *tappurisa*s when followed by words beginning with *si* (the nominative case ending).
In the case of *abyayībhāva*:
*upamaṇikaṃ adhitthi* (he stands near the water-jar), *upavadhu* (near the wife).
In a collective compound (samāhāra-digu):
*catuddisaṃ*, *dasitthi*, *dasavadhu*.
In a collective dvanda: [examples follow].
The mouth and nose; the jaw and neck.
In a tappurisa compound:
*salabhacchāyaṃ* (the shadow of a moth); *brahmasabhaṃ* (the assembly of Brahmas).
360. *Ghappassantassāppadhānassa* (ka. 403; rū. 354; nī. 858; caṃ. 2.2.86; pā. 1.2.48).
In the case of *syādi* [words], there is shortening of the *gha*-sound that is either internal (*anta*) or non-principal (*appadhāna*).
In a *bahubbīhi* compound—
A family with many female slaves, a person with many women, a family with many wives, a family with many daughters-in-law.
In the case of *abyayībhāva* compounds: *upamaṇikaṃ* (near the water-jar), *adhitthi* (concerning the woman), *upavadhu* (near the daughter-in-law).
What is meant by "internal" (*antassa*)? A man whose wealth is faith (*saddhādhana*).
What is meant by "of one who is not primary" (*appadhānassa*)? A princess, a royal maiden, or a daughter of a Brahmin (*brahmabandhū*).
361. *Gossu ka* (Pāṇini 1.2.48). *Kaśyapa*, *Rūpāvatāra*, *Niruttidīpanī*, *Candavicitravyākaraṇa*. Pāṇini 1.2.48.
The substitution *u* occurs for the word *go* when it is included within a compound (*anta*) and is not the primary member (*appadhāna*).
Examples: *tiṭṭhagu*, *cittagu*.
Why say "not the primary member"? Consider *rājagavo*.
"Anta" means what? "Gokula.
Thus [are] the rules for the shortening of vowels in compounds (*samāsantarassarāsi*). The rule for the extension of the masculine gender (*pumbhāvātidesarāsi*).

362. *Itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumitthī pumāvekatthe* (Ka. 331; Rū. 353; Nī. 714; Caṃ. 5.2.29; Pā. 6.3.34). "In the sense of a single referent" (*ekatthe*) means in a coordinate construction (*tulyādhikaraṇe*).

When a word of feminine gender that has been mentioned as masculine occurs, followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) in the sense of a single referent, that feminine-gendered word sometimes becomes like a masculine.
This rule consists of four conditions: the preceding member (*pubbapada*), its being of feminine gender, [the subsequent member], and the sense of a single referent.

A word may be masculine when used as the latter member of a compound, and it may be of the feminine gender and in grammatical agreement with the preceding member when used as the first member. For example:
*dīghajaṅgho* (long-shanked) refers to a man; *dīghajaṅghā* refers to a woman; *dīghajaṅghaṃ* refers to a family.
Furthermore, in this context, there are words which take masculine forms in some instances, while in others they take feminine forms by being joined with feminine suffixes.

Those are called "masculine by usage" (*bhāsitapuma*), such as: *dīgho maggo* (a long road), *dīghā ratti* (a long night), *gato puriso* (a man who has gone), *gatā itthī* (a woman who has gone), *kumāro*, *kumārī*, *brāhmaṇo*, *brāhmaṇī*, and so forth.
However, those which are joined with feminine suffixes and always possess a feminine gender-form are not called "masculine by usage."

Examples include *kaññā*, *paññā*, *saddhā*, *nadī*, *itthī*, *pathavī*, and so forth. Likewise, words that possess feminine gender by their very nature (*sabhāva-itthilinga*) or are fixed in the masculine or neuter genders (*niyata-punnapuṃsakalinga*) do not become masculine when used as nouns (*bhāsita-pumā*);
examples include *devatā*, *ratti*, *dhenu*, *vadhū*, *sakko*, *devo*, *brahmā*, *ratanaṃ*, and *saraṇaṃ*.
However, in this context, the word *dīgha* (long) is masculine—as in the phrase *dīgho bālānaṃ saṃsāro* (Dhammapada 60)—and it follows the gender of the qualified noun (*visesya*).
Here, a word with a feminine gender-sign (*itthiliṅga-saddo*) that is connected to the condition of being feminine (*itthipaccaya-yutto*) is what is meant.

When the substitution of the masculine state (*pumbhāva-atideso*) has been made by this sutta, the *ā*-suffix disappears therein. By the sutta “*ghapassantassāppadhānassā*,” there is the shortening of the long vowel *ā* at the end of the compound;
for example, one whose wife is a maiden (*kumārī*) is called *kumārabhariyo*, which involves the cessation of the *ī*-suffix. One whose wife is a young woman (*yuvati*)...

Thus, there is the elision of the *tipaccaya* suffix in *yuvajāya*. One whose wife is a *brahmabandhu* is called *brahmabandhubhariyo*; here, there is the elision of the *ūpaccaya* suffix. Why [is the word] "woman" (*itthī*) mentioned? [Consider:
one whose jewel is a maiden is *kumārīratano*, a man. In this case, the subsequent member (*parapada*) does not possess the feminine gender;
therefore, the extension of the masculine state (*pumbhāvātideso*) should not be applied. If one were to apply it, [the form would be] *kumāro ratanaṃ yassa kumāraratano*.
In this way, the meaning would be undesirable.

What is meant by "in the same referent" (*ekatthe*)? For example: one whose devotion is toward maidens is a *kumārībhattika*. Likewise, a *samaṇībhattika* (one devoted to female ascetics), a *brāhmaṇībhattika* (one devoted to Brahmin women).

In these cases, the suffix *-ka* occurs at the end of the compound; here, the subsequent member (*parapada*) does not share the same referent as the prior member (*pubbapada*), and therefore the extension of the masculine state (*pumbhāva-atideso*) does not apply.
[The suffix] -ika should be applied; if one were to apply it [in this way], then "one who has devotion (*bhatti*) toward princes" would result in the undesirable form *kumārabhattiko*.
What is the meaning of *itthi* (female)? It is *diṭṭhi* (view) in the sense of being seen. One by whom the clan of the village headman (*gāmaṇi*) is seen is *gāmaṇidiṭṭhi*;
here the word *gāmaṇi* is masculine when spoken, but here, because it denotes a clan, it stands in the neuter gender, and thus the feminine suffix [-ī] is applied.
It does not exist; therefore, there is no need for the function of extending [the application] from the masculine state.
What is the purpose of the term *bhāsitapuma* (expressed as masculine)? [Consider: *saddhā pakati yassa so saddhāpakatiko* ("one whose nature is faith" = *saddhāpakatika*). Likewise, *paññāpakatika*.
Here, because the preceding member (*pubbapada*) is fixed in the feminine gender, it is not "expressed as masculine. [Examples: *saddhādhana*, *paññādhana*, *saddhādhura*.
In this case, there is a deficiency of two factors [for a *dvanda* compound]. However, in the *kammadhāraya*, according to Ka. 332; Rū. 343; Nī.

716, the word "in a single meaning" (*ekattha*) does not constitute a separate factor, because a "multiple meaning" (*anekattha*) is impossible here. Thus, "she who has a long shank" is *dīghajaṅghā*; [and] *kumārī*.
And "she is both a wife and a maiden," thus *kumārabhariyā*. Likewise, "a daughter of a khattiya" (*khattiyakaññā*), "a daughter of a brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇakaññā*);
"she is both a young woman and a wife," thus *yuvabhariyā*; "she is both a kinswoman of Brahmā and a wife," thus *brahmabandhubhariyā*.
[Question: What is the purpose of the word "itthi" (woman)? [Answer: "She is both a maiden and a jewel," thus *kumārīratanaṃ*. Likewise, *samaṇīpadumaṃ* (the lotus-like female ascetic).
What is meant by "itthī" (feminine)? "Gāmaṇidiṭṭhi" means that it is both a village headman's family and a view.
What is meant by "bhāsitapumo" (masculine when spoken)? "Saddhāpakati," "gaṅgānadī," "taṇhānadī," and "pathavīdhātu.

However, among words denoting perception (*saññā*), even when joined with the four factors (*caturaṅgayutta*), the rule does not apply: such as "nandādevī," "nandāpokkharaṇī," "kāyagatāsati," "paṭhamāvibhatti," "dutiyāvibhatti," "pañcamīvibhatti," "chaṭṭhīvibhatti," and so forth.
When a suffix follows, a word of the feminine gender that has been spoken as masculine sometimes remains masculine.

For example: *byattatarā*, *byattatamā*. Here, the meaning is: "a woman who is more or most clever among clever women" (*byattānaṃ itthīnaṃ atisayena byattā*). Likewise: *paṇḍitatarā*, *paṇḍitatamā*, and so forth.
364. *Sabbādayo vuttimatte* (Kaccāyana 331; Rūpasiddhi 353; Niddesa 714; Cāndra 5.2.41; Pāṇini 6.3.35).
In the sense of being used as a compound member (*vuttimatte*), the words beginning with *sabba*, known as pronouns (*sabbanāma*), function only as masculine. For example:

*sā pamukhā yassa so tappamukho* ("he for whom she is the chief is 'one whose chief is she'"). Likewise: *tappadhāno* ("one whose main part is she"), and *taṃsampayutto* ("associated with her" or "associated with them").
