"Sā eva pamukhā tappamukhā" means "that itself is the foremost; that is the chief. Likewise, "tappadhānā" [is explained as follows]: its mouth is "tammukhaṃ"; in that verse or in those verses it is "tatra";
from that verse or from those verses it is "tato"; at that time it is "tadā," and so forth.
And here, "vutti" refers to a compound (*samāsa*), while words ending in *taddhita* suffixes and so on, as well as those ending in case-suffixes (*vibhatti-paccaya*), are called nouns (*nāma*).
Thus ends the section on the extended application (*atidesa*) of the masculine gender. Section 365:
The suffixes for compound endings (*samāsanta*). Rule 338: *Lti-itthiyūhi ko ka*. [Referenced in: Rūp 356; Nī 725; Caṃ 4.4.140; Pā 5.4.152.

In the domain of the meaning of another word (*aññapadattha*), when suffixes such as *kattū* and others ending in *ltu* denote a feminine, the suffix *ī* is applied; furthermore, the suffix *ka* is frequently added after words ending in long *ū*.
For example: *bahukattuko* (a place where there are many agents); likewise, *bahuvattuko*. *Bahunadiko* (a place where there are many rivers);
likewise, *bahuitthiko* (a village where there are many women), *bahuitthikā* (an assembly where there are many women), and *bahuitthikaṃ* (a family where there are many women).
Thus, *bahukumārikaṃ* (many maidens) and *bahubrahmabandhuko* (many Brahmin women).

Here, the short form *brahmabandhu* refers to a Brahmin, while the long form *brahmabandhū* refers to a Brahmin woman; when the suffix *-ka* follows, they desire the shortening of long vowels according to the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*). Why [is the word] *bahu* mentioned?
[To exclude: *bahukattā* (having many agents), as in *gāmo* (a village).
366. *Aññato ka*. (Kaṭṭhaka 338; Rūpasiddhi 356; Nyāsa 725; Cāndra 6.2.72; Pāṇini 5.4.152).

In the sense of another word (*aññapadattha*), after words ending in *a*, *avaṇṇa*, *ivaṇṇa*, or *uvaṇṇa*—provided they are followed by feminine suffixes (*itthi*) or the suffix *ū*—the suffix *ka* generally occurs optionally.
First, from those ending in *avaṇṇa*:
*Agāmakaṃ*, *araññaṃ*, *bahugāmako*, *janapado*, *sasotako*, *asotako*, *salomako*, *sapakkhako*, *bahumālako*, *bahumālo*, *bahumāyako*, *bahumāyo*. From stems ending in *ivaṇṇa*:

one whose view is beautiful is *sammādiṭṭhiko*, [also] *sammādiṭṭhi*; *micchādiṭṭhiko*, [also] *micchādiṭṭhi*; a woman who has killed her husband is *matapatikā*; one characterized by faith is *saddhāpakatiko*; one characterized by wisdom is *paññāpakatiko*; one with many hands is *bahuhatthiko*; one with many staffs is *bahudaṇḍiko*.
From *uvaṇṇanta* [stems]:
*sahetuka*, *ahetuka*, *sacakkhuka*, *acakkhuka*, *sabhikkhuka*, *abhikkhuka*, *dīghāyuka*, *appāyuka*, *bahudhenuka*, *vaja*, *bahurattaññuka*, *bhikkhusaṅgha*.

When followed by a word beginning with the feminine suffix *kam*, the vowel *a* at the end of the stem frequently becomes *i*—either by the general rule (*mahāvutti*) or by the specific sutta “*adhātussa ke…*”—as in *bahuputtikā* (a woman with many sons), or *bahuputtakā*; likewise, *ekaputtikā*, *ekaputtakā*, and so forth.
Thus ends the group of suffixes forming compound endings.
Group of suffixes forming compound endings, 367.
*ka*: Kaccāyana 337; Rūpasiddhi 350; Nyāsa 722; Cāndra 4.4.52; Pāṇini 5.4.68; [‘tva’ occurs in many instances].
‘*Samāsanto +a*’: this consists of two words. The meaning is that, having become the end of a compound (*samāsanta*), it becomes a suffix (*apaccaya*).
This is a governing rule (*adhikāra-sutta*). 368. *Pāpādīhi bhūmiyā ka.* (Kaccāyana 337; Rūpasiddhi 350; Nyāsa 722; Canda-vutti 4.4.72; ...pe... 5.4.75; ‘godāvarīnaṃ’ [in many manuscripts]).

The suffix *ka* is added to the word *bhūmi* when it follows *pāpa* and others in a compound. Although one could have simply said “of the word *bhūmi*,” the term “*bhūmiyā*” is used here in order to demonstrate its fixed feminine gender. The same applies elsewhere as well.

*Pāpabhūmaṃ*: the ground of evils; the meaning is "the ground of the arising of evils. *Jātibhūmaṃ*: the ground of birth; the land where the Teacher was born. Likewise, *pacchābhūmaṃ*: the western region;

the country situated to the west of the Middle Country (*majjhima-desa*). 369. [Sanskrit Rule: *saṅkhyā-bhūmy-aḥ*. When *bhūmi* follows numerals, the suffix *a* is applied at the end of the compound. *Pāpānaṃ bhūmi pāpabhūmaṃ*, *pāpānaṃ uppattibhūmi*—this is the meaning. *Jātiyā bhūmi jātibhūmaṃ*, the land where the Teacher was born. Likewise, *pacchābhūmaṃ*, the western part of the Middle Country.
369. By numerals: *ka.* 337; *rū.* 350; *nī.* 722; *caṃ.* 4.4.73; *pā.* 5.4.75. After numerals, the final vowel of *bhūmi* becomes *a* in a compound.
That which has two planes (*bhūmi*) therein is "two-planed" (*dvibhūmo*), "two-storeyed" (*dvibhūmako*), or "a two-storeyed palace" (*pāsādo*);
or alternatively, those things which have three planes, or which are included within three planes, are "three-planed phenomena" (*tebhūmakā dhammā*).

Likewise, there are "four-planed phenomena" (*catubhūmakā dhammā*), "three-planed" (*tebhūmikā*), or "four-planed" (*catubhūmikā*). In the case of reduplication of the syllable *gu*, one says "two planes" as *dvibhūmaṃ*, "three planes" as *tibhūmaṃ*, and "four planes" as *catubhūmaṃ*, and so forth.
370. *Nadīgodhāvarīnaṃ* (Kaṇḍa 337; Rūpa 350; Niddesa 722; Candra 4.4.73; Pāṇini 5.4.75).
The word-final vowel of *nadī* and *godhāvarī* becomes *a* when following numerals in a compound.
For example: *pañca nadiyo* = *pañcanadaṃ*; or, that region which has five rivers is *pañcanadaṃ*. *Satta godhāvariyo* = *sattagodhāvaraṃ*.
371. *Aññāsaṅkhyatthesu* (in the sense of "other" and "innumerable"): *ka.* 337; *rū.* 350; *nī.* 722; *caṃ.* 4.4.74; *pā.* 5.4.86.
The compound *aññāsaṅkhyatthā* consists of *aññattha* (the sense of "other") and *asaṅkhyattha* (the sense of "innumerable").

Here, *aññattha* refers to a *bahubbīhi* compound whose referent is something else (*aññapadattha*), while *asaṅkhyattha* refers to an *abyayībhāva* compound signifying an innumerable sense. It does not mean "those that have other and innumerable senses."

In compound formations other than those where *asaṅkhyā* (innumerable) functions as the final member—excluding compounds where *aññāsaṅkhyā* is the final member—the suffix *a* occurs after *aṅguli* when it follows prefixes (*upasagga*) or numerals (*saṅkhā*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), forms such as *sugat’aṅgulena* and *pamāṇ’aṅgulena* are established. That which has emerged from the fingers is *niraṅgula*;
that which exceeds the fingers is *accaṅgula*; these two are *amādi*-compounds. That which is the sum of two fingers is *dvaṅgula*.
Regarding the phrase "in meanings other than 'not another'": what is it? "Five fingers are in this" is *pañcaṅguli*, meaning "hand. *Upaṅguli* means "near the finger.

In such instances as, "having drawn back the ear by four *aṅgulas*," "an eight-*aṅgula* tooth-stick," "at most two *aṅgulas*," "at most four *aṅgulas*," "at most eight *aṅgulas*," and so forth, the word *aṅgula* ending in the vowel *a* is a distinct term denoting measurement.
372. *Dārumhaṅgulyā* (Ka. 337; Rū. 350; Nī. 722; Caṃ. 4.4.97; Pā. 5.4.114): ‘*dārumhaṅgulyā*’ (found in many texts).
The suffix *-a* occurs at the end of a compound following the word *aṅguli* when it refers to another word (*aññapadatthe*) meaning “wood” (*dāru*).

For example, *pañcaṅgulaṃ dāru* (“a piece of wood five finger-breadths long”). Here, the specific measure of grain and other things, which has the finger as its unit of measurement, is called “wood” (*dāru*).
373. *Dīghāhovaṣseka-deśebhyaśca rātryāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.87). The compound *dīgho ca aho ca vasso ca ekadeso ca* is a *dvanda*.

Regarding the term "part" (*ekadeso*): when preceded by words such as *dīgha*, *ahna*, or *vassa*, or by numerals (*saṅkhyā*)—whether they are expressed as prior members, as initial members (*parādi*), or otherwise—the suffix *a* is applied to the end of the compound with the word *ratti* (night), provided that the numeral is not used in the sense of "another" (*anañña*). By the use of the particle *ca*, [the rule also applies] to numerals.
“Cirarattan” is established [as a compound].
Long nights are “dīgharattaṃ”; the meaning is a long succession of nights and days.
Day and night is “ahorattaṃ. A night moistened by rain is “vassarattaṃ. The first part of the night is “pubbarattaṃ”; the latter part of the night is “pararattaṃ.”
Half of the night is *addharattaṃ*; the night having passed is *atiratto*; two nights is *dvirattaṃ*.

Likewise, *tirattaṃ*, *caturattaṃ*, *pañcarattaṃ*, and *chārattaṃ* [are formed]. Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*), the forms *ekarattaṃ* and *ekarattī* are established. What is the purpose of the phrase "in the sense of non-otherness and number" (*anaññāsaṅkhyatthesu*)?
*Dīgharatti*: that in which the night is long; it refers to the winter season (*hemanta*). *Uparatti*: near to the night.
374. *Go* [receives] *a* in place of *alopa*, except when meaning "cowherd" (*acattha*). (Kacc 337; Rūp 350; Nī 722; Candra 4.4.77; Pāṇini 5.4.92).

The word *go* ("cow"), when occurring except in the sense of "cowherd" (*acattha*) and in the senses of "not another" (*anañña*), "innumerable" (*asaṅkhya*), and so on, takes the suffix *a* in place of the elision (*alopa*) at the end of a compound.

Examples: *Rañño go*: *rājagavo* (the king's cow); *attano go*: *sagavo* (one's own cow); *paresaṃ go*: *paragavo* (another's cow); *pañca gāvo*: *pañcagavaṃ* (five cows); *pañca gāvo*: *pañcagavaṃ*. Likewise, *dasagavaṃ* (ten cows).

What is elided? [In the word] *pañcagu*, meaning "bought for five cows," there is the elision of the taddhita suffix in this sense; therefore, this *ap*-suffix does not occur, and by the rule *gossū*, the *o* of *go* is replaced by *ava*.
Why say "when it means bought" (*acatthe*)? Consider *gavajā ca gāvo ca gavajagavo*; here, in the *yo*-compound, the substitution of *go* by *gava* occurs.
Why say "not when meaning another or a number" (*anaññāsaṅkhyatthesu*)? Consider *cittagu* and *upagu*.
375. *Rattidiva*, *dāragava*, *caturassa*. These three words ending in *-anta* are treated as indeclinables (*nipacca*).

*Ratti* (night) and *divā* (day) form *rattidivaṃ*; *dārā* (wife/woman) and *gāvo* (cows) form *dāragavaṃ*; that which has four mares (*assiyo*) is *caturasso*. Here, the suffix (*apaccaya*) is absent, and the *issa* of *assissa* becomes *attaṃ*.
When extension (*āyāma*) is implied, the form *anugava* is derived [from *anu* + *go*].
A cart that has followed behind the cows is called *anugava*.
What is *āyāma*? It is that which follows behind cattle (*guṇṇaṃ*).
377. *Akkhimhāññatthe ka*: [Pāṇini 5.4.113; Kaccāyana 337; Rūpasiddhi 350; Nyāsa 722; Cāndra 4.4.96].
The suffix *ka* is added after the word *akkhi*, when it occurs in a compound signifying something other than its own meaning.
He whose eyes are broad is *visālakkho*; he whose eyes are deformed is *virūpakkho*;
he whose eyes are many thousands is *sahassakkho*; he whose eyes are red is *lohitakkho*. Likewise for *nīlakkho* or *nīlakkhi*.
Due to the governing rule of abundance (*bahulādhikāra*), even when there is no other meaning [than the literal], it refers to that which is directly before the eyes; [it is] of the eyes...
*Parabhāga* becomes *parokkha*; *tirobhāga* of the eyes becomes *tirokkha*. Here, by the word "eye" (*akkhi*), the five sense-faculties are intended.
According to the *Mahāvutti*, in certain instances, the suffixes *-a*, *-ā*, and *-i* occur at the end of a compound.
Among these, when the suffix *-a* is absent:

A friend of the wind is a "wind-friend" (*vāyusakha*); or, one who has a friend reckoned as the wind is a "wind-friend"—this refers to fire. One who is a friend to all—whether loved, unloved, or neutral—is a "friend-to-all" (*sabbasakha*);
or, one who has all beings as friends is a "friend-to-all"—this refers to one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārī*).

"Friend to all, companion to all" is the text from the *Theragāthā* (verse 648). A friend of the wicked is a "wicked-friend" (*pāpasakha*); or, one for whom the wicked are companions is a "wicked-friend."
Or one with evil friends. “One with evil companions, one with evil friends”—this is the Pāḷi at Dīgha Nikāya 3.253.
One by whom the self has been sent forth is *pahitatto*; one whose middle state or intrinsic nature is balanced is *majjhatto*;
one whose internal continuum or constitution is emaciated (as in the root text) is *chātajjhatto*; one whose self is satisfied is *suhitatto*; [and] one whose self is restrained is *yata*.
*Yassa*: one whose self is restrained (*yatatta*); "one whose self is established" (*ṭhitatto*), and so forth.
Regarding the *ā* suffix:

"one for whom the Dhamma is directly perceived" (*paccakkhadhammā*); "it covers" (*chādeti*) thus it is a covering (*chado*), namely delusion (*moha*); "one from whom the covering is removed" (*vivaṭacchadā*), [referring to] the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*).
Regarding the conditional relation (*paccaya*): one who has a beautiful scent is *sugandhi*; one who has a foul scent is *duggandhi*; one who has a putrid scent is *pūtigandhi*;
one who has a fragrant scent is *surabhigandhi*. The canonical text (*pāḷi*) reads: “I am endowed with the fragrance of virtue, possessing the sweet scent of the body.”
Thus ends the section on the group of *samāsanta* suffixes.
Section 378: The Group of Various Locales (*Nānādesarāsi*). Rule 333–334; Rūpasiddhi 344–345; Nyāsa 717–718: [The suffix] *ka* is applied when the following word (*uttarapada*) is present.
The meaning is that a grammatical rule applies when a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) follows a preceding word (*pubbapada*).
This is a governing rule (*adhikārasutta*). In compounds such as *abrāhmaṇo*, *anariyo*, *abhikkhuko*, and *ananto*, when a subsequent word follows, the letter *na* becomes *a* or *ana*.
Words such as *nakha* and others are established as *napakatika*.
*Nakha*: that which has no *kha*; here *kha* means pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*dukkha*).
*Nakula*: that which has no *kula* (family); a Brahmin of that name. *Pum-ssaka*: there is no male (*puṃsaka*) belonging to it; *napuṃsaka*: that in which there is no male.
*Khañjana* means moving with deficiency; *khatta* is that which has no *khañjana*, thus it is *nakkhatta*.
*Kaṃ* is said to mean happiness (*sukha*); because it is opposed to that, *akaṃ* is said to mean suffering (*dukkha*). That in which there is no *akaṃ* is *nāka*, [meaning] heaven (*sagga*).
He does not release, thus he is *namuci*, [meaning] Māra. It does not dissolve, it does not fall away, thus it is *nagara*; when referring to a house, the word *agāra* is established.

380. *Nago vā pāṇini* (Pāṇini 6.3.77; Kaccāyana 333–334; Rūpasiddhi 344–345; Nyāsa 717–718; Cāndra 5.2.96; Amarakośa 2.5.10). In many instances, the form *naga* is established even when it does not follow *pāṇi*.
Thus, *na gacchanti* means "they do not move," referring to trees (*rukkhā*);
*nagā* refers to mountains (*pabbatā*). Similarly, *agā* refers to trees (*rukkhā*) and *agā* refers to mountains (*pabbatā*).

What is an example of *apāṇinī*? "Ago vasalo kiṃ tena" (What is a wretched outcaste to him?). Here, *ago* means a person in distress; *vasalo* means a lowly person; *kiṃ tena* is a word of reproach. There is also a reading as *sītena*. Thus: *neke*, *aneke*, *nekāni*, *anekāni*, and so forth.

This concludes the section on the group of *na*-compounds. 381. *Sahassa soññatthe ka.* (In the sense of emptiness, *sa-* is substituted for *saha-*. Kaccāyana 404; Rūpasiddhi 370; Niddesa 859; Cāndra 5.2.97; Pāṇini 6.3.82.)
In a compound where another word’s meaning [is expressed] and when followed by a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), *sahassa* optionally becomes *sa*.
*Saputto* (or *sahaputto*) means "one who exists together with a son. Why say "in another meaning"?
[Consider: *saha katvā* (having done together), *saha yujjhitvā* (having fought together).
382. When a compound name (*saññā*) is to be formed, the word *sahassa* becomes *so* when followed by a following member (*uttarapada*). For example:
*saha āyattaṃ* becomes *sāyattaṃ*; *saha palāsaṃ* becomes *sapalāsaṃ*. This is a designation for that which does not show respect.
383. *Apaccakkhe* (Kaccāyana 404; Rūpasiddhi 307; Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā 859; Canda-vutti 5.2.99; Pāṇini 6.3.80).
When the sense of "not being present" (*apaccakkhe*) is implied, and an *uttarapada* follows, the substitution of *so* for *saha* occurs.
That by which one is caught is *oḍḍi*, meaning a snare. That which exists together with a snare is *soḍḍi*, meaning a pigeon. Here, [the word] is *oḍḍi*.
“Not visible. There is also a reading, “*sāggi kapoto*”; it is *sapicukā* because it occurs together with cotton (*picu*), that is, a whirlwind.
And that is not visible; it is to be known by seeing a mass of cotton whirling about in the sky after having risen up.
There is also a reading, “*sapisācā vātamaṇḍalikā*. Thus [are described] the dusty winds, the wind with demons, and the night.

384. *Saha* becomes *sa-* when it does not mean "time," provided it is the primary element signifying its own meaning (*sakattha*) and is followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). (Ka. 404; Rū. 370; Nī. 859; Caṃ. 5.2.110; Pā. 6.3.81).

In the case of the word *saha*, when it denotes its own meaning (*sakattha*) and is not used in the sense of time (*akāle*), the *sa-* substitution occurs when a subsequent word follows. Examples: *sabrahmaṃ* ("together with Brahmins"), *sacakkaṃ* ("together with the wheel").

What is the meaning of *akāle*? It means "together with forenoon" (*saha pubbaṇhaṃ*), "together with afternoon" (*saha paraṇhaṃ*), or "forenoon and afternoon occurring together with a favorable constellation" (*sunakkhattena saha pavattaṃ pubbaṇhaṃ, paraṇhaṃ*).

385. Regarding the rule for *ganthanta-ādhikye ka*: [Kaccāyana 404; Rūpasiddhi 370; Nītattha 859; Cāndra 5.2.101; Pāṇini 6.3.79]. *Ganthassa anto* is *ganthanto*. *Ādhikyaṃ* is the state of being excessive (*adhikabhāvo*).

When the word *saha* occurs before a following word (*uttarapade pare*) that signifies either the end of a treatise (*ganthante*) or an excess (*ādhikye*), the substitution of *ka* takes place. For example, the *Uṇādi-kappa* is the end of the Kaccāyana treatise (*yathā taṃ kaccāyanaganthassa anto uṇādikappo*). Thus, when expressing the sense of "at the end of a treatise" or "in excess," the form becomes *sahaka*.

That which is studied together with the *uṇādi* [suffixes] is called *soṇādi*; the meaning is that the entire *Kaccāyana* has been studied. *Samuhuttaṃ*: "He studies the entire *Joti* together with a *muhutta*";

*joti* refers to the science of astrology (*nakkhattasattha*). Regarding excess: *sadoṇā*, *khārī*, *sakahāpaṇaṃ*, *nikkhaṃ*, *samāsakaṃ*, *kahāpaṇaṃ*. This sutta has the sense of constancy (*niccattha*).
386. *Samānassa pakkhādīsu vā* (Ka. 404; Rū. 370; Nī. 859; Caṃ. 5.2.103–4; Pā. 6.3.84–86).
In the case of the northern regions beginning with *pakkha*, the suffix *sa-* optionally replaces *samāna*.
Thus: *samāno pakkho sahāyo* becomes *sapakkho*; or, that which has a similar side (*samāno pakkho yassa*) is *sapakkho*, or *samānapakkho*. Likewise: *sajāti*, *samānajāti*, *sajanapado*, *saratti*.
That woman whose husband (*pati*) is the same is *sapati*. Similarly: *sanābhi*, *sabandhu*, *sabrahmacārī*, *sanāmo*. [The same applies to] *avhayaṃ*.
It is called *nāma*; he whose name (*avhaya*) is equal to *canda* (moon) is *candasavhaya*.
He who has the same clan (*sagotta*) as *inda* is *indasagotta*. [The following are] *sarūpa* (identical in form) and *saṭṭhāna* (identical in place). *Hari* is called gold;
he whose color (*vaṇṇa*) is equal to *hari* is *harissavaṇṇo*, with the doubling of the *s*. Likewise: *siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo*, *savayo*, *sadhano*, *sadhammo*, *sajātiyo*.
In "pakkhādīsū" and so forth, what [is meant]? One who is of like character (*samānasīla*).
387. *Udare iye ka*. When *udara* follows a word joined with *iya*, the substitution of *sa* for *samāna* optionally occurs. 404; *rū.* 370; *nī.* 859; *caṃ.* 5.2.105; *pā.* 6.3.88.
When *udara* follows a word joined with *iya*, the substitution of *sa* for *samāna* optionally occurs.
One born from the same womb is a *sodariya* (uterine brother); [the term] *samānodariya* [is derived from] *samāna-udara*.
What does this signify? It signifies the state of having the same womb.

This application of *samāna-* occurs with other words as well; for example, "one whose splendor is equal to the moon" is *candassasirīkaṃ*, referring to a face. Likewise, *padumassasirīkaṃ* refers to a countenance.
By the great rule (*mahāvutti*), it applies to *santa* and the others as well: that which has hair (*loma*) existing in it is "hairy" (*salomaka*).
Likewise, "having wings" (*sapakkhaka*). Those in whom taints (*āsava*) exist are "with taints" (*sāsavā*); those in whom conditions (*paccaya*) exist are "with conditions" (*sappaccayā*);
those in whom there exist states (*dhamma*) superior to themselves are "surpassable" (*sauttara*). A person who is good is a "true person" (*sappurisa*). So too is a "virtuous person" (*sajjana*).
"Saddhamma" (the true Dhamma), "santassa bhāvo" (the state of being peaceful), "sabbhāvo" (existence), and so forth.
Thus ends the *sa*-group.
388. Regarding this, [refer to] Ka. 129; Rū. 222; Nī. 305.
When a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) follows, *imassa* becomes *idaṃ*.
This is the meaning of this, thus it is *idamatthī*; with the suffix *-ī* at the end of the compound, it is *idamatthī*. The state of being one who has this as their object is *idamatthitā*.
These are the conditions for these, thus they are *idappaccayā*; the state of being such conditions is *idappaccayatā*. "The conditions of these are *idappaccayā*."
Some also construe it thus: "The state of having this as its condition (idappaccayatā) is simply this-conditionality (idappaccaya). There is also the indeclinable word *idaṃ*;
for example, in the Mahānidāna Sutta: "Bhikkhus, if form here were the self... if feeling here were the self... if perception here were the self...
if mental formations here, bhikkhus, were the self... and so forth. 20.
389. *Puṃ* for *pumassa* optionally. (Ka. 82; Rū. 149).
When followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*), the form *puṃ* optionally replaces *pumassa*.

*Pumassa liṅgaṃ* = *pulliṅgaṃ* (masculine gender); *pumassa bhāvo* = *pumbhāvo* (the state of being male); *pumā ca so kokilo ca* = *puṅkokilo* (a male cuckoo); *pumā ca so go ca* = *puṅgavo* (a bull). [In this case], by the rule “*go* when not expressing its own meaning...,” there is no suffix (*apaccaya*), and it is neuter.
What does it blow?
A man and a woman. 390. *Ṭa* [is substituted] for *nta* and *ntūnaṃ* [before] a following word. (Kaccāyana 126; Rūpasiddhi 101; Nyāsa 301).
When a subsequent word follows, *ṭa* optionally replaces *nta* and *ntūnaṃ* in some instances.

Those for whom existence (*bhava*) is the foundation are "existence-foundationed" (*bhavaṃpatiṭṭhā*); this is due to the addition of the suffix *-i*. Those whose root is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) are "rooted in the Blessed One" (*bhagavaṃmūlakā*), namely the teachings (*dhammā*). Likewise, the teachings have the Blessed One as their refuge (*bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā*).
Because of the predominance of the suffix *-tara* and others following a frequent usage, "greater than great" (*mahantīnaṃ atisayena mahā*) is *mahattarī*;
the state of being great among those long-versed is "greatness of long-standing" (*rattaññumahattaṃ*). Thus [are explained] greatness of birth, greatness of virtue, and greatness of merit.
The state of an *arahant* is *arahatta*.
When a following word (*uttarapada*) begins with a vowel, the suffixes *-nta* and *-ntu* become *-a*.

*Vijjāyonisambandhīnam ā tatra catthe ka.* (Pāṇini 6.3.25) [This rule prescribes the substitution of the vowel *ā* for the final vowel of the first member in compounds denoting relationship through knowledge (*vijjā*) or birth (*yoni*), when the second member begins with a consonant. *Vijjāyonisambandhīnam ā tatra catthe ka*: In this context, the vowel *ā* is substituted [for the final vowel of the first member] in words denoting relationship through knowledge or birth, before a word beginning with a consonant. *Rū*: 158; *Nī*: 736; *Caṃ*: 5.2.21; *Pā*: 6.3.25.

In a compound of two words, the substitution of *ā* occurs for those related by knowledge—such as *ltu*, *pitā*, and so on—and for those related by birth, when these very same words follow immediately after [the preceding word].

(*Jāyaṃ patimhi*—*Bahūsu*); *Rūp* 358; *Nī* 731. When *pati* follows, the word *jāyā* becomes *jāyaṃ*.

According to the *Mahāvutti*, from the word *pati* (husband) with the suffix *suja*, *sujātā* (wife) is formed; likewise, from *dāra* (child/wife), *daṃ* is formed.

One who gives birth to a son is called a *jānī*. Thus, it is logical to say *jānī* and *pati* together as *jānīpati*. The reading is *tudaṃpatī*. And in the *Kaccāyana*, it says: ‘*tu daṃjāni patimhi*’.
Therein, the word *tu* serves merely to complete the meter. 406. *Saññāyam udodakassa ka*:
[In the sense of a name, the letter *ka* is substituted for the final vowel of *uda* and *udaka*. (Kaccāyana 404; Rūpasiddhi 370; Niddesa 257; Cāndra 5.2.65; Pāṇini 6.3.57).
When the word *saññā* (name) is understood, the substitute *uda* takes the place of *udaka* when followed by a subsequent member of a compound.
It holds water, thus it is *udadhi*; it holds great water, thus it is *mahodadhi*. They drink water here, thus it is *udapāna*; they drink water by means of this, thus it is *udapānī*. 407.
In the case of *kumbha* and so forth, *ka* [is substituted] according to Kaccāyana 404; Rūpasiddhi 370; Niddesa 257; Cāndra 5.2.69; Pāṇini 6.3.59.
In words such as *kumbha* and others, there is optionally the elision (*uda*) of the word *udaka*.

Thus, *udakassa kumbho* becomes *udakumbho* or *udakakumbho*. Likewise, *udapatto*, *udakapatto*, *udabindu*, and *udakabindu*. According to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), even in the case of feminine endings (*sy-ādi*), the Pāḷi reads:
“*nīlodā pokkharaṇī*” (a blue-lotus pond). 408. In words such as *sota*, there is the elision of *ka*. (Aṭṭhakathā 404; Rūpasiddhi 370; Niddesa 256).
In the case of *udaka* when followed by *sota*, etc., there is elision (*lopa*) of the *u*.

Thus: *udakassa sotaṃ* becomes *dakasotaṃ*; *udake rakkhaso* becomes *dakarakkhaso*; those whose abode (*āsaya*) is water are *dakāsayā*, namely living beings (*pāṇā*). According to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), even in the case of *syādi* [suffixes], there is the Pāli:

The suffix *ṇha* is substituted for *aha* when preceded by *pubba*, *apara*, *ajja*, *sāya*, or *majjha*.

Apart from the application of the *syādi*-case endings, words beginning with *ku-* and *pā-* are always in apposition (*ekattha*) with a word ending in a *syādi* case ending.
A contemptible brahmin is a "bad brahmin" (*kubrāhmaṇa*). "Slightly warm" is "lukewarm" (*kaduṇha*). "Having become manifest" means *pātubhūta*;
it is also seen as *āvī* or *āvi*, meaning "having become visible" (*āvibhūta*). "Having become silent" means *tuṇhībhūta*. "Foremost" refers to a leader or guide (*nāyaka*).
Having performed in a particular manner is "having performed" (*pakaritvā*); what is done in such a manner is "done in a particular way" (*pakataṃ*); or, it is "done first" (*paṭhamaṃ kataṃ*).

"Pakataṃ" (done) means a man who is ugly is a "duppuriso" (ill-done man). Likewise, "dukkataṃ" (badly done) [means] a man who is handsome is a "supuriso" (well-done man). Likewise, "sukataṃ" (well-done) [is used in compounds such as]:

*abhidhammo* (the highly praised doctrine), *abhitthuto* (highly extolled), *bhusaṃ kaḷāro* (exceedingly beautiful) becomes *ākaḷāro*, and *bhusaṃ bandho* (a very firm bond) becomes *ābandho*, and so forth.

Words beginning with *pāda-* become synonymous with words beginning with *pakata-* when they follow the first case (nominative) in a compound; for example, *pakato ācariyo* (a well-trained teacher) becomes *pācariyo*. Likewise, *payyako paro antevāsī* (a very excellent student) becomes *pantevāsī*; *paro putto* (an excellent son) becomes *paputto*; *paro nattā* (an excellent grandson) becomes *panattā*.
Words such as *ati* and others [are used] with the second case in the sense of "having transcended" (*atikkanta*), etc.; for example, *mañcam atikkanto* = *atimañco*. Likewise, *atibālo*, *ativeḷā*.

Words such as *ava* and others [are used] with the third case in the sense of "abandoned" (*kuṭṭha*), etc.; for example, *kokilāya avakuṭṭhaṃ vanaṃ* = *avakokilaṃ*. They say that "*avakuṭṭha*" means "abandoned" (*chaḍḍita*). Likewise, *avamayūraṃ*.
Words such as *pari* and others [are used] with the fourth case in the sense of "incapable" (*gilāna*), etc.; for example, *ajjhāyituṃ gilāno* = *pariyajjheno*.

The particles *ni*, etc., [are used] after a word in the ablative case in the sense of "departing from" (*nikkhanta*). For example: *nikkosambi* (departed from Kosambī), *vānato nikkhantaṃ nibbānaṃ* (Nirvana departed from craving). Why say "in the sense of departing, etc."? [Observe:
*rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate* (it flashes toward the tree). 411.
*Cī* is used after words expressing the sense of "doing" (*kiyattha*). (Pāṇini 1.4.60, 61) *caṃ* (the particle *ca*) [is used]. (Kaccāyana 2.2.25)
A word ending in the suffix *cīpa* becomes synonymous with words expressing an action (*kriyā*).
[Examples: *balasā kiriyā* (an act by force), *balīkiriya*, *pākaṭīkiriya*, *pākaṭībhuyya*, *pākaṭībhaviya*. 412.
[The suffix] *caṃ* is used together with words such as *bhūsana* (adornment), *ādara* (respect), and *anādara* (disrespect). (Pāṇini 1.4.63, 64).
The words *alaṃ* and so forth become co-referential (*ekattha*) with these verbal derivatives (*kriyattha*) in the senses of adornment and the like.

"He performed adornment" is *alaṃkiriya*; "he performed equal respect" is *sakkacca*; "he performed unequal disrespect" is *asakkacca*. [In the latter two cases,] there is the substitution of the following form (*pararūpattaṃ*) for the nasal dot (*bindu*).

[Question: Why is it said "in the senses of adornment and the like"? [Answer: *Alaṃ bhutvā gato* ("having eaten enough, he went"); here *alaṃ* means "sufficient. *Sakkatvā gato* ("having honored, he went"); [here *sakka* means] "beautiful."

The meaning is: having made [the word] *katvā* the primary sense. The intention is that the designation of "having the same meaning" (*ekattha-saññā*) applies only to those forms established together with abbreviated secondary members (*upapada*), such as *kacca* and *kiriyā*, and not to those established separately with unabbreviated forms like *katvā*.
Furthermore, other words frequently become co-referential (*ekattha*) with words ending in case-suffixes (*syādi*) that denote the sense of an action (*kriyāttha*).
"To be beyond" (*abhavīti*) is *parobhuyya*. Likewise: *tirobhuyya*, *parokiriya*, *tirokiriya*, *urasikiriya*, *manasikiriya*, *majjhekiriya*, *tuṇhībhuyya*.

Words such as *tya* and others, having attained the status of technical designations (*saññā*), are indeclinables (*nipāta*) and take the form of case-suffixes (*syādi*). Therefore, they too are included in this sutta.
A cow that has milk; a woman whose children are not dead. Being present as a condition is a *atthipaccaya* (presence-condition).
Likewise for the *natthipaccaya* (absence-condition). "Kamma that has been" is *ahosikamma*; "come and see" is *ehi-passa*. That which deserves such an injunction is *ehipassika*.

"Itihāsa" (tradition) refers to that which exists here as a procedure that has occurred thus, as the ancients have said, or as they existed thus in the past;

it is an ancient text (*purāṇagandha*). "Aññāsikoṇḍañño. Some, however, [explain it as] "he realizes," "he attends to," "he makes manifest," "he reveals," "he displays," or "he adorns."
They state that [words] such as *sakkaroti*, *pabhavati*, and *parābhavati* also possess a single meaning (*ekatthībhāva*). Herein, forms ending in the suffix *-tu* and others are also included:
one who desires to go is *gantukāmo*; likewise *kattukāmo* (one who desires to do) and *daṭṭhukāmo* (one who desires to see).

421. From *acattālīsā* onwards, *bā* optionally replaces *dvi*. (Ka. 380; Rū. 255; Nī. 810).
After *acattālīsā*, *dvi* becomes *bā* optionally.
Examples: *bārasa*, *dvādasa*; *bāvīsati*, *dvāvīsati*; *bāttiṃsa*, *dvattiṃsa*.
What is "forty-two"? Forty-two (dvācattālīsaṃ).
422. *Catussa cuco dase ka*: When *da* follows, *cu* and *co* optionally replace *catu*. (Kaccāyana 390; Rūpasiddhi 256; Nyāsa 826).
When *da* follows, *cu* and *co* may optionally take the place of *catu*.
Cuddasa, coddasa, catuddasa. 423.
In the cases of *vīsa* and *dasa*, the fifth [vowel] becomes *paṇṇa* or *pannā* respectively (Ka. 404; Rū. 370; Nī. 814).
In these instances, the fifth vowel becomes *paṇṇa* or *pannā* according to the respective order.
Twenty-five, twenty-five, fifteen, fifteen. 424.
*Cha* followed by *sa* becomes *so*. (Ka. 374; Rū. 408; Nī. 806).
When *da* follows, *cha* becomes *so*.
Sixteen.
425. From *ekaṭṭhāna* up to *ā ka*: [the rule] applies from 383; 253; 815.
When ten or more follow, there is one [consonant], and *a* becomes *ṭṭhāna*.
Eleven, eighteen.
426. *Ra* optionally replaces *ka*. (Kacc 381; Rūp 254; Nīti 812).
The letter *ra* optionally occurs in place of the following *das* after numerals beginning with *eka*.

In *ekārasa*, *ekādasa*, *bārasa*, *dvādasa*, *pannarasa*, *pañcadasa*, *sattarasa*, *sattadasa*, *aṭṭhārasa*, and *aṭṭhādasa*, [the substitution of *l* for *d*] occurs invariably before the suffixes *-desa* and *-panna*. Here it does not occur:
*catuddasa*. 427. *Chatīhi ḷo ca ka*. (Pāṇini 6.1.172; Rūpasiddhi 258; Nyāsa 809).
After *cha* and *tī*, the *da* of the following word becomes *ḷa*, and *ra* is substituted [for the final vowel].
Sixteen, thirteen, thirteen.
428. Regarding “aḍḍhuḍḍhatiyā”: the analysis is *aḍḍha* + *uḍḍhatiyā*.
For the fourth and third [vowels] following *aḍḍha*, they become *uḍḍha* and *tiyā* respectively. (Ka. 387; Rū. 411; Nī. 819).
With *addha* [prefixed], the fourth becomes *addhacatuttha*; with *addha*, the third becomes *addhatiya*.
When the suffix *ṇya* is used in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*), it becomes *addhateyya*. 429.
For the second [ordinal], *saha* [is prefixed] to form *diyaḍḍha* and *divaḍḍha*. (Ka. 387; Rū. 411; Nī. 819).
From "half" (*aḍḍha*) and "another" (*parassa*), with the addition of "second" (*dutiya*), there arise *diyaḍḍha* and *divaḍḍhā*.
With "half" and "second," there are *diyaḍḍho* and *divaḍḍho*.
And just as the words one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten [combine] individually with their own...
The words *vīsati*, *tiṃsati*, *cattālīsa*, *paññāsa*, *saṭṭhi*, *sattati*, *asīti*, and *navuti* each fall [into grammatical application] within their own respective meanings;
however, they do not undergo the grammatical operations (*kāriya*) of the word *dasa*.
It should be understood that the same applies to the words *sata* and *sahassa*.
Beyond that, ten thousands are a "ten-thousand" (*dasasahassa*), which is also called a "myriad" (*nahuta*);

one hundred thousands are a "hundred-thousand" (*satasahassa*), which is also called a "lac" (*lakkha*); and ten hundred-thousands are "ten-hundred-thousands"—thus these terms are formed by way of numerical compounds (*digusamāsa*).
Two hundred is *dvisataṃ*, three hundred is *tisataṃ*, two thousand is *dvisahassaṃ*, and three thousand is *tisahassaṃ*;
these and others are already explained under the section on doubling (*digumha*). In the system of calculation (*gaṇanapatha*), however, there are seven places:

the place of ones, the place of tens, the place of hundreds, the place of thousands, the place of ten thousands, the place of hundred thousands, and the place of ten hundred thousands; these are successively multiplied by ten.
They exist. In that context, "single place" refers to one, two, three, and so forth. "Ten places" refers to ten, twenty, thirty, and so forth.
"Hundred places" refers to a hundred, two hundred, three hundred, and so forth.
"Thousand places" refers to a thousand, two thousand, three thousand, and so forth. It is the same for the higher numbers as well. And in each single place, there are nine.
There are nine steps, both intermediate and final. This is called the "ground of the root" (*mūlabhūmi*).
Beyond that is the "ground of the limit" (*koṭibhūmi*). Within that, there are seven stages, such as the single place, the ten places, the hundred places, and so forth.
Therein, having taken the final place of the ground of the root and multiplied it by ten, [one reaches] the ground of the limit.
There is one place; here too, seven places are each multiplied by ten in succession, so that here the final place becomes one hundred thousand times ten million (100,000,000,000).
Beyond that is what is called the "ground of the koṭi" (pakoṭibhūmi). Here too there are seven places. Among those, the final place of the ground of the koṭi—
Having taken [the numbers] and multiplied them tenfold, they become one place on the level of ten million (koṭi);

here too, the seven places are likewise multiplied by ten, with one hundred thousand times ten million (100,000 × 10,000,000) being the final place. In this manner, the transition from stage to stage and the differentiation of the places across all levels should be understood.

Now, the sequence of stages here is as follows: the root stage (*mūlabhūmi*), the limit stage (*koṭibhūmi*), the beyond-limit stage (*pakoṭibhūmi*), the beyond-limit-beyond-limit stage (*koṭipakoṭibhūmi*), the myriad stage (*nahutabhūmi*), the beyond-myriad stage (*ninnahutabhūmi*),

the unshakeable stage (*akkhobhiṇībhūmi*)— the forms *bhinī* and *bhanī* are also seen [for this], the drop stage (*bindubhūmi*), the *abbuda* stage (*abbudabhūmi*), the beyond-*abbuda* stage (*nirabbudabhūmi*),
the *ahaha* stage (*ahahabhūmi*), the *ababa* stage (*abababhūmi*), the *aṭaṭa* stage (*aṭaṭabhūmi*), the *sogandhika* stage (*sogandhikabhūmi*), and the *uppalaka* stage (*uppala-bhūmi*).

The twenty-one planes— the *kumuda* plane, the *puṇḍarīka* plane, the *paduma* plane, the *kathāna* plane, the *mahākathāna* plane, and the *asaṅkhyeyya* plane— constitute one hundred and forty-seven locations. Furthermore, in the sequence of the hell-planes,
there are the *abbuda* plane, the *nirabbuda* plane, the *ababa* plane, the *aṭaṭa* plane, and the *ahaha* plane.

It should be stated as: "the ground of white water-lilies (kumuda), the ground of fragrant water-lilies (sogandhika), the ground of blue lotuses (uppala), the ground of white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), and the ground of red lotuses (paduma).

And herein, since in the Pali language there is no seventh place called a hundred thousand, but only six places exist, the teachers, having bypassed the seventh place according to the method found in the commentaries (Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 1.181):
When explaining the transition between planes from the sixth stage upwards, they speak by multiplying by a hundred:
a hundred times a hundred thousand is a *koṭi*, and a hundred times a hundred thousand *koṭis* is a *pakoṭi*, and so forth.
In that context, "a hundred times a hundred thousand" is simply ten times a hundred thousand; therefore, it is as follows:
It should be understood that even when they speak of the various grounds (*bhūmi*) and all locations, they are speaking specifically of the accomplishment of the ten qualities.
Furthermore, because the "path of calculation" (*gaṇanapatha*), which is synonymous with the grounds of calculation, is of various kinds according to the inhabitants of different regions,
[the author] has excluded the *akkhobhiṇī*, *bindu*, *kathāna*, and *mahākathāna* from the *Dīpavaṃsa* and followed the method of the Pāḷi [tradition], resulting in seventeen [grounds].
The planes (*bhūmi*) have already been mentioned. In Kaccāyana (Ka. 394, 395; Rū. 416, 417), twenty-one planes were previously shown;
in the Sakkata texts, there are more than that number of planes; however, in some places, sixty planes are recorded, ending with the *Mahābalakkhandha*.

Among these, the factors exceeding their respective planes are said to be beyond the path of calculation (*gaṇanapathavītivatta*); as for those which possess even only the root plane, even their mere millions of factors are indeed transcendent of the path of calculation.
Moreover, "beyond the path of calculation," "transcending the path of calculation," and "incalculable" (asaṅkhyeyya) are identical in meaning.
Therefore, here too, it is precisely twenty planes multiplied successively by ten that are called the "path of calculation.
However, the term "incalculable" refers specifically to a plane that transcends the path of calculation, being free from even tenfold multiplication.

For from the point of transcending the stage of the Great Discourse (*mahākathānabhūmi*) onwards, even all the dust particles of the infinite great earth are included here within the stage of the incalculable (*asaṅkhyeyya*). Otherwise, it would be contradictory for something to be both "incalculable" and "within the range of calculation.
And in the *Dīpavaṃsa*, it is said: "Beyond that is no ground; it is called 'incalculable' (*asaṅkhyeyya*). In that context, "no ground" (*abhūmi*) means—

By means of speech, the very ground of the path of calculation (*gaṇanapathabhūmi*) is excluded, but there is no separate ground called "the incalculable" (*asaṅkhyeyya*) that transcends the path of calculation.
In the *Cariyāpiṭaka-vaṇṇanā* as well, this meaning has been stated in the eight introductory narratives (*nidānakathā*).

Furthermore, even regarding the ground of the incalculable, its many divisions—such as the "small incalculable" (*cūḷa-asankheyya*) and the "great incalculable" (*mahā-asankheyya*)—should be illustrated by the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta* (Majjhima Nikāya 142).
In the *Saddanīti* (Nī. 833), however, adopting the method of the Pāḷi, it is stated that "twenty Abbudas make one Nirabbuda;
twenty Nirabbudas make one Ababa," and so forth, asserting that even the enumeration of the Nirabbuda and other hells increases by a factor of exactly twenty.
That is not tenable. For in the hells, [the duration] of the Abbuda, Nirabbuda, and others does not increase by a factor of exactly twenty.
The names of those ten hells are established. However, the teachers, having taken those names, included them within the numerical sequences of the ten-fold siddhis;
therefore, they are similar merely by name, but the method of their qualities (*guṇa-vidhi*) is indeed different.
Having done so, it is stated even in the Pāḷi, in the *Baka-Brahmā Sutta* (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.175): "A hundred thousand *nirabbudas*..."

"I know your lifespan, O Brahmā," it is said. And here, if even on the path of calculation there were only twenty *nirabbudas* to constitute one *abbuda*, then a "hundred thousand *nirabbudas*" would not be mentioned.
Furthermore, in the *Jātaka-ṭṭhakathā* (JA II 421), it says: "One hundred thousand *nirabbudas* is called one *ahaha*."
"It is said that this much of the lifespan remained for the Brahmā Baka in that existence.
Therefore, it is established that once one has reached this path of numerical stages, there is no such thing as a "twenty-fold" multiplication.
The terms *akkhobhiṇī*, *bindu*, *kathāna*, and *mahākathāna* may have been inserted by taking them from elsewhere. And regarding these fourteen numbers thus inserted, in the Kaccāyana [grammar]:
"But the desire for liberation may be posteriorly arisen.
Thus ends the fourth section, the Section on Compounds, in the Elucidation of Moggallāna’s Grammar, known as the Elucidation of Etymology.
5. Taddhita.
Now the exposition of *taddhita* suffixes is illuminated.
That which is called *taddhita*-formation is manifold; it especially brings benefit to those of diverse wisdom. Therefore, for their sake—
"Beneficial for those sons of good family" is *taddhita* (a secondary derivative); this is the name for all types of derivation in this section.

That, moreover, is eightfold: *apacca* (patronymic), *anekattha* (polysemous), *assatthi* (possessive), *bhāvakamma* (abstract action), *parimāṇa* (measure), *saṅkhyā* (numeral), *khuddaka* (minor), and *nānātta* (differentiation).
Apaccā-rāsi 430. *Ṇo* or *vāpacce* (*ka*). [Kaccāyana 344; Rūpasiddhi 361; Nyāsa 752; Cāndra 2.4.16; Pāṇini 4.1.92; cf. ‘*sarānamādissā…*’ in many texts.
The suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs after a noun ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) in the sense of “belonging to that” (*tassa apaccanti*). The word *vā* indicates an alternative.
The purpose of this [rule] is to provide an alternative for compounds; it follows from hereafter, and by means of it, the rules for alternatives are established in all instances.

The suffix *ṇ* has *ā* as its *anubandha* (indicatory letter) for the purpose of vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*); it may or may not be employed. By this sutta, in the sense of "Vasiṭṭha’s descendants," the suffix *ṇa* is added after *vasiṭṭha*.
This [suffix] expresses both the sense of equality (*sāmyattha*) and the sense of descendants (*apaccattha*), and it involves both the genitive case and the word *apacca* (descendant).

Thus they become names of what has been stated; the word *vasiṭṭha* (descendant of Vasiṣṭha) is synonymous with the *paccaya* (suffix), and the meaning is that both together constitute the name of the son. Then, by the rule "due to synonymy" (*ekatthatāya*), there is the elision of the genitive case;
however, the word *apacca* (descendant) is elided merely because its meaning has already been expressed. For that [word] is indicated in the sutta as being the primary element, not the genitive case.
Or, there is the elision of words according to the great grammatical tradition (*mahāvutti*).
This applies everywhere. 431. *Padānamādissāyuvaṇṇassāeo ṇānubandhe ka* (Pāṇini 7.1.2). Rule 365; Nīti 860:

When a suffix with *ṇ* as its *anubandha* follows, the *vṛddhi* vowels *ā*, *e*, and *o* replace the initial *a*, *i*, or *u* of words. Thus, by the rule "the *vṛddhi* vowel *ā* replaces the initial *a* of words," the *ā-vṛddhi* occurs, and the case endings beginning with *si* arise.

A man of the Vāsiṭṭha [lineage] is a *vāsiṭṭha*, a woman of the Vāsiṭṭha [lineage] is a *vāsiṭṭhī*, a family of the Vāsiṭṭha [lineage] is a *vāsiṭṭha* clan, the son of Vasiṣṭha is a *vāsiṭṭha*, the daughter of Vasiṣṭha is a *vāsiṭṭhī*, and the family of Vasiṣṭha is the *vāsiṭṭha* [clan].

Thus it is appropriate to apply [the term] in this way as well. In that context, by the phrase “of Vasiṣṭha” (*vasiṭṭhassa*), one refers to the original ancestor who is the father of the lineage itself. Why? Because it is a word denoting a lineage (*gotta*). For when this is the case, all people subsequently born into that lineage are called his descendants (*apacca*).
In the middle of words, the vowels *a*, *i*, and *u* optionally become their respective *vuddhi* (increment) vowels—*ā*, *e*, and *o*—in certain instances.

Thus: *vāseṭṭho*, *vāseṭṭhī*, *vāseṭṭhaṃ*. By means of the word *vā* (“or”), one may form either the analytical sentence (*vākya*)—"the son, daughter, or family of Vasiṣṭha"—or the compound (*samāsa*)—"the son of Vasiṣṭha," "the daughter of Vasiṣṭha," or "the family of Vasiṣṭha.
This applies everywhere. The descendant (*apacca*) of Bharadvāja is Bhāradvāja; likewise for the descendant of Visāmitra-Bharadvāja... Vesāmitra... (as per the grammatical forms).
The offspring of Vesāmitta is Vesāmitta; the offspring of Gotama is Gotama; the offspring of Kassapa is Kassapa;
the offspring of Vasudeva is Vāsudeva. So too is Bāladeva.

Regarding the phrase “the offspring of Upagu,” here [the rule] applies: “uvaṇṇa becomes avaṅ before a suffix with a nasal as its marker (ṇānubandha). Thus, *uvaṇṇa* becomes *avaṅ* when followed by a suffix having *ṇ* as its marker.
[The suffix] *a* occurs [after these]. For example: *opagava*, *opagavī*, *opagavam*; the offspring of *manu* is *mānava*; the offspring of *bhaggu* is *bhaggava*;
the offspring of *paṇḍu* is *paṇḍava*; the offspring of *upavindu* is *opavindava*, and so forth. 433.
After *vaccha* and others, the suffixes *ṇa*, *āna*, *ṇya*, and *naka* [are applied]. (Kaccāyana 345; Rūpasiddhi 366; Niddesa 754; Pāṇini 4.1.93, 94, 162, 163).
After the sixth group of words beginning with *vaccha*—namely, the class of words known as *gotta* (clans)—the suffixes *āna*, *āya*, and *na* optionally occur to denote "his descendant.
Thus, from *vaccha*, the forms are *vacchāno*, *vacchāyano*, *vacchānī*, *vacchāyanī*, *vacchānaṃ*, and *vacchāyanaṃ*.
Likewise: *kaccāno*, *kaccāyano*; *kātiyāno*, *kātiyāyano*; *sākaṭāno*, *sākaṭāyano*; *kaṇhāno*, *kaṇhāyano*.
*Moggallāna*, *moggallāyana*, *aggivessāna*, and *aggivessānī* are also seen (Dīgha Nikāya 1.176;
Majjhima Nikāya 1.353, etc.), as are *aggivessāyana*, *muñcāna*, *muñcāyana*, *kuñcāna*, *kuñcāyana*, and so forth. 434.
From *kattika*, *vidhava*, and others, the suffixes *ṇeya*, *ṇa*, and *era* are applied (Kaccāyana 346; Rūpasiddhi 367; Niddesa 755; Pāṇini 4.1.120, 123, 126, 127, 128, 129, 131).

The suffix *eya* occurs after words ending in the sixth case, such as *kattikā*, etc., and after words like *vidhavā*, etc., to denote offspring (*apacca*); it is applied according to the sequence [of the respective bases], or else the suffix *eyya* is used.
Examples of the suffix *eyya*: the offspring of the divine maiden named Kattikā is *Kattikeyyo*; the offspring of the goddess named Vinatā is *Venateyyo*;
the offspring of the goddess named Rohiṇī is *Rohiṇeyyo*; the offspring of a sister is *Bhāgineyyo*.
The offspring of a woman named Nadi is *nādeyya*. Likewise, [the offspring of] an *anteyyā*, an *āheyyā*, and a *kāmeyyā*;
the offspring of a *suci* is *soceyya*; the offspring of a *bālā* is *bāleyya*, and so forth.
Regarding the suffix *-ṇera*: the offspring of a *vidhavā* is *vedhavero*; a *vidhavā* is a woman whose husband has died. The offspring of a *bandhuki*...
Bandhukera is the son of a woman named Nāḷikiyā, thus he is called Nāḷikera; a novice monk (sāmaṇera) is the son of a male ascetic (samaṇa), his preceptor (upajjhāya);
a female novice (sāmaṇerī) is the daughter of a female ascetic (samaṇī), his presiding nun (pavattinī), and so forth.
435. The suffix *Ṇya* [is added] after words such as *ditya*, etc. (Ka. 347; Rū. 368; Nī. 756; Caṃ. 2.4.2; Pā. 4.1.85).
After the sixth case endings, such as *diti* and others, the suffix *ya* optionally occurs with the meaning "belonging to that" (*tassa apaccati*).
436. *Lopovaṇṇivaṇṇānaṃ ka.* 261; *rū.* 369; *nī.* 509.
"When *ye* follows, there is the elision of *avaṇṇa* and *ivaṇṇa*. Thus, when the suffix *ṇya* follows, there is the elision of *avaṇṇa* and *ivaṇṇa*.
The offspring of the divine maiden named Diti is Decca; the offspring of Aditi is Ādicca.

Therein, upon the elision of the *ivaṇṇa* vowel, by the rule “for the *tavagga* and *varaṇa* [consonants], there are the *cavagga* and *bayañña* [substitutes] when followed by *ya*,” the *tavagga* becomes the *cavagga* before the following *ya*. Then, by the rule “those [substitutes] are replaced by the preceding form when followed by a *vagga* or a *lasa* [consonant],” the *ya* is replaced by its preceding form.
The offspring of Kuṇḍanī is Koṇḍañño. 437. *Uvaṇṇassāvaṅ sare*: When a vowel follows, *avaṅ* is substituted for *uvaṇṇa*. (Kaccāyana 348; Rūpasiddhi 371; Nyāsa 757).

"avaṅ becomes [the substitute] for uvaṇṇa"—this is the substitution of ava for uvaṇṇa. By the rule "tavaggavaraṇāna... there is the substitution of ba for va; then, by the rule "vaggalasehi te," there is the prior-form (pubbarūpa) substitution of ya for y.
The offspring of a brother is *bhātabyo*. 438. *Ā ṇi ka.* 347; *rū.* 368; *nī.* 756; *caṃ.* 2.4.19; *pā.* 4.1.95.

After a short vowel ending in the letter *ā*, when the sense is not that of offspring (*apaccattha*), the suffix *ṇā* (with *ṇ* as its *anubandha*) optionally functions as a short vowel (*rassī*) suffix.
The offspring of Dakkha is Dakkhi. Likewise, [the offspring] of Doṇa is Doṇī; of Vāsava, Vāsavi; of Sakyaputta, Sakyaputti; of Nāṭaputta, Nāṭaputti; of Dāsa, Dāsī;
the offspring of Dāruṇa is Dāruṇī—this is to be analyzed in this manner. The offspring of Varuṇa is Vāruṇī. Likewise, [the offspring] of Kaṇḍu is Kaṇḍī;
of Bāladeva, Bāladevī; of Pāvaka, Pāvaki; of Jinadatta, Jenadatti; of Suddhodana, Suddhodanī; of Anuruddha, Anuruddhī, and so forth.
When descent (*jāti*) is implied, the suffix *-ña* optionally occurs after the word *rājan*, provided there is no sense of offspring (*apacca*).
*Rañño apaccaṃ rājañño*: the offspring of a king, meaning a son of the royal family.
What is meant by "jāti" (genus)? For example: *rājaputto* (a prince).
440. *Khattā yiyā ka*. When genus (*jāti*) is implied, the suffixes *ya* and *iya* occur after the word *khatta*, provided that a case-ending other than the accusative (*apaccatthe*) follows.
*Rū*: 368; *Nī*: 756; *Caṃ*: 2.4.69; *Pā*: 4.1.138. When genus is understood, the suffixes *ya* and *iya* are applied after the word *khatta* when it does not bear the sense of the accusative case.
The offspring (*apacca*) of the *khatta* clan is a *khatya*, that is, a *khattiya*.
Is it only by birth (*jāti*) [that one is so called]?
A *khattiya*. [Note: This entry refers to grammatical rules for the derivation of the term *khattiya* from *khatta* according to various Pali grammatical treatises.]
When *jāti* (birth/species) is being expressed, the suffixes *ssa* and *na* occur after the word *manu* when no further derivative meaning is intended.
The offspring of *manu* is a *manusso* or a *mānuso*. *Manu* was the first Kṣatriya, King Mahāsammata, in the [first] eon (*kappa*). In the feminine, it is *manussī* or *mānusī*.
Only when expressing *jāti*? [Answer: *Māṇavo*.

442. From a name of a country (*janapada*), the suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word denoting a Kṣatriya, and [it denotes] both a king and his descendant. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.52; Rūpasiddhi 376; Nyāsa 765; Candra-vyākaraṇa 2.4.96; Pāṇini 4.1.168). “From a name of a country, after a word denoting a Kṣatriya... (as found in many texts).
From a name of a country that denotes people and also denotes a Kṣatriya, the suffix *ṇo* occurs to denote both a king and a descendant.
For example: the king of the people of Pañcāla is *Pañcāla*; the descendant of the Kṣatriya Pañcāla is *Pañcāla*. Likewise: *Kosala*, *Māgadha*, *Okkāka* (Dīgha Nikāya 1.267).
What is the purpose of the rule *janapadanāmnaḥ sma*? [Examples: The son of King Daśaratha is *Dāśarathi* or *Dāśarathi*.
Why [is it] *janakhattiyāt*? The descendant of the Brahmin Pañcāla is *Pañcāli*.
443. *Ṇya* after *Kuru* and *Sivi*; *ka* [after others]. (Pāṇini 4.1.172; Rūpasiddhi 367; Nyāsa 755; Cāndra 2.4.101 …pe…)
After *kuru* and *sivi*, the suffix *ṇya* occurs when meaning "descendant" (*apacca*) or "king" (*raññe*).

The descendant of King Kuru is a *korabya*. [Aṇ 1.14.228, 232, 236] The king of those dwelling in the kingdom of Kuru is a *korabya* or *korabba*; this is due to the restoration of the original form (*pubbarūpatta*). The descendant of King Sivi is a *sebya*; the king of those dwelling in the kingdom of Sivi is a *sebya*. The section on descendants is concluded.
Anekattharāsi 444. *Ṇa*:
"Ratta" [is derived] from *rāga*. (Ka. 347; Rū. 368; Nī. 756; Caṃ. 3.1.1 …pe… 4.2.1).
That by which one is colored is *rāga*—that is, the substance for coloring. From a word expressing *rāga*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs in the sense of "colored by that."

A cloth dyed with *kasāva* (safflower) is called *kāsāva*; likewise *kāsāya*. Similarly, [a cloth] dyed with *kosumbha* (madder) is *kosumbha*; dyed with turmeric is *hālidda*; dyed with *pāṭaṅga* is *pāṭaṅga*; as well as *mañjiṭṭha*, *kuṅkuma*, and so forth.

However, in expressions such as "a blue cloth" (*nīlaṃ vatthaṃ*) or "a yellow cloth" (*pītaṃ vatthaṃ*), words like *nīla* and *pīta*, being quality-words (*guṇasadda*), denote the substance that is the substratum of the quality without requiring a suffix.

This applies to all quality-words (*guṇasadda*), genus-words (*jātisadda*), and proper nouns (*nāmasadda*). 445. At the time when the moon is joined with a lunar mansion... [Kaccāyana 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa 765; Candra 3.1.5; Pāṇini 4.2.3].
When a time is characterized by a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*) joined with the moon (*indu*), the suffix *ṇo* occurs after words denoting that lunar mansion. For example:

*phussā ratti*, "the night marked by the full moon and the Phussa lunar mansion"; *phusso aho*, "the day [marked by] Phussa. Similarly: *māgho* [ratti], etc. Why say "by a lunar mansion"? [To exclude:
*garugahena lakkhitā ratti*, "a night marked by a malignant planet."
What is the meaning of *induyuttena*? A muhutta marked by Phussa.
What is the meaning of *kāle*? Prosperity (*atthasiddhi*) marked by Phussa.
446. *Sā assa devatā puṇṇamāsī* (Ka. 352; Rū. 376; Nī. 765; Caṃ. 3.1.18, 19 …pe… 4.2.21–24).
The word *sā* (she) becomes *sā* [with the suffix] when it means "his deity" or "his full-moon day"; thus, the nominative singular ending *ṇo* occurs.

*Buddho assa devatā* means "the Buddha is his deity," i.e., *buddho*. This is the name for one who wanders about honoring the Buddha as if he were his own protective deity, or who constantly utters the words "Buddha, Buddha. *Sugato assa devatā*... [means "the Sugata is his deity"].
*Sogata* means the deity Mahinda; thus he is *Māhinda*. Likewise for *Yāma*, *Soma*, and *Vāruṇa*.

*Phussī* refers to the full-moon day; thus it is the month *Phussa*. Likewise for *Māgha*, *Phagguṇa*, *Citta*, *Vesākha*, *Jeṭṭhamūla*, *Āsāḷha*, *Sāvaṇa*, *Poṭṭhapāda*, *Assayuja*, *Kattika*, and *Māgasira*. What is meant by "full-moon day"?
It refers to the fifth lunar date (*tithi*) of the month of *Phussa*.
447. *Tam adhīte tam jānāti* (Kaṇikā 351; Rūpasiddhi 374; Niddesa 764; Canda-vutti 3.1.37 …pe… 4.2.59).
In these senses, the suffixes *ṇo*, *ko*, and *ṇiko* are added to a word ending in the accusative case. With the suffix *ṇa*:

one who studies or knows grammar (*byākaraṇa*) is called a *Veyyākaraṇo* (Dīgha Nikāya 1.256). In the alternative [with the suffix *ika*], *Veyyākaraṇiko* and, likewise, one who studies or knows the phrasing (*byañjana*) is called a *Veyyañjaniko*—these are formed with the suffix *ṇika*.
In the sense of *adhīte* (he studies) or *jānāti* (he knows), *chanda* [forms] *chandika*: one who studies or knows the *Chandas*. Likewise, *padaka*, etc. (Dīgha Nikāya 1.256), and *nāmaka*.
In the sense of *adhīte* or *jānāti*, *vinaya* [with the suffix] *ṇika* forms *venayika*: one who studies or knows the Vinaya; likewise, *suttantika* and *ābhidhammika*.
And here, for the word *veyyākaraṇo*, the sentence is "one who has studied grammar" (*byākaraṇaṃ adhīte*); for the word *veyañjaniko*, [the sentence is "one who has studied the phonetics"].

Regarding the phrase "he has studied the phonology": in the subsequent sections such as "the gatekeeper" (*dovāriko*) and "leading to heaven" (*sovaggikaṃ*), although the sentences would be "appointed to the gate" (*duvāre niyutto*) and "conducive to a good realm" (*suvaggāya saṃvattati*), when explaining the meaning, one should state them as *dvāra* and *saggāya*.
This is because the status of these as *taddhita* (secondary derivative) suffixes is established only through the words *dvāra* and *sagga*.
448. *Tassa visaye dese* (Kaccāyana 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa 365; Cāndra 3.1.61; Pāṇini 4.2.52, 53).
The suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case when it denotes a region (*desa*) as its object (*visaya*).

For example: *thūyamigā vasātino nāma*, [meaning] "the deer of Thūya are called Vasātins"; *vasātīnaṃ visayo deso vāsāto*, "the region that is the domain of the Vasātins is Vāsāta. In this instance, because it does not denote a region, *ṇo* does not occur: *cakkhussa visayo rūpaṃ*, "the object of the eye is visible form."
449. *Nivāse tannāme* (Kaccāyana 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa 365; Canda-vutti 3.1.64; Pāṇini 4.2.69).
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word ending in the genitive case when it denotes a place of residence that bears that same name. For example:

*Sivīnaṃ nivāso deso sebyo* ("The country which is the residence of the Sivis is Sebya"). Those who eat fat (*vasa*) are called *vasādā*, such as tigers or lions; the country which is the residence of the *vasādā* is *vāsāda*.
450. *Anubhave* (Kaccāyana-vutti 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā 765; Canda-vutti 3.1.65; Pāṇini 4.2.70).
That which exists nearby is *anubhavaṃ*; there is also a reading, *adūrabhave*. In the sense of a place named after that, the suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case.
For example: *vidisāya anubhavaṃ* = *vedisaṃ* (a city); *udumbarassa anubhavaṃ* = *odumbaraṃ* (a celestial mansion).
The suffix *ṇo* is applied after a word in the third case when it denotes a place produced by that [person or thing].
*Kosambī*: [the city] produced by the seer named Kusamba; in the feminine, the suffix *ī* is added, hence it is a city (*nagarī*). Likewise, *kākandī*, *mākandī*.
Produced by a thousand pieces of wealth, it is "sāhassī" (worth a thousand); this [term] is a moat (*parikhā*).

This third [suffix] is appropriately applied according to the context to the cause (*hetu*), the agent (*kattar*), and the instrument (*karaṇa*). 452. *Tamidhatthi* (Ka. 352; Rū. 376; Nī. 765; Caṃ. 3.1.67; Pā. 4.2.67).
The suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case when it means "this exists here," referring to the meaning itself or to a place bearing that name.
For example: because *udumbarā* (fig trees) exist in this place, it is called *odumbaro*; because *badarā* (jujube trees) exist in this place, it is called *bādaro*. Likewise, *pabbajo*. 453.
The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of "existing there" (*tatra bhave*). [Kacc 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa 765; Candra 3.2.48; Pāṇini 4.2.133].
In that context, the suffix *ṇa* occurs after a word ending in the seventh case (*sattamī*).
*Udake bhavo* (that which exists in water) is *odaka*, as in a fish; *urasi bhavo* (born from the breast) is *orasa*, as in a son; *sāgama*. *Nagare bhavo* (existing in the city) is *nāgara*.

Likewise, *jānapada* (belonging to the country), *māgadha* (of Magadha), and *kapilavatthumhi bhavo* (born in Kapilavatthu) is *kāpilavatthava*. [This is according to the rule: “*uvaṇṇassa avaṅ*... (the *avaṅ* substitution for *u-vaṇṇa*...).
*Ussa-avattaṃ*. That which exists in Kosambī is *kosamba*; that which exists in *mettā* is *mettā*; that which exists in a city (*pura*) is *porī*, as in *vācā* (Dīgha Nikāya 1.9);
that which exists in the mind (*manas*) is *mānasa*.
Here, however—[refer to] *Manādīnaṃ saka* (Kaccāyana-vutti 404; Rūpasiddhi 370; Nyāsa 859).

When a suffix marked with the *Ṇ* anubandha follows, the augment *s* is inserted at the end of words such as *manas*. Thus, in all instances, the augment *s* is added to the end of the group of words beginning with *manas*:

*mānaso*, *rāgo*, *mānasā*, *taṇhā*, *mānasaṃ*, *sukhaṃ*. Likewise: *cetaso*, *cetasā*, *cetasaṃ*. In some cases, it is also appropriate to consider that *mano* itself is *mānasaṃ*, and *ceto* itself is *cetaso*.
455. From *ajja* etc., the suffix *tana* [is added]. (Kaccāyana 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa 765; Candra 3.15; Pāṇini 4.2.105).
In this context, the suffix *tana* is applied after words such as *ajja* (today) when the sense is "being" (*bhava*).
Thus: *ajja bhavo* = *ajjatano*, meaning "belonging to today"; [with case endings: *ajjatani*; [with *dvitta* doubling: *ajjatanaṃ*; [with *hita*: "beneficial for today. *Sve bhavo* = *svātano*;
by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), the substitution of *ātta* occurs for *e*. *Hiyyo bhavo* = *hiyyattano*; [with case endings: *hiyyattano*, *hiyyattanaṃ*.
*ossa attaṃ dvittañca*. 456.
*Purāto ṇo ca ka*. 352; *rū.* 376; *nī.* 765.
In the sense of "therein" (*tatra*), the suffixes *ṇo* and *ka* occur after the word *purā*.
The pure being is ancient; here there is no further connection, whether ancient or primordial.
457. *Amātvacco* (from *amā* + *tvacca*). Rule 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa 765; Candra-vyākaraṇa 3.2.13; Pāṇini 4.2.104.
After the word *amā*, the suffix *-acca* occurs in the sense of "being" (*bhava*). *Amā* is a term expressing "together with."
An *amacca* is one who exists together with the king in royal affairs (*rājakiccesu raññā saha bhavati*), according to the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* (1.339, 458);

the *Majjhimādi-niddesa* (ka. 353; rū. 378; nī. 767); the *Candavuttasaṅgaha* (3.2.82); and the *Pāṇini-sūtra* (4.3.8, 22), where it says: “The suffix *ima* occurs after [the group] beginning with *majjha* in the sense of ‘being there’ (*bhavatthe*)” (in many texts, it reads *majjhāditvimo*).
Thus, the suffix *ima* is applied after words such as *majjha* when expressing the state of being therein.
*Majjha* becomes *majjhima*. Likewise: *antima*, *heṭṭhima*, *uparima*, *orima*, *pacchima*, *abbhantarima*, *paccantima*, *puratthima*.
(Pāṇini 5.3.35–46). These five suffixes are added to words ending in the locative case when expressing the sense of "being in" (*bhav-attha*).

Born in Kaṇṇakujja-Kusinārā is a Kaṇṇakujjaka; born in Magadha is a Māgadha; [born in] the forest is a forest-dweller (āraññaka); [born in] a monastery is a monastic (vihāra). Born by the Gaṅgā is a Gaṅgeyya;
born on a mountain is a mountaineer (pabbateyya); born in the forest is a forest-born (vāneyya).

Born in Koṭṭhaka is a Koṭṭhakeyyaka; born in Kosala is a Kosaleyyaka; born in Bārāṇasī is a Bārāṇaseyyaka; born in Campā is a Campeyyaka; born in Mithilā is a Mithileyyaka; here there is no further increase.
*Gammo*: that which exists in a village (*gāma*). *Dibbo*: that which exists in heaven (*diva*). *Iya-gāmiyo*, *gāmiko*:

[suffixes] for one who goes to a village. *Odariyo*, *odariko*: that which exists in the belly (*udara*). *Diviyo*: that which exists in heaven (*diva*). *Pañcāliyo*: [one who belongs to] Pañcāla. *Bodhipakkhiyo*: [that which pertains to] the wings of enlightenment.
*Lokiyo*: [that which pertains to] the world (*loka*). 460. The suffix *ṇika* (forms the word *lokiyo*): Ka. 351; Rū. 374; Nī. 764; Caṃ. 3.2.40, 41, 42; Pā. 4.2.126, 127, 128.
The suffix *ṇika* occurs after the word *bhava* when it ends in the locative case (*sattamī*).
Examples: *sāradiko divaso* (an autumn day), *sāradikā ratti* (an autumn night), *sāradikaṃ pupphaṃ* (autumn flowers).

Furthermore, by means of the word *bhava*, other meanings are also indicated here: a river that has descended from a mountain is called *pabbateyyā*; that which is born in the cocoon of silkworms is called *koseyyaṃ*.
Cloth. Thus: *siveyya* (cloth from Sivi), *bārāṇaseyya* (cloth from Benares). 461.

In the senses of "this is his craft," "this is his habit," "this is his merchandise," "this is his weapon," or "this is his purpose," the suffix *-ika* is added after a word in the nominative case. (Kaccāyana 3.4.49–66; Rūpasiddhi 374; Niddesa 764; Candasiddhanta 4.4.47–65). That is to say:

when the meanings are "this is his craft," "this is his habit," "this is his merchandise," "this is his weapon," or "this is his purpose," the suffix *-ika* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case.

**Craft:** Lute-playing is his craft; he is a lute-player (*veṇiko*). And here, by the word "lute" (*vīṇā*), lute-playing is meant. For this is [an example of] the power of forming a compound (*ekatthībhāva*). So it is in all cases. Likewise for the drum-player (*modiṅgiko*), the cymbal-player (*pāṇaviko*), and the flute-player (*vaṃsiko*).
**Virtue:** Wearing rag-robes is his virtue; he is a rag-robe wearer (*paṃsukūliko*). Or, he is a rag-robe wearer because wearing rag-robes is his habit (*sīla*).
And here, by the word "virtue" (*sīla*), vows (*vata*), duties (*dhamma*), and expressions of approval (*sādhukāra*) are also included; [it means] he wears rag-robes.

"By virtue of his virtue" (*sīlena*) also applies to the term *paṃsukūlika*. Likewise, one who possesses the three robes is a *tecīvarika*. As for *piṇḍapāta*: it is that which falls from morsel to morsel;
food obtained by wandering for alms (*piṇḍācāra*); or his virtue consists in subsisting on alms-food—thus he is a *piṇḍapātika*.
Furthermore, he is a *piṇḍapātika* because his virtue, observance, duty, and respect consist in subsisting by means of alms-food.
‘Paṇya’ means an article for sale; one who has perfume as his merchandise is a *gandhika*. Likewise, a *telika* (oil-seller) and a *goḷika* (sugar-candy seller).
That by which they strike is a *paharaṇa*, a weapon; one who has a bow as his weapon is a *cāpika*. Likewise, a *tomarika* (lance-thrower) and a *muggarika* (club-wielder).

‘Payojana’ means a result or purpose; merit that has acquisition (*upadhi*) as its purpose is *opadhika*. That which has a hundred as its purpose is *sātika*. Likewise, *sāhassika* (worth a thousand).
462. *Taṃ hantārahāti gacchatuñchati carati ka.* (A. 3.5.1; Rū. 374; Nī. 764; Cāndra 3.4.27–43; Pāṇini 4.4.28–46).

The suffix *ka* is added to a word in the accusative case when it has the sense of "one who kills that," "one who deserves that," "one who goes to that," "one who gathers that," or "one who wanders for that.
For example: one who kills birds with the help of birds is a *pakkhika*. Likewise, a *sākuṇika* (also seen as *sākunika*) [is one who lives by killing birds]. (A. ni. 2.263).

A *māyūrika* is one who kills peacocks; a *macchika* is one who kills fish with fish. Likewise, a *dhenuka* is one who kills cows; a *māgavika* is one who kills deer with deer—the vowel *ā* occurs in the middle.
Likewise, a *hāriṇika* is one who kills antelopes—here, "antelope" (*hariṇa*) refers specifically to a deer. A *sūkarika* is one who kills pigs; here there is no vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*).
That which is worth a hundred is *sātika*; likewise, that which is worth a thousand is *sāhassika*.
One who goes to another’s wife is a *pāradārika*, or a *paradārika*. Likewise, a *pathika* (wayfarer) and a *maggika* (roadster).
One who gleans or seeks among *badara* fruits is a *bādarika*. Likewise, an *āmalakika* (one who gathers *āmalaka* fruits).
One who practices the Dhamma is a *dhammika*. Likewise, an *adhammika* (one who practices what is not Dhamma).

463. *Tena kataṃ, kītaṃ, baddhaṃ, abhisaṅkhataṃ, saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, hataṃ, hanti, jitaṃ, jayati, dibbati, khaṇati, tarati, carati, vahati, jīvati ka.* (Kaccāyana 350; Rūpasiddhi 373; Niddesa 364; Canda-vutti 3.4.1–26; Pāṇini 4.4.1–27).
In the senses of "done by that," "bought by that," and so forth, up to "living by that," the suffix *-ika* is added to a word in the third case.
*By the body done*: *kāyikaṃ*. Likewise, *vācasikaṃ* (verbal), *mānasikaṃ* (mental). *Done by the wind*: *vātiko*, [referring to] a disease.
Goods bought for a hundred [coins] with a hundred added is "with a hundred" (*sātika*). Likewise for "with a thousand" (*sāhassika*).
That which is bound with leather is "leather-bound" (*vārattika*); that bound with iron is "iron-bound" (*āyasika*), with an addition. Likewise for "cord-bound" (*pāsika*).
That which is prepared or mixed with ghee is "ghee-based" (*ghātika*). Likewise for "molasses-based" (*goḷika*), "curd-based" (*dādhika*), and "milk-based" (*māricika*).
A "jālika" is a fish caught by a net;
one who kills with a net is a "jālika," meaning one who is addicted to nets. Thus it is for a fisherman (bāḷisika).
Wealth won by dice is "akkhika"; thus it is for a gambler (sālākika).
One who wins or plays with dice is called *akkhika*.
One who digs with a spade is called *khāṇittika*. Likewise for *kuddālika*; here there is no vowel lengthening (*vuddhi*).
One who crosses by means of a raft is called *oḷumpika* or *uḷumpika*. Likewise for *nāvika*. [And] *gopucchika*.
One who travels by cart is a *sākaṭika*. Likewise, a *rathika* (charioteer), a *yānika* (carriage-bearer), and a *daṇḍika* (staff-bearer).
One who carries on the shoulder is a *khandhika*. Likewise, an *aṃsika* (shoulder-carrier) and a *sīsika* (head-carrier);

here there is no suffix *i*. One who lives by wages is a *vetanika*. Likewise, a *bhatika* (hireling), a *kasika* (ploughman), a *kayika* (buyer), and a *vikkayika* (seller); in the case of *bhatika* and so forth, there is no suffix *i*.
464. *Tassa saṃvattati* (It leads to that). [Kaccāyana 351; Rūpasiddhi 374; Niddesa 765; Cāndra 3.4.67–69; Pāṇini 4.4.66–68].
In the sense of "it leads to that," the suffix *ṇika* is applied to a word ending in the fourth case (*catutthī*).

For example: *puna-bhavāya saṃvattati* ("it leads to renewed existence") becomes *ponobbhaviko*. Here, *puna* remains as it is, and *bhassa* undergoes doubling (*dvitta*), resulting in *ponobbhaviko*. [The feminine form is] *ponobbhavikā*.
“Mahāva. 14: ‘It leads to the world,’ thus it is worldly (*lokika*); ‘it is truly the highest (*agga*)’ thus it is heaven (*sagga*);

‘it leads to heaven,’ thus it is heavenly (*sovaggika*), [namely] merit (*puñña*). Thus [there is merit] pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*).
465. ‘That which has arisen from that, has come from that’: Ka. 351; Rū. 374; Nī. 765; Caṃ. 3.3.49–51; …pe… 4.3.77–79.”
The suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the fifth case (ablative) in the sense of "originated from that" or "come from that. For example:
*mātito sambhūtaṃ āgataṃ vā mattikaṃ pārā* ("originated from or come from the mother—maternal"). [Pāṇini 4.3.24] *dvittaṃ rasso ca*: likewise *pettikaṃ*.

The suffixes *ṇya* and *ṇiya* are also seen: *surabhito sambhūtaṃ sorabhyaṃ* ("originated from a fragrant source—fragrance"), *thanato sambhūtaṃ thaññaṃ* ("originated from the breast—breast-milk"), and *pitito...* [originated from the father].
*Sambhūta* [is derived from *pitṛ*] with the suffix *ya*. Similarly, *mattiya* [from *mātṛ*]. In the sense of "one who belongs to" (*ṇyamhi*), *macca* [is used].
466. Regarding the rule: *Tattha vasati vidito bhatto niyutto ka* (Kaccāyana 351; Rūpasiddhi 374; Nyāsa 765; Cāndra 3.4.70–75; ...pe... 4.4.69–74):
the suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the locative case when these meanings are intended: "dwelling there," "known," "served," or "appointed."
"One who dwells at the foot of a tree" is a *rukkhamūlika*. Likewise for the *āraññika* (forest-dweller) and the *sosānika* (charnel-ground dweller).

And here, although the word "dwells" (*vasati*) is a general term, the meaning should be understood according to the sense of "having that as one's habit," "practicing that," "having that as one's nature," or "doing that well," because secondary suffixes (*taddhita-paccaya*) indicate well-known meanings. For it is not [the case that] at the foot of a tree...
One who dwells for even a mere moment [at the foot of a tree] is designated as a "tree-root dweller" (*rukkhamūlika*).
That which is known in the world is "worldly" (*lokiya*).
Those whose food is among the Four Great Kings are the "Four Great Kings' Realm Devas" (*cātumahārājikā*; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081).
*Dovārika* means one appointed at the gate. Likewise for *bhaṇḍāgārika* (treasurer) and *navakammika* (superintendent of works); here there is no increase [of the suffix].

In words such as *jātikiya* and *andhakiya*, the suffix *-kiya* is applied by the general rule (*mahāvutti*). 467. Regarding this, see Kaśikā 3.51; Rūpasiddhi 374; Nyāsa 764; Cāndra 3.3.85–102; Pāṇini 4.3.120–133.
In the sense of "belonging to him" (*tassa idaṃ*), the suffix *-ika* is applied after a word ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*).
This belongs to the Saṅgha; it is the Saṅgha’s monastery, the Saṅgha’s land, this belongs to the Saṅgha, it is the Saṅgha’s property.

In the same way, [one speaks of] what belongs to an individual (puggalika), what belongs to a group (gaṇika), or what belongs to the multitude (mahājanika). "He is one belonging to the Sakyan son" (sakyaputtassa eso) is *sakyaputtiko*. Likewise, *nāṭaputtiko* and *dāsaputtiko*. 468.
The suffixes *ṇika*, *siya*, or *ka* [are applied]. (Kacc 404; Rūpasiddhi 370; Nyāsa 756).
The *iya* vowel optionally replaces the suffix *ṇika*. Examples include *sakyaputtiyo* and *sakyaputtiko*, and so forth.
469. *Ṇo ka*. (Kaṭantra 3.52; Rūpāvatāra 376; Nyāsa 765; Cāndravyākaraṇa 3.3.85; Pāṇini 4.3.120).
The suffix *ṇo* occurs after the sixth case-ending when the sense is "belonging to this.
This [work] belongs to Kaccāyana, thus it is the *Kaccāyana* grammar (*byākaraṇa*). Likewise: *Sogata*, *Sāsana*, *Māhiṃsa*, *Maṃsādi*. 470.
[The suffix] *ya* follows words such as *go* (cow), etc. (Ka. 353; Rū. 378; Nī. 781).
*Tassidaṃ* means "this is its [suffix]. Regarding the rule *gavādīhi yo hoti* (471):
according to *yamhi gossa ca ka* (Pāṇini 7.1.50; Rūpasiddhi 31;

In cases such as *go* (cow), *asso* (horse), and *manusso* (human)—which are genus-words (*jāti-sadda*)—the [suffixes] *manta*, etc., do not apply, because they are capable of denoting a substance (*dabba*).

Likewise, in cases such as *nīlo paṭo* (blue cloth) and *sukko paṭo* (white cloth)—which are quality-words (*guṇa-sadda*)—and in cases such as *tisso* and *phusso*, which are proper-name words (*nāma-sadda*), [they do not apply].
However, they do apply only to those [words] that lack the capacity to denote a substance, such as *buddhimā* (intelligent) and *paññavā* (wise).

The suffix *vantu* occurs in the sense of the possessive suffix *mant*, after a word ending in the nominative case that has become *avaṇṇa*.

One who possesses virtue (*sīlavā*) is so called because he has virtue that is purified by constant observance, or because such virtue exists in him. One who possesses qualities (*guṇavā*) is so called because he has praiseworthy qualities, or because they exist in him.

Thus, in all cases, the specific meaning of the suffix *-vant* should be stated according to the sense of the word-base. One who possesses wisdom (*paññavā*) is so called because he has wisdom accompanied by rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
In some instances, there is shortening of long vowels when a *paccaya* follows. That by which one finds (*vidati*) is "finding" (*vido*).

According to Pāṇini 5.2.115–116 (which corresponds to Kaccāyana 366, Rūpasiddhi 400, Nyāsa 790, and Candra 4.2.118–121): after words such as *daṇḍa*, the suffixes *ika* and *ī* optionally occur in the sense of possession (*mantvatthe*).
Thus, [from *gāṇḍīva*] we derive *gāṇḍīvika* or *gāṇḍīvī*.
One who has constantly taken up a staff (*daṇḍa*) is *daṇḍika*; or one in whom it exists is *daṇḍiko*, *daṇḍī*, or *daṇḍavā*.
Likewise: *gandhiko*, *gandhī*, *gandhavā*; *rūpiko*, *rūpī*, *rūpavā*. When speaking of the owner of a debt, [the suffix] *-ika* is added to *dhana*:

And here, one who has a purpose (*attha*) by means of a purpose not present [to him] is "one who has a purpose" (*atthika*); one who has a great value is "one who has a great value" (*mahagghatthika*).
Likewise, *dhanatthika*, *puññatthika*, and *seyyatthika*. That which has this purpose is "this-purpose" (*idamatthi*);
