However, in the case of *vaṇṇa-saddanta*, it is exactly the same: one who possesses the color (*vaṇṇa*) and the shape (*saṇṭhāna*) of a Brahmā is called *brahmavaṇṇī*.
Alternatively, the color of a Brahmā is *brahmavaṇṇa*; one whose color is like the color of a Brahmā is *brahmavaṇṇī*.
In the same way is *brahmavacchasī*. Here, "head" (*sīsa*) is [the meaning of] *vacchasa*; this is a compound word ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). In the same way is *devavaṇṇī*.

After *hattha*, *danta*, and so forth, the suffix *ī* is used in the sense of birth (*jāti*): *hatthī*, *dantī*, *gajo*, *dāṭhī*, *kesarī*, *sīho*; [but] after *hattha* and *danta*, the suffix *vā* is used instead.
When expressing one who practices the holy life (*brahmacārin*), the suffix *ī* alone is used for color (*vaṇṇa*): *vaṇṇī*; [but] after *vaṇṇa*, the suffix *vā* is used instead.

After *pokkhara* and so forth, the suffix *ī* alone is used in the sense of place (*desa*); *pokkhara* is said to mean a lotus; thus, *pokkharaṇī*. Furthermore, after feminine bases ending in *i*, the suffix *nī* is applied, [and] there is the substitution of *ī* for the preceding *i*.
*Uppalinī*, *kumudinī*, *bhisinī*, *muḷālinī*, *sālukinī*, and *paduminī*: because there are lotuses (*paduma*) in this place, it is called *padumī*;
from that, by adding the feminine suffix *nī*, it becomes *paduminī*. The shortening of the previous long vowel [to *i*] occurs;
this is the name for either a lotus pond or a cluster of lotuses. Except for the case of the "lotus-hand" (*pokkharahatthī*), where here the trunk is called a "lotus" (*pokkhara*).

*Sikhī*, *sikhāvā*; *mālī*, *mālāvā*; *sīlī*, *sīlavā*; *balī*, *balavā*. Even at the end of a compound (*samāsanta*), *-ī* occurs: *niddāsīlī*, *sabhāsīlī*, *bāhubalī*, *ūrubalī*. With *sukha* and *dukkha*, only *-ī* is used: *sukhī*, *dukkhī*, and so forth.
After *tapa* and similar words, *-sī* optionally occurs in the sense of the suffix *-mant*.

One who possesses austerity (*tapas*) or for whom austerity exists is a *tapassī*; this is a formation with the suffix *-in*. Likewise, *yasassī* and *tejassī*. One who has mind (*manas*) is a *manassī*. Why is it not *yasavā*? [Because of the following rule: 478. *Ṇo tapā ka.* (Pāṇini 5.2.103; Kaccāyana 370; Rūpasiddhi 405; Nyāsa 795;

When expressing something auspicious (*kalyāṇa*), the suffix *no* occurs after the word *aṅga* in the sense of the possessive suffix *-mant*.
A woman (*aṅganā*) is one who possesses beautiful limbs (*kalyāṇaṃ aṅgaṃ*);

thus she is called *aṅganā*. (Pāṇini 5.2.100). The suffix *mantu* is added after the word *loman* in the sense of possession. (Kaccāyana 364; Rūpasiddhi 398; Niddesa 787; Candasandhi 4.2.104; Pāṇini 5.2.100).
The suffix *mantu* occurs after *loman* in the sense of possessing that.
"One who has many hairs" is *lomaso*. Here, by the analysis of the sutta, forms such as *sumedhaso* and *bhūrimedhaso* are also established.
The section on the agent (*assatthi*) is completed.
Now, the section on the object (*kammarāsi*).
490. *Tassa bhāvakammesu tta tā ttana ṇya ṇeyyaṇiya ṇa iyā ka.* (Kaccāyana 360; Rūpasiddhi 387; Niddesa 780; Cāndra 4.1.136–153; Pāṇini 5.1.119–136).
In the sense of "its state" (*tassa bhāvo*) or "its action" (*tassa kammaṃ*), these eight suffixes generally occur after a word ending in the sixth case.
Among these, *bhāva* means that from which understanding arises; it is the cause for the initial arising of words within their own respective meanings.
And there is the cause for its occurrence over a long period of time. In this context, the cause for occurrence at the beginning is called the "sign of attainment" (*byappatti-nimitta*).

The cause for occurrence over a long period of time is called the "sign of occurrence" (*pavatti-nimitta*). Both of these are fivefold, according to the categories of genus (*jāti*), substance (*dabba*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and name (*nāma*).
In this context: "The state of a cow is 'cowness'"—here, the genus of the cow is what is called "state.
"'The state of one possessing a staff' is 'staff-ness'"—here, the possession of the staff is what is called "state.
"'The state of a blue cloth' is 'blueness'"—here, the quality of blue is what is called "state."
In the phrase “the state of being a cooker is ‘cooker-ness’” (*pācakassa bhāvo pācakattan*), the act of cooking is what is called “state.
In the phrase “the state of a person named Tissa is ‘Tissa-ness’” (*tissanāmassa janassa bhāvo tissattan*), the name Tissa is what is called “state.

In that context, the meaning of “the state of a cow” (*gossa bhāvo*) is: upon hearing the word “cow,” the cause for the application of the designation “cow” either through the cognition of a cow regarding the substance, or upon seeing the substance, regarding that very substance. In the same way, the meaning should be understood accordingly for the remaining cases as well.

*Tamhi*: the state of being of such-and-such a clan (*gotta*), the state of being punished (*daṇḍitta*), the state of being a cooker (*pācakatta*), the state of being Tissa (*tissatta*), and so forth.
*Tāmhi*: delight in society (*saṅgaṇikārāmatā*), delight in sleep (*niddārāmatā*), delight in talk (*bhassārāmatā*), and so forth.

*Ttanamhi*: the state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjanattana*), the state of being feeling (*vedanattana*), the state of being a paramour (*jārattana*), the state of being a husband (*jāyattana*), and so forth.
The state of one who is inactive (*ṇyamhi-ala*) is *ālasya*; the state of a recluse (*samaṇa*) is *sāmañña*; the state of a brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*) is *brāhmañña*.

The qualities of virtue, concentration, and wisdom are called both *sāmañña* and *brāhmañña*. The state of an ascetic (*tāpasa*) is *tāpasya*; the state of one who is skillful (*nipuṇa*) is *nepuñña*;
the state of one who is extensive (*vipula*) is *vepulla*; the state of a king (*rājā*) is *rajja*; [the state] of a field that has reached the mountains...
The state (*bhāva*) of being a mountain is *āpabbatya*; the state of an heir is *dāyajja*; the state of unevenness is *vesamma*;
the state of a friend is *sakhya*; the state of merchants is *vāṇijja*, and so forth.
In the case of the suffix *-ṇeya*: the state of purity is *soceyya*. Likewise, *ādhipateyya* and so on.
In the suffix *ṇi*: *ālasyaṃ* (laziness), *madiyaṃ* (the state of being intoxicated). Likewise, *dakkhiyaṃ* (skill); *porohitiyaṃ* (the office of a domestic priest);
*veyyattiyaṃ* (the state of one who is proficient); *veyyāvaṭiyaṃ* (the state of one who is occupied)—these two are established like the words of the ancient grammarians (*pubbe veyyākaraṇapadaṃ*).
In the suffix *ṇaṃ*: *gāravo* (respect), *pāṭavaṃ* (proficiency), and so forth.

The state of being a lord is *adhipatibhāva*, [and the corresponding abstract noun] is *adhipatiyaṃ*; the state of being wise is *paṇḍitabhāva*, [and the corresponding abstract noun] is *paṇḍitiyaṃ*; the state of being learned is *bahussutabhāva*, [and the corresponding abstract noun] is *bahussutiyaṃ*; the state of being naked is *naggassa bhāvo*, [and the corresponding abstract noun] is *naggiyaṃ*; the state of being brave is *sūrabhāvo*, [and the corresponding abstract noun] is *sūriyaṃ*;

the state of being a hero is *vīrabhāvo*, [and the corresponding abstract noun] is *vīriyaṃ*—and so forth. In the sense of the object (*kamma*), "object" (*kamma*) means action (*kriyā*). The object of one who is lazy is *alasassa kammaṃ*, [and the corresponding abstract nouns are] *alasattaṃ*, *alasatā*, *alasattanaṃ*, *ālasyaṃ*, *ālaseyyaṃ*, *ālasiyaṃ*, *ālasaṃ*, *alasiyaṃ*—and so forth.
491. *Bya-vaddha-dāsā vā ka.* 360; *rū.* 387; *nī.* 780.
*Bhāva* (the state) and *kamma* (the action) [are formed] from *vaddha* with the suffix *-bya*, or it becomes *dāsebya*.

The state or action of one who is grown (*vaddha*) is *vaddhabbaṃ*, *vaddhattā*, *dāsabbaṃ*, *dāsatā*, or *dāsatā*; here, when the suffix *ṇa* follows, there is optionally the augment *va* [after *vaddha*].

492. *Naṇa yuvā bo ca vaye ka.* (Kaccāyana 361; Rūpasiddhi 388; Niddesa 781; Cāndra 4.1.146; Pāṇini 5.1.130; [variant reading: *...vassa*]). [Note: This rule concerns the substitution of *bo* for the final vowel and following consonant of *yuvan* when the suffixes *na*, *ṇa*, or *ka* follow.]
When the suffix *ya* is applied, there is neither elision (*lopa*) nor substitution (*vāgama*) for the final vowel of the word.
The state of being young (*yuvan*) is "youth" (*yobbanam*). Is it only in this case? No; [it also applies to] "youthfulness" (*yuvattaṃ*) and "the state of being young" (*yuvatā*).
493. *Aṇvādīhim o* (Ka. 360; Rū. 387; Nī. 780; Caṃ. 4.1.139; Pā. 5.1.122): ‘*aṇvāditvimo*’ (in many texts).
The suffix *ima* optionally occurs after these [words] in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*). The state of being minute is *aṇimā*; the state of being light is *laghimā*.
494. *Kassamahatamime kasamahā* [Ka. 404; Rū. 370; Ni. 859; cf. ‘kassaka…’?].
When the suffix *ima* follows, the words *kassa* and *mahanta* respectively become *kasa* and *maha*.

Thus: the work of a farmer (*kassaka*) is *kasimā*; those who are small and great (*kisa-mahantā*) are *kasamahā*. When the suffix *ima* follows, the words *kisa* and *mahanta* [become *kasa* and *maha*].
The state of being *kasa* (thin) is *kasimā*; [the suffix] *mā* is used after *kisa*. (4-133) The state of being great (*mahant*) is *mahimā*.
The state of being *sumana* (joyful) is *somanassa*; [here] the augment *ṇya* is added, and by the rule “*vaggalasehi te*,” there is the substitution of the subsequent form for *y*.
Similarly, [there is] *domanassa*. That in which there is beautiful speech is *suvaca*; the state of being *suvaca* is *sovacassa*. Similarly, [there is] *dovacassa*.
In such expressions as “ārāmarāmaṇeyyakaṃ,” “uyyānarāmaṇeyyakaṃ,” and “bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ,” the word *ramaṇa* means that which is to be enjoyed (*ramitabba*).
That which possesses enjoyment is *rāmaṇo*, namely, a grove (*ārāmo*). The state of being a grove that is enjoyable is *ārāmarāmaṇeyyakaṃ*.

[The suffix] *-ṇeyya-* is used in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*), and how is the meaning of *rāmaṇiya* established? It is established by the suffix *-ka-* in the sense of the base itself, as in the word *kanthā*; thus it signifies the excellence of the grove (*ārāmasampatti*).
"Glory of the grove" (ārāmasirī) is what is meant. The same applies to the remaining [examples].
The section on abstract nouns (bhāva) and the section on action-nominals (kamma) are concluded. Now, the section on measure-words (parimāṇa).
495. *Tamassa parimāṇaṃ* [ṇiko ca]. (Kaccāyana 351; Rūpasiddhi 374; Niddesa 764; Cāndra 4.1.62; Pāṇini 5.1.57, 58).
The suffix *ṇika* and *ka* are added after a word in the nominative case in the sense of "that is its measure" (*tamassa parimāṇaṃ*).
That by which something is measured is "measure" (*parimāṇaṃ*). One whose measure is a *doṇa* is *doṇiko*. Likewise, *khāriko*, *kumbhiko*. One whose measure is eighty years is... [asītivassiko].
"Eighty years" (*āsītiko*), "age. Likewise, "ninety years" (*nāvutiko*). That which has half a body as its measure is *upaḍḍhakāyika*;
a bolster (*bimbohanaṃ*). That which has two as its measure is *duka*. Likewise, *tika*, *catukka*, *pañcaka*, *chakka*, *dvitta*.
*Dasaka*, *sataka*. 496. *Yatetehi ttako ka* (Kaccāyana 391; Rūpasiddhi 423; Niddesa 830; Pāṇini 5.1.22, 23).
In the sense of "the measure of that," the suffix *ttaka* occurs as a substitute for the words *ya*, *ta*, and *eta*.
That which is its measure is *yattaka*; likewise, *tattaka*. 497.
*Etasseṭa ttake ka* (Pāṇini 5.2.40; Rūpasiddhi 370; Nyāsa 859).
The word *eta* becomes *eṭa* before the suffix *para*. That which has this as its measure (*parimāṇa*) is *ettakaṃ*;

that which has as its measure "as far as" (*yāva*) is *yāvattakaṃ*. Similarly, there are *tāvattakaṃ* and *etāvattakaṃ*. By the statement "by *yata*, *ita*, and *eta*," the words *yāva*, *tāva*, and *etāva* are also included.
498. *Sabbā ca ṭāvantu* (Kaccāyana 391; Rūpasiddhi 423; Nyāsa 830; Candra 4.2.43; Pāṇini 5.2.39; 'sabbā cacavantu' [in many manuscripts]).
The suffix *vanta* occurs after the words *tama*, *parimāṇa*, *attha*, *ya*, *te*, *ete*, and *sabbato*;
this [suffix] undergoes doubling (*dvitta*). That which has all as its measure is *sabbāvanta*; [its forms are]:
*sabbāvā*, *attho*, *sabbāvanto*, *sabbāvantā*, *atthā*, *sabbāvati*, *atthe*, *sabbāvantesu*, *atthesu*. In the feminine, [it is] *sabbāvatī*, *sabbāvantī*, [or] *parisā*.
In this manner: *yāvā*, *yāvantā*, *yāvanto*, *tāvā*, *tāvantā*, *tāvanto*, *ettāvā*, *ettāvantā*, *ettāvanto*, and so forth.
In some instances, by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is the elision of one *ta*-sound: *yāvatako kāyo, tāvatako byāmo* (Dīghanikāya 3.200); *yāvatikā yānassa bhūmi* (499). From *kiṃ*:
*rati*, *rīva*, *rīvataka*, *rittaka* (Kaccāyana 391; Rūpasiddhi 423; Niddesa 830; Candra 4.2.45; Pāṇini 5.2.41).
The suffixes *ta*, *ka*, *tu*, and *tva* occur after the word *kiṃ* (what) in the sense of "its measure" (*taṃ assa parimāṇaṃ*).
500. *Rānubandhentasarādissa ka.* (Pāṇini 5.2.39; Rūpasiddhi 558; Nyāsa 1124).

When a suffix with *r* or *n* as its *anubandha* follows, there is elision of the final vowel (*sarādi*) of the word-base (*pada*), and by the word "beginning" (*ādi*), the final consonant (*byañjana*) of the word-base is also included. By the analysis of the sutta, the suffixes *rīvantu* and *rittāvantu* also occur.
"What is its measure? means "how many" (*kati*). Examples include: "How many aggregates (*khandha*) are wholesome, and how many are unwholesome?
(*Vibha* 151); "How many years have you been ordained, monk? "I have been ordained for one year, Blessed One" (*Mahāva* 78). "What is its measure?
means "how much" (*kīvaṃ*), as in "How far is the village from here? Similarly, there are *kīvatakaṃ* and *kittakaṃ*.
In *rīvantumhi*—“How many may there be, O people, who are supplicants? (2.20.103).

In *rittāvantumhi*—“To what extent is there the designation of aggregates for the aggregates? (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.82); “To what extent, venerable sir, is it called ‘form’? To what extent, venerable sir, is it called ‘Māra’? (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.161).
In *ṭāvantumhi* according to the previous sutta—“To this extent is there the designation of aggregates for the aggregates; to this extent is it called ‘form’; to this extent is it called ‘Māra’.”

That by which something is measured is *māna*. It is twofold: *ummāna* (height/measure) and *parimāṇa* (circumference/measure). *Ummāna* is vertical measurement; measurement other than that is *parimāṇa*.
However, because this sūtra uses a general term (*sāmaññavacanattā*), both types are applicable. In these two cases...
When the suffix *matta* occurs in the sense of "that which has such-and-such as its measure," it follows words such as *hattha*.
For example: *hatthamattaṃ* means that which has a cubit as its measure; *dvihatthamattaṃ* means that which has two cubits as its measure;
*dvaṅgulamattaṃ* means that which has two fingers as its measure. Likewise, *caturaṅgulamattaṃ*, *vidatthimattaṃ*, and so forth.
“Only a league” (*yojanamattaṃ*); “measuring three leagues” means having a measure of three leagues (*tiyojanamattaṃ*);
“only a nāḷi,” “only a *pattha*,” “only a *doṇa*”; a *pala* is said to be a specific measure known as a weight;
“having a *pala* as its measure” means measuring a *pala* (*palamattaṃ*); “fivefold” means together with five hundred monks; “thirtyfold,” “sixtyfold.”

“About a hundred,” “about a thousand,” “about ten million,” “about a jar,” “about a bowl,” “about an elephant,” “about a mountain,” and so forth. Alternatively, *mattā* is another word signifying measure (*parimāṇa*);
thus, “an elephant is its measure” is *hatthamattaṃ*. In this way, compounds such as *dvihatthamattaṃ* (measuring two cubits) and others are also appropriate.
However, by means of figurative identification (*abhedūpacāra*), taking the measure of a cubit itself as “a cubit,” one says “two cubits.”
“vatthaṃ, doṇo vīhi, doṇo māso” is thus established. 502.
*Taggha* [occurs] after *uddhaṃ* [in the sense of] “that much. (Ka. 328; Rū. 352; Nī. 708; Caṃ. 4.2.39; Pā. 5.2.37).
The suffix *taggha* and *mat* occur in the sense that words functioning with respect to a measure (*uddhamāna*) are the measure (*parimāṇa*) of that [substance].
*Jaṇṇuparimāṇam assā* means "having the knee as its measure," thus *jaṇṇutagghaṃ*, [or] *jaṇṇumattaṃ*. Regarding *Ṇo ca purisā*: [Pāṇini 5.2.38] ...pe...
From the word *purisa* (man), when it occurs in the sense of measuring upwards (*uddhamāne*), the suffix *Ṇo* is applied, and the words *taggha* and *matta* are also used [as substitutes].
That which has a man of four cubits as its measure is "porisaṃ" (human-sized); thus there is "tiporisaṃ" (three men high), "sataporisaṃ" (a hundred men deep), and "gambhīraṃ" (deep).
Likewise, they say that "porisa" refers to the human measure of five cubits, including the hand extended upwards—namely, what is worth a man or equal to a man.
Regarding the phrase "ekūnatīso vayasā" from the *Dīghanikāya Aṭṭhakathā* (2.214), here "ekūnatīsa" means twenty-nine.

"His measure of lifespan is twenty-nine years," thus it is "twenty-nine. Likewise, "twenty," "thirty," "forty," "fifty," "a thousand-fold Brahmā," "a two-thousand-fold Brahmā," and "a ten-thousand-fold Brahmā.
And here, [the forms] such as "a thousand-fold" (sahassa) are established by means of the suffix -ṇa, according to the rule:
"That which has a thousand as its measure is 'a thousand-fold' (sahassa)," and so forth.
The section on measures (*parimāṇa-rāsi*) is concluded.
The section on numbers (*saṅkhyā-rāsi*): 504. *Eka* [is used] when there is no companion (*asahāya*). (Kaccāyana 391; Rūpasiddhi 423; Niddesa 835; Cāndra 4.2.67; Pāṇini 5.3.52).
In the sense of "without a companion," after the word *eka*, the forms *ka*, *ākī*, or *ā* may occur.
Thus: *asahāyo eko*, *ekako*, *ekākī*, or simply *eko*.
In the feminine: *ekikā*, *ekākinī*, or *ekā*; [the change to *i*] occurs when *ka* follows by the rule *adhātussa ke*.
505. *Dviti* [is used] for the suffixes *tīya* and *ttha*. (Ka. 385; Rū. 409; Nī. 817; Tisatthā?).
In the sense of "the completion of that by means of those," the suffixes *tīya* and *ttha* occur.
506. For the words ending in *dvitī*, *duta* [is substituted] before *tīya*. (Ka. 386, 410; Nī. 818; Tiye?).
In the case of *tīye*, the word *ti* becomes *du* before the suffix *pare*; that is, the substitutes for the word *ti* become *du*.
This is seen in the readings of the Sixth Council (*Chaṭṭhasaṃgīti*) as *dutīyo* (the second), and so forth, meaning "that which completes two.

Thus: *dutīyā* (feminine) means "that which completes two," and *dutīyaṃ* (neuter) means "that which completes two. Likewise: *tatīyo*, *tatīyā*, *tatīyaṃ*. *Catuttho* means "that which completes four."
The fourth, the fourth. 507.
*Ma* [is substituted] after *pañca* and so forth, and after *kati*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.49; Kaccāyana 373; Rūpasiddhi 406; Nyāsa 802; Cāndra 4.2.55; Pāṇini 5.2.49).
After words beginning with *pañca* and after *kati*, the suffix *ma* occurs in the sense of "that which completes it."
*Pañcamo*, *pañcamī*, *pañcamaṃ*. Likewise, *sattamo*, *aṭṭhamo*, *navamo*, *dasamo*, *ekādasamo*, etc. [The suffixes] *-naṃ*, *-pūraṇo*, *-katimo*, *-katimī*, and *-tithī*.
508. Regarding the rule *tassa pūraṇekādasādito vā*: (Kaccāyana 374; Rūpasiddhi 412; Niddesa 805; Cāndra 4.2.51; Pāṇini 5.2.48). That by which something is filled is a "filler" (*pūraṇa*).
In the sense of "the filler of that," starting from *ekādasa* (eleven) and so on, the suffix *ap* with the marker *ṭā* is optionally applied.
The eleventh is *ekādaso*, *ekādasī*, *ekādasaṃ*, or *ekādasamo*. Likewise: the twelfth (*dvādaso*, *dvādasamo*);
the thirteenth (*teraso*, *terasamo*); the fourteenth (*cuddaso*, *cuddasamo*); the fifteenth (*pañcadaso*, *pañcadasamo*, *pannaraso*, *pannarasamo*);
the sixteenth (*soḷaso*, *soḷasamo*); the seventeenth (*sattaraso*, *sattarasamo*); the eighteenth (*aṭṭhāraso*, *aṭṭhārasamo*).
509. *Ṭe satissa tissa ka.* (Kaṇḍa 389; Rūpasiddhi 413; Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā 824).
When *ṭe* follows, there is the elision of the letter *t* of *sati*; thus, for *vīsati*, *tīsa*, and *tiṇṇaṃ*, there is the elision of *t*. [The forms are:

*ekūnavīso*, *ekūnavīsatimo*, *vīso*, *vīsatimo*, *tīso*, *tīsatimo*, *cattālīso*, *cattālīsamo*, *paññāso*, *paññāsamo*. From *saṭṭhi* onwards, by the preceding sutta, *mo* is substituted: *saṭṭhimo*, *sattatimo*, *asītimo*, *navutimo*.
After *sata* and other such words, the suffix *ma* occurs in the sense of completing that [number], and the final vowel of *sata* and the others becomes *i*. Thus:
the completer of a hundred is *satima*, *dvisatima*, *tisatima*, *sahassima*.
511. *Cha-ṭṭha-ṭṭhamā* (ka. 384; rū. 407; nī. 803).
In the sense of "completing that [number] by six," the suffixes *ṭṭha* and *ṭṭhamā* occur.
Thus: *chaṭṭho*, *chaṭṭhī*, *chaṭṭhaṃ*, *chaṭṭhamo*, *chaṭṭhamī*, *chaṭṭhamaṃ*.

512. *Saṅkhyāya saccutīsāsadasantāyādhikāsmiṃ satasahasse* [Pāṇini 5.2.45, 46; Kaccāyana 328; Rūpasiddhi 352; Niddesa 701; Candra 4.2.50–51]. The suffix *ap*, which has *ṭ* as its *anubandha*, occurs after numerals ending in *sati*, *uti*, *īsa*, *āsa*, and *dasanta*, in the sense of “in this hundred-thousand there is an excess of that. Here, the phrase “in a hundred-thousand” (*satasahasse*) means either “in a hundred” or “in a thousand.

*Note:* Regarding the rule *‘...ḍo’* (in the case of many), it applies when the numeral refers to many instances. Thus, from numerals ending in *sati*, *uti*, *īsa*, *āsa*, and *dasanta*, the suffix *ap* with the *anubandha* *ṭ* is added in the sense of “in this hundred-thousand there is an excess of that.
In this context, “hundred-thousand” (*satasahassa*) signifies either a hundred or a thousand.
In this context, by the term "thousand" (*sahassa*), a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, and a million are included.
The sequence should be understood as follows: *dasanta*, *satyanta*, *īsanta*, *āsanta*, and *utyanta*.
Among these, the numbers from ten up to eighteen—starting from eleven—are called *dasanta* (ending in ten).
Twenty; from twenty-one up to twenty-eight, the number nine, and thirty are called "ending in *na*. From thirty-one up to thirty-eight, the number nine, and forty are called "ending in *sa*.
Forty; from forty-one up to forty-eight, the number nine, and fifty are called "ending in *i*.
Fifty; from fifty-one up to fifty-eight, the number nine, and sixty are called "ending in *ā*."
From ninety up to ninety-eight, the nine numbers beginning with ninety are called "ending in -u" (*-utanta*).

The remaining numbers ending in *-ṭṭh* and *-ty* are also included here. Those ending in *-ṭṭh* are the nine numbers beginning with sixty and sixty-one. Those ending in *-ty* are the nine numbers beginning with seventy and seventy-one, as well as the nine numbers beginning with eighty and eighty-one.
Regarding those ending in *-das*: that hundred in which ten are added is a "ten-hundred" (*dasasata*). Likewise, a "ten-thousand" (*dasasahassa*) and a "ten-hundred-thousand" (*dasasatasahassa*).
That hundred in which eleven is added is "one hundred and eleven" (*ekādasasataṃ*). Likewise, "eleven thousand" (*ekādasasahassaṃ*) and "one hundred and eleven thousand" (*ekādasasatasahassaṃ*).

In the same way, there are "one hundred and twelve" (*dvādasasataṃ*), and so forth. In those [compounds] ending in *sata*—when [the suffix] *-ṭaṃ* occurs, the letter *ti* is elided; thus, that hundred in which twenty is added is "one hundred and twenty" (*vīsasataṃ*). Likewise...

One hundred and twenty-one, one hundred and twenty-two, and so forth; that hundred in which thirty is added is "one hundred and thirty" (*tīsasataṃ*). Likewise, one hundred and thirty-one, one hundred and thirty-two, and so forth.
This same method applies to the thousand as well. Regarding those ending in *ī*:

that hundred in which forty is added is "one hundred and forty" (*cattālīsasataṃ*). Likewise, one hundred and forty-one, one hundred and forty-two, and so forth. This same method applies to the thousand as well.

In those [numbers] ending in *ā*: when fifty (*paññāsa*) is added to a hundred, that is "one hundred and fifty" (*paññāsasata*). Likewise, "one hundred and fifty-one," "one hundred and fifty-two," and so forth. This same method applies to the thousand as well. In those [numbers] ending in *ṭṭhu*:

when sixty (*saṭṭhi*) is added to a hundred, that is "one hundred and sixty" (*saṭṭhisata*). Likewise, "one hundred and sixty-one," "one hundred and sixty-two," and so forth. This same method applies to the thousand as well. In those [numbers] ending in *ty*:
they should be expressed by adding "seventy" (*sattati*), "seventy-one" (*ekasattati*), "eighty" (*asīti*), "eighty-one" (*ekāsīti*), and so on.

"Utyantāsu" means that in which there is a hundred increased by ninety; this is "ninety-hundred. In the same way, there are "one-hundred-and-ninety," "two-hundred-and-ninety," and so forth. This method applies to the thousands as well.
Alternatively, "ending in ten" refers to the numbers starting from one up to ten.
"Ending in hundred" refers to the numbers starting from eleven up to twenty.
The group ending in *ī* consists of ten numbers beginning from thirty-one.
The group ending in *ā* consists of ten numbers beginning from forty-one.
In the same way, those ending in *ṭṭhi*, *ti*, and *u* are also to be understood.
“One hundred with one added to it is ‘one hundred and one’ (ekasataṃ), as in the Pāḷi passage: ‘Now here there were one hundred Khattiyas, illustrious followers’ (Jā.
2.22.594). ‘Two hundred with two added to it is “two hundred” (dvisataṃ)’—in this manner, everything should be stated;
this method of formation is most versatile.”
Just as "one and ten" (*eko ca dasa ca*) results in *ekādasa*, or "ten with one added" (*ekādhikā vā dasa*) results in *ekādasā*,
so too here, when it is said "ten and a hundred" (*dasa ca satañca*), resulting in *dasasataṃ*, or "a hundred with ten added" (*dasādhikaṃ vā sataṃ*), resulting in *dasasataṃ*, and so forth—
all such formations are established by means of compound (*samāsa*).

In that regard, however, compounds formed by numeral multiplication (digusamāsa) are established as follows: "two hundreds" (*dve satāni*) and "two hundred" (*dvisataṃ*), "three hundreds" (*tīṇi satāni*) and "three hundred" (*tisataṃ*), and so forth;
as well as "two thousands" (*dve sahassāni*) and "two thousand" (*dvisahassaṃ*), "three thousands" (*tīṇi sahassāni*) and "three thousand" (*tisahassaṃ*), and so forth;

and "two hundred-thousands" (*dve satasahassāni*) and "two hundred-thousand" (*dvisatasahassaṃ*), "three hundred-thousands" (*tīṇi satasahassāni*) and "three hundred-thousand" (*tisatasahassaṃ*), and so forth.
513. *Vārasaṅkhyāyakkhattuṃ* (Ka. 646; Rū. 419; Nī. 1282; Caṃ. 4.4.5; Pā. 5.4.17).
Numerical words related to "times" (*vāra*) take the suffix *-kkhattuṃ*.

For example: two times is *dvikkhattuṃ*; likewise, three times (*tikkhattuṃ*), four times (*catukkhattuṃ*), five times (*pañcakkhattuṃ*), ten times (*dasakkhattuṃ*), a hundred times (*satakkhattuṃ*), and a thousand times (*sahassakkhattuṃ*).
514. *Kati-mhā ka.* 646; *rū.* 419; *nī.* 1282; *caṃ.* 4.4.6; *pā.* 5.4.20. After words meaning "times" (*vāra*) that are related [to the action], the suffix *kkhattum* is used.
Example: *kati vārā katikkhattum* ("how many times"). 515. *Bahumhā dhā ca paccāsattiyā* (Ka.

646; Rū. 419; Nī. 1282; 'paccāsattiyaṃ' [in the plural]). After the word *bahu*, the suffix *dhā* is also used when there is proximity (*paccāsatti*). [Note: The term *paccāsattiyaṃ* appears in the plural form in some sources.]
The word *bahu* (many), when connected with the sense of frequency (*vāra*), becomes *dhā* and *kkhattuṃ* due to proximity (*paccāsatti*).
Thus, *bahuvārā* becomes *bahudhā*, and *bahukkhattuṃ*. By means of the word *bahu*, it characterizes "many times" as "several times" (*anekavāraṃ*);
thus, "several times" becomes *anekadhā*. Proximity (*paccāsatti*) is said to be the close succession of occurrences.
He eats many times during the day; he eats in many ways. When there is a great distance between the turns [of eating], those requisites do not suffice;
he eats many times within a month.
*Ekavāram* is either a derivative form of *ekam* or a contraction of *sakim*.
"He eats once" means "he eats one time.
The section on numerical groups is concluded.
Khuddakarāsi, Pakārarāsi 517. *Dhā* [is used] with numerals: Ka. 397; Rū. 420; Nī. 836; Caṃ. 4.3.20; Pā. 5.3.42.
The suffix *dhā* occurs after words expressing numbers (*saṅkhyāvācī*) to denote manner (*pakāra*).
From two ways: *dvidhā*. Likewise: *tidhā*, *catudhā*, *pañcadhā*, *dasadhā*, *satadhā*, *sahassadhā*, *bahudhā*, *ekadhā*, *anekadhā*.
518. *Vekā jjhaṃ ka.* (Kaccāyana 397; Rūpasiddhi 420; Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā 837; Cāndra 4.3.24; Pāṇini 5.3.46)
The suffix *jjhaṃ* optionally occurs after the word *eka*.
[It means] "in one way" (*ekena pakārena*) or "all at once" (*ekajjhaṃ*), or "in a single manner" (*ekadhā*).
519. From the rule *dvitīhedhā ka* (Kaccāyana 404); see Rūpasiddhi 420–370; Nyāsa 859; Candra-vyākaraṇa 4.3.24; Pāṇini 5.3.46.
After the words *dvi* and so forth, the suffix *edha* optionally occurs in the sense of manner (*pakāra*).
Thus: *dvedhā*, *tedhā*, *dvidhā*, or *tidhā*. 520.
After the words *sabba* and so forth, the suffix *thā* is substituted for *ka* [in the sense of manner]. (Kaccāyana 398; Rūpasiddhi 421; Nyāsa 844; Cāndra 4.3.26; Pāṇini 5.3.69).
A specific distinction (*visesa*) that differentiates a general category (*sāmañña*) has many divisions; the suffix *thā* occurs after words such as *sabba* to denote a manner (*pakāra*).
In every manner: *sabbathā*. By all manners: *sabbathā*. In whatever manner: *yathā*. By whatever manners: *yathā*. Likewise: *evam*, *tathā*. Otherwise: *aññathā*. In both ways: *ubhayathā*.
In the other way: *itarathā*. 521. *Katham*, *ittham*, *ka*. 399; *rū*. 422; *nī*. 845; *pā*. 5.3.24, 25.
These words are declined in various modes (*pakāra*).

In what mode? In which way? By this mode, thus (*itthaṃ*). By this sutta, what [is meant]? From the word *ima*, by applying the suffixes *thaṃ* and *tthaṃ*, the substitution of *ka* for *kiṃ* and the substitution of *ita* for *ima* are performed.

The word *tabba* means "that which has such a quality" (*so pakāro assa atthīti tabbo*). In the phrase *tasmiṃ tabbaṃ*, the meaning is "in that which possesses such a quality" (*pakāravante dabbe*). From a word expressing a common characteristic (*sāmañña*), the suffix *jātiya* is added to form *tabba*.

For example: one who is especially sharp in nature is called *paṇḍito paṭujātiyo* (a wise person of a sharp nature); a substance that is especially soft in nature is called *mudujātiyaṃ* (of a soft nature).
523. [The suffix] *ka* is used in the sense of desire and manner (*vīcchā-pakāresu*). (Kaccāyana 397; Rūpasiddhi 420; Nyāsa 836; Candra 4.4.2 ...pe... 5.4.43)
The suffix *sopaccaya* occurs in the sense of distribution (*vīcchā*) and in the sense of manner (*pakāra*). In the sense of distribution:

*Padaṃ padaṃ vāceti* (he recites word by word) becomes *padaso vāceti*. *Khaṇḍaṃ khaṇḍaṃ karoti* (he makes into pieces) becomes *khaṇḍaso karoti*; *bilaṃ bilaṃ vibhajjati* (he divides hole by hole) becomes *bilaso vibhajjati*, and so forth. And here, in cases such as *padaṃ padaṃ*, the accusative case is used for an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāvisesana*).
In the case of *pakāre*—such as in "in many ways" (*bahūhi pakārehi*), "separately" (*puthuso*), "in all ways" (*sabbehi pakārehi*), "in every respect" (*sabbaso*), and so forth.

However, in expressions such as "systematically" (*yoniso*), "by means of" (*upāyaso*), "by way of the occasion" (*ṭhānaso*), "by way of the cause" (*hetuso*), "by way of the meaning" (*atthaso*), "by way of the Dhamma" (*dhammaso*), "by way of the Sutta" (*suttaso*), and "by way of the phrasing" (*anubyañjanaso*), the suffix *-so* is applied to the third case singular by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*). Likewise in cases such as "lengthwise" (*dīghaso*) and "from the breast" (*oraso*).
Thus ends the section on the letter *pa*.
Section 524:
The Section on the Letter *ka* (*Kularāsi*). From the father [comes] the brother: *reyyaṇa ka*. (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā 765).
From the word *pitu* (father), the suffix *reyyaṇa* occurs in the sense of "his brother.
Thus, *pitu bhātā* becomes *petteyyo* (A. ni. 6.44). According to the rule “*rānubandhentasarādissā*” [Kacc. 351], there is the elision of *ussa*, and its doubling (*dvitta*) occurs.
525. From the mother, the suffix *cha* is used for the sister: *mātito ca bhaginiyaṃ cho* (Kacc. 352; Rūp. 376; Nī. 765).
A sister is [derived] from both the mother’s side and the father’s side.
A mother’s sister is *mātucchā* (mother’s sister); a father’s sister is *pitucchā*.
[The suffix] *-maha* is applied after the words *mātā*, *pitā*, *svasā*, and *mātula*. *Kaccāyana*: 352; *Rūpasiddhi*: 376; *Niruttidīpanī*: 765; *Candavutti*: 3.1.60; *Pāṇini*: 4.2.36.
They have grandparents for their own parents;

the mother’s mother is the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*), the mother’s father is the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*); the father’s mother is the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*), and the father’s father is the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*).
Thus ends the section on the family lineage.
Beneficial, good, you are worthy. 527.
Regarding "beneficial" (*hite reyyaṇa*): Ka. 352; Rū. 376; Nī. 765.
It is beneficial for them to dwell with their mother and father.
Beneficial to his mother, he is *metteyya*; beneficial to his father, he is *petteyya*. He is one who has practiced rightly toward his mother and father.
(528) In the sense of "beneficial to him," there is the suffix *-iya-* (as in *hita-ya*). 356; Rūp 381; Nī 773.
In the meaning of "beneficial to him" (*tassa hita*), the suffix *-iya* occurs.

That which is beneficial for the clingings (*upādāna*) is *upādāniya*. Likewise, there are [terms ending in] *-iya* such as *oghaniya*, *yoganiya*, *ganthaniya*, and *nīvaraṇiya*. In other instances, the suffix *-iya* also occurs in the *Suttavibhaṅga*.
For example, one who has slept in the same womb is *sodariya*. 529. Regarding the rule "after *cakkhu* and so forth, the suffix *-ssa-* [is applied]" (Ka. 353; Rū. 378; Nī. 767):
when the sense of "beneficial for that" is intended, the suffix *-ssa-* occurs after words beginning with *cakkhu*.

*Cakkhussaṃ* (beneficial for the eye): that which is beneficial for the eye, such as wholesome form (*subharūpa*) and eye-medicine (*cakkhubhesajja*). *Āyussaṃ* (beneficial for life): that which is beneficial for life, namely the methods for increasing longevity (*āyuvaḍḍhanavidhi*).
530. The suffix *Ṇya* occurs in the sense of "good or fit for that" (*tasmiṃ sādhūti atthe*). [Referenced: Kaccāyana 353; Rūpasiddhi 378; Niddesa 767; Cāndra 3.4.100, 103; Pāṇini 4.4.98, 103, 105.
In the sense of "good for that," the suffix *Ṇya* is applied.

*Sabhāyaṃ sādhu* means "good in an assembly"; *sabbho* means one who is skillful, fit, or beneficial. *Mettaṃ* is the welfare (*hitaṃ*) of friends. According to the analysis of the *Sutta*, the suffix *-ṇya-* occurs even outside [the specific rules]; for example, that which carries a chariot (*rathaṃ vahati*) is a *racchā*, meaning a carriage road.
531. Regarding *kammāniyaññā* (Kacc 353; Rūp 378; Nī 767):
the suffixes *-niya-* and *-ñña-* occur after a noun in the sense of "good in that" (*tasmiṃ sādhu*). *The suffixes -niya and -ñña occur after a noun in the sense of "good in that."*
*Kamme sādhu kammaniyaṃ, kammaññaṃ.* (That which is good for work is *kammaniya* or *kammañña*).
532. Regarding the suffix *-ika* after words such as *katha*: *ka.* 353; *rū.* 378; *nī.* 767; *caṃ.* 3.4.104; *pā.* 4.4.102.
In that context, the suffix *-ika* occurs after words beginning with *katha* in the sense of "good for" (*sādhu*).

In discourse, one who is skilled is a *kathika*; in discourse on the Dhamma, one who is skilled is a *dhammakathika*; in battle, one who is skilled is a *saṅgāmika*; in village life, one who is skilled is a *gāmavāsika*; in fasting, one who is skilled is an *upavāsika*.

According to the rule *pathādīhi ṇeyyo* (Kaccāyana 352; Rūpasiddhi 376; Nyāsa 765; Cāndra 3.4.105; Pāṇini 4.4.104), the suffix *ṇeya* is applied after words such as *patha* in the sense of "one who is skilled" (*sādhu*).
In this context, the suffix *ṇeya* occurs after *patha* and other such terms when the meaning is "one who is proficient."

That which is good for a journey is called "provisions" (*pātheyya*); it is wealth. That which belongs to that [wealth] is *sapati*; in the sense of belonging to one who possesses it, there is the term *sāpateyya*. 534.
Regarding the suffix *ṇeya* after the word *dakkhiṇā* in the sense of being worthy (*araha*): *Kaccāyana-vutti* 352; *Rūpasiddhi* 376; *Niruttisamuccaya* 765; *Candavutti* 4.1.80; *Pāṇini* 5.1.69.
The suffix *ṇeya* is applied after the word *dakkhiṇā* in the sense of being worthy of it.
One who is worthy of an offering (*dakṣiṇā*) is called *dakkhiṇeyya*.
[Grammatical rule: “*Āyo* after words ending in *tum*”: *ka* 352; *rū* 376; *nī* 765; ‘*rāyo tumantā*’ (in many texts).
The suffix *āya* occurs after a word ending in *tum* in the sense of being worthy (*arahattha*).

"One who deserves to be killed" is *ghātetāyo*; "one who deserves to be caused to recite" is *jāpetāyo*—here, "to cause to recite" means to cause to abandon (*hāpetuṃ*). "One who deserves to be ordained" is *pabbājetāyo*. According to the great grammatical rule, there is the elision of the *ussa* (the suffix *-ya-*) after a long vowel followed by a nasal (*sabinduno*).
Thus: *hitarāsi*, *sādhu-rāsi*, *araharāsi*, *vikatirāsi*.

536. Regarding its products (*vikāra*) and parts (*avayava*): *ṇa*, *ṇika*, *ṇeya*, and *maya*. (Kaccāyana 352, 351, 372; Rūpasiddhi 376, 374, 385; Niddesa 765, 764, 798; Candra 3.3.103; Pāṇini 4.3.134).

The suffixes beginning with *ṇa* occur in the senses of "its product" (*tassa vikāro*) and "its part" (*tassa avayavo*). A "product" (*vikāra*) is the attainment of a different state beyond the original nature (*pakati*).

A product of the *udumbara* tree is *odumbaraṃ*, such as ashes. A part of the *udumbara* tree is *odumbaraṃ*, such as leaves and so forth. A part of a pigeon (*kapota*) is *kāpotaṃ*, such as its flesh, blood, feathers, and so forth.
In the case of *Ṇika*: a derivative product (*vikati*) of cotton is *kappāsikaṃ*, namely thread and cloth.
In the case of *Ṇeyya*: a part of a black antelope (*eṇi*) is *eṇeyyaṃ*, namely its meat. A derivative product of silkworms (*kosakimi*) is *koseyyaṃ*, namely thread and cloth.

In the case of *Maya*: a derivative product of grasses is *tiṇamayaṃ*. Likewise, there are *dārumayaṃ* (made of wood), *naḷamayaṃ* (made of reeds), and *mattikāmayaṃ* (made of clay). A derivative product of cows (*gonna*) is *gomayaṃ*, namely dung (*karīsaṃ*).
537. *Jatuto mayaṇa vā* (Ka. 372; Rū. 385; Nī. 798; Caṃ. 3.3.108; Pā. 4.3.138): *jatuto saṇa vā* (in the sense of many).
After the word *jatu*, the suffix *mayaṇ* optionally occurs in the senses of a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*).
A modification of lac (*jatu*) is *jatumayaṃ*.
Thus ends the section on *vikati*.

**Section on *visesa* (Distinction):** 538. The suffix *ka* occurs after a word denoting excellence (*atisaya*) when that excellence is expressed through a comparative degree (*taratama*). [Referenced: Ka. 363; Rū. 390; Nī. 786; Caṃ. 4.3.45; Pā. 5.3.55, 57.]
These suffixes occur in the sense of intensity (*atisaya*).

One who is exceedingly wicked is *pāpatara*, *pāpatama*, *pāpissika*, *pāpiya*, or *pāpiṭṭha*; in the feminine, *pāpatarā*. There is also a suffix for intensity applied to an already intense degree: one who is exceedingly wicked is *pāpiṭṭhatara*. 539.
After words such as *vaccha* ("calf"), when expressing smallness (*tanutta*), the suffix *tara* is added. (Kaccāyana 363; Rūpasiddhi 390; Nyāsa 786; Cāndra 4.3.74; Pāṇini 5.3.91).
It is "tara" when there is a diminution of all qualities [of the base].
A calf that is excessively young is *vacchataro*; in the feminine, it is *vacchatarī*.
When youth has diminished among those who have reached youth, an ox that is excessively young is *ukkhataro*. When the state of being a horse has diminished, a young horse is *assatara*.
*Itthiyaṃ assatarī*: a female mule. *Sāmatthiyassa tanutte taruṇausabho usabhataro*: among those capable [of work], a young bull is the "buller" (*usabhataro*).

540. Regarding the rule for selection (*niddhāraṇe*): *taratamā ka*. When the word *kiṃ* is used to express selection, the suffixes *-tara* and *-tamā* are applied. (Note: *ratara ratamā* appears in many manuscripts.
When the sense of selection is understood from the word *kiṃ*, the suffixes *-tara* and *-tamā* occur.

"Which of you is Devadatta? Which of you is Yaññadatta? Who among you is Devadatta? Who among you is Yaññadatta?"—cross over by means of the sutta "Of what is which"? Among these, it is the agent of "of what.
Thus is the aggregate of distinction (*visesarāsi*). The aggregate of collection (*samūharāsi*).
In the sense of "its collection," the suffixes *kaṇ*, *ṇa*, and *ṇikā* are applied.
First, from words ending in the patronymic suffix *tā*: a collection of *rājaññas* is *rājaññakaṃ*; [a collection of] humans is *mānussakaṃ*.
A collection of oxen (*ukkha*) is *okkhaka*; a collection of lips (*oṭṭha*) is *oṭṭhaka*;
a collection of rams (*urabbha*) is *orabbhaka*. Likewise, *rājaka*, *rājaputtaka*, *hatthika*, and *dhenuka*.
Those who eat or consume hares (*sasa*) are *sasādakā*; a collection of them is *sasādakaka*. *Ikkhaṇikaṃ*.
In the sense of the suffix *ṇa*, a collection of enemies (*amittānaṃ*) is called *amittaṃ*.
In the sense of the suffix *ṇika*, a collection of cakes (*apūpānaṃ*) is *āpūpikaṃ*; a collection of birds (*sakuṇānaṃ*) is *sākuṇikaṃ*; a collection of *saṃkula* flowers is *saṃkulikaṃ*. 542.
From *jana* and other words, the suffix *ka* [is applied]. (Kaccāyana 3.55; Rūpasiddhi 380; Nyāsa 771; Cāndra 3.1.69; Pāṇini 4.2.43).
The suffix *tā* occurs in the sense of "a collection" (*samūha*).

Examples include: *janatā* (a collection of people), *rājatā* (kingship), *bandhutā* (kinship), *gāmatā* (village-ness), *sahāyatā* (companionship), and *nāgaratā* (citizenship)—that is, a collection of city-dwellers—and so forth.
[Grammatical rules: *Ayūbhadvitīhaṃse* (Kaśikā 3.54; Rūpamālā 379; Nyāsa 771; Cāndra 4.2.47, 48; Pāṇini 5.2.43, 44).
From *ubha*, *dvi*, and *tīhi* there arises the suffix *-aṃsa*.

That which has both parts (*ubho aṃsā bhāgā*) is *ubhayaṃ*; that which has two parts is *dvayaṃ*; that which has three parts is *tayaṃ*, as in *vatthuttayaṃ* (the triad of bases) and *ratanattayaṃ* (the triple gem). That which has two or three parts is *dvattayaṃ*.
Thus ends the section on collections and aggregates.
Datta, [meaning] "given," [is formed from the root] *dā* with the suffixes *la* and *iyā*, according to Ka. 358, 356; Rū. 383, 381; Nī. 778, 773.
In the sense of "given by him" (*tena dattaḥ*), the suffixes *la* and *iyā* occur. By the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), the word *dinna* becomes *datta*.
*Devalo* means "given by a god" (*devena datta*). Jā. 1.8.65. Is it also *devilo* or *devīlo*? The canonical text (*pāḷi*) reads *deviyo* or *devadatto*.
Similarly, *brahmalu*, *brahmiyo*, *brahmadatto*. *Sīvalo* means "given by King Siva, Bissanudeva"; [the forms are] *sīviyo*, *sīvali* (in the feminine), *sīviyi*;
[here] the vowel of *sissa* is long. 545. *Tena nibbatte* (Ka. 353; Rū. 378; Nī. 767); "'imo' [is used] when something is produced by that."
By that [cause], this is produced.
That which is produced by cooking is *pākima*; that produced by froth is *pheṇima*; that produced by wrapping is *veṭhima*. Likewise, *vedhima*.
That produced by the ankle is *gopphima*, etc. Eight. 2.431. A flower-garland; by means of the instrument (*karaṇena*).
*Nibbatta*, *kittima*, or *kuttima* are derived from the root *kit* (to fashion) by means of the suffix *mahāvutti*. From the root *kṛ* (to do/make), *kitta* and *kutta* are formed.
By means of the *suttavibhatta* (analytical rule), forms such as *saṃhārima* and *āhārima* are established.
Thus ends the section on *datta* and the group of derived (*nibbatta*) words.
*La*, *ita*, *karāsi* 546.
*Tannissite loka*. 358; *rū.* 383; *nī.* 778; ‘*llo*’ (in many texts). The suffix *lo* occurs in the sense of "depending on that" (*tannissita*).
*Vedaṃ* is derived from *ñāṇa* with the suffix *-lla*; *duṭṭhullaṃ* is derived from *duṭṭhu-nissitaṃ*.
Words such as *madanīyaṃ*, *bandhanīyaṃ*, *mucchanīyaṃ*, *rajanīyaṃ*, *gamanīyaṃ*, and *dassanīyaṃ* are formed by means of the suffix *-anīya* in either the instrumental or locative sense.

In the passage beginning with “*dhūmāyitattan*,” [it is explained as follows]: that which acts like smoke (*dhūma*) toward itself is *dhūmāyita*; the sky is *dhūmāyita*, and the state of being so is *dhūmāyitatta*.

The suffix *-tta* is used here in the sense of the base itself (*sakatthe*). Likewise, *timirāyitatta* is established from the verbal root *timira* by means of the suffix *-āya* (as found in *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 3.87, etc.).

Regarding the word *sañjātatārakā*: it is derived from the root *tāraka* with the suffix *-ita* (according to *Kaccāyana* 555; *Rūpasiddhi* 612; *Niddesa* 1142; *Candavutti* 4.2.37–5.2.36). [The reading] “*sañjātan*” occurs in many manuscripts.
The suffix *ita* occurs after words such as *tāraka* in the sense of "those [things] have arisen from it.
For example: "stars have arisen from it" is *tārakitaṃ*, namely the sky. "Flowers have arisen from it" is *pupphitaṃ*.
Likewise, *phalito* refers to a tree. "Sprouts have arisen from it" is *pallavitā*, namely a creeper. "Suffering has arisen from it" is...
One who has experienced suffering is *dukkhita*; one for whom happiness has arisen is *sukhita*.
*Paṇḍā* is said to be wisdom (*paññā*); one for whom wisdom has arisen is *paṇḍita*. One for whom a staff has been applied is *daṇḍita*.
According to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), that which has had dirt produced upon it is *malina*. Likewise, that for which thirst has arisen is [called *pipāsita*].
One who has thirst is *pipāsita*; one in whom hunger has arisen is *jighacchita*; one in whom a desire to eat has arisen is *bubhukkhita*; one in whom fainting has arisen is *mucchita*;
one in whom loss of consciousness has arisen is *visaṇñita*; one in whom blame has arisen is *nindita*. Likewise, one in whom pregnancy has arisen is *gabbitha*;
one in whom strength has arisen is *dabbitha*. One in whom an internal [excrement] has arisen is *antarita*; one in whom feces have arisen is *vaccita*.

548. Regarding *nindā*, *aññāta*, *ppapaṭibhāga*, *rassa*, *daya*, and *asaññā*: *ko* [is the suffix] after a noun when these meanings are to be expressed. (Koṭṭhaka 391; Rūpasiddhi 423; Niddesa 835; Canda-vutti 4.3.62, 63, 64; Pāṇini 5.3.73–79, 96, 97).
When *nindā* (blame) and so forth are to be indicated, the suffix *ko* occurs after a noun.
In the sense of blame: a contemptible ascetic is a *samaṇako*. Likewise: *muṇḍako*, *assako*, *uddhumātakaṃ*, *vinīlakaṃ*, *vipubbakaṃ*, *aṭṭhikaṃ*, and so on.
In the sense of "known": *aññāto*—*aññāto asso* means "a horse whose owner is known," as in "whose horse is this? or "one who has a known horse" (*assako*), and so forth.
In the sense of "small": *appatthe*—*appakaṃ telaṃ* becomes *telakaṃ*. Likewise, *ghatakaṃ*, *khuddakaṃ dhanu* becomes *dhanukaṃ*, *rathakaṃ*, *gāmakaṃ*, and so forth.
In the sense of "likeness" (*paṭibhāga*): *hatthirūpakaṃ* becomes *hatthikaṃ*. Likewise, *assakaṃ*, *balībaddako*, and so forth.
In the sense of "race" or "kind": *manusso* (human) and *manussako* (human); likewise *rukkhako*, *pilakkhako*, and so forth. In the sense of "pity":
*dayāyaṃ anukampito putto* (a son who is pitied) is called *puttako*; likewise *vacchako*, *itthikā*, *ambakā*, *kumārikā*, and so forth. In the sense of "perception":
by means of a mere name, like a peacock (*moro*) one says *morako*, and so forth.
Thus, *la*, *ita*, and *ka* are the groups [of suffixes].
549. *Abhūtatadbhāvarāsi*:

In the sense of "the becoming of what was not so before" (*abhūtatadbhāva*), when there is the application of the suffix *ka* expressing a transformation (*vikāra*), [the suffix] *ka* is applied. (Kaccāyana 391; Rūpasiddhi 423; Nyāsa 835; Cāndra 4.4.35; Pāṇini 5.4.50).

The becoming of that which previously did not exist as such at some time is "the state of becoming what was not" (*abhūtatabbhāva*). When this *abhūtatabbhāva* is to be expressed, the suffix *ī* occurs after a noun denoting a modification resulting from the conjunction of the element *bhū*. For example: *adhavalaṃ dhavalaṃ karoti* → *dhavalīkaroti* (he makes what is not white white);

*adhavalo dhavalo siyā* → *dhavalīsiyā* (what was not white may become white); *adhavalo dhavalo bhavati* → *dhavalībhavati* (what was not white becomes white). Likewise: *dhavalīkāro* (the act of making white) and *dhavalībhūto* (become white). Why say "in the state of becoming what was not"? [Because it does not apply to cases like:
*ghaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a pot), *ghaṭo atthi* (there is a pot), or *ghaṭo bhavati* (it becomes a pot).
What is the example for "in connection with becoming something else" (*karāsabhūyogeti*)? "The non-white becomes white. Why "in connection with a modification" (*vikārāti*)?

[Example: "He makes gold into an earring. What is meant is that in the world, the making of an earring from gold is called its "natural form" (*pakatirūpa*). Thus: "Gold may become an earring," or "Gold becomes an earring. This is the group concerning the transformation of what was not into what it is (*abhūtatabbhāvarāsi*).
*Sakattharāsi* 550. Regarding the sense of the word itself (*sakattha*): *ka.* 178, 360, 372; *rū.* 224, 387, 385, 378; *nī.* 364, 780, 798, 767.

Suffixes (*paccaya*) are seen even in the sense of the word itself. “The sense of the word itself” (*sakattha*) means the sense of its own base (*sakapadattha*); what is meant is the sense of the base according to its natural gender (*pakatiliṅga*).
The inferior is indeed the inferior; the young is indeed the youth; a deity is indeed a divinity; as it has become is indeed as it truly is; compassion is indeed pity;
the opportune time is indeed the right occasion; the infinity of space is indeed the base of infinite space;
proficiency is indeed proficiency; wieldiness is indeed wieldiness; giving is indeed that which consists of giving; virtue is indeed that which consists of virtue. Thus...
“Consisting of development” (bhāvanāmaya), and so forth.

And just as the sons of ministers are called “those belonging to the ministers” (amaccaputtiyā), so too it is appropriate to say: “One who is a son of the Sakyans alone is a Sakyan-puttiya; one who is not an ascetic is a non-Sakyan-puttiya,” and likewise “Nāṭa-puttiya,” “Dāsa-puttiya.

The suffixes -vantu and -mantu are also appropriate even when they do not possess their own specific meaning, as in “one who sees fear” (bhayadassivā) and “one who sees the goal” (atthadassimā). [And] “possessing the color of Brahmā” (brahmavaṇṇī).
Regarding the term *devavaṇṇī*: here, the "color of Brahmā" is *brahmavaṇṇo*.
When the analysis is "one who has a color like the color of Brahmā," the suffix *ī* functions solely as a grammatical affix (*paccayattha*) and does not possess its own meaning (*sakattha*).

However, when the analysis is "one whose color is like the color of Brahmā," it possesses its own meaning (*sakattha*). Furthermore, there are two types of compounds regarding a single external referent (*aññapadattha*).

It is also logical that they function as *taddhita* [secondary] suffixes; likewise, in such cases as “the state of being proficient (*paguṇa*) is proficiency (*pāguññatā*),” two *taddhita* suffixes have the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*).
Thus ends the section on the group of primary meanings (*sakattha-rāsi*). Now follows the section on the group of specified suffixes (*niddiṭṭha-paccaya-rāsi*).
551. *Aññasmiṃ* (In other [meanings]).
The suffixes beginning with *ṇa*, which were previously taught, are seen in other meanings as well than those already specified.

For example: *māgadho* ("born in the Magadhas"), *māgadho* ("reared in the Magadhas"), *māgadho* ("dwelt in the Magadhas"), or *māgadho* ("lord of the Magadhas or in the Magadhas")—such are examples of the suffix *ṇa*.
“Kāsiya” means “worth of Kāsi,” [the suffix] -iya being a diminutive (cūḷava). 376. The word “kāsī” refers to a hundred or a thousand, while “iya” is the suffix.
In this way, other suffixes (paccaya) should also be understood according to their respective applications.
552. Other suffixes are also seen: ka. 351, 352; rū. 374, 376; nī. 764, 765.
Other conditions are also seen in meanings both indicated and not indicated among the conditions previously explained.
*Vimātaro* means stepmothers; those who are different or various (*visadisā vividhā*) are stepmothers. Their sons are *vemātikā*; [the suffix] *ikaṇ* is added according to *Netti* 95.

*Pathāvino* means those who go on a path: *pathamhi gacchantīti pathāvino*, according to *Moggallāna-nirutti* 2.347. *Aghāvī* means one who goes toward misfortune (*agham*), suffering, or evil: *agham dukkham pāpam vā gacchatīti aghāvī*; [the suffix] *āvī* is added.
"One who has envy" (*issā*) is *issukī*; [the suffix] *-ī* is added according to Pāṇini 5.2.122.
"Those who bear the burden" (*dhuraṃ vahanti*) are *dhorayhā*; [the suffix] *-yhaṇa* is added according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.129.
"Favorable to greed" (*lobhassa hitā*) are *lobhaneyyā*. Likewise, *dosaneyyā*, *mohaneyyā*, and *aneyyo*.
That which is worthy of being seen is *dassaneyyo*. Likewise, [the suffix] *-eyyo* is used in *vandaneyyo*, *pūjaneyyo*, *namassaneyyo*, etc.

That which is beneficial for the floods (*ogha*) is *oghaniyā*; likewise, *yoganiyā*, *ganthaniyā*, *kammaniyaṃ*, *attaniyaṃ*, *dassaniyaṃ*, *pūjaniyo*, *namassaniyo*, and so forth—these end in *-aniyo*.
That whose measure is such is *yāvaṃ*; the state of being *yāvaṃ* is *yāvatvaṃ*. Likewise, *tāvatvaṃ* and *tva*.
The state or action of the supreme persons (parama-purisā) is *pāramī*; the state or action of those who are in harmony (*samagga*) is *sāmaggī*. [This is] from the *Nighaṇṭu*.

In such expressions as "possessing the nature of an elephant" (*nāgavata*), "possessing the nature of a lion" (*sīhavata*), and "possessing the nature of a thoroughbred horse" (*ājaññavata*), they accept the suffix *-vanta* in the sense of state (*bhāva*).
[Furthermore,] the brother of one's mother is *mātula*; [this is formed with] the suffix *-ula*.
Thus ends the section on the group of demonstrated conditions.

Regarding the section on vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*): by the rule “*padānamādissāyuvaṇṇassāeo ṇānubandhe*,” there is *ā* as the strengthening for the vowels *a*, *i*, and *u* when they occur at the beginning of a word. Thus, *ā*, *e*, and *o* are the strengthened forms.
Ādicca, Vāsiṭṭha, Venateyya, Menika, Pettika, Odumbara, Oḷumpika, Odagya, Dobhagga, Sobhagga, and so forth. Why does [the rule] specify "followed by the suffix -ṇa"?
[Examples without -ṇa: Nāmaka, Padaka, Purātana.
By the rule "in the middle," there is also vṛddhi in the middle of a word: Vāseṭṭha, Aḍḍhateyya, and so forth.
553. *Saṃyoge pi kvaci* (Ka. 405; Rū. 365; Nī. 864; ‘pi’ is absent in many manuscripts).
When a suffix having *Ṇ* as its *anubandha* follows, a vowel-vṛddhi occurs in some instances even when there is a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).

Examples include: *petteyyo*, *pettikaṃ*, *decco*, *pāmokkhaṃ* (meaning "good at the head"), *pāmojjaṃ* (the state of one who is delighted), *vākyaṃ* (that which is to be spoken), *bhāgyaṃ* (that which is to be shared), *bhoggaṃ*, *yoggaṃ*, and so forth.
Thus ends the section on augmentation (*vuddhi*).
Regarding the section on elision (*lopa*): by the rule “*Lopovaṇṇivaṇṇānan*,” there is the elision of *avaṇṇa* and *ivaṇṇa* when followed by the suffix *ṇya*.

In this regard, *avaṇṇa* [substitutes] occur as follows: *paṇḍiccaṃ* (skill), *tacchaṃ* (truth), *dāyajjaṃ* (inheritance), *dvejjhaṃ* (duplicity, from *dvidhā-bhāvo*), and *kāruññaṃ* (compassion, from *karuṇā*).
In *ivaṇṇa*, for example: *ādhipaccaṃ* (lordship, from the state of *adhipati*), and likewise *ādicco* (the sun) and *koṇḍañño* (Koṇḍañña).
Regarding *uvaṇṇa*: "When a vowel follows, *uvaṇṇa* becomes *avaṅ*. Thus, when a vowel follows, *uvaṇṇa* is replaced by *avaṅ*.

The state of being light (*lahu*) is *lāghava*; [the suffix] *rāghava* [is formed similarly]. That which exists in the *jambu* tree is *jambava*. Likewise, that which exists in Kapilavatthu is *kāpilavatthava*, as in "the forest. The offspring of a brother is *bhātabya*; [similarly] *gabya* and *dabya*.
Regarding the rule “*Ṭe satissā…*,” there are twenty forms when the suffix *ṭa* is applied; the elision of the *ti* occurs for *tīsa* and *tīna*.
That which completes twenty is *vīsa*, as in *ekūnavīsa* (nineteen). Similarly, *tīsa* and *ekūnatīsa* (twenty-nine).

‘*Rānubandhentasarādissa*’: when a suffix (*paccaya*) having *r* as its consonantal ligature (*anubandha*) follows, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel (*sara*) and the following consonants of the base.
Examples: *metteyyo*, *petteyyo*, *kivaṃ*, *kittakaṃ*, *īdī*, *īdikkho*, *īdiso*, *āhacca*, *upahacca*, *sakkacca*, *adhikicca*, *kiriyā*, *vedagū*, *pāragū*, and so forth.
554. The elision of suffixes [is taught] in Ka. 391; Rūpasiddhi 423; Nīti-kaṇḍa 830; and in Moggallāna, it is seen simply as “elision” (*lopo*).
In certain instances, there is the elision of case-suffixes (*paccaya*). For example:
*buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ*, *cakkhu suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā* (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.85). Here, the suffix of the abstract noun (*bhāva*) is elided:

the state of being a jewel is "jewel" (*ratana*); the state of being oneself is "self" (*attā*); and the state of belonging to oneself is "one's own" (*attaniya*). Thus, there is an elision of the abstract noun suffix.

In expressions such as "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati*) and "recollection of the Dhamma" (*dhammānussati*), the elision of the suffix should be understood according to the method: "the state of the Buddha is the Buddha" (*buddhassa bhāvo buddho*), "this quality of the Buddha is the Buddha" (*buddhassa ayaṃ guṇo buddho*), and so forth.
*Lopa vīmantuvantūnaṃ ka.* (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī 268; Rūpasiddhi 397; Nyāsa 518):
When *iyi* or *iṭṭha* follow, there is the elision of *vī*, *mantu*, and *vantu*.

One who is exceedingly wise among the wise is *medhiya* or *medhiṭṭha*; one who is exceedingly mindful among the mindful is *satiya* or *satiṭṭha*; one who is exceedingly virtuous among the virtuous is *guṇiya* or *guṇiṭṭha*.
Thus ends the section on elision (*lopārāsi*). The minor section (*khuddakarāsi*) is finished.
Nānāttarāsi 556.
When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow, the word *vuddha* undergoes the substitution *ja*. (Note:
This rule corresponds to Pāṇini 5.3.61–62, which prescribes the substitution of *jya* for *vṛddha* before the taddhita suffixes *cha* [iya] and *ṭhañ* [iṭṭha].)
One who is superior among the aged is to be known as *vuddha*, [and thus] *jeṭṭha*.
557. Regarding the derivation of *bāḷha*, *antika*, and *pasattha*: Ka. 263, 264, 265; Rū. 392, 393, 394; Nī. 512, 514, 515; Caṃ. 4.3.49, 51; Pā. 5.3.60, 63; ‘...dasā’ (in many texts).
When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow, the words *bāḷha*, *antika*, and *pasattha* undergo the substitutions *sādha*, *neda*, and *sa* respectively.

*Balha* (strong) becomes *sādhiya*, *sādhiṭṭha*, meaning "exceedingly strong"; *antika* (near) becomes *nediya*, *nediṭṭha*, meaning "very near"; and *pasattha* (praised) becomes *seyya*, *seṭṭha*, *jeyya*, *jeṭṭha*, meaning "most excellent.
558. Regarding *kaṇa* and *kana* for *appa* and *yuvan*: [Ka. 266, 267; Rū. 395, 396; Nī. 516, 517; Caṃ. 4.3.53; Pā. 5.3.64].
When the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha* follow, the words *appa* and *yuvan* undergo the substitutions *kaṇa* and *kana* respectively.

*Appānaṃ*: One who is exceedingly small among those who are small is *kaṇiyo* or *kaṇiṭṭho*. *Yuvānaṃ*: One who is exceedingly young among the young is *kaniyo* or *kaniṭṭho*. A maiden (*kaññā*) is one who exists in that youthful age (*kaniye vaye*). 559.
*Kosajja-ajjava-pārisajja-suhajja-maddava-arisya-āsabhājañña-theyya-bāhusaccā* (Ka. 360, 361; Rū. 387, 388; Nī. 780, 781; “...rissā... [in many texts]).

The suffix *ṇa* is attached after these words when they denote an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an action (*kamma*), provided no other suffix follows. Among them, the words *ajjava*, *maddava*, and *assabha* are formed with the suffix *ṇa*; the remainder are formed with the suffix *ṇya*.

In this context, the state of being upright (*ujju*) is *ajjava*; by this sutta, the suffix *-ṇam* is replaced by *-atta*, and according to the rule “*uvaṇṇassāvaṅ*...”, the *-us* is changed to *-avaṅ*.
Likewise, the state of being mild is *maddava*; the state of a bull (*usabha*) is *āsabha*, with the *-us* changed to *-ātta*.

The state of one who is lazy (*kusita*, *kusīta*) is *kosajja*; by this [rule], there is the elision of the vowel *i*, and that [suffix] is changed to *-jja*. One who has arisen among the assembly is *pārisajja*.
Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā 2.215: *dāgama* (the addition of *d*); *suhadayo va suhado* (from *suhṛdaya*, the *y* is elided, resulting in *suhada*;

the state of being *suhada* is *sohajjaṃ*, according to Jaṭa 1.5.23). *Ārisyaṃ* (this belongs to the *isi*, thus *issassa ārittaṃ*); *ājaññaṃ* (the state of a *ājāniya* or *ājanīya* is also seen as such;
the *y* is elided, then by the rule "the elision of *vaṇṇi* and *vaṇṇānaṃ*," the *i* is elided; thereafter, the form is produced by *sandhi*; or it is simply *ājāniyo*).
*Ājañña*: *jā* (born) + suffix *ṇya* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). *Theyya* is the state or action of a thief (*thenassa bhāvo vā kammaṃ*). *Nassattaṃ* is the state of one who has perished.
*Bāhusaccaṃ* is the state of one who has heard much (*bahusutassa bhāvo*). *Ussattaṃ* is the state of one who has risen. Again, this is a form of euphonic combination (*sandhirūpaṃ*). 560.

According to Pāṇini, the suffix *ka* is applied after a word that is not a primary element (*adhātussa*), and in the case of *canda*, it is seen as ending in the ablative case, as in *‘kāka’*. [This is indicated by] *syādito ghessi ka* (Pāṇini 5.4.40), *rū.* 370, and *nī.* 859.
‘Ghessi’: this is a sutta consisting of six words.
When *gha* follows a non-affixal (*adhātu*) stem-final *a*, the preceding *a* is frequently replaced by *i* when *ka*—which is based on *ni*—follows, provided that *gha* begins with *a*.
Examples: *bālikā*, *ekikā*, *hatthipotikā*, *mahallikā*, *kumbhakārikā*, *kammakārikā*, *annadāyikā*, *upāsikā*, *sāvikā*, *dhammavācikā*.
What is the meaning of *adhātu*? *Kulupakā-bhikkhunī*, *dhenupakā*, *khīrupakā-vacchī*; here, even the letter *k* in place of a root (*dhātu*) receives the designation of a root.
What is the meaning of *ka*? *Vedanā*, *cetanā*.
What is the meaning of *asyāditō*? *Bahuparibbājakā-rājadhānī*.
What is the meaning of *assā*? It means "a hall with many attendants.
Here, the analysis (*viggaha*) is: "that which has many wanderers (*paribbājaka*) is 'one with many wanderers' (*bahuparibbājaka*). The word *paribbājaka* is a word belonging to the *syādi* class;
therefore, because the vowel *ā*—which is designated as *gha*—of the suffix *kan* follows a word ending in *syādi*, the preceding [consonant] [is doubled].
There is no *itta* (suffix) for this. If there were, there would be the undesirable consequence (*atthappasaṅga*) that there would be many female wanderers (*paribbājikāyo*) belonging to him.
Thus ends the section on diversity (*nānāttarāsi*).
Thus ends the Moggallāna-grammar known as the Elucidation of Etymology (*Niruttidīpanī*).
The fifth chapter, on Taddhita suffixes, in the *Dīpanī*.
6. The Chapter on Verbs: Forms with the Simple Active Agent (*suddhakatturūpa*).

Now, the verb (*ākhyāta-pada*), which is established through roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*paccaya*), and which indicates distinctions of tense, agent, person, and number; which is devoid of gender distinctions; which expresses action as its primary meaning; and which ends in *ti* and so forth, will be explained.

In this context, that which "bears" (*dhāreti*) action is called a root (*dhātu*). It is threefold: by way of the original root (*pakati-dhātu*), the derivative root (*vikati-dhātu*), and the nominal root (*nāma-dhātu*).
Among these, *bhū*, *hū*, *gamu*, *paca*, and so forth are called original roots because they are established by their own inherent nature (*sabhāva*).
*Titikkha*, *tikiccha*, *bubhukkha*, *jighacchā*, and so forth, are called "verbal roots" (*vikati-dhātu*) because they are established by way of being conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*).

*Puttīya*, *pabbatāya*, and so forth, are called "nominal roots" (*nāma-dhātu*) because, while being nouns, they stand in the position of a verbal root through connection with suffixes that express action.
Furthermore, the "natural root" (*pakati-dhātu*) is twofold, according to whether it is transitive or intransitive.

Among these, that which expresses an action dependent upon an object is called "with an object" (*sakammikā*). Examples include *gāmaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to the village") and *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks rice").
That which expresses an action independent of an object is called "without an object" (*akammikā*). Examples include *bhavati*, *hoti*, *tiṭṭhati*, and *seti*.
Those with objects are further divided into two types: those with a single object and those with two objects.

In this context, that which speaks of an action dependent on a single object is called "single-object" (*ekakammikā*). Examples include: "He goes to the village" (*gāmaṃ gacchati*) and "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*).
That which speaks of an action dependent on two objects by way of a primary and a subordinate object is called "double-object" (*dvikammikā*).
And that is twofold, according to the [verb] classes beginning with *nī* and those beginning with *duh*.

In this context, that verbal root whose purpose is leading away is called *ni-ādi* (the group beginning with *ni*). For example: "He leads the goat to the village," "He carries the load to the village," "He drags the branch to the village.
The remaining roots, which take two objects, are called *duh-ādi* (the group beginning with *duh*). For example:

"He milks milk from the cow," "He asks the brahmin for a blanket," "He begs alms from the donor," "He shuts the bull in the pen," "He asks the Blessed One a question," "He teaches the Dhamma to the pupil."
The Blessed One instructs the bhikkhus; he spoke this word, "A king speaks these words to his minister," and so forth.

In that context, when a form is established within a verbal root (*dhātu*), they call it the primary object (*padhānakamma*) in cases such as the *vibhatti* (case endings) and *paccaya* (suffixes) beginning with *ny-*.

In cases such as *duh-* (to milk), they call it the secondary object (*apadhānakamma*). In all roots, when there is a connection with a causal suffix (*kārita*), it is called the causal object (*kāritakamma*). All of this—
This is stated according to the primary meaning of the verbal roots (*dhātu*);

however, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, when expressing a different sense or when joined with various prefixes (*upasagga*), those that are intransitive become transitive, and those that are transitive become intransitive.
First, regarding the expression of a different sense:
Vida in the sense of existence: a phenomenon exists, is found.
Vida in the sense of knowing: one knows a phenomenon.
Vida in the sense of acquisition: one acquires wealth.
*Vida* in the sense of experiencing: "He experiences pleasure; he experiences the ripening [of kamma]" (M.N.

3.303). *Vida* in the sense of announcing: "I announce, venerable sir; let it be remembered of me that 'he announces'" (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā 102), as in "he makes known the cause" or "he penetrates the Dhamma," and so forth.
When not joined with a prefix (*nānupasaggayoge*): [vida].

In the sense of "going on foot" (*pada-gati*), it means: one goes along the path (*maggaṃ pajjati*), one enters upon it (*paṭipajjati*); the path arises (*maggo uppajjati*), one lies down upon it (*nipajjati*), one succeeds (*sampajjati*);

it becomes wealth (*bhogo bhavati*), it comes into being (*sambhavati*); one enjoys wealth (*bhogaṃ anubhavati*), one overcomes craving (*taṇhaṃ abhibhavati*), one treats it with contempt (*paribhavati*), one masters it (*adhibhavati*);

one reaches the forest (*araññaṃ abhisambhavati*), one plunges into it (*ajjhogāhati*)—this is the meaning. Furthermore, it means that while going, one reaches or arrives at the path (*gacchantaṃ magge abhisambhavati, sampāpuṇāti*)—and so forth.
The case endings (*vibhatti*) are those which assist either through the perfection of phonetic form or through the perfection of meaning; they are called "conditions" (*paccaya*).
In that regard, there are eight types beginning with *ti* and *tvā*, and ninety-six types according to their specific forms.

Among these, the forty-eight forms belonging to the first group of six are called the "active voice" (*parassapada*). The forty-eight forms belonging to the second group of six are called the "middle voice" (*attanopada*).

In this context, some say that those words which occur frequently in connection with the welfare of others are called *parassapada*, while those which occur frequently in connection with one’s own welfare are called *attanopada*.

Others, however, maintain that "other" (*para*) refers to the agent because he is common to all actions, and "self" (*atta*) refers to the object because it is common to its respective individual action;
thus, words expressing the other are *parassapada*, and words expressing the self are *attanopada*.

*Attā* is said to be the referent (*padatthāna*) consisting of the action (*kriyā*) that has become the body; however, in the sense of being accomplished by an agent (*kattā*), the forms of action are *bhāva*, and even objects (*kamma*) are called *attā*. Others say that the agent (*kattā*), being distinct from them in the sense of being the accomplisher, is called *para*.
Some also say: *attā* is said to be the meaning of the first person (*amha*), while *para* is said to be the meaning of the second person (*tumha*), the meaning of the name;

because the first group of six [tenses] have the suffix *-ra* as predominant, they are called *parassapada*, whereas the second group of six are called *attanopada* by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhī*).
This is not tenable, because even the mere abundance of that [term] is not established in the case of the *parachakkas*.

However, when reaching the language of the Pāḷi, no difference in occurrence is seen between the two sets of six—whether in terms of one's own welfare and the welfare of others, or in terms of those who act for these three purposes;
therefore, it should be understood that those two names are not included in this treatise.
The suffixes (*paccaya*), however, are fourfold: by way of *vikaraṇa* (conjugational suffix), *kicca* (grammatical operation), *kārita* (causative), and *dhātu-paccaya* (verbal root suffix).

Among these, those which cause the words beginning with *ty-*, etc., and the words beginning with *tabba-*, etc.—which are already established from the verbal roots—to assume mutually different forms according to the division of grammatical classes (*gaṇa*) are called *vikaraṇa*-suffixes, such as *la*, *ya*, *ṇo*, and so forth.
The suffix *kyo*, which has the sense of state (*bhāva*) or object (*kamma*), is called a *kicca*-suffix.
The *ṇi* and *ṇāpi* suffixes occurring in the sense of an instigating agent’s activity—known as commanding others—are called *kārita*-suffixes.
Those suffixes such as *kha*, *cha*, *sa*, and so forth, which are themselves verbal roots (*dhātu*) expressing various specific actions, are called *dhātupaccaya* (root-suffixes).

Regarding the phrase “the distinctions of tense, case-role (*kāraka*), person, and number,” the distinction of tense is fourfold, according to the past, present, future, and time-free (*kālavimutta*).
In this regard, these three case endings—*hiyyattanī*, *ajjattanī*, and *ajjatanī* (the latter being common in many texts), as well as *parokkhā*—function with reference to the past tense.
Two endings, *vattamānā* and *pañcamī*, function with reference to the present.
One ending, *bhavissantī*, functions with reference to the future.

The seventh [case], *kālātipatti* (the lapse of time), occurs in two instances where [the action] is independent of time; this, it is said, is the sequence of the ancient case-endings (*vibhatti*), and it indeed accords with the Canon (*pāḷi*). As it is said:
“All those who revere the true Dhamma have lived and do live;
they will also live—this is the nature of things for the Buddhas” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.21).
“Those Buddhas who have passed away, those who are present, and those yet to come”—this is the Pāḷi from Thera 1.1.588.
In this sequence, both names—*pañcamī* (the fifth) and *sattamī* (the seventh)—are established according to their literal meaning (*anvatthavasena*).
However, later on, teachers arrange the various case endings according to their own preference.

The agent (*kattṛ*), the action (*kamma*), and the state (*bhāva*) constitute what is called the "distinction of the factors" (*kārakabheda*). Among these, state (*bhāva*) is twofold: by way of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and by way of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

It is further distinguished as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*). In this context, the activity that is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is called the "state to be accomplished" (*sādhyabhāva*). The activity that is the meaning of the suffix (*paccaya*) is called the "state of the means of accomplishment" (*sādhanabhāva*).
Among these, the state to be accomplished is manifold according to the various verbal roots. The state of the means of accomplishment pertains to the meanings of the various verbal roots.
In the sense of being a single function known as the mode of occurrence, it is one alone.

However, just as birth, while remaining on the side of the unarisen, appears as if it were producing conditioned phenomena, so too this [occurrence], while remaining merely within the sphere of conventional designation, appears as if it were manifesting the existence of all elements;
therefore, it is called both the "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) and the "agent" (*kāraka*). Just as...
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena that arise by way of birth (jāti) exclusively specify that birth through such expressions as "thinking has arisen" or "contact has arisen";

likewise, even those whose meanings consist of various bases (nānādhātu) that manifest by way of the sense of conditionality (paccayattha) exclusively specify that sense of conditionality through such expressions as "it is being," "it is going," "it is cooking," "being," "going," or "cooking."

However, in the case of words functioning as abstract nouns (*bhāvasādhana*), it is indeed appropriate to speak of the non-differentiation between the meaning of the verbal root and the meaning of the suffixes according to one’s wish.
But here, what is intended is the state of being an agent (*sādhana*) with respect to two [types of] actions.
The first, middle, and third persons (*purisa*) are the distinctions of person. And regarding "person" (*purisa*), it refers to "whatever this person or individual (*puggala*)..."
“He experiences pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure. (MN 3.1) Here, it is the self (*attā*) that is spoken of.
And that self is called the “agent” in the passage: “He acts, he experiences” (AN 6.43; Vism 2.580).
Thus, the term “person” (*puriso*) refers precisely to the agent.
And that meaning of the personal endings (*nāmattha*) is threefold: the second person (*tumhattha*), the first person (*amhattha*), and so forth.

In this context, because it constitutes one's own internal continuum (*ajjhattasantāna*), the first person (*amhattha*) is called the "supreme person" (*uttamapurisa*); the others, however, are called the "first person" (*paṭhamapurisa*) and the "middle person" (*majjhimapurisa*) respectively.

The case-endings (*vibhattiyo*), moreover, receive the names "first person" and so on because they indicate those [persons]. And this naming [of persons] occurs according to the distinction of the agent (*kāraka*).
"Having considered that it is already included [within what has been stated], it is not taken up in this treatise.
The distinction of number is twofold: by way of singularity and plurality.

Regarding "devoid of distinction of gender": in such cases as "a man goes," "a woman goes," and "a family goes," there is no variation in form following the gender of the denoted words—such as "man"—within the verbal form.

Regarding the phrase “expressing the action as the primary meaning”: here, the intention is that it expresses the action itself as the primary [meaning], and not the substance as the primary [meaning] like a noun (nāmapada).

In this context, "action" (kriyā) refers to the state of the meaning of a verbal root (dhātu); and that is fourfold according to time: past action, present action, future action, and action free from time.

Furthermore, there are many varieties of action, such as the action of commanding, the action of requesting, the action of permission, the action of supposition, and the actions of fitness, ability, injunction, invitation, and exhortation.

*Bhū* [means] "existence" (*sattā*). The state of being existent is "existence" (*sattā*); in that existence, the root *bhū* functions in the sense of existence. The meaning is that it functions in the sense of the existence of all word-meanings by way of their being present as objects of cognition through speech.
*Kriyatthā* (Ka. 432, 455; Rū. 362, 530; Nī. 905, 936; Pā. 3.1.91). This is a governing rule (*adhikāra-sutta*). The meaning is:
"after those whose meaning is action (*kriyā*), case-endings (*vibhatti*) and suffixes (*paccaya*) occur. Action is the meaning.

*Yassa* means "of which" and functions as a verb-root (*kriyāttha*). The root (*dhātu*) is threefold: by way of the natural root (*pakatidhātu*), the modified root (*vikatidhātu*), and the nominal root (*nāmadhātu*);

even the forms of suffixes used for the function of a root (*kāritapaccaya*) are included within the modified root. 562. In the present tense (*vattamāna*), the personal endings are: *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, *mhe*, *ka*. (Aṭṭhasālinī 414; Rūpasiddhi 428; Nyāsa 872; Cāndra-vyākaraṇa 1.2.82; Pāṇini 3.2.123).
A state that has begun but has not yet reached its conclusion is called "present" (*vattamāna*).
By metaphorical extension, the time associated with that state is also called "present. When the present tense occurs, the case endings beginning with *tya* follow verbal roots (*kriyāttha*).
Furthermore, because this set of suffixes beginning with *tya* pertains to the domain of the present time, they are established as "present" (*vattamānā*).
