563. Among the first and subsequent sets of six [case endings], when two or more remain from among the [three] persons (*tumhaṃ*, *amhaṃ*, and the remainder), the two middle and the highest [endings] of each set are used.

When the three names—namely, the name for "you" (*tumhanāma*), the name for "we" (*amhanāma*), and the name for the remainder (*tadubhayato sesanāma*)—are being employed or implied, whether in a single or multiple meanings, the two middle and highest [endings] of both the preceding and succeeding sets of six are applied. *Ka.* 408; *Rū.* 431; *Nī.* 867.

When the three names—namely, the name for "you" (*tumhanāma*), the name for "we" (*amhanāma*), and the name for the remainder (*tadubhayato sesanāma*)—are being employed or implied, whether in a single or multiple meanings, the two middle and highest [endings] of both the preceding and succeeding sets of six are applied.
The first case endings (vibhattiyo) occur. "‘Uttama’ means ‘subsequent’ or ‘last’," as stated in the *Cūḷamoggallāna*.
Furthermore, here, by way of prescribing the case endings, the prescription of their respective technical names (*saññā*) is also established.
How so? *Ti*, *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*—these are called the "first group of six" (*pubbachakka*).
*Te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, and *mhe* are called the "posterior six" (*parachakka*).
In the "anterior six," *ca* and *ti* are called the first pair; *si* and *tha* (the two) are called the middle pair; and *mi* and *ma* (the two) are called the highest pair.
It is the same for the posterior six. In that regard, when the remaining names—which function as the same substratum—are being employed or are implied, the first pair occurs.
Thus, for you there is the middle dyad (*majjhimaduka*), and for us there is the highest dyad (*uttamaduka*).
Regarding the duals, the singular number is used when one object is to be expressed, and the plural number is used when many are to be expressed.

Here, because meanings are dependent on nouns, the sense of the agent (*katvattha*) and the sense of the object (*kammattha*) are called "the meaning of the noun" (*nāmattha*). [The sense of] the agent...

The nominal meaning (*nāmattha*)—in which case endings such as *tyādi* occur within the category of "action-conditioned" (*kammasaṅkhāta*)—is called the "stated meaning" (*vuttattha*), as it is the expressed object (*vāccabhūta*) specifically of those [suffixes] that denote *tyādi* [case endings]. It is not the expressed object of case endings such as *syādi*.

A nominal word (*nāmapada*) that denotes the gender-meaning (*liṅgattha*) based on the stated agent (*kattu*) or object (*kamma*) is called the "denoted word" (*abhidheyyapada*); this very same thing is also called a "word with a common substratum" (*tulyādhikaraṇapada*).
The case endings beginning with *am* (the accusative), which express a specific meaning, find no place here;
only the nominative case ending, which indicates the mere sense of gender, finds its place.
With reference to such words that serve as the common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) of the expression, it is stated in the Sutta: “In the remainder after *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ*.”
And this sutta is to be understood as applying to two pairs of sentences each: those joined with pure pronouns, and those joined with remaining names (nouns) either in combination or mixed.

Therein, when joined with pure pronouns, individual dyads are formed. For example: *so gacchati* (he goes), *te gacchanti* (they go), *tvaṃ gacchasi* (you go), *tumhe gacchatha* (you [plural] go), *ahaṃ gacchāmi* (I go), *mayaṃ gacchāma* (we go).
Likewise, it applies to pure duals. For example: *so ca so ca gacchati* (he and he go), or *gacchanti*; *te ca te ca gacchanti*.
"He and they go; you and you go; or you two go. "You all and you all go; you and you all go.

However, in compound sentences joined by *missaka* (mixed) conjunctions, because of the convention that "in case of negation" (*vippaṭisedhe*) [the first member takes the plural], only the subsequent forms find scope.
They take [the endings], and among them, only plural forms are used. For example? "He and you two go" (*so ca tvañca gacchatha*);
"He and I go" (*so ca ahañca gacchāma*); "You and I go" (*tvañca ahañca gacchāma*); "He and you and I go" (*so ca tvañca ahañca gacchāma*).

This is the tetrad of singular forms. "They and you two go" (*te ca tumhe ca gacchatha*); "They and we go" (*te ca mayañca gacchāma*); "You and we go" (*tumhe ca mayañca gacchāma*); "They and you and we go" (*te ca tumhe ca mayañca gacchāma*). This is the tetrad of plural forms.
He and you go; he and we go; you and I go; he and you and I go. This is the tetrad based on the singular. They and you go; they and I go; you and I go; they and you and I go.
This is the tetrad based on the plural. Furthermore: you and he go; I and he go; you and I and he go.
The following sets of four should also be understood: "You and he go; we and he go; you and they go; I and they go," and so forth. Here are the scriptural passages:
"You, son, daughter-in-law, and grandson—may you dwell at home in harmony, O lady. (1.8.7) "I, son, daughter-in-law, and grandson—may we dwell at home in harmony, O lady. (1.8.7)
"Now I and the venerable Sāriputta shall lead the community of monks" (MNI 2.160).
"I and these monks sat down in meditative concentration" (MN 2.160).
"I and my wife were both donors" (Jā 2.22.1593).
“I and my husband were both lords of almsgiving,” etc.
Furthermore, when it should be said, “He goes and you go,” the expression “you two go” (*tumhe gacchatha*);
or when it should be said, “He goes and I go,” the expression “we two go” (*mayaṃ gacchāma*)—these are simply plural forms used as the base form (*pakati-bahuvacana*).

It is not the plural form of *paropurisa*. And as for the rule in Kaccāyana— “When all [of these] are expressed together, it is *paro puriso*” (Nīti 216)— the sūtra found there also refers to the case where all [of them],
whether two or three, being mixed together, are expressed collectively as "you" (*tumhaṃ*) or "we" (*amhānaṃ*).
In a compound consisting of two words, the meaning "the subsequent masculine [word] should be joined" is not impossible.
(564) *Kattari lo* (Pāṇini 3.4.67).

When suffixes such as *māna*, *nta*, and *tya* follow roots expressing action (*kriyāttha*) that are not proximate (*aparokkha*), the suffix *la*, which has *a* as its *anubandha*, occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). The presence of the *anubandha* *l* in *la* serves as a qualifier in the rule *ūlasse*.

By this [rule], it is made known that where suffixes such as *māna*, *anta*, and *tya* function in the sense of the agent (*kattari*), this suffix *la* likewise denotes the agent; this same principle applies to rules such as "kyo bhāvakammesu...
and so forth. Furthermore, here the *vikaraṇa* suffixes serve only to complete the phonetic form (*byañjanapūraṇā*) and not to fulfill a semantic purpose (*atthapūraṇā*);
therefore, they occur only in those instances where, without them, the word-form cannot be established. Where it is already established, there [they do not occur].
They do not occur; this *lapaccaya* also occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when a vowel of a case-ending (*vibhatti-sara*) or a vowel of an augment (*āgama-sara*) is absent.

However, when such a vowel is present—as in *pacāmi*, *pacāma*, *pacāhi*, *gameti*, *gamenti*, *vajjeti*, *vajjenti*, and so forth—it occurs for the purpose of another grammatical operation (*kāriyantara*).
Furthermore, wherever the elision (*lopa*) of suffixes is prescribed, there [the *lapaccaya* applies] to prevent the contingency of other groups (*gaṇa*) or other forms (*rūpa*).
It applies here, but does not apply elsewhere. 565.
*E* replaces the *yu* and *vaṇṇa* vowels before an affix (*paccaya*). [Referenced: Ka. 485; Rū. 434; Nī. 975; Caṃ. 1.1.82; Pā. 3.1.60.
Case endings (*vibhatti*) and affixes (*paccaya*) are called "affixes" (*paccaya*). *I*, *kī*, *khī*, *ci*, *ji*, and so forth, are called *ivaṇṇa*. *Cu*, *ju*,...
The vowels *bhū*, *hū*, and so forth, are called *uvaṇṇa*. When a suffix follows, the *ivaṇṇa* and *uvaṇṇa* vowels at the end of monosyllabic roots undergo *e*-vṛddhi and *o*-vṛddhi respectively.
By the rule "the following [vowel] is sometimes elided," there is elision of the subsequent *sara* vowel.
Thus: *saṃpubba*—*sambhoti*, *sambhonti*, *sambhosi*, *sambhotha*, *sambhomi*, *sambhoma*.

*Anupubbo* [is used] in the sense of experiencing (*anubhavana*). Thus: "He experiences wealth," "They experience wealth," "You experience wealth," "You (plural) experience wealth," "I experience wealth," or "We experience wealth.

In this context, just as in the phrase "a blue cloth" (*nīlo paṭo*), the meaning of the word "blue" (*nīla*) is twofold: the expressed meaning (*vāccattha*) and the denoted meaning (*abhidheyyattha*).
Therein, the primary meaning consisting of the quality (*guṇa*) is called the expressed meaning.
The meaning based on qualities (*guṇanissaya*) is called the expressed meaning (*abhidheyyattha*), which is the substance (*dabbattha*).

However, the word "blue" (*nīla*) expresses its denoted meaning (*vāccattha*) directly; one who hears the mere word "blue" understands the blue quality directly. Therefore, the expressed meaning of the word "blue" is indicated by another term, namely "cloth" (*paṭa*).
Likewise, in the phrase "he experiences" (*anubhoti*), the meaning of the word "triad" (*tisa*) is twofold: the denoted meaning and the expressed meaning.
In this context, the meaning of the agent (*kattu*), which is comprised within the category of sentient beings (*satti*), is called the expressed meaning (*vāccattha*).
The meaning of the gender (*liṅga*) based on that sentient being is called the denoted meaning (*abhidheyyattha*).
However, the word *ti* expresses only the expressed meaning directly, not the denoted meaning. [The term] "experiences" (*anubhoti*) includes the action to be accomplished along with its object.
The meaning is that it knows only the agent as straight, and not any object whatsoever. Therefore, the referent of the word *ti* is explained by the intervening word *so*;
however, since the expressed meaning has already been stated directly by the word *ti*, there is no further need to explain the third case ending (*tatiyāvibhatti*).
The nominative case (*paṭhamāvibhatti*) is used in the word expressing the referent merely for the purpose of indicating its grammatical gender.
"Thus it proceeds. This method applies everywhere.
566. *Eonam ayavā sare ka*: When a vowel follows, *e* and *o* become *aya* and *ava* respectively.
The letter *a* in *aya* and *ava* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇattha*).
*Bhavati*, *bhavanti*, *bhavasi*, *bhavatha*.
567. *Himimesvassa ka. 478; rū. 438; nī. 959*:
When *hi*, *mi*, or *mesu* follow, the long vowel (*dīgha*) occurs for the letter *a*.
*Bhavāmi*, *bhavāma*.
In the sixth person: *bhavate*, *bhavante*, *bhavase*, *bhavavhe*, *bhave*, *bhavamhe*.
With the prefix *pa-*, in the sense of the occurrence of becoming, it is *pabhavati* (it originates).
The prefix *adhi* signifies injury; it appears in *adhibhavati*, meaning "to overcome" or "to surpass.
The prefix *vi* signifies destruction, manifestation, and beauty; it appears in *vibhavati*.
The prefix *parā* signifies defeat; it appears in *parābhavati*.
The prefix *abhi* is used in the sense of attainment (*patti*), plunging deeply (*ajjhogāha*), and so forth—as in *abhisambhavati*, *tathā pātubbhavati*, *āvibhavati*, etc.
Thus ends the pure active form (*suddhakatturūpa*).
Now, the pure passive-objective form (*suddhabhāvakammarūpa*).

568. In the case of the suffixes *māna*, *nta*, and others beginning with *ty* (excluding those used for the remote past), when following verbal roots (*kriyattha*) in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an object (*kamma*), the suffix *ya* with the *kā*-anubandha is employed.
Due to the rule of "frequent occurrence" (*bahulādhikāra*), it is also used in some instances for the agent (*kattar*). Examples:

*Rūpaṃ vibhuyyati* ("Form is being manifested"), *So pahīyissati* ("He will be abandoned")—Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249, *Bhattaṃ paccati* ("The meal is being cooked"), *Gimhe udakaṃ chijjati* ("In summer, the water is cut off"), *Kusūlo bhijjati* ("The granary is being broken"). [References: Ka. 440; Rū. 445; Nī. 920; Caṃ. 1.1.80; Pā. 3.1.67.]
569. In the case of *kānubandha* (followed by a consonant) and *nāgama* (vowel increment), for the vowels *i* and *u*, there is no *e* or *o*, nor *assa* or *te*;

thus, there is no *vṛddhi* in the *ky*-affixes. For example: *kamme*—by that man, enjoyment is experienced (*anubhūyati*); by him, enjoyments are experienced (*anubhūyanti*); by him, you are experienced (*anubhūyasi*).
By that you experience it; by that I experience it; by that we experience it. For that which has the dual number and the short vowel, [the forms] *anubhuyyati* and *anubhuyyanti* are used.

In this context, regarding the word *anubhūyati*, the meaning of the word *ti* when accompanied by the suffix *kyap* is twofold: the expressed meaning (*abhidheyyattha*) and the implied meaning (*vāccattha*).
In this context, the meaning of the word *saka* (one’s own), which is designated as "power" (*satti*), is called the expressed meaning (*vāccattha*).
The meaning of the gender (*liṅga*) based on that power is called the denoted meaning (*abhidheyyattha*).
However, the word *ti*, when accompanied by the suffix *-ya*, expresses directly only the expressed meaning, not the denoted meaning. [As in the phrase] “it is experienced” (*anubhūyati*).
Hearing it, one understands only the power of the action (*kamma-satti*) together with its accomplishment (*sādhya-kriyā*), and not any substance (*dabba*);
this is what is meant. The rest is exactly as explained previously.
[The passive forms are: *anubhūyate*, *anubhuyyate*; *anubhūyante*, *anubhuyyante*; *anubhūyase*, *anubhūyavhe*; *anubhūye*, *anubhuyye*; *anubhūyamhe*, *anubhuyyamhe*.
570. After a short vowel preceded by a heavy syllable, *re* is the substitute for the endings *-nti* and *-ntīnaṃ*. (Ka. 517; Rū. 488; Nī. 1105; “*guru…*” [in many texts]).
When a short vowel is preceded by a heavy syllable, *re* is substituted for the endings *-nti* and *-ntīnaṃ*.
Examples: *jāyare*, *jāyanti*; *jāyare*, *jāyante*; *gacchare*, *gacchanti*; *gacchare*, *gacchante*; *gamissare*, *gamissanti*; *gamissare*, *gamissante*.
What is the meaning of *garupubba*? Examples are *pacanti* and *pacante*. What is the meaning of *rassa*? Examples are *pācenti* and *pācante*.

Furthermore, by means of this grammatical rule (*sutta*), these canonical phrases are established: “*sabbaṃ hidaṃ bhañjare kālapariyāyaṃ* (Jā. 1.15.370), *muñcare bandhanasmā* (Jā. 2.22.1648), and *jīvare vāpi sussatī* (Jā. 2.22.840).”

In this context: *bhañjare* means "it breaks"; *muñcare* means "let them release"; *jīvare vāpi* means "or even while living. [The forms] *anubhūyare*, *anubhūyanti*, *anubhūyare*, and *anubhūyante* [are used].

What is called "state" (*bhāva*) is the process of becoming, such as the act of going and so forth; it is qualified by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself through a relationship of grammatical coreferentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇabhāva*), not by a nominal word (*nāmapada*).
Therefore, in that case, there is no application of specific dual endings such as *tumhaṃ* or *amhaṃ*, nor the group beginning with *tyādi*, according to the remaining nominal bases.
In this context, there is only the first pair [of forms]. And because that [term] *dabba* itself possesses the nature of being unskilled (*abyatta*), there is no distinction in number;
it remains in the singular alone.
By means of that, the sense is: "wealth is experienced," "is being experienced," "is experienced," "is being experienced," or "the experiencing occurs."
Thus end the pure bhāva-kamma-rūpas.
571. Hetu-kattū-rūpa:
"The suffix *ṇa* and also *ka* [are used] in the sense of the operation of an instigator" (Pāṇini 3.1.26; Rūpasiddhi 540; Nyāsa 914).

When one prompts a pure agent (*suddhakattā*), the suffixes *ṇi* and *ṇāpi* occur after that prompting agent (*payojaka*) in the sense of the action (*kriyattha*). The *ṇā*-suffixes have *vuddhi* as their purpose.
Among those, after a root ending in long *ā*, only *ṇāpi* occurs according to the rule *ato* (Moggallāna-vyākaraṇa); thus: *dāpeti*, *dāpayati*.
After a root ending in *uvaṇṇa* (u, ū), only *ṇi* occurs; thus: *sāveti*, *sāvayati*.
From the perspective of meaning, there are two types: *pāceti*, *pācayati*, *pācāpeti*, and *pācāpayati*.

Since the activity of the instigator (*payojaka-byāpāra*) is itself an action, the case endings follow after the suffixes *ṇi* and *ṇāpī* which express that meaning; furthermore, there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) of the final element of the root in the case of *ṇi* and *ṇāpī*.

Examples: *So maggaṃ bhāveti* (He develops the path). *Te maggaṃ bhāventi* (They develop the path). *Tvaṃ maggaṃ bhāvesi* (You develop the path). *Tumhe maggaṃ bhāvetha* (You [plural] develop the path). *Ahaṃ maggaṃ bhāvemi* (I develop the path). *Mayaṃ maggaṃ bhāvema* (We develop the path).
572. *Āy* and *āvā* [are substituted] when there is no following nasal consonant (*aṇ-anubandha*). (Ka. 515; Rū. 541; Nī. 1029).

When a suffix (*paccaya*) beginning with a vowel (*sarādi*) that does not have a following nasal consonant follows, *āya* and *āvā* are substituted for *e* and *onaṃ* respectively, in accordance with the rules of the grammatical system (*suttavibhatti*); this substitution occurs even when the suffix has no following nasal consonant.
In the root *ge* (to sing): *gāyati*, *gāyanti*.
If preceded by *apa*, the root *pūj* [undergoes the following changes]: *apacāyati*, *apacāyanti*.
For the root *jhi* in the sense of "thinking": *jhāyati*, *jhāyanti*, *ujjhāyati*, *nijjhāyati*, and so forth. 573.
By means of the affixes *ṇi*, *ṇāpi*, and *āpi*, [the rule] "or" (*vā*) [applies] in many instances.
The suffix *lo* optionally occurs after the causative markers *ṇi*, *ṇāpi*, and *āpī* when denoting the agent (*kattari*). Thus:
*kārayati*, *kārāpayati*, *saddāpayati*.

By this rule, in places where there is no vowel (*asare*), the letter *a* follows the substitution of *ay*; thus: *so maggaṃ bhāvayati*, *bhāvayanti*, *bhāvayasi*, *bhāvayatha*, *bhāvayāmi*, *bhāvayāma*.
Thus end the forms of the causal agent (*hetukattā*). Regarding *tyādi*:
in the rule “*kyo bhāvakammesu…*,” the suffix *ṇi* is applied; from that suffix *ṇi*, the suffix *ya* follows.
The affix *īña* is substituted for the initial [vowel] of the suffix *kyā* when it follows a verbal root (*kriyattha*).
By that, the path is cultivated; by that, paths are cultivated; by that, you are cultivated; by that, you (plural) are cultivated; by that, I am cultivated; by that, we are cultivated.
In the case of shortening: *bhāviyati*, *bhāviyanti*. In the case of doubling:
*bhāviyyati*, *bhāviyyanti*. Likewise: *bhāvayīyati*, *bhāvayīyanti*.
In the case of shortening: *bhāvayiyati*, *bhāvayiyanti*.
In the second [tense], there will be *bhāvayiyyati* and *bhāvayiyyanti*.
Even a root that is intransitive (*akammikā*) becomes transitive with one object (*ekakammikā*) when the causative suffix (*kārita*) is added;
likewise, it may have one object, two objects, or even three objects.

Thus, within a single element (*dhātu*), four types of derived matter (*nipphanna-rūpa*) are found: pure agent-form (*suddha-katturūpa*), pure object-form (*suddha-kammarūpa*), causal agent-form (*hetu-katturūpa*), and causal object-form (*hetu-kammarūpa*).

Herein, the "agent-object form" (*kamma-katturūpa*) is also included under the category of agent-form; for example: *kusūlo bhijjati* (the granary breaks), *bhijjanadhammo bhijjati* (that which is subject to breaking breaks).

Furthermore, the "agent-agent-form" (*kattu-kammarūpa*) is also included under the category of object-form. Among these, when a word that expresses an agent becomes an object-form by its verbal form, it is called "agent-object-form" (*kattu-kammarūpa*); this is frequently seen in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
"Form is analyzed away; it is transcended, surpassed, and overcome;
the sign is mastered," thus [it is called] *gotrabhū*.
"The occurrence is mastered, death is mastered, and rebirth is mastered," thus [it is called] *gotrabhū*, and so forth. (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.59)
Likewise: "He might be abandoned, or he might not be abandoned" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249); "He will be abandoned" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249); "His fame is lost" (Dīgha Nikāya 3.246);
"He is lost" means "the person is being lost" (Jātaka 1.15.348); "He goes away" means "he is falling away" (Jātaka 1.15.348);
"Noble steeds are laughed at" (Jātaka 2.22.2369); "The heart of the distressed man is tormented" (Jātaka 2.22.1350), and so forth.

Regarding the Kaccāyana rule which states, “In this [section], after the roots *dā*, *dhā*, *mā*, *thā*, *hā*, *pā*, *maha*, *matha*, etc., there is *ī*,” they maintain that it applies to the object (*kamma*);
however, it is more appropriate for the agent (*kattar*) because of the actual occurrence of the insertion of *ivaṇṇa* in the object.

In the *Saddanīti*, however, it firmly asserts that the forms of the words “he will abandon” (*so pahīyissati*) and so forth are abstract nouns (*bhāvarūpa*), yet those very forms are indeed both agentive and objective (*kattukammarūpa*).

And herein, the present tense (*vattamāna*) is fourfold: constant occurrence (*niccapavatta*), occurrence not yet ceased (*pavattāvirata*), occurrence already ceased (*pavattuparata*), and proximate occurrence (*samīpavattamāna*).
Regarding constant occurrence: "Here this mountain stands; the moon and sun revolve; the quarters shine resplendent" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.69).
Regarding occurrence not yet ceased: "Is alms given in your family, householder?"—"Alms are given in my family, venerable sir" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.20).
And here, as long as there is enthusiasm for giving, the act of giving continues exactly as it has proceeded; it is said to be "present" because the enthusiasm has not ceased.
When the activity has stopped—such as "He does not eat this meat," "He does not kill a living being" (A.N.
3.67), or "He does not take what is not given" (A.N. 3.67)—here, as long as he does not perform the action opposed to that [virtue], the act of abstention is indeed said to be "present."

In the sense of proximity (*samīpe*): "From where indeed are you coming? "I am coming from Rājagaha" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.130). In the sense of the future (*anāgate*): "I shall teach the Dhamma to you; listen well.

This case ending occurs even in the past when used in connection with *sutta-vibhatta* ("the analysis of the discourse"): "Shaking off the bark garments, I was then going through the sky" (Buddhavamsa 2.37).
In connection with *yāva*, *pure*, and *purā*, it occurs even in the future: "Stay right here meanwhile, until I come," or "What if I were now... (Yaṃnūnāhaṃ).
I shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya in the assembly. (Eight. 1. The First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā):
"Previously, non-Dhamma shone forth, and the Dhamma was obstructed. (Cūḷavaṃsa 437) "Cut these teeth before I die!

(Jātaka 1.16.127) "Even for the sake of a single truth, I shall surely go to hell; of this there is no doubt for me. (Jātaka 2.22.331) "Even regarding that which is certain to happen: 'I shall certainly become a Buddha. (Buddhavamsa 2.109) "Or: 'He will certainly become a Buddha. (Buddhavamsa 2.81)

Even in the case of an indeclinable (*aniyama*), if one speaks or acts with a clear mind, it is called *citta* because it thinks (*cinteti*)—DhsA 1; it is called *phassa* because it touches (*phusati*)—DhsA 1; he is called *Buddha* because he awakens (*bujjhati*).
Even in the case of a combination of tense and person: "When does he go? means "he goes" (*karahi gacchati*) or "he will go" (*gamissati*). Such are the forms beginning with *iti*.
Now, the *tvādi* (suffixes beginning with *tvā*) are explained. 575.
*Tu*, *antu*, *hi*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *taṃ*, *antaṃ*, *su*, *vho*, *e*, *āmase*, and *ka*. 424; Rūp. 450; Nī. 897; Caṃ. 1.3.122; Pā. 3.3.162.

In the present tense, the verbal roots *kṛ* (to do) and others, along with the suffixes *tvā* and so forth, occur in the senses of questioning (*pañha*), aspiration (*patthanā*), and injunction (*vidhi*). In the sense of questioning:
"Dhamma or Vinaya—what shall you study? (dhammaṃ vā tvaṃ adhiyassu vinayaṃ vā pāci). [This is identical in meaning.
By the term "aspiration" (*patthanā*), blessings and the like are also included.
Therein, regarding aspiration: "Wandering through various states of existence, may I be endowed with faith and free from stinginess.

Regarding prayer: "By this utterance of truth, may the rain-cloud pour down its rain everywhere. (Cariyāpiṭaka 3.89). "May all beings behold what is auspicious" (Jātaka 1.2.105). "May all beings be free from enmity" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.22).
Regarding entreaty: "Give me one eye" (Cariyāpiṭaka 1.59).
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.68); "Let the Blessed One exhort me" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.1);
"Let the Sugata instruct me" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.1); "May the Saṅgha lift me up, venerable sir" (Mahāvagga 71);
"Forgive us who have transgressed, O elephant among kings" (Jātaka 2.21.181); "Come, tigers, turn back! (Jātaka 1.3.66).
By the term "injunction" (*vidhi*), such things as enjoining (*niyojana*) are also included.

Among these, regarding injunctions: "Abandon the unwholesome; enter upon and abide in the wholesome" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.30; Pārāyana 19); "Think thus; do not think thus" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.30). Regarding enjoinings:

"Come, monks, be virtuous" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.114); "Accomplish [your task] with diligence" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.185); "Come, take it, bind it" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.342); "Do not let go of anything" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.342).
In the case of *ajjhesana* (request): "Venerable sir, let the Elder recite the Pātimokkha," Mahāvagga 155.
In the case of *āṇatti* (command): "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs," Pārājika 368.
In the case of *pesana* (sending): "Go, you, Sāriputta," Pārājika 432.
At the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*): "Let the Saṅgha speak to me, venerable sirs. (Aṭṭha. 213); "Speak, venerable sirs, according to what is needed. (Pārā. 290). In granting permission:
"Use it, or dispose of it, or do with it as you see fit. (Pāci. 374). In the granting of a boon:
"O Phussatī, of excellent complexion and radiance, choose ten boons. (Jā. 2.22.1655); "Whatever is desired or wished for by you, may it be fulfilled quickly. (A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.192).
"Ask me a question, Vāsava, whatever you desire in your mind" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.356).
"Having been granted the opportunity, ask" (Sutta Nipāta 1036).
"So be it" (in acceptance) (Dīgha Nikāya 2.419).
In the sense of abuse: "May your head split into seven pieces! (Jātaka 1.16.295); "May the thieves cut you into pieces! (Majjhima Nikāya 1.8). In the sense of an oath:
"By this utterance of truth, may a son be born to me, O Lord" (Jātaka 1.14.104); "If I speak falsely, may my head split into seven pieces!

(Jātaka 1.14.104). In the sense of address: "Let King Vessantara come! (Jātaka 2.22.2341); and in such instances as "Come, monk, lead the holy life" (Mahāvagga 28) and "Come, monks, be virtuous," the words *ehi* and *etha* stand in the sense of address.
“May the Blessed One accept my invitation, venerable sir, for a meal on the morrow at Pārā.

[Regarding the forms] *anubhotu*, *anubhontu*, *anubhohi*, *anubhotha*, *anubhomi*, *anubhoma*, *bhavatu*, *bhavantu*: because of the rule "himimesvassa," the long vowel occurs in place of *hi*, *mi*, and *mesu*; thus, "be wise, you."
576. *Hissa lopo ka.* (Pāṇini 6.4.105). There is elision of *hissi* following an *a*-vowel.
Why [is it said] "following an *a*-vowel"?
[Consider: *brūhi*, *dehi*, *hohi*.
By this [rule], there is the elision of *hi* from *ato*: "May you be wise" (*tvaṃ paṇḍito bhava*).
"May you (plural) be wise" (*tumhe paṇḍitā bhavatha*), "I am" (*bhavāmi*), "we are" (*bhavāma*).

In the subsequent group of six: "May he be" (*so bhavatu*), "may they (plural) be" (*te bhavantu*), "may you (singular) be" (*tvaṃ bhavassu*), "may you (plural) be" (*tumhe bhavavho*), "may I be" (*ahaṃ bhave*), "may we (plural) be" (*mayaṃ bhavāmase*). These are the forms for the simple agent (*suddhakattarūpāni*).
*Anubhūyatu*, *anubhūyantu*, *anubhuyyatu*, *anubhuyyantu*, and so forth, are examples of the pure passive form (*suddhakamma-rūpa*).
*Bhāvetu*, *bhāventu*, *bhāvayatu*, *bhāvayantu*, and so forth, are examples of the causal active form (*hetukatturūpa*).

*Bhāvīyatu*, *bhāvīyantu*; when the vowel is shortened: *bhāviyatu*, *bhāviyantu*; when doubled: *bhāviyyatu*, *bhāviyyantu*. Likewise, *bhāvayīyatu*, *bhāvayīyantu*, and so forth, are examples of the causal passive form (*hetukamma-rūpa*).
By the sutta beginning with "eyyāthasse," *tha* becomes *vho*: *tumhe bhavavho* or *bhavatha*. Thus ends the section on *tvā* and so forth; next is the section on *eyya* and so forth.
Now, *eyya* and so forth are explained. 577.

In the sense of cause (*hetu*) and effect (*phala*), *eyya*, *eyyuṃ*, *eyyāsi*, *eyyātha*, *eyyāmi*, *eyyāma*, *etha*, *eraṃ*, *etho*, *eyyāvho*, *eyyavho* (according to Moggallāna and others), or *eyyaṃ*, *eyyāmhe*—or *ka*. (Moggallāna 416; Rūpasiddhi 454; Nītattha-saṅgaha 880; Canda-vutti 1.3.120; Pāṇini 3.3.156).
The verbal suffixes beginning with *eyya* optionally occur in the sense of action denoting a cause and in the sense of action denoting an effect when they are mutually related.
In the case of cause and effect as well, the particle *vā* sometimes serves to indicate the occurrence of another grammatical analysis, such as:
"If he obtains a vehicle, he will go; if he does not obtain one, he will not go," and so forth.
"If the conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) were permanent, it would be called pleasant; if he were wise, he would be happy."
578. Regarding the rules for interrogative propositions (*pañhapatthanāvidhi*), [Pāṇini 3.3.161; Candra 1.3.121]: *eyya* and other suffixes occur in these cases. In an interrogation:
"Kinnu kho tvaṃ vinayaṃ vā adhiyyeyyāsi dhammaṃ vā? ("Would you perhaps study the Vinaya or the Dhamma?")
In the *Patthana* [it is said]: "May I be born in a birth after birth. In the context of the positive injunction (*vidhi*):
one should not kill living beings, one should not take what is not given, one should give gifts, and one should guard moral virtue.
579. *Sattārahesveyyādī* (Ka. 416; Rū. 454; Nī. 881–4; Caṃ. 1.3.128; Pā. 3.3.169–172; *Satyarahesveyyādī* in many manuscripts).
The optative suffixes (*eyya*, etc. occur in the sense of capability (*satti*) and worthiness (*arahatta*).
"May your majesty rule the kingdom," "your majesty is capable of ruling the kingdom," or "your majesty is worthy to rule the kingdom"—this is the meaning.
He should disentangle this tangle (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.23).

580. *Sambhāvane vā* (Ka. 416; Rū. 854; Nī. 881, 883–4; Caṃ. 1.3.118–9; Pā. 3.3.154–5). Even in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvana*), the optative suffixes beginning with *eyya* may optionally occur.
For example: "He might even split the mountain with his head"—*bhideyya*, *bhaveyya*, *bhaveyyuṃ*, *bhaveyyāsi*, *bhaveyyātha*, *bhaveyyāmi*, *bhaveyyāma*.
*Parachakke so bhavetha*, *te bhaveraṃ*, *tvaṃ bhavetho*, *tumhe bhaveyyāvho*, *ahaṃ bhaveyyaṃ*, *mayaṃ bhaveyyāmhe*—these are the forms of the pure agent (*suddhakatturūpāni*).
*Anubhūyeyya*, *anubhūyeyyuṃ*. With the shortening of the vowel in the dual, *anubhuyyeyya*, *anubhuyyeyyuṃ*, etc.—these are the pure object forms (*suddhakammarūpaṃ*).
*Bhāveyya*, *bhāveyyuṃ*, *bhāvayeyya*, *bhāvayeyyuṃ*, etc.—these are the causal agent forms (*hetukatturūpaṃ*).

*Bhāvīyeyya*, *bhāvīyeyyuṃ*. In the short vowel form: *bhāvayiyeyya*, *bhāvayiyeyyuṃ*. In the doubled form: *bhāviyyeyya*, *bhāviyyeyyuṃ*. Likewise, *bhāvayīyeyya*, *bhāvayīyeyyuṃ*, and so forth—these are the causal passive forms (*hetukamma-rūpa*).
581. *Eyya-eyyāsi-eyyaṃ-naṃ ṭe ka.* (Pāṇini 3.3.162; Rūpasiddhi 488; Nyāsa 1105).
For *eyya*, *eyyāsi*, and *eyyaṃ*, the suffix *ṭe* optionally occurs.
"A wise person should abandon even a small amount of suffering if they see abundant happiness" (Dhp 290). "Why do you, Sutasoma, grieve?
(Jā 2.21.399). "One should see the wise and listen to the wise; one should dwell together with the wise" (Jā 1.13.94), and so forth.

582. *Eyyuṃsuṃ* (Ka. 517; Rū. 488; Nī. 1105). For *eyyuṃ*, *uṃ* may optionally be substituted.
These are the canonical examples:
*vajjuṃ vā te na vā vajjuṃ, natthi nāsāya rūhanā jā* (Jā. 1.3.33), and *upayānāni me dajjuṃ, rājaputta tayī gata* (Jā. 2.22.26).
583. *Eyyāmassemu* and *ka*. (Kaṇḍa 517; Rūpasiddhi 488; Niddesa 1105). For the optative (*eyyāma*), there is *emu*, and for the ending, there is *u*.

Regarding the phrase “or in the case of [one’s] esteem,” the word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative (*avuttavikappana*). By this, hypothetical supposition (*parikappa*), the conditional mood (*kriyātipanna*), and so forth, are included.
Therein, hypothetical supposition (*parikappa*) is twofold, by way of what is factual (*bhūta*) and what is non-factual (*abhūta*).
In that regard, concerning the conception of what has come to be (*bhūtaparikappa*): whoever would associate with a fool, he too would become a fool.

Concerning the conception of what has not come to be (*abhūtaparikappa*): when a threefold cloak made of tortoise hair might exist; when a ladder well-constructed from the horns of hares might exist. Concerning the past conditional (*kriyātipanna*):
had he lived as a householder, he would have been a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattī rājā*).
Thus, *eyya* and so forth.
Now, the past tense (*hiyyattanī*) is explained.
584. *Anajjattane ā ū o ttha a mhā ttha tthuṃ se vhaṃ iṃ mhase ka.* (Ka. 418; Rū. 456; Nī. 886; Caṃ. 1.2.77; Pā. 3.2.111).
After a verbal root (*kriyattha*) expressing an action, when referring to a past time other than the present (*ajjatta*), the suffixes beginning with *ā* and so forth occur.
585. *Ā ī ssādīsvaña vā ka.* (Ka. 519; Rū. 457; Nī. 1032). When the suffixes beginning with *ssā* follow, the substitution of *ā* for *i* is optional.
In the cases beginning with *āicca* (aorist), *īicca* (perfect), and *ssādi* (precative), there is optionally another form at the beginning of those [suffixes].

Those verbal roots which receive the substitution of *ā* (āyādesa) without the suffix *Ṇānubandha* are called "ending in *e*" (*edanta*).

Therefore, those ending in *ā* and those ending in *e* are for the most part identical in form.

A collection (*samudāya*) is that wherein constituent parts (*avayava-dhammā*) arise together (*samudenti*); a method (*pariyāya*) is that by which things come in a distinct or complete manner (*paribyattaṃ āyanti*).

Now, the roots ending in consonants.
The Tudādigaṇa of Verbal Roots that Do Not Undergo Vowel Strengthening (Avuddhi).

Now, the forms of verbal roots ending in consonants are being stated. These are twofold: those that do not undergo vowel strengthening (avuddhika) and those that do (savuddhika). Among these, first the ones that do not undergo vowel strengthening are stated.
*Khipa*, *guha*, *tuda*, *disa*, *pisa*, *phusa*, *likha*, *vadhādi*.
Here, the vowel at the end of the verbal roots (*dhātu*) serves the purpose of pronunciation; it is not employed in the formation of word-forms (*rūpavidhāna*).
628. [The suffix] *ka* follows *tuda* and the rest. (Kaccāyana 445; Rūpasiddhi 433; Nyāsa 925; Cāndra 1.1.92; Pāṇini 3.1.77).
The suffix *kā* with a *kā*-anubandha becomes a zero-suffix (*apaccaya*). The *kā*-anubandha serves the purpose of indicating that no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) occurs.
From the root *khip* (in the sense of throwing): *khipati*, *pakkhipati*, *ukkhipati*, *okkhipati*, *nikkhipati*, *vikkhipati*, *paṭikkhipati*, *saṃkhipati*.
In the passive voice (*kamme*): *khipīyati*.

*Kārite* means "he causes to throw": *khipeti*, *khipayati*, *khipāpeti*, *khipāpayati*; or *khepeti*, *khepayati*. It means he throws water, he throws away craving, or he causes destruction (*khayāpeti*).
*Guha* is in the sense of concealing: *guhati*, *nigguhati*. In the passive voice (*kamme*), it is *guhiyati*.

In the active voice (*assa*), it becomes *tudeti* and *tudenti*. In the passive voice (*kamme*), it becomes *tudīyati*.

By the rule “for the letters *tavagga* and *varaṇa*, there are *cavagga* and *bayañā*,” the *da* of *dassa* becomes *ja*; thus, by the rule “for *vaggalasa*, there is *te*,” the original form of the *ya* becomes *tu*, resulting in *tujjati*.
*Kārite*: *tudeti*, *tudayati*, *tudāpeti*, *tudāpayati*. *Disī*: *uddisane*;

*Vadha* means killing; [the verb forms are] *vadhati*, *vadheti*.

When *dha* becomes *jha*, that is its prior form. In the causative (*kārita*), one should state *vadheti*, *vadhayati*, *vadhāpeti*, *vadhāpayati*; likewise, when the master causes a person to go along a path, one should state *gameti*, *gamayati*, *gamāpeti*, *gamāpayati*, and so forth.
Thus ends the *tudādigaṇa*. [Now follows] the forms with the honorific suffix (*savuddhikarūpa*).

In the future tense (*bhavissanti*), the conditional (*hīyyattani*), and the past non-evident (*parokkhā*), as well as in the past beyond the range of sight (*kālātipatti*), the root *atthi* becomes *bhū* before suffixes beginning with *ss-*.
This rule is intended to apply this substitution to these case endings of *atthi* as well. The resulting form is likewise simply *bhū*.
Thus: *so babhūva*, *te babhūvu*, *so abhavā*, *te abhavū*, *so bhavissati*, *te bhavissanti*, *so abhavissā*, *te abhavissaṃsu*, and so forth.

By this rule, [the forms] beginning with *ty-*, *tv-*, *eyy-*, etc., [are derived].

however, in the remaining four case-endings and in the suffixes beginning with *tabba*—excluding *nta*—the substitution of *bhū* for *atthi* is applicable. The root *āsa* means "to sit near.

*tumhe jagamittha* (you [plural] went), *ahaṃ jagamaṃ* (I went), *mayaṃ jagamimha* (we went). *so jagamittha* (he went), *te jagamire* (they two went), *tvaṃ jagamittho* (you went), *tumhe jagamivho* (you [plural] went), *ahaṃ jagamiṃ* (I went), *mayaṃ jagamimhe* (we went).

Or, by the rule “*vācchaṅa* for *gam*, *ami*, *sa*, and *sadisa*,” the *ma* of *gami* becomes *ccha* in all case-endings: *gacchati*, *gacchanti*, *gacchare*.

Regarding the rule: "The suffix *cchaṅ* optionally replaces the final vowel and consonant (*vasa*) of the roots *labh*, *vas*, *chid*, *gam*, *bhid*, and *rud*, when followed by the suffix *ssena* in case-endings containing *ss*. (Kaccāyana 481; Rūpasiddhi 524; Nyāsa 966, 968).

This means that for these [roots], *cchaṅ* optionally occurs before case endings containing *ss*, as well as for the suffix *sus* according to the sutta division, as in the canonical passage: *“nadīva avasucchatī”* (Jātaka 2.22.2140).
He will obtain, he will receive; he did not obtain, he did not receive; he will go, he will dwell; he did not go, he did not dwell;

Regarding the rule *disa-pekkhane*, etc., for the arising [of forms], the suffix *lo* is used in the sense of the agent (kattari). According to *Disassa passadassadasadadakkhā* (Kaṇḍa 471; Rūpasiddhi 483; Nāmamālā 951):
for the verbal root *dis* (to see), these substitutions—*passa*, *dassa*, *dasa*, *da*, and *dakkha*—occur optionally.

Vipassanā; the Blessed One Vipassī; Sudassī; Piyadassī; Atthadassī; Dhammadassī; "Sudassaṃ vajjamaññesaṃ" (DhP 252); the city of Sudassana; the king named Mahāsudassana (Dīgha Nikāya 2.242). Regarding the ten substitutes:
"The Lord who sees the Four Truths" (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā, Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā); "the Dhamma is difficult to see" (Mahāvadāna Sutta 7;

It is said that [the truth] is to be sought. "Behold the Dhamma, which is difficult to understand; herein the ignorant are utterly deluded. [The forms] *daṭṭhabbaṃ*, *daṭṭhā*, and *daṭṭhuṃ* [are derived from the root *dis*].
By this sutta, for the root *dis*, in all case endings (*vibhatti*) as appropriate, there are the substitutions *passa*, *dassa*, and *dakkha*;
and in the case of vowels such as *ā* and *ī*, there are the substitutions *da* and *dā*. Furthermore, the forms *dissati* and *dissanti* are [derived] because of the preceding form [of the root].
