In the *ī*-class (*īādi*), the forms are: *avaci*, *vaci*.

With the form *mahāvuttinā* (according to the Great Rule), together with the augment (*sāgamo*), [the forms are]: *avacāsi*, *vacāsi*, *avacuṃ*, *vacuṃ*, *avaciṃsu*, *vaciṃsu*. For the second person: *tvaṃ avaco*, *avaca*, *avaci*, *avacāsi*, *avacittha*, *avacittho*; for the plural: *tumhe avacittha*. By the rule *mhāthānamuña*, [the forms are]:

*tumhe avacuttha*, *vacuttha*. For the first person: *ahaṃ avaciṃ*, *vaciṃ*, *avacāsiṃ*, *vacāsiṃ*; for the plural: *mayaṃ avacimhā*, *vacimhā*, *avacimha*, *vacimha* or *mayaṃ avacumhā*, *vacumhā*. For the third person singular: *so avacā*, *vacā*.
*Rassatte-avaca, avacittha, vacittha vā, ahaṃ avacaṃ, avaca, vaca vā, mayaṃ avacimhe, vacimhe.* (652) *Īādīsu vacassoma ka.* (477;
Rūp 479; Nī 958; Cāndra 6.2.69; Pāṇini 7.4.20). In the case of the root *vac*, when followed by *ī* and other [affixes], the letter *o* is substituted for *mā* as an indicatory marker (*anubandha*).

*So avoci*, *te avocuṃ*, *avociṃsu*, *tvaṃ avoci*, *tumhe avocuttha*, *ahaṃ avociṃ*, *mayaṃ avocumhā*, *so avoca*. [In the case of] the short vowel, *bhagavā etadavoca udā*. 20. Regarding words beginning with *s*: 653.

For *vaca*, *bhuja*, *muc*, and *visāna*, the substitute *kkhaṅ* is applied [to the following *a*]. (Kaccāyana 481; Rūpasiddhi 524; Niddesa 963; "For *bhuja*, *muc*, *vaca*, and *visāna*, *kkhaṅ* [is substituted for the following *a*]"—this is found in many texts).
In the future tense (*ssayuttāsu vibhattīsu*), the final consonant of *vac* and other roots becomes *kkha*.

Examples: *vakkhati*, *vacissati*, *vakkhanti*, *vakkhare*, *vacissanti*, *vacissare*, *vakkhasi*, *vakkhatha*, *vakkhāmi*, *vakkhāma*, *vakkhate*, *vakkhante*, *vakkhase*, *vakkhavhe*, "I shall speak" (*ahaṃ vakkhaṃ*), *vacissaṃ*.
We shall say: *vakkhāmhe*, *vacissāmhe*.
By virtue of the governing rule "ssena," the substitution of *kkh* for the end of the verbal root is also obtained even without an explicit governing rule: *vakkhissati*, *vakkhissanti*.
Before suffixes beginning with *ss-*: *avakkhā*, *avacissā*, *avakkhaṃsu*, *avacissaṃsu*.
In the section on verbal forms (*vada-viyattiyaṃ*): [Active voice] *vadati*, *vadanti*; *ovadati*, *ovadanti*; *vadasi*, *vadatha*; *vadāmi*, *vadāma*.
[Present optative] *vade*, *vadetu*; *vadentu*; *vadesi*, *vadetha*; *vademi*, *vadema*.
[Passive voice] *vadīyati*, *vadiyyati*; *ovadīyati*, *ovadiyyati*.
When *da* is substituted for *ca*, the preceding form becomes *va*: *vajjati*, *vajjanti*, *ovajjati*, *ovajjanti*.
In the causative (*kārita*), [the forms are]: *bheriṃ vādeti*, *vādenti*, *vādayati*, *vādayanti*; *guruṃ abhivādeti*, *abhivādenti*, *abhivādesi*, *abhivādetha*, *abhivādemi*, *abhivādema*.
According to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), there is the substitution of *i* for this [root], resulting in either *abhivādiyāmi*, *abhivādiyāma*, or *abhivādayāmi*, *abhivādayāma*.
The meaning is: "I pay homage, I pay homage. For one who pays homage causes [the other] to utter auspicious words such as "May you be happy," and such speech is the duty toward one worthy of homage.
In the causative suffix *ṇāpi*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening; thus: *vadāpeti*, *vadāpayati*.

In the phrase “*gamavadadānaṃ ghammavajjadajjā vā*,” there is a substitution (*ādesa*) of *vajja* for *vaja*. In the rule “*ūlasse*,” there is the substitution of *etta* for *lassa*. [Thus one says] *vajjeti*, *vajjenti*.
In the passive (*kamma*), it is *vajjīyati*, *vajjīyanti*.
In the causative (*kārita*), it is *vajjāpeti*, *vajjāpayati*.

In the case of *eyya* and other [optative] suffixes, according to the rule “*eyya*, *eyyāse*, *eyyaṃ*, *naṃ*, *ṭe*,” there is the substitution of *et* for the singular forms of *eyya* and the rest: *vade*, *vadeyya*, *vajje*, *vajjeyya*, *vadeyyuṃ*, *vajjeyyuṃ*.
In the case of the substitute *vajja*, by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is the substitution of *ā* for *eyya*;

there is the elision of the word *eyya* in *eyyum* and the others: *so vajjā*, *te vajjuṃ*. Alternatively, there is the elision of the syllable *yyā* in *eyya* and the rest: *tvaṃ vajjāsi*, *vajjesi*, *tumhe vajjātha*, *vajjetha*, *ahaṃ vajjāmi*, *vajjemi*, *mayaṃ vajjāma*, *vajjema*, *ahaṃ vajjaṃ*, *mayaṃ vajjāmhe*, *vajjeyyāmhe*.
Whether this Pāli passage is correct or not, there is no growth of the nose, O lady (Jātaka 1.3.33); "Mother, may you speak of health;
and you, dear father, may you be happy" (Jātaka 2.22.2148); "Mother, may you all speak of health;
this Brahmin is leading us away" (Jātaka 2.22.2174), and so forth.
In the past (*hiyyattanīya*): *so avadā*, *vadā*, *avajjā*, *vajjā*; *te avaduṃ*, *vaduṃ*, *avajjuṃ*, *vajjuṃ*.
In the present (*ajjattanīya*): *so avadi*, *vadi*, *avajji*, *vajji*; *te avaduṃ*, *vaduṃ*, *avajjuṃ*, *vajjuṃ*, *avadiṃsu*, *vadiṃsu*, *avajjiṃsu*, *vajjiṃsu*.
In the future beginning with the suffix *-ss-*: *vadissati*, *vajjissati*.
Examples include *avadiṭṭhā* and *avajjiṭṭhā*. The root *vid-* means "to know";

thus, *vidati*. According to the rule “yuvaṇṇānam iyaṅuvaṅa sare” (the vowels *u* and *v* are replaced by *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* before a vowel), there is the substitution of *iya* before the vowel; thus, *te vidiyanti*.
*Kārite* means *nivedeti*, *paṭivedeti*, *nivedayati*, or *paṭivedayati*. In the passage *paṭivedayāmi vo bhikkhave* (MN 1.416), the meaning is "I make you know.
In the *Cūḷavagga* (Aṭṭhakathā 102), it says: *vedayāmahaṃ bhante, vedayatīti maṃ saṅgho dhāretu* ("Venerable sir, I make myself known;
may the Saṅgha remember me as one who makes himself known"). Alternatively, the meaning is "I make [it] known" or "I make it manifest."

“‘I feel, venerable sir; let the Saṅgha remember me as one who feels’—this is the reading in the *Cūḷavagga* (Vinaya Piṭaka), VIII.10.2. In that context, the substitution of *iyā* is appropriate when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant (*apaccaya*).
In the case of suffixes beginning with *ey*, we have: *videyya*, *vidiyeyya*, *videyyuṃ*, *vidiyeyyuṃ*. In the case of suffixes beginning with *ī*, [we have]:
*avedi* (from the root *vid* ‘to know’) for the destruction of conditions, and *te viduṃ*, *vidiṃsu*.”
*Kārite* (in the causative): *nivedesi*, *nivedayi*, *paṭivedesi*, *paṭivedayi*, *nivedayuṃ*, *nivedayiṃsu*, *paṭivedayuṃ*, *paṭivedayiṃsu*.
In the sense of "to see" (*vid-*) beginning with the root *sas*: *vidissati*, *vedissati*; "it is seen to be pure," thus I shall know it as great, etc.
(Mahāvaṃsa 134). In the sense of "dwelling" (*vas- nivāse*): *vasati*, *vasanti*, *nivasati*, *nivasanti*.

*Kamme-adhi*: preceded by *ā*, by which a village is inhabited, dwelt in, or presided over. Regarding the word *assu*: through the sutta [Pāṇini 6.4.19], the vowel *u* is substituted for the letter *a*;

thus one lives (*vussati*), they live (*vussanti*), or they dwell (*vussare*). The canonical passage at *Majjhima Nikāya* 1.257 reads: "The holy life is lived under the Blessed One" (*bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati*). In the causative form:
one causes to dwell (*vāseti*), one endures (*adhivāseti*), one causes to dwell (*vāsayati*), or one causes to endure (*adhivāsayati*).
In the *ṇāpi* [causative] suffix, there is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*): *vasāpeti*, *vasāpayati*.
In those beginning with *ī*: *avasi*, *vasi*, *avasum*, *vasum*, *avasimsu*, *vasimsu*.

In the case of *ssat* and other suffixes, according to the rule "for the roots *labh*, *vas*, *chid*, *gam*, *bhid*, and *rud*, [the suffix] *cchaṅ* [is applied]," the final consonant of the root combines with *ss*.
Covering; he will dwell, he will dwell, they will dwell; I shall dwell depending upon the Venerable One, Mahāva.
77. I do not go into his presence, Jā. 2.22.1933; they did not dwell, they will not dwell, they dwelt, they will have dwelt.
*Visa* in the sense of entering: he enters, they enter.
In the passive voice: *pavisīyati*, *pavisīyanti*, *pavisīyate*, *pavisīyante*.
In the future tense: *pavissati*, *pavissanti*, *pavissare*, *pavissate*, *pavissante*, *pavissare*.
In the causative: *paveseti*, *pavesayati*.
*Kamme-pavesīyati*, *pavesīyanti*.
Optionally, there is a long vowel for the prefix beginning with *ī*: *pāvisi*.

By the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), *kkha* is substituted for the end of the root: *pāvekkhi pathaviṃ cecco jā* (1.19.98), *so pāvekkhi kāsirājā jā* (1.15.266), *so tassa gehaṃ pāvekkhi jā* (1.15.303). [The forms] *pāvisuṃ*, *pāvisiṃsu*, *pāvekkhiṃsu*.
In the case of *satya* and other words, when combined with the suffix *ssa*, the final vowel of the verbal root is replaced by *kha* according to the rule "vaca bhuja muca visānaṃ kkhaṅa.
Thus: *pavekkhati*, *pavisissati*, *pavekkhanti*, *pavisissanti*, *esa bhiyyo pavekkhāmi*, *vammikaṃ sataporisaṃ jā.* (Ja 1.4.100), *pāvekkhā*, *pavisissā*, *pāvekkhaṃsu*, *pavisissaṃsu*.

In the case of *saṃsīdana*, the augment *īma* optionally occurs after the vowel of roots such as *sīda* (to sink), as in *sīdamīma vā*. Thus: *sīdati*, *sīdanti*, *lābūni sīdanti* (the gourds sink), *silā plavanti* (the stones float). [Pāṇini 1.1.77]. Likewise: *saṃsīdati*, *visīdati*, *osīdati*, *avasīdati*.
With the prefix *ni-*, it means sitting: *nisīdati*, *nisīdanti*.
With the prefix *pa-*, it means to have confidence: *pasīdati*, *pasīdanti*.

Even when used in the causative (*kārita*), there is no increase [of syllables] because of the substitution of another letter: *sīdeti*, *sīdayati*; *saṃsīdeti*, *saṃsīdayati*; *osīdeti*, *osīdayati*; *osīdāpeti*, *osīdāpayati*; *nisīdāpeti*, *nisīdāpayati*.
When preceded by *pa-*, the vowel *ī* does not occur: *pitā puttaṃ buddhe pasādeti*, *pasādayati*, *pasādenti*, *pasādayanti*.
In the passive (*kamma*), it is *pasādīyati*, *pasādīyanti*.
*Hana* means non-injury; it occurs in the sense of going (*gatīsu*). It takes the forms *hanati* and *hananti*.

By the rule "kvaci vikaraṇānam" (sometimes there is elision of the suffix), when the *la*-suffix is elided, we have *hanti*. Examples include: "The fruit destroys the plantain tree" (*phalaṃ ve kadaliṃ hanti*, Cūḷavagga 335); "Honour destroys the base man" (*sakkāro kāpurisaṃ hanti*, Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.64); and "An angry worldling destroys [himself]" (*hanti kuddho puthujjano*, Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.64).

According to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), there is sometimes elision of the final part of the root: "Crying out with intense [cries], they kill each other, one by one" (*vikkosamānā tibbāhi, hanti nesaṃ varaṃ varaṃ*, Jātaka 2.22.2370); "Hunters kill the deer"; "Fishermen kill the fish."
In the causative (*kamma-*) [suffix], there are *hanīyati* and *hanīyanti*.
When the final consonant of the root belongs to the *ca*-group, there is the substitution of the preceding form for *ya*, resulting in *haññati* and *haññanti*.
In the causative—
654. *Hanassa ghāto ṇānubandhe* (Ka. 591; Rū. 544; Nī. 1195).
The substitution of *ghā* occurs for *han* when a suffix with a nasal as its following consonant (*ṇānubandha*) follows.
[Examples: *ghāteti*, *ghātayati*, *ghātāpeti*, *ghātāpayati*.
In the active voice: *ghātīyati*, *ghātāpīyati*.
In the passive (*kamme*): *ahani*, *hani*, *ahaniṃsu*, *haniṃsu*;
*ahaññi*, *haññi*, *ahaññiṃsu*, *haññiṃsu*.
In the section beginning with *Ssatya*—655. Regarding *hanā jekhā*: Ka. 481; Rū. 524; Nī. 967, 969. “…*chakhā*” (in many instances), “*chekhā*” (in some places).

After *han*, the substitutes *je* and *khā* optionally occur for the letter *s* of another word; by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is the substitution of the following form (*pararūpatta*) for the final of the verbal root.
Hajjeti, hanissati, hajjenti, hajjesi, hajjetha, hajjemi, hanissāmi, hajjema, hanissāma.

By the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), the final consonant of the verbal root becomes a stop (*vagganta*) before the suffix *khādes*: *paṭihaṅkhati*, *paṭihanissati*, *paṭihaṅkhanti*, *paṭihaṅkhasi*, *paṭihaṅkhāmi*, *paṭihaṅkhāma*, *paṭihanissāma*.
*Hara* means "to take away": *harati*, *haranti*.
In the active voice (*kamme*): *harīyati*, *harīyanti*.
In the causative (*kārite*): *hāreti*, *hārayati*.
In the causative with the suffix *-āpi-* (*ṇāpimhi*), there is no *vṛddhi*: *harāpeti*, *harāpayati*.
*Kamme* means it is carried or caused to be carried.
Regarding *ā*, *ī*, and so forth—656. In the case of *ā*, *ī*, and so forth, there is the substitution of *sā* for *har*.
In the case of *ādi* and *īdi*, the letter *r* of *har* optionally becomes *ā*; thus, it becomes *ahā*, *aharā*.
In the case of *īdi*: *so ahāsi*, *ajini maṃ ahāsi me dha pa.* (Dhp.
3–4), *attānaṃ upasaṃhāsi*, *āsanaṃ abhihāsi*, *sāsane vihāsi*, *vihāsi purisuttamo gavesitabbaṃ*, *dhammaṃ payirudāhāsi*, *ahari*, *hari*.
They took, they seized, or they harmed [thinking], "May they not take my roots and fruits from there" (Jātaka 2.18.22, Pāli);
they took, they took, they took, they took, they took, they took; you took, you took, you all took, you all took;
I took, I took, I took—delighting in the teaching (Apadāna Thera 1.2.84); we took, we took.
In *parachakke assa tthattaṃ*, it becomes *so ahāsittha*, *aharittha*. Regarding *ssatya* and the others—657.
In the case of *harassa cāhaṅa sse*, it becomes *hāssa cāhaṅa ssena* (according to many manuscripts).
In the *ssakāravatī* (suffixes containing *ss*), the letter *r* of both *harati* and *karoti* optionally becomes *āhaṅ*. When the augment *iu* (*i*) is added, it becomes *hāhi*;
and when the suffix *khāri* (*jā*) is added, it becomes *hāhi*. [Examples: *hāhati* or *harissati*, *hāhinti*, *hāhanti*, *harissanti*, *hāhasi*.
"O monk, you shall dwell in happiness" (*sukhaṃ bhikkhu vihāhisi*). [From Dhammapada 379. *hāhatha*, *hāhāmi*, *hāhāma*, *harissāma*.

According to the *Mahāvuttin*, there is also elision (*lopa*) of the final consonant of the root when followed by *harassa*: the canonical texts read, “*yo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye appamatto vihassati*” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.185), “*purakkhatvā vihassāma*” (Therīgāthā 121), and “*ahaṃ udakamāhissaṃ*” (Jātaka 2.22.1931).
In the case of roots beginning with *ss-*: *ahāhā*, *aharissā*, *ahāhaṃsu*, *aharissaṃsu*.
With the prefix *ā-* in the sense of wishing or praying: *āsīsati*, *āsīsanti*, *paccāsīsati*, *paccāsīsanti*.
658. *Ādismā sarā caṃ* (Candaviveka 5.1.3; Pāṇini 6.1.2):

A single-syllable form that is the first sound following a vowel at the beginning [of a word] becomes double. By this rule, for roots and words preceded by a vowel, when doubling occurs, two forms arise:
*āsīsa* and *sīsa*. 659. *Loponādibyañjanassa caṃ* (Candaviveka 6.2.112; Pāṇini 7.4.60).
In the case of a doubling (dvitta), there is the elision (lopa) of one initial consonant; thus, in the preceding forms *āsīsissati* and *āsīsissanti*, there is the elision of the letter *s*.

Likewise, according to the rule *parokkhāyañca* ("and in the parokkhā tense"), by the word *ca* ("and") in that sutta, when doubling is applied to verbal roots such as *kam*, the rule *loponādibyañjanassa* ("there is elision of the initial consonant") applies.
In the preceding word-forms, there is the elision of the initial consonant; by the rule “for the *ka*-vaggas, the *ca*-vaggas,” the remaining *ka*-vaggas become *ca*-vaggas;
and by the rule “and the *niggahīta*,” there is the insertion of the *niggahīta*. Thus: *caṅkamati*, *caṅkamanti*, *caṅkamatu*, *caṅkamantu*, *caṅkameyya*, *caṅkameyyuṃ*, and so forth.
In *kucasaṅkocane*: *caṅkocati*, *caṅkocanti*.
In *calacalane*: *cañcalati*, *cañcalanti*.
According to the *Mahāvutti*, when the *niggahīta* undergoes the substitution of the following form (*pararūpa*) and the breaking apart (*bhijjana*), [we have] *jajjarati*, *jajjaranti*.
In *daḷa-ditti*, [the forms] *daddallati* and *daddallanti* occur;
in *moha-vecitta*, *momuhati* and *momuhanti* occur, as exemplified by the great rule (*mahāvutti*).
Likewise, in the sense of sound (*ru-sadde*), *roruvati* and *roruvanti* occur.
Examples include *lupa-giddhe*, *loluppati*, and *loluppanti*.
Reduplication (*padadvitta*) is used for the purpose of indicating intensity (*atisaya*) of the word-meaning;

however, in cases of repetition (*vicchā*), such as *ponopuñña*, or in instances of confusion (*sambhama*) and the like, there is no elision of the initial consonant (*anādibyañjanalopa*) when reduplicated, as in *gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo*. Likewise, it occurs in some cases even when indicating intensity.
Form-form, suffering-suffering, internal-internal, god-god, sage-sage, king-king, Brahma-Brahma,
excellent-excellent, foremost-foremost, eldest-eldest, best-best, praised-praised, risen-risen, superior-superior,
inferior-inferior, weak-weak, powerless-powerless, great-great, and so forth.
The *bhūvādi* class is finished.
Now the *rudhādi* class is being stated.

The word *kattari* (in the sense of the agent) recurs; and because of the governing rule of multiplicity (*bahulādhikāra*), it indicates that the occurrence of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) is fixed for the agent, but not fixed for the state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), as they occur optionally.
Therefore, the occurrence of verbal suffixes should be understood to apply to the state, to the object, and to forms expressing causality (*kārita*).
*chida*, *bhida*, *bhuja*, *muca*, *yuja*, *rica*, *rudha*, *lipa*, *vida*, *sica*, *subha*. 660. According to *Mañjūsāsaddanīti* (ka.
446; rū. 509; nī. 926; caṃ. 1.1.93; pā. 3.1.78): after the roots beginning with *rudh* used in the sense of action (*kriyāttha*), the suffix *lo* occurs in the agent (*kartari*).
Furthermore, following the final vowel of those roots beginning with *rudh*, there is a *niggahīta* [anusvāra].
The prefix *ā-* occurs here for the purpose of indicating the preceding part [of the root]; the vowel *a-* is for the sake of pronunciation;
by the word *ca* ("and"), the suffixes *i*, *ī*, *e*, and *o* following roots such as *subha* are included; the final consonant of the group (*vagganta*) replaces the nasal (*niggahīta*).
Thus: *rundhati*.
In the sense of "cutting into two," [the forms are] *chindati*, *chindanti*.

In the passive voice (*kamme kyo*), by the rule “*tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā*,” the final *y* of the root becomes *c*; and by the rule “*vaggalasehi te*,” the *y* undergoes the substitution of its preceding form (*pubbarūpatta*).
Thus: *chijjati*, *chijjanti*. By the rule “*garupubbā rassā re ntentīnaṃ*,” the *re* is substituted for the four endings *nte* and *ntīnaṃ*: *chindate*, *chijjate*, *chijjante*, *chijjare*.
By this [rule], the insertion of the nasal (niggahītāgama) is elided: *chindīyati*, *chindīyanti*, *chindīyate*, *chindīyante*.
In the causative: *chedeti*, *chedayati*, *chedāpeti*, *chedāpayati*, *chindeti*, *chindayati*, *chindāpeti*, *chindāpayati*.
In forms beginning with *ī*: *acchindi*, *chindi*, *acchinduṃ*, *chinduṃ*, *acchindiṃsu*, *chindiṃsu*.

According to the *Mahāvuttin*: "The final consonant of the root becomes *cch*, and there is doubling of the preceding [consonant]. Thus: *acchecchi taṇhaṃ, vivattayi saṃyojanaṃ* (he cut off craving, he cast off the fetters). 53. Furthermore, the reading *divādi* is seen as *acchejjī*; for example:
*acchecchuṃ vata bho rukkhaṃ* (O, they have indeed cut down the tree) [Jātaka 2.22.1788]. In the passive (*kamma*): *acchijji*, *chijji*, *acchindiyi*, *chindiyi*. In the causative (*kārita*):
*chedesi*, *kaṇṇanāsañca chedayi* (and he caused the ears and nose to be cut off) [Jātaka 1.4.49], *chindesi*, *chindayi*.
In the *ssādi* [future tense]: *acchecchā*, *acchindissā*, *acchecchaṃsu*, *acchindissaṃsu*.
In the sense of splitting (*bhida-vidāraṇe*): *bhindati*, *bhindanti*.
In the passive (*kamme*): *bhijjati*, *bhijjanti*, *bhijjare*, *bhindiyati*, *bhindiyanti*.

In the passive voice: *bhikkhū bhikkhūhi bhedeti* (he causes the monks to be divided by the monks), *mahāva*. 107. [Present tense: *bhedayati*, *bhedāpeti*, *bhedāpayati*, *bhindeti*, *bhindayati*, *bhindāpeti*, *bhindāpayati*.
In the passive: *bhedīyati*, *bhedāpīyati*. In the *ī*-class and others:
*abhindi*, *bhindi*, *abhinduṃ*, *bhinduṃ*, *abhindiṃsu*, *bhindiṃsu*.
*Kamme*: *abhijji*, *bhijji*, *abhindiyi*, *bhindiyi*.
*Kārite*: *abhedesi*, *bhedesi*, *abhedayi*, *bhedayi*, *bhedāpesi*, *bhedāpayi*.
In the presence of *ss* and so forth—by the rule beginning with “*labhavasa…*” and so on, there is the substitution of *cch* for *d* together with *ss*: *bhecchati*, *bhindissati*, *bhecchanti*.
They will break; you will break; you [plural] will break; I will break; we will break; we [plural] will break; “I shall break that for you with wisdom”—this is the *Suttanipāta* (Su.Ni.
445 reading. In forms beginning with *ssā*, there are such examples as *acchecchā* and *acchindissā*.
In the sense of protecting the arms or in the sense of dealing with transactions: *bhuñjati*, *bhuñjanti*.
In the passive sense (*kamme*): *bhujjati*, *bhujjanti*.
In the causative sense (*kārite*): *bhojeti*, *bhojayati*, *bhojāpeti*, *bhojāpayati*.
*Kamme* (in the passive sense): *bhojīyati*, *bhojāpīyati*.

In the presence of *ss-* and so forth, by the rule "for *vac*, *bhuj*, *muc*, and *vis*, there is *kkha*," the final consonant of the root becomes *kkha*, the initial vowel undergoes *vuddhi*, and [the forms are]: *bhokkhati*, *bhuñjissati*, *bhokkhanti*, *bhokkhasi*, *bhokkhatha*, *bhokkhāmi*, *bhokkhāma*, *bhuñjissāma*.
In the presence of *ssā-* and so forth: *abhokkhā*, *abhuñjissā*, *abhokkhaṃsu*, *abhuñjissaṃsu*, and so on.
In the sense of releasing: *muñcati*, *muñcanti*, *muñcare*.
In the passive sense (*kamma*): *muccati*, *muccanti*, *muñcīyati*, *muñcīyanti*.
In the causative sense (*kārita*): *mocāpeti*, *mocāpayati*.
In the present tense (īādi): *amuñci*, *muñci*, *amuñciṃsu*, *muñciṃsu*.
In the causative (*kārita*): *amocesi*, *mocesi*, *amocayi*, *mocayi*, *amocesuṃ*, *mocesuṃ*, *amocayuṃ*, *mocayuṃ*, *amociṃsu*, *mociṃsu*, *amocayiṃsu*, *mocayiṃsu*.

In the future tense beginning with *-ss-* (*ssatthādi*), the suffix *-ssa* is added along with the change of *ca* to *kkha*: *mokkhati*, *muñcissati*, *mokkhanti*. Examples: *mārabandhanā dha* (Dhp. 37); *na me samaṇa mokkhasi* (Saṃ. Ni. 1.140). *Mokkhatha*, *mokkhāmi*, *mokkhāma*, *muñcissāma*.
*Sādi* (to begin): *amokkhā*, *mokkhā*, *amuñcissā*, *muñcissā*, *amokkhaṃsu*, *mokkhaṃsu*, *amuñcissaṃsu*, *muñcissaṃsu*.

*Yuj* (in the sense of "joining"): *yuñjati* means he joins in the Buddha’s teaching; the meaning is that he exerts himself. *Yuñjanti*: they devote themselves to negligence, as in the verse: "Fools of dull wit... (*Dhammapada* 26). *Yuñjasi*, *yuñjatha*: "Exert yourselves in the Buddha’s teaching" (*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.185).
*Yuñjāmi*, *yuñjāma*. In the passive voice: *yuñjīyati*, *yuñjīyanti*.
*Kāreti*: yojeti, payojeti, niyojeti, uyyojeti, yojayati, payojayati, niyojayati, uyyojayati.
*Kamme*: yojīyati, payojīyati, niyojīyati, uyyojīyati.
*Rudha* (to obstruct): rundhati, rundhiti, rundhīti, rundheti, rundhoti, rundhanti, orundhati.
*avarundhati*, *rundhāpeti*, *rundhāpayati*, *avarodheti*, *avarodhayati*, *uparodheti*, *uparodhayati*, *rodhāpeti*, *rodhāpayati*.
In the passive voice: *avarodhīyati*, and so forth.
In the sense of smearing: *lipati*, *limpati*, *limpanti*.
In the passive (*kamma*):
*limpiyati*. In the causative (*kārita*): *limpeti*, *limpayati*, *limpāpeti*, *limpāpayati*, *lepeti*, *lepayati*, *lepāpeti*, *lepāpayati*, and so forth.
In the sense of obtaining life: *vindati*, *vindanti*.
In the passive sense: *vindīyati*, *vindīyanti*.
In the causative sense: *vindeti*, *vindayati*, *vindāpeti*, *vindāpayati*.
In the section beginning with *ī*: *avindi*, *vindi*; "they found mud there in the courtyard," *jā* 1.1.2; *avindiṃsu*, *vindiṃsu*, and so forth.
In the root *sic* (to sprinkle): *siñcati*, *siñcanti*. In the passive (*kamma*): *siñcīyati*, *siñcīyanti*.
In the causative (*kārite*): *siñceti*, *siñcayati*, *siñcāpeti*, *siñcāpayati*; or "he should sprinkle" (*siñceyya*) or "he should cause to sprinkle" (*siñcāpeyya*), [resulting in] *pāci*.

140. Thus and so forth. In the sense of striking (*sampahāre*): "He strikes us like cattle" (*yo no gāvova sumbhati*). 2.22.2132. *Sumbhanti*, *sumbhasi*, *sumbhatha*; "I strike the ground with speed" (*bhūmiṃ sumbhāmi vegasā*). 1.5.51. *Sumbhāma*, *sumbhiti*, *sumbhīti*, *sumbheti*, *sumbhoti*, and so forth.
The root *gaha* is also included here. In the sense of grasping (*upādāne*): by the rule "and for *rudh*-type roots," the suffix *lap* is added together with the nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*).
661. *Ṇo* replaces the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). (Kaccāyana 490; Rūpasiddhi 518; Nyāsa 982).
The *ṇo* is substituted for the *niggahīta* occurring after the verbal root *gaha*. By the alternative rule (*vikappa*) of the *Mahāvutti*, the long vowel is substituted for the *la*.
Thus: *gaṇhāti*, or *gaṇhati*; *gaṇhanti*; *gaṇhasi*; *gaṇhatha*; *gaṇhāmi*; *gaṇhāma*.
In the active voice (kamme): *gaṇhīyati*, *gaṇhīyanti*.
Regarding the substitution of *ha* for *ya*: it is a reversal (*vipariyāso*) of *ya*; thus [the forms] are *gayhati*, *gayhanti*, *gayhare*.
In the causative (kārite): *gāheti*, *gāhayati*, *gāhāpeti*, *gāhāpayati*, and so forth.
662. *Gahassa gheppa* (ka. 489; rū. 519; nī. 901).
In the case of suffixes such as *nta*, *māna*, and *ty-*, the substitution of *gheppa* for *gaha* optionally occurs.
Examples: *gheppati*, *gheppanti*.
It is grasped by action; they are grasped. In the *ī*-class: *agaṇhi*, *gaṇhi*.

By the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), there is elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), and the augment *iñ* becomes *etta*; thus: *aggahesi*, *paṭiggahesi*, *anuggahesi*; *aggaṇhiṃsu*, *gaṇhiṃsu*; *aggahesuṃ*, *paṭiggahesuṃ*, *anuggahesuṃ*.
In the *sattya* group (the sixth class), there are forms such as *gaṇhissati*, *gahessati*, *gaṇhissanti*, and *gahessanti*.
The *rudhādi* group is finished. Now, the *divādi* group (the fourth class).
Now the *div-ādi-gaṇa* (the class beginning with *div*) is stated.
Here, the sequence of roots (*dhātu*) is to be understood according to their final consonants, because they are entirely similar in form.
*Muca*, *vica*, *yuja*, *luja*, *vija*, *gada*, *pada*, *mada*, *vida*, *idha*, *kudha*, *gidha*, *budha*.

*yudh* (to fight), *vidh* (to arrange), *sidh* (to succeed), *sudh* (to purify), *man* (to think), *han* (to kill), *kup* (to be angry), *dīp* (to shine), *lup* (to cut off), *vap* (to sow), *sup* (to sleep), *div* (to play), *siv* (to sew), *tas* (to perish), *tus* (to satisfy), *dis* (to show), *duṣ* (to corrupt), *sis* (to sharpen), *sus* (to extract juice), *dah* (to burn), *nah* (to bind), *muh* (to be confused). 663.
The suffix *yaka* is added after roots beginning with *div*. (Kāśikā 3.1.69; Rūpamālā 510; Nīḍāna 928; Cāndra 1.1.87; Pāṇini 3.1.69).

The suffix *ya*, which has *kā* as its consonantal bond (*anubandha*), occurs after roots beginning with *div* when used in the sense of an action (*kriyāttha*) and denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). [Examples:
*dibbati*.

[From the root] *muc* in the sense of releasing (*muttiyaṃ*): because of the substitution of the preceding form (*pubbarūpattaṃ*) for *ya*, we have *muccati* and *vimuccati*. Since these are intransitive (*akammaka*), the pure passive form (*suddhakammarūpaṃ*) is not obtained.
In the causative: *moceti*, *mocayati*, *mocāpeti*, *mocāpayati*. In the passive: *mocīyati*, *mocāpīyati*;
[imperative] *muccatu*; [optative] *muccantu* (may they be released from suffering).
In the sense of "liberation" (*mokkha*), etc., the final consonant of the root becomes *kkha*: *mokkhati*, *mokkhanti*.
In the sense of separation (*vica-viveke*): *viviccati*, *viviccanti*.
In the causative sense (*kārite*): *viveceti*, *vivecayati*, *vivecāpeti*, *vivecāpayati*.
In the passive sense (*kamme*): *vivecīyati*, *vivecāpīyati*, and so forth.
In *yuj*—meaning "to join": *yujjati*, *yujjanti*.
In *luj*—meaning "destruction": *lujjati*, *lujjanti*.
In *vij*—meaning "fear" and "movement": *saṃvijjati*, *saṃvijjanti*.
In the causative: *saṃvejeti*, *saṃvejayati*, *saṃvejenti*, *saṃvejayanti*, and so forth.
*Gada* in the sense of thundering: *megho gajjati*, *gajjanti*.
*Pada* in the sense of going: *uppajjati*, *uppajjanti*; *nipajjati*, *vipajjati*, *sampajjati*, *āpajjati*, *samāpajjati*, *paṭipajjati*.
By means of the *kamme*-suffix: one incurs an offense (*āpatti*), enters into a meditative absorption (*jhāna*), or proceeds upon the path (*magga*).
When the suffix *yaka* occurs after a causative (*kyamhi*) verb: by that [suffix], an offense is incurred; a meditative absorption is entered into;

the path is proceeded upon. In the causative (*kārite*): one causes to arise, causes to arise; causes to produce, causes to produce; causes to accomplish, causes to accomplish. One causes to fulfill, causes to fulfill; causes to bring about, causes to bring about; causes to lead toward, causes to lead toward; causes to cause to proceed, causes to cause to proceed.
It is produced by action (*kamma*); it is brought forth, accomplished, attained, and realized.
"May it arise! May they arise! May it arise! May they arise! How indeed might a bowl arise for my co-resident? How might a robe arise?
How might requisites arise?"—thus, indeed, [he thinks]. These, moreover, are the verbal forms of the agent and the action.
In the beginning of a word: *uppajji*, *nipajji*, *vipajji*, *sampajji*, *āpajji*, *samāpajji*, *paṭipajji*.
664. In some cases, there is the substitution of *ka* for verbal suffixes (vikaraṇa). Rule 517; Rūpasiddhi 488; Nīti-mālā 1105.
In certain instances, there is the elision (*lopa*) of verbal suffixes.
“Vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, light arose” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081), and so forth; [the verbs] *uppajjiṃsu* and *nipajjiṃsu*.
In the sense of intoxication and madness: *majjati*, *majjanti*.
In the sense of existence: *vijjati*, *saṃvijjati*.
*Idha* means "here"; it signifies success (*ijjhati*, *samijjhati*).
*Kudha* means "anger"; it signifies being angry (*kujjhati*, *kujjhanti*).
*Budha* means "understanding"; it signifies awakening (*bujjhati*, *sambujjhati*).
The prefix *paṭi-* [is used] in the senses of awakening from sleep, blooming, and [repeatedly] waking up (*paṭibujjhati*).

Regarding the passive voice: by means of that [prefix], one wakes up to the Dhamma (*dhammo bujjhati*), [the Dhamma] is awakened to, they are awakened to, it is being awakened to, they are being awakened to (*bujjhare*, *bujjhīyati*, *bujjhīyanti*).

Regarding the causative voice: one causes to awaken, one causes to awaken [someone], one causes to be awakened, one causes to be awakened, one causes to be awakened to, one causes to be awakened to (*bodheti*, *bodhayati*, *bodhāpeti*, *bodhāpayati*, *bujjhāpeti*, *bujjhāpayati*).

In the sense of combat: a wrestler fights with a wrestler; two armies fight; two rams fight; two bulls fight; two elephants fight; two cocks fight. In the sense of an object (kamma): *yujjhati*, *yujjhanti*.
In the sense of causing another to act (kārita):
*yodheti*, *yodhayati*, *yujjhāpeti*, *yujjhāpayati*; as in the Pāli text at Dhammapada 40: “*Yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhena*” (“Fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom”).
In the sense of piercing (*vidha-tāḷane*): one pierces a deer with an arrow;

one penetrates the Dhamma; they penetrate [it]. There is also a form where the object is treated like the agent: by that, one penetrates the Dhamma; they penetrate the Dhammas; it is penetrated; they are penetrated. In the causative (*kārite*):
he causes to pierce, he causes to cause to pierce; he causes to penetrate, he causes to cause to penetrate, and so forth.
In the *Siddhasaṃsiddhi*: *sijjhati*, *sijjhanti*, *sijjhare*.
In the causative (*kārita*), by the *Mahāvutti* rule, the substitution of *ātta* for *issa* occurs: *sādheti*, *sādhayati*, *sādhenti*, *sādhayanti*.
In the passive (*kamma*): *sādhīyati*, *sādhīyanti*, and so forth.
In the sense of purification: *sujjhati*, *sujjhanti*, *visujjhati*, *parisujjhati*.
In the causative: *sodheti*, *sodhayati*.
In the sense of conceiving or imagining: *maññati*, *avamaññati*, *atimaññati*; *maññanti*, *avamaññanti*, *atimaññanti*, and so forth.
*Hana* (to strike): *hana-vighāta*, *saṅghātesu*, *haññati*, *vihaññati*, *haññanti*, *vihaññanti*, etc.
*Kupa* (to be agitated): *paro parassa kuppati*, *kucchivāto kuppati*, *rogo kuppati*, *paṭikuppati*, *tejodhātu pakuppati* (M.N.
1.305). In the causative (*kārita*): *kopeti*, *kopayati*, etc.
In *dīpa-dittiyaṃ*, [the forms] *dippati* and *dippanti* occur; previously, in the *Cūḷava*, it was stated that unrighteousness (*adhamma*) shines forth.
437. In the passive (*kamma*), [the forms] *dīpīyati* and *dīpīyanti* occur.
In the causative (*kārita*), because of the heavy suffix *-panta*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening; thus, [the forms] *dīpeti*, *dīpayati*, *dīpenti*, and *dīpayanti* occur, and so forth.
In the sense of "not seeing," there are *luppa-dassane*, *luppate*, and *luppante*.
In the causative, there are *lopeti*, *lopayati*, and so forth.
In the sense of "sowing seeds," there are *vappa-bīja-nikkhepe*, *vappate*, *vappante*, and so forth.
In *suppa* (to sleep): *suppati*, *suppanti*. By the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is initial vowel strengthening (*ādivuddhi*): *soppati*, *soppanti*. In *sam* (calmness) and *upa-sam* (dwelling):

*sammati*, *visammati*, *upasammati*, *vūpasammati*. In *assama* (hermitage), it is *sammati*; where it is *sammati*, the word *temiya* is born [as an example]. (2.22.73) *sammanti*. In the causative (*kārita*), there is no strengthening: *sameti*, *vūpasameti*, and so forth.

In the sense of playing, desiring victory, legal dispute, praise, beauty, going, and power, for the letters *ta*, *tha*, *da*, and *dha*, *ya* is substituted according to the rule “for *ta*-group and *va-raṇa* [consonants], *ya* is substituted for *ca*-group and *ba-ya*” (*tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā*);
and for the letter *sa*, *ya* is substituted according to the rule “for *vaggas* and *las*, *te*” (*vaggalasehi te*). Thus, one has *dibbati*, *dibbanti*, and so forth.
In the sense of sewing, for the root *sivu*, one has *sibbati*, *sibbanti*, *sibbeyya*, or *sibbāpeyya*, and so forth. (Pāci 176).

In the sense of being terrified (*tasa-santāse*), it means "he is terrified" (*tassati*). According to the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), *tassa* becomes *trattaṃ*; thus, *utrassati* means "he is greatly terrified" or "he is agitated. In the sense of thirsting, it means "he thirsts" (*tassati*) or "he is distressed by thirst" (*paritassati*).
In the causative form, it appears as *tāseti*, *tāsayati*, and so forth.
In the sense of satisfaction (*tusa-pīti*): *tussati*, *santussati*.
Also in the sense of action (*kamma*): *tussati*, *santussati*, *tussīyati*.
In the causative (*kārita*): *toseti*, *tosayati*, and so forth.
*Disa-paññāyane*: it is seen, it is clearly seen, it is perceived. "Fools and the incompetent are seen," *Mahāvaṃsa* 76;
"signs are clearly seen," *Buddhavamsa* 2.82; "these qualities are perceived in me," *Majjhima Nikāya* 3.253;
"and I am perceived among these qualities" (*Majjhima Nikāya* 3.253—slightly different).
In the sense of "resisting what is disagreeable," one hates (*dussati*). One hates those things that provoke hatred (*dosaneyyesu*). [The forms] *padussati*, *dussanti*, and *padussanti* occur.
In the causative, the vowel is lengthened: *dūseti*, *dūsayati*.
In the passive, *dūsīyati*, and so forth.
*Sisa* in the sense of "remaining" (*asabbayoge*): *sisati*, *avasissati*. "The remains shall remain. In the causative:
*seseti*, *sesayati*, etc. *Susa* in the sense of "drying up" (*sussane*): *sussati*.
"Let the bones, the sinews, and the skin remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up" (M.N. 2.184). [Note: this passage is slightly different. Etc.
*Daha* (to burn): *dāho*, *ha*; the opposite is *vipariyāyo*. [Examples: *dayhati*, *dayhanti*, *ekacitakamhi dayhare*.
In the causative: *dāheti*, *dāhayati*, etc.
*Naha* (to bind): *sannayhati*, *sannayhanti*, etc.
*Muha*: *muyhane*, *muyhati*, *sammuyhati*, *sammuyhāmi*, *pamuyhāmi*. "All directions are bewildered by me.
(2.22.2185). In the causative: *moheti*, *mohayati*, etc.
The *div-ādi* class is concluded.
The *svādi-gaṇa*:
Now the *svādi-gaṇa* is stated:
*gi*, *ci*, *mi*, *vu*, *su*, *hi*, *āpa*, *saka*.
The term ‘kā’ is being discussed. 665.
After roots beginning with *svād* that have *kṇ* as an affix, *ka* [is substituted]. (Moggallāna 4.48; Rūpasiddhi 512; Nyāsa 929; Cāndra 1.1.95; Pāṇini 3.1.74; cf. *svādibhyaḥ...* in many texts).
After roots beginning with *svād* that signify an action (*kriyārtha*), two suffixes, *ṇa* and *ṇo*, both having *kā* as their indicatory letter (*kānubandha*), occur.
666. *Na te kānubandhanāgamesu*:

When followed by suffixes or augments (*āgama*) having *k* as their consonantal adjunct (*kānubandha*), the letters *i*, *u*, and *a* do not undergo the changes to *e*, *o*, and *ā*. This is a prohibition against *vuddhi* (vowel strengthening).
Examples: *suṇāti*, *suṇoti*.
In the root *gi* (to take): *giṇāti*, *giṇoti*, *anugiṇāti*, *paṭigiṇāti*.
By the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbassaralopa*), we have *anugiṇanti*, *paṭigiṇanti*.

In the root *ci* (to pile up): by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is the substitution of *ṇa* for *na*; thus, a mason (*vaḍḍhakī*) piles up (*cināti*, *cinoti*), builds up (*ācināti*, *ācinoti*), or dismantles (*apacināti*, *apacinoti*)—the meaning being that he destroys.
There is elision of the preceding vowel: *cinanti*, *ācinanti*, *apacinanti*.
In the passive (*kamma*): *cīyati*, *ācīyati*, *apacīyati*, *cinīyati*, *ācinīyati*, *apacinīyati*.
In the causative (*kārita*): *cayāpeti*, *cayāpayati*, *cināpeti*, *cināpayati*, and so forth.
*Mi*, in the sense of measuring: *miṇāti*, *miṇoti*, *mināti*, *minoti*.
*Vu*, in the sense of covering: *saṃvuṇāti*, *saṃvuṇoti*, *āvuṇāti*, *āvuṇoti*.
*Su*, in the sense of hearing: *suṇāti*, *suṇoti*, *suṇanti*, *suṇāsi*, *suṇosi*.
Listen attentively, O Great Nāga! 126. *Suṇātha*, *suṇotha*, *suṇāmi*, *suṇomi*, *suṇāma*, *suṇoma*.
In the passive (*kamme*), by the rule “the vowel becomes long before a primary suffix (*kyamhi*)”, we have *sūyati*, *sūyanti*, *suyyati*, *suyyanti*, *suṇīyati*, *suṇīyanti*.
In the causative (*kārite*): *sāveti*, *anusāveti*, *sāvayati*, *anusāvayati*, *suṇāpeti*, *suṇāpayati*.
*Kamme* (in the passive sense): *sāvīyati*, *anusāvīyati*.
[Optative forms]: *suṇātu*, *suṇantu*; *suyyatu*, *suyyantu*; *sāvetu*, *sāventu*; *suṇe*, *suṇeyya*, *suṇeyyuṃ*; *sūyeyya*, *suyyeyya*, *sūyeyyuṃ*, *suyyeyuṃ*; *sāveyya*, *sāveyyuṃ*.
In the case of roots beginning with *ī*: *asuṇi*, *suṇi*.
667. Among those [verbs], *suta* [is formed as follows]: *kṇo*, *kṇānaṃ roṭa* (Kaṇḍa 517; Rūpasiddhi 488; Nyāsa 1105).

In those verbal forms beginning with *ī* and others that possess the letter *ss*, the *kṇo* and *kṇānaṃ* suffixes following the root *su* undergo the substitution of *roṭ*. The letter *r* is an *anubandha* for the purpose of indicating a universal replacement (*sabbādesa*). By the rule “*rānubandhentasarādissā*” (the initial vowel of the suffix is elided), the initial vowel is dropped, and doubling (*dvitta*) occurs.
Thus: *assosi*, *assosuṃ*, *assosi*, *assosittha*, *assosiṃ*, *assosimhā*, *assosumhā*, *assosittha*, and so forth.

In the *satya*-class (*sacca-vagga*), [the forms] will be: *suṇissati*, *sossati*, *suṇissanti*, *sossanti*, *suṇissasi*, *sossasi*, *suṇissatha*, *sossatha*, *suṇissāmi*, *sossāmi*, *suṇissāma*, *sossāma*. Thus it is in the second group (*parachakka*). In the *ssādi*-group:
*asuṇissā*, *asossā*, *asuṇissaṃsu*, *sossaṃsu*, and so forth.
With the prefix *pa-* in the sense of sending, [we have]: *pahiṇāti*, *pahiṇoti*, *pahiṇanti*.

In the word *īdādīnam* [in the rule], he sent a messenger (*dūtaṃ pahiṇi*), they sent [messengers] (*pahiṇiṃsu*). By the rule "kvaci vikaraṇānaṃ," there is the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*); by the *Mahāvutti*, see that the vowel is longened. He sent the messenger (*dūtaṃ pāhesi*) to the other shore (*pārā*); 297; *Mahāvaṃsa* 198, and so on, such as "they sent" (*pāhesuṃ*).
With the prefix *pa-*, [the root] *āp-* means "to reach. — 668. Regarding *sakāpānaṃ kukku ṇe ka*: 517; *Rūpasiddhi* 488; *Nirutti* 1105; "...*kukakū ṇe*" (found in many texts).
In the case of the roots *pā* and *pari*, when the suffix *kṇa* follows, the letters *k* and *u* respectively become augmentations (*āgama*).
Thus: *pāpuṇoti*, *pāpuṇanti*, *sampāpuṇanti*.
With the prefix *pari*, it means "to master" (*pariyatti*): *pariyāpuṇāti*, *pariyāpuṇanti*.
The prefix *sam-* [is used in the sense that] one attains (*samāpuṇāti*), one completes (*parisamāpuṇāti*), or one reaches the conclusion (*niṭṭhānaṃ gacchati*). What about the root *kaṇ*?
It means "to obtain" (*pappoti*).
In the passive voice (*kamme*): *pāpīyati*, *pāpīyanti*.
In the causative (kārita): *pāpeti*, *pāpayati*, *pāpenti*, *pāpayanti*.
In the passive (kamma): *pāpīyati*, *pāpīyanti*.

Āpa, kamu, gaṇa, ghaṭa, cinta, ceta, cura, dhara, pāla, pūja, manta, māna, vida. 692. From *cur* etc., *ṇi*. Kaccāyana 452; Rūpasiddhi 525; Nyāsa 933; Candra 1.1.45;

Pāṇini 3.1.25; ‘*ṇi* after *cur* etc. (in many texts). The suffix *ṇi* occurs after roots beginning with *cur* when they have the sense of "action" (*kriya*), provided that the word formed has the same meaning as the root itself (*sakattha*).
*Coreti*, *corayati*.
With the prefix *vi-*, in the sense of spreading: *byāpeti*, *byāpayati*.
In the sense of desiring: *kamu-*; *kāmeti*, *kāmayati*, *kāmenti*, *kāmayanti*, *nikāmeti*, *nikāmayati*, *nikāmenti*, *nikāmayanti*.
In the passive: *kāmīyati*, *kāmīyanti*.
In the causative: likewise with *-āpi-*, as in *kāmāpeti*, *kāmāpayati*.
In the passive of the causative: *kāmāpīyati*, *kāmāpayīyati*.
In the enumeration of the *gaṇas*: for *gaṇa*, because it belongs to the *tudādi* class, there is no *vṛddhi*; thus, *gaṇeti* and *gaṇayati*.
For *ghaṭa*, in the sense of "to strive," [the forms are] *ghaṭeti* and *ghaṭayati*.
For *cinta*, in the sense of "to think," because it ends in a heavy syllable (*garu*), there is no *vṛddhi*; thus, *cinteti* and *cintayati*.
In the passive voice: *cintīyati*, *cintīyanti*.
In the causative: *cintāpeti*, *cintāpayati*.
In the passive causative: *cintāpīyati*, *cintāpayīyati*.
In the root *ī* (to think): *cintesi*, *cintayi*, *cinteyuṃ*, *cintayuṃ*, *cintesi*, *cintayi*, *cintayittha*, *cintesim*, *cintayim*, *cintesimhā*, *cintayimhā*.
In the root *cet* (to perceive): *cetāyaṃ*, *ceteti*, *cetayati*, *cetenti*, *cetayanti*.
In the root *cur* (to steal): *theyye*, *coreti*, *corayati*, *corenti*, *corayanti*.
Dhara (in the sense of holding): *dhāreti*, *dhārayati*, *dhārenti*, *dhārayanti*.
Pāla (in the sense of protecting): *pāleti*, *pālayati*, *pālenti*, *pālayanti*. Pūja (in the sense of honoring):
because it is heavy [to pronounce], there is no vowel lengthening; *pūjeti*, *pūjayati*, *pūjenti*, *pūjayanti*.
Regarding *mant-*, when used in the sense of "guarding speech," one says: *manteti*, *mantayati*, *mantenti*, *mantayanti*.
With the prefix *ā-* (*āpubba*), it means "speaking" or "addressing": *āmantayāmi vo bhikkhave* (DN 2.218); the Blessed One addressed the monks (*āmantesi*) (DN 2.208).
With the prefix *ni-* (*nipubba*), it means "inviting": *nimanteti*, *nimantayati*.
In the sense of "speaking," [the forms] are: *mantesi*, *mantayi*, *āmantesi*, *āmantayi*, *nimantesi*, *nimantayi*, *mantesuṃ*, *mantayuṃ*, *mantayiṃsu*—used by those who have gone into seclusion;
as well as *mantessati*, *āmantessati*, *nimantessati*, *mantayissati*, *āmantayissati*, *nimantayissati*, and so forth.
In the sense of honoring (*māna-pūjā*): *māneti*, *mānayati*, *mānenti*, *mānayanti*, and so forth.
In the sense of experiencing (*vida-anubhavane*): *vedeti*, *vedayati*, *paṭisaṃvedeti*, *paṭisaṃvedayati*.
With the prefixes *paṭi*, *ni*, and *pa*: in the sense of making known (*ācikkhane*): *paṭivedeti*, *paṭivedayati*, *nivedeti*, *nivedayati*, *pavedeti*, *pavedayati*, and so forth.
The curādigaṇa is finished.
The collection of vikaraṇa suffixes is finished.
The general section on consonants, *cha*, and vowels is finished.
Now, the suffixes based on verbal roots (dhātupaccaya) are being explained.

Suffixes that have the nature of verbal roots by virtue of expressing an action are "dhātupaccaya"; what is meant is "suffixes whose meaning is an action. Therefore, from them as well, there arises the occurrence of all the suffixes beginning with *ty* and those beginning with *tabba*, along with their respective case-endings (*vibhatti*).
[The roots are: *tija*, *māna*, *kita*, *gupa*, *badha*.
693. *Tijamānehi khasā khamāvīmaṃsāsu* (Ka. 433; Rū. 528; Nī. 906–9; Caṃ. 1.1.17, 28; Pā. 3.1.5).

After the verbal roots *tij* (to sharpen) occurring in the sense of patience (*khamā*) and *mān* (to measure) occurring in the sense of investigation (*vīmaṃsā*), the suffixes *kha* and *sa*, respectively, follow.
By the rule *tija-khamāyaṃ*, the suffix *kha* is applied here.
694. Regarding the single vowel of *khacchasānam* [and] *ekassaradveka*: Ka. 458; Rū. 461; Nī. 939; Caṃ. 5.1.1; Pā. 6.1.1, 9; “…mekasarodi…” (in many texts).
When the first phonetic form of verbal roots ending in *kha*, *cha*, or *sa* along with their suffixes becomes a single vowel, it takes two forms;

thus, when the two forms *tij-a*, *tij-a* have been made, by the rule “there is elision of the initial consonant” (*loponādibyañjanassā*), there is the elision of the letter *ja*, which constitutes the initial consonant.
There is elision (*lopa*). By the rule “*apararūpamayakāre byañjane*,” the final *j* of the root undergoes the substitution of the following form (*pararūpa*).

By the rule “*catutthadutiyesvesaṃ tatiyapaṭhamā*,” the *kh* that begins the consonant cluster becomes *k*. Thus, the form of the root and suffix is *titikkha*; from this, the personal endings such as *-ti* arise.
[Thus we have] *titikkhati*, *titikkhanti*.
In the passive sense: it is endured. In the causative sense: he causes [something] to be endured; it endures; he causes [someone] to endure; he causes [someone] to cause [something] to be endured.
In the passive causative sense: it is caused to be endured; they are caused to be endured.
*Titikkhatu*, *titikkhantu*, *titikkheyya*, *titikkheyyuṃ*, and so forth. What do they endure (*khamāyanti*)?
The root *tij* means to sharpen; it sharpens, they sharpen. In the causative, it is *tejeti*.
The Pāli passage from the *Majjhima Nikāya* (3.276) reads: “*Samuttejeti sampahaṃseti*” (He incites and gladdens).

In this analysis of *māna*, it is therefore accompanied by its condition. According to the rule “for *kha*, *cha*, and *sa*, when followed by a single consonant, [the preceding vowel] becomes double,” the forms *māna* and *māna* are each doubled.
695. Regarding *māna*, for the following *vī* and for the *maṃ* of the subsequent *māna*: [Kaccāyana 463–7; Rūpasiddhi 532–3; Nyāsa 944].
When doubled, the *vī* of the preceding *māna* occurs, and for all of the subsequent *māna*, the *maṃ* occurs.
He investigates; they investigate. In the passive:
it is investigated; they are investigated. In the causative:
he causes to investigate; he causes [them] to investigate; he causes to be investigated; he causes [them] to be investigated.
*Kamme-vīmaṃsāpīyati*, *vīmaṃsāpīyanti*.
What do they inquire about (*vīmaṃsāyanti*)? It means to honor, to respect, to revere, and to worship.
The root *kit* is used in the sense of removing disease and in the sense of doubt.
696. *Kita* is used in the senses of healing (*tikicchā*) and doubt (*saṃsaya*). [Kacc 433; Rūpasiddhi 528; Niddesa 906–9; Candra 1.1.18; Pāṇini 3.1.5].
After the verbal root *kit*, which occurs in the senses of healing and doubt, the suffix *cha* is applied.
When the two forms *kita* and *kita* are thus produced—
697. *Kitassāsaṃsaye* (or *ka*). Rule 463; Rūpasiddhi 532; Nyāsa 944.

When the root *kit*, which occurs in the sense of "to cure" (*tikicchati*), is reduplicated, the form *kitassa* optionally replaces the preceding *kit*. By the rule “*pararūpamayakāre byañjane*,” there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and by the rule for the first letter of a conjunct, the *c* becomes *t*.
Thus: *tikicchati*, *tikicchanti*. “Even the gods cure him, the man who supports his mother and father” (Jātaka 2.22.408).
In the passive (*kamme*): *tikicchīyati*, *tikicchīyanti*.
In the causative (*kārite*): *tikiccheti*, *tikicchayati*, *tikicchāpeti*, *tikicchāpayati*.

By means of the particle *vā*, when the letter *t* is absent, according to the rule "for gutturals (*ka-vagga*), there is a palatal (*ca-vagga*) substitute," the preceding [consonant] becomes a palatal in the reduplication (*dvitte*): *cikicchati*, *cikicchanti*, *cikicchīyati*, *cikicchīyanti*.
What is meant by "asaṃsaya" (without doubt)? It means *vicikicchati* (he doubts) or *vicikicchanti* (they doubt).

When it has a meaning other than the sense of doubting—that is, in the sense of buying (*kitattha*), knowing (*ñāṇattha*), and dwelling (*nivāsattha*)—it appears as *ketati*, *saṃketati*, and *niketati*.

Regarding the rule for *gup* in the sense of censure (*nindā*). 698. In the sense of censure, after the roots *gup* and *badh*, the suffix *cha* is applied, and the *b* of *gup* becomes *bh*. (Kaccāyana 433; Rūpasiddhi 528; Candra 1.1.19, 20; Pāṇini 3.1.5, 6; Kātantra).

When used in the sense of censure, the suffix *cha* follows the roots *gup* (to protect) and *badh* (to bind/hurt), and the *b* of *gup* becomes *bh*. When the double form has been produced, there is the elision of the initial consonant.
699. *Gupissi ka*. 465; *rū*. 463; *nī*. 946; ‘*gupissussa*’ (in many texts).

When *gupi* is reduplicated, the vowel *u* of the preceding syllable becomes *i*. The *g* undergoes substitution by the palatal group (*cavagga*), the final of the verbal root undergoes substitution by the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and the first member of the consonant cluster undergoes substitution by the first letter.
[Thus: *jigucchati*, *jigucchanti*.
In the active voice (kamme): *jigucchīyati*, *jigucchīyanti*. In the causative (kārite):
*jiguccheti*, *jigucchayati*, *jigucchāpeti*, *jigucchāpayati*. [Optative forms: *jigucchatu*, *jigucchantu*, and so forth. To what does it refer when used in the sense of censure (*nindā*)?
[The root] *gup* means "to conceal" (*saṃvaraṇe*); [forms: *gopeti*, *gopayati*.
In the case of *badha-nindāyaṃ*, when [the suffix] *-dvirūpa-* and so forth have been applied—700. Regarding *khachasessi* (Ka. 465; Rū. 463; Nī. 946; ‘khachasesvassi’ in many texts):

when *kha*, *cha*, or *sesu* follow, the *i* of the preceding *assa* becomes *it*, and there is elision (*bhattaṃ*) of the subsequent letter *ba*; furthermore, the final vowel of the root undergoes the formation of a single substitute (*pararūpādi*).
*Bibhacchati* means "he becomes deformed"; the sense is that he is loathsome. *Bibhacchanti*: what do they revile?
[The words] *badha* and *bandhana* [mean] regarding injuries; *bādheti*, *bādhayati*. "You obstruct the wind with a net," *jā*.
1.12.8. In the passive (*kamme*): *bādhīyati*, *bādhīyanti*; *bajjhati*, *bajjhanti*.
Thus ends the section on the common [sandhi] of *kha*, *cha*, *sa*, and *ra*.

Regarding the rule for the elision of *tuṃ* when expressing desire (*tumicchātthe*) with *kha*, *cha*, *sa*, and *ra*: *Tumsmā lopo cicchāyaṃ te ka.* (Pāṇini 3.1.7) [Reference: Kha 434; Rūpa 534; Nīti 910; Cāndra 1.1.22; Pāṇini 3.1.7.]
In the sense of desire (*icchattha*), *tum* becomes *kha*, *cha*, and *sā*, and there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *tum*.
This rule is intended to demonstrate that when the sense of desire is possible, *kha*, *cha*, and *sā* occur after all verbal roots and words.

Therefore, having applied the suffixes *sa* and *cha* in the sense of desire, [one applies] the augment *ī* at the beginning of *sa* and *cha* according to the rule "ū byañjanassa" (a vowel is substituted for a consonant).
Having formed [the suffix], the following are established: *puttīyati* (he wishes to treat as a son), meaning he wishes to behave toward one who has no son as if toward a son;
*pabbatāyati* (he wishes to act like a mountain), meaning he wishes to behave as if he were a mountain; *dicchati* (he wishes to give).
[The roots] are: *bhuja*, *ghasa*, *hana*, *ji*, *hara*, *pā*, *su*.

In the sense of "he wishes to eat," the suffix *kha* is added to the root *bhuj*, the suffix *tuṃ* is elided, doubling occurs, the initial vowel of the preceding syllable is elided, the first letter of the consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) is substituted for the preceding form, and the *bha* of the preceding syllable becomes *bba*. Thus:
*bubhukkhati*, *bubhukkhanti*; *bubhukkhiyati*, *bubhukkhiyanti*; *bubhukkheti*, *bubhukkhayati*; *bubhukkāpeti*, *bubhukkāpayati*.

*bubhukkhāpīyati*, *bubhukkhāpīyanti*, *bubhukkhatu*, *bubhukkhantu*, *bubhukkheyya*, *bubhukkheyyuṃ*, *bubhukkhi*, *bubhukkhiṃsu*, *bubhukkhissati*, *bubhukkhissanti*, *bubhukkhissā*, *bubhukkhissaṃsu*. Regarding the root *ghasa* in the sense of eating:
in the sense of "he desires to eat," the suffix *cha* is applied; there is doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*), etc.; and the *gha* of the preceding root becomes *ga*.
The forms *jigacchati*, *jigacchanti*, *jigacchīyati*, *jigacchīyanti*, *jigaccheti*, and *jigacchāpeti*—and so forth—are derived from the root *gas* with the suffix *-it*.
Regarding the sense "he desires to kill" (*hantuṃ icchati*) from the roots *han* and *hiṃs*:

the suffix *-cha* is applied; the doubling of the consonant (*dvitta*) and other operations occur; by the rule "for gutturals (*ka-vagga*), there are palatals (*ca-vagga*)," the preceding *h* becomes *j*; and for the following *a*, there is *it-tva* (vocalization).
702. *Ghaṃ* replaces *han* when followed by *se*.
When *se* follows, *ghaṃ* is substituted for the subsequent *han*.
Examples: *jighaṃsati*, *jighaṃsanti*.
In *ji-jaye*, meaning "one who wishes to conquer," the suffix is present;
this is a doubling (*dvitta*). 703. *Jiharānaṃ gī ka. 462, 474; rū. 467, 535; nī. 943-954*.
When there is a doubling of *ji* and *harānaṃ*, the substitute *gī* occurs for the subsequent *ji* and *harassa* when *se* follows.
*Jigīsati*, *jigīsanti*, *vijigīsati*, *vijigīsanti*. [The root] *hara* means "to take away.

[When followed by] a suffix beginning with a double consonant (*dvittādi*), the *gī* of the following syllable is substituted, and the *ha* of the preceding syllable becomes *ja*; the *a* of that [syllable] becomes *it*. Thus: *jigīsati*. The meaning is "he desires to take away" (*harituṃ icchati*). *Jigīsanti*. [The root] *pā* means "to drink.

In the sense of "he desires to drink" (*pivituṃ icchati*), when there is a suffix, [the *pā* becomes *pipā*], and the *dvittaṃ* (doubling) occurs. By the rule "there is shortening of the preceding [vowel]" (*rasso pubbassā*), [the vowel is shortened]; the *a* of that [syllable] becomes *it*. Thus: *pipāsati*, *pipāsanti*, *pipāsīyati*, *pipāsīyanti*.
In the sense of "desiring to hear" (*su-savane*, *sotuṃ icchati*), when there is reduplication (*dvitte*),
the following word is reduplicated: *sussusati*, *sussūsati* (in many instances), *sussusanti*, *sussusīyati*, *sussusīyanti*, *sussuseti*, *sussusayati*,
*sussusāpeti*, *sussusāpayati*, *sussusāpīyati*, *sussusāpīyanti*, *sussusatu*, *sussusantu*, and so forth.

In the sense of "he wishes to endure" (*titikkhituṃ icchati*): for one who endures (*titikkhato*), there is a suffix (*sapaccayo*). Because of the state of having a suffix (*sapaccayaparattā*), there arises again the contingency of doubling (*dvitta*).

704. *Na puna caṃ*: When doubling has already occurred once, doubling does not occur again; thus, there is an absence of further doubling (*puna dvittābhāvo*). By the rule “*ū byañjanassā*,” the augment *ū* is added.
*Titikkhisati*, *titikkhisanti*, and so forth. Likewise, "he desires to treat" is *tikicchisati*, *tikicchisanti*, *cikicchisati*, *cikicchisanti*, and so forth.
Thus, in the sense of desiring to do (*tumicchattha*), there are the groups of *kha*, *cha*, and *sa*. This is the section on verbal roots (*nāmadhāturāsi*).
Regarding the sense of “he desires a son” (*puttam icchati*):
705. *Īyo kammā ka.* 437; *rū.* 538; *nī.* 912; *caṃ.* 1.1.23, 24; *pā.* 3.1.8, 9. The suffix *īya* occurs after a word in the objective case (*kamma*) in the sense of desiring.

Thus, from the word *putta*, which functions as the object, the suffix *īya* is applied in the sense of desire, resulting in the form *puttīya*—a combination of a verbal root and a suffix. From that, the inflectional endings such as *-ti* arise.
*Puttīyati*, *puttīyanti*, *puttīyeti*, *puttīyayati*, *puttīyāpeti*, *puttīyāpayati*, *puttīyāpīyati*, *puttīyāpīyanti*.
Likewise, *cīvarīyati*, *cīvarīyanti*, *pattīyati*, *pattīyanti*, *parikkhārīyati*,
*parikkhārīyanti*, and so forth.
Regarding the meaning "he behaves toward a pupil who has no father as if toward his own son":
*Upamāṇācāre ka.* (Kaśikā 4.3.105); *Rū.* 537; *Nī.* 912; *Caṃ.* 1.1.25; *Pā.* 3.1.10. That by which a thing is compared—that which is to be compared—is called *upamāna*.
From a word functioning as the object (*kamma*) of the act of comparison, the suffix *īya* is added in the sense of behaving (*ācāra*). Thus, [the form] *aputtīya* is derived.
*Puttīyati*, *puttīyanti*: "he treats the pupil like a son.

In the passive sense (*kamma*), even one who is not a son acts as if he were a son: *puttīyīyati*, *puttīyīyanti*, *puttīyeti*, *puttīyayati*, *puttīyāpeti*, *puttīyāpayati*, *puttīyāpīyati*, *puttīyāpīyanti*. Likewise: *sissīyati*, *sissīyanti*.
In the sense of "he behaves toward the palace as if it were a hut": [the same forms apply].
The suffix *īya* is added after a noun in the sense of conduct (*ācāra*) when it functions as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or as a locus (*ādhāra*). Examples:

*kuṭīyati*, *kuṭīyanti pāsāde* (he behaves like a hut, he behaves like huts in the palace); *nadīyati*, *nadīyanti iccādi* (he behaves like a river, they behave like rivers, and so forth). This occurs as if [one were] in a river, [as if] in the ocean.
One behaves in the city as if in the forest; thus one is "forest-like" (*araññīyati*), and [others] are "forest-like" in the city. Likewise, one is "householder-like" (*gehīyati*) in the monastery.
In the sense that one behaves toward oneself like a mountain in the sense of being unshakable by worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), [the suffix -iya is applied].
[Grammatical notes: *Kattutāyo* (Ka. 435; Rū. 536; Nī. 911; Caṃ. 1.1.27; Pā. 3.1.11).

The suffix *āya* occurs after a noun in the sense of "acting like" (upamāna) or "acting as" (kattubhūta). Thus, from the word *pabbata*, we have *pabbatāya*. From that, the formation of the verb begins:

*pabbatāyati saṅgho* ("the Saṅgha acts like a mountain"), *pabbatāyanti*. Just as one makes the sound *cicciṭa*, so one acts like oneself [making that sound]: *cicciṭāyati*; thus, the sound. Likewise: *paṭapaṭāyati*, *kaṭakaṭāyati*, *dhūmadhūmāyati*, *dhūpāyati*, *sandhūpāyati*.
In the sense of "becoming intensely (*bhusaṃ*) even though not previously intense (*abhusaṃ*")— [End of excerpt]
709. *Jhatthe* (ka. 435; rū. 536; nī. 911; caṃ. 1.1.30; pā. 3.1.12, 13). The meaning of the suffix *cī* is the state of becoming something that was not previously so;
this is called *jhattha*. When the sense of *jhattha* follows the agent (*kattū*), the suffix *āya* occurs.

*Bhusāyati*, *bhusāyanti*: even though it is not a cloth, it becomes a cloth—*paṭāyati*, *paṭāyanti*. Even though it is not red, it becomes red—*lohitāyati*. Likewise: *nīlāyati*, *kamalāyati*, *candāyati*, *candanāyati*, *kañcanāyati*, *vajirāyati*.
Why is it *kattu-tot-eva*? It means "it performs intensely" or "it makes a sound.
Regarding the meanings [of the suffix], [the rule] is: 710. *Saddādīhi karoti ka* (Kaccāyana 435; Rūpasiddhi 536; Niddesa 911; Candra 1.1.36; Pāṇini 3.1.17, 18; 'saddādīni' occurs in many texts).
The suffix *āya* occurs in the sense of "doing" after nouns ending in the second case, such as *sadda*.
For example: *saddāyati*, *saddāyanti*; *veraṃ karoti* becomes *verāyati*, *verāyanti*; *kalahaṃ karoti* becomes *kalahāyati*, *kalahāyanti*;
*mettaṃ karoti* becomes *mettāyati*, *mettāyanti*; *karuṇaṃ karoti* becomes *karuṇāyati*, *karuṇāyanti*.
One produces gladness, one is gladdened, they are gladdened; one produces equanimity, one is equanimous, they are equanimous;
one produces remorse, one is remorseful, they are remorseful; one produces affection, one is affectionate, they are affectionate;
one produces conviction through reliance, one has conviction, they have conviction; one produces craving, one craves, they crave.
*Taṇhīyati* or *taṇhīyanti*: the suffix *-īya-* has the sense of "to do. *Mamāyati* means "he makes it his own" (*mama idam iti karoti*); *mamāyanti* [is the plural].
In the sense of "he pays homage" (*namo karoti*), [the rule] applies: 711. *Namotvasso caṃ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.19)
The suffix *assa* occurs in the sense of "making" (*karoti*) after the word *namas*.
[Examples: *namassati*, *namassanti*.
In the sense of "making equal" (*samānaṃ*) or "making similar" (*sadisaṃ*): [examples follow].
712. *Dhātvatthe nāmasmim pā.* (Pāṇini 3.1.21, 25).

The meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvattha*) is said to be any action whatsoever. After a noun (*nāma*), the suffix *i* occurs when the meaning of a verbal root is intended. By the rule “*yuvaṇṇānameo paccaye*,” the *i* of *samāneti* becomes *e*.
Thus: *samāneti*, *samānenti*.
In the expression “*kappam-ayāvā sara*,” there is the substitution of *ayā*. In the rule “*ṇi-ṇāpy-āpīhi vā*,” by means of the word “*vā*,” the suffix *la* is applied:
*samānayati*, *samānayanti*; *piṇaṃ karoti* becomes *piṇeti*, *piṇayati*; he asks about what is wholesome (*kusalaṃ pucchati*) becomes *kusaleti*, *kusalayati*;
it becomes pure (*visuddhaṃ hoti*) becomes *visuddheti*, *visuddhayati*; he sings near the lute (*vīṇāya upagāyati*) becomes *upavīṇeti*, *upavīṇāyati*.
He surpasses by means of wisdom; he over-wisdoms, he is over-wise. He makes excrement; he excretes, he causes excretion. He makes urine;
he urinates, he causes urination. He presses with strength; he strengthens, he causes strengthening.
It is strengthened for him; they are strengthened. “The weak are strengthened”—this is the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
Regarding the sense of "he makes true" (*saccaṃ karoti*):
713. The suffix *āpi* is also added after [roots] beginning with *sacca*, according to the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*; *Rūp* 540; *Nī* 914; *Pā* 3.1.25.
The suffix *āpi* occurs after verbal roots when followed by nouns beginning with *sacca*.
He makes true, they make true; he analyzes the meaning, they analyze the meaning;
he makes known the Veda, they make known the Veda; he dries up, they dry up; he makes happy, they make happy;
he makes suffering, they make suffering; he makes hot, they make hot, and so forth.

7. Kitakaṇḍa: The Section on the End of Elements and the Group of Transformations, and the Group of the Form of Disjunction.

Now, the *kitaka* word—which is established through roots (*dhātu*) and suffixes (*paccaya*), which illuminates the distinctions of tense, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), gender, number, and action, and which expresses the substance as the primary meaning—is explained.
Among these, the distinctions of tense are called "past" and so forth.

The seven means of accomplishment—namely, the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*kamma*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the recipient (*sampadāna*), the point of departure (*apādāna*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the abstract state (*bhāva*)—are called the "distinctions of grammatical relations."
The distinction of gender refers to the differences such as the feminine gender and so forth.
The distinction of number refers to the difference between singularity and plurality.

Its functions are: the function of its own nature, the function of its associated qualities, the function of performing its proper task, the function of self-satisfaction, and the function of repetition.

The various types of action (*kriyā*) include: the act of attaining Arhatship (*arahakriyā*), the act of being a Sakka, the act of sending, the act of transgression, the act of announcing the proper time, and the act of what is inevitable, and so forth.

In expressions such as "going occurs" (*gamanaṃ bhavati*) or "he knows how to cook" (*pacanaṃ jānāti*), the state (*bhāva*) which constitutes the meaning of the suffix is of the nature of an instrument (*sādhana*).

Like a genus (*jāti*), it is endowed with the three genders because it serves as the means of accomplishing the action to be accomplished (*sādhya-kriyā*), which is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, because it is established as *hoti*, *kriyā*, *kāro*, and *karaṇaṃ*, it is also associated with numerical distinctions;

for there is the possibility of formal variation (*sarūpabheda*) through the distinction between various verbal roots (*dhātu*), agents (*kartr*), objects (*kamma*), and [temporal factors] such as time. Therefore, since that too is subsumed under "substance" (*dabba*) itself, it is stated as "denoting substance as the primary meaning.
All the rest has already been explained in the section on nouns (*tyādikaṇḍa*) within the analysis of the abstract derivation (*bhāvasādhana*).

The terms ‘bahula’ (variously) and ‘kriyārthā’ (denoting action) are employed here. Pāṇini 3.2.102: *Kartari bhūte kta-ktavantu-ktāvī-kak* (Pāṇini 1.2.66 …pe… 3.2.102). In the sense of the past tense (*bhūte*), when denoting the agent (*kartari*), the suffixes *kta*, *ktavantu*, and *ktāvī* are applied after verbal roots (*kriyārthā*) that have *ka* as their indicatory letter (*kānubandha*).

Regarding the indicatory letter *ka*: it serves as a qualifier according to the rule *na te kānubandhanāgamesu* (it is not [included] among those suffixes that have *ka* as their indicatory letter in the context of elision). Thus, *abhavī* means “he was,” “he existed,” or “he passed. When the past tense is to be expressed, the suffixes *ta*, *tavantu*, and *tāvī* occur after verbal roots having *ka* as their indicatory letter, provided they denote the agent. The indicatory letter *ka* is for the purpose of specification.

In this context, the meaning of the *kitapaccayas* (nominal suffixes) is twofold: the expressed meaning (*vāccattha*) and the denoted meaning (*abhidheyyattha*). All of this should be understood according to the method explained in the *Tyādikanda* (the section on *ty-ādi* suffixes).

However, among the six preceding modes of derivation (*sādhana*), the denoted meaning of the suffixes is stated by means of another word, whereas in the mode of derivation by state (*bhāvasādhana*), it is stated by the verbal root itself.
In that regard, when expressing the literal meaning— consisting of the power of the agent (*kattusatti*), the power of the object (*kammasatti*), the power of the instrument (*karaṇasatti*),

the power of the recipient (*sampadānasatti*), the power of the source (*apādānasatti*), and what is termed the power of the locus (*adhikaraṇasatti*)— the *kitapaccayas* (primary suffixes) express themselves with the same gender,
case-ending, and number as their own denoted word-base.
How so? First, regarding the agent: a man has experienced wealth; men have experienced wealth... [and so on] ...when men have experienced wealth;
a woman has experienced wealth; women have experienced wealth... [and so on] ...when women have experienced wealth; a family...

Thus, interrogative pronouns (*kitavācaka*), having become identical in gender, case-ending, and number with their own expressed referent (*abhidheyyapada*), express that respective grammatical factor (*sādhana*).

When there is a qualifier (*visesana*) for two qualified things (*visesya*) that are prior and subsequent actions, and their agent is one and the same, then in the case of the prior action, the suffixes *tuna*, *tvāna*, and *tvā* occur with the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvattha*).

By virtue of the rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikārā*), the suffixes *tuṇ* and so forth occur even when there is a subsequent action (*aparakiyāsu*) or when there are different agents (*nānākattukāsu*). Because [the suffix] *tta* is seen [in such forms], the occurrence of *tuna*, etc., after the agentive [suffix] is logical.

In the sense of remembering (*saraṇa*), the suffix *-ta* applies across the three tenses due to its frequent occurrence; thus: *sarati*, *asari*, *sarissati* = *sato*, *anussato*, *patissato*.
In the sense of taking away (*haraṇa*): *harīyittha* = *hato*, *āhato*, *nihato*.
For that [root], there are the forms *ṭatta*, *āhaṭa*, *nihaṭa*, *udāhaṭa*, *samudāhaṭa*, and *avahaṭa*.

The root *hana* means "to injure"; thus, that which was struck (*haññittha*) is called *hata*, as in *vihata* and *samūhata*. In the case of non-separation, it is *mahāva*. (Mahāva 145). In the case of the complete removal of a boundary, it is *mahāva*. (Mahāva 146).
Due to the rule of abundance (*bahulādhikāra*), there is elision of the internal vowel even when the suffix begins with the letter *a*. That which is performed first is the *pakati*; the vowel *ā*—
Appearance is *ākati*; modification is *vikāra* or *vikati*; singing is *gāyana*, *gīti*, *uggīti*, *saṅgīti*, *anugāyana*, or *anugīti*;

going is *gamana* or *gati*—it is called *gati* because it is that which should be gone to, or because they go there; coming is *āgamana*; [there are] good destination (*sugati*) and bad destination (*duggati*); meeting is *samāgamana* or *saṅgati*;
birth is *janana* or *jāti*—it is called *jāti* because they are born by means of it, or because they are born there; standing is *ṭhāna* or *ṭhiti*.
*Saṇṭhiti* is stability; *avaṭṭhiti* is persistence; *santati* is the continuous stretching out again and again. They sustain by means of this, thus it is *dhīti*;

it is the state (*īttaṃ*) of great conduct (*mahāvuttinā*). Bending is *nati*; rising up is *unnati*; rising up completely is *samunnati*; bowing down is *onati*; bending down is *avanati*. It is to be borne, thus it is *bhati*. One knows by means of this, thus it is *mati*.
Diverse knowledge is *vimati*. Delighting is *rati*; delighting intensely is *ārati*; desisting is *virati*.
*Abhiramaṇaṃ* is delight (*abhirati*); *paṭiviramaṇaṃ* is abstention (*paṭivirati*). *Saraṇaṃ* is mindfulness (*sati*); or, it is mindfulness because they remember by means of it;
thus there is *anussati* (recollection) and *paṭissati* (counter-recollection).
*Upahananaṃ* is destruction (*upahati*). Regarding the suffix *-tavant*: *akāsīti* means "one who has done" (*katavā*); *ahanīti* means "one who has killed" (*hatavā*).
In the case of the *tāvī* suffix: *katāvī*, *hatāvī*.
In the case of *tuṃ* and so forth—728. *Tuṃ*, *tuṇa*, and *tabba* may optionally [be used].
In the case of the verbal root *kar*, the letter *r* optionally becomes *ā* before the suffixes *tuṃ*, *tuna*, and *tabbe*. By the word *tuna*, both *tvāna* and *tvāpi* are included.
729. *Karassā tave*:
In the suffix *tave*, the letter *r* of the verbal root *kar* becomes *ā*.
*Kātuṃ*, *kātave*, *kātuna*, *kātabbaṃ*.

Just as for *karassa*, so by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*) the form of *harassa* is established: *hāthuṃ*, *hātave*, *hātuna*. "By their snout, having released the previously incurred debt" (*tesaṃ tuṇḍena hātūna, muñce pubbakataṃ iṇaṃ*). 1.14.10.
"In me there is the state of being yours (*tvāmhi āssa ittaṃ*), having placed [it], having placed water in the trunk" (*āhitvā, soṇḍāyudakamāhitvā*). 1.10.9 (...*hatvā*).
Thus ends the aggregate of material form as dissociation.
Now, the aggregate of material form as similar conjunction is explained.
Regarding the *tupacca* (the suffix *tu*):

730. When a consonant follows that is not the letter *y*, the final consonant of all verbal roots undergoes the change to the form of the following sound (*pararūpa*). That is, when a consonant suffix other than *y* follows, the final consonant of every root assumes the same form as that following consonant.

One who does is a *kattā* (doer); one who is worthy to do, able to do, whose nature is to do, whose quality is to do, or who does with diligence—this is the meaning. One who supports is a *bhattā* (supporter); one who carries is a *hattā* (carrier).
In forms such as *tvā*, the letter *r* becomes *ā*, and when followed by a conjunct consonant, it becomes short;

thus: *katvā*, *katvāna*. Through the rule of subsequent form (*pararūpatta*), [we have] *kattuna*, *kattuṃ*, *kattabbaṃ*; *bharaṇaṃ* becomes *bhattuṃ*, *bhattave*; *haraṇaṃ* becomes *hattuṃ*, *abhihattuṃ*, *hattave*.
Āpa, ṇāpa, khipa, gupa, caja, ñapa, ñāpa, tapa, dīpa, dhūpa, pada, bhaja, bhuja, mada, mida,
yuja, rica, ranja, lipa, lupa, vaca, vatu, vada, vapa, vica, sanja,
sica, sambhu, sūca, sūda, supa.

The final consonant of a verbal root takes the form of the following vowel when the suffix *ta* follows; however, when preceded by the prefix *vi*, it becomes *āpa* in the sense of pervading (*byāpana*). One who can pervade quickly through the pervasion of knowledge is called *byatto* (learned) or *viyatto*.
The prefix *pari-* is used in the sense of mastering (*pariyāpuṇana*) and abundance (*pahutta*);
thus, one who has mastered is *pariyatto*. The prefix *sam-* is used in the sense of completeness (*paripuṇṇabhāva*); one who has brought something to its conclusion is *samatto* or *parisamatto*.
The prefix *ā-* is used before the root *ṇā* in the sense of commanding;

thus, *āṇāpīyittha* means "he was commanded," and [the past participle] is *āṇatto*. The root *khipa* means throwing; thus, *khipīyittha* means "it was thrown," and [the past participles are] *khitta-daṇḍo* ("a thrown staff"), *khittā-mattikā* ("thrown clay"), and *khittaṃ-leṭṭhu* ("thrown stone"). It is the same in all these cases: *pakkhitto*, *ukkhitto*, *nikkhitto*, *vikkhitto*, *okkhitto*, *saṃkhitto*. The root *gup* means protection;
thus, *gopīyittha* means "it was protected," and [the past participles are] *gutto* and *saṃgutto*.
In *caja-cāge* (the act of giving up), because it was caused to be given up (*cajīyittha*), it is "abandoned" (*catto*).

In *upa-paññāpane* (the act of establishing), because it was caused to be established (*paññapīyittha*), it is "laid down" (*paññatto*)—as in "the discipline is laid down," "the training rule is laid down," or "the seat is laid down.

In *ñāpa-ñāpane* (the act of making known), this is the root *vikaṭi*; because it is caused to be made known (*kāritantattā*), that which was caused to be made known is "made known" (*paññatto*), that which was caused to be fully made known is "fully made known" (*saññatto*), and that which was caused to be specifically made known is "specifically made known" (*viññatto*).
In *tapa* (heat), from *atappī* comes *tatto*, meaning "heated" (*santatto*).
In *dīpa* (light), from *adīpittha* comes *ditto*, meaning "blazing," "inflamed," or "set on fire" (*paditto*, *āditto*).

In *dhūpa* (incense/smoke), from the sense of "smoking," one who has smoked, will smoke, or does so is called *dhutto*; for example, a drunkard (*surādhutto*) or a gambler (*akkhadhutto*). (Saddanīti 106)
In the sense of going to a place (*pada-gati*), *apajji* means "attained," "reached," or "arrived.
In the sense of associating (*bhaja-sambhatti*), one who associates is called *bhatto* or *sambhatto*.
With the prefix *vi-*, it signifies separation; thus, "he divided" is *vibhatto*.
In the sense of protecting the arms and in the sense of conducting business: *bhuñjittha*, *bhuñjīyittha*, or *bhutto* means "enjoyed" or "consumed.
In the sense of intoxication and madness: *majjittha* means "intoxicated," "drunk," "negligent," or "insane.
In the sense of moistening with affection: *mijjati* means "a friend" (*mitto*).
In *yuja* (joining), that which joins is *yutta*, *payutta*, *uyyutta*, *niyutta*, *viyutta*, *saṃyutta*, and *saññutta*.
In *rica* (leaving), that which leaves is *ritta*.
In *ranja* (coloring/dyeing), that which colors is *rakta*, *sārakta*, and *virakta*.
From the root *limpa* (to smear): that which has been smeared (*limpīyittha*) is *litto*, as in *ullitto* (smeared over) and *avalitto* (smeared down).
From the root *lupa* (in the sense of disappearance): that which is destroyed (*luppati*) is *lutto*. From the root *vaca* (in the sense of distinctness of speech): it refers to speech (*vācāyaṃ*).
731. *Vac*-ādīnam *vassa uṭa vā ka*. (Ka. 579; Rū. 629; Nī. 1182).

After the words beginning with *vac*, the suffix *uṭ* optionally replaces the *vas* [of the present participle] before a suffix beginning with *ta*, provided it does not have *tvā* as its initial letter.

Examples: *vuccittha* → *uttodhammo* (the Dhamma spoken), *uttākathā* (the discourse spoken), *uttaṃ vacanaṃ* (the speech spoken), *nirutto* (etymology), *niruttā* (etymological analysis), *niruttaṃ* (etymology), *rāgamo* (the arrival).
The vowel *assa* (the short *a*) is substituted for [the final vowel] of words such as *vutta*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *ta* that excludes those starting with *tvā*.
Examples: *vuttodhammo*, *vuttākathā*, *vuttavacanaṃ*.
In *vatu*, the sense is "to turn": thus it is *vatta* (a turn), *pavatta* (proceeding), and *nivatta* (returning).
In *vapa*, the sense is "the sowing of seed": thus it is *vutta-bīja* (sown seed); it is said, "it was sown" (*assa*).
In *vica*, the sense is "separation": thus it is *vivitta* (secluded).
From *sañj* (to cling), *sañjatīti satto*: one who clings, attached, thoroughly attached.
From *sic* (to sprinkle), *siñcīyitthāti sitto*: that which has been sprinkled, drenched, poured over, or anointed. From *sūca* (to indicate), *atthaṃ sūcetīti suttaṃ*:
that which indicates the meaning is called a "thread" (*sutta*).
In *sūda-paggharaṇe*, that which clarifies the meaning is *sutta*.
In *supa-soppane*, one who sleeps is *sutto*, and so forth.
In the case of the suffix *-ti*: pervading is *byatti* or *viyatti*; mastery is *pariyatti*; and attainment is *samatti*.
*Parisamatti* is completion; *āṇatti* is commanding; *gutti* is guarding; *ñatti* is making known; *paññatti* is prescribing;
*saññatti* is informing; *viññatti* is requesting. *Titti* is the act of satisfying;
its form *itthaṃ* is derived from the root *tappati* with the suffix *mahāvuttinā*. *Ditti* is illumination; *patti* is reaching.

*Āpatti* (occurrence), *uppatti* (arising), *nippatti* (accomplishment), *vipatti* (failure), *sampatti* (success), *bhajanaṃ* (sharing) and *bhatti* (devotion), *sambhatti* (companionship), *bhuñjanaṃ* (eating) and *bhutti* (consumption), *yuñjanaṃ* (joining) and *yutti* (application), *riñcanaṃ* (leaving) and *rittī* (emptiness). It is called *nirutti* because meaning is expressed by means of it;
it is called *vutti* because the meaning of the Sutta is expressed by means of it. It is also said: "The meaning of the Sutta is unfolded by means of it, thus it is *vuttī*."
They say: *vattana* is *vutti*, meaning the mode of livelihood (*jīvitavutti*) or a mode dependent on that; *assa* is the root *as*. *Vivecana* is *vivitti*;
*sajjana* is *satti*, *āsatti*, *visatti*, and so forth.
In the case of the *tu*-suffix: *khipati* thus *khittā*; *gopeti* thus *guttā*; *cajeti* thus *cattā*.
Herein, *chida*, *bhida*, and so forth should also be mentioned: one who cuts is a cutter (*chettā*); one who breaks is a breaker (*bhettā*);
one who divides is a divider (*bhattā*); one who eats is an eater (*bhuttā*) or a consumer (*bhottā*); one who is joined is a joiner (*yuttā*); one who is smeared is a smearer (*littā*);
