one who is cut off is a cutter-off (*luttā*); one who speaks or says is a speaker (*vattā*); one who is secluded is a secluder (*vivittā*); one who is attached is a being (*sattā*); one who sleeps is a sleeper (*suttā*), and so on.
In the *tavantū* suffix: *khittavā* means "one who has thrown," *guttavā* means "one who has guarded," *cattavā* means "one who has abandoned," and *chettavā* means "one who has cut.
In the sense of distribution (*puthakkaraṇe*), *bhajitthā* becomes *bhattavā* or *vibhattavā*; *abhuñji* becomes *bhuttavā*;
*ayuñji* becomes *yuttavā*, and so forth. In the *tāvī* suffix: *khittāvī*, *guttāvī*, *cattāvī*, *chettāvī*, *vibhattāvī*, *bhettāvī*, *bhuttāvī*, *yuttāvī*, and so forth.

In the case of *tvādīsu* (the suffixes -tu and -tave), according to the Mahāvutti rule, there is elision of the initial consonant of the three types of consonants; for example: *chetvā*, *chetvāna*, *chettuna*; *vibhatvā*, *vibhatvāna*, *vibhattuna*; *bhutvā*, *bhutvāna*, *bhuttuna*, and so forth.

In the case of the suffixes *-tuṃ* and *-tave*, there is elision of the initial consonant: *chettuṃ*, *chettave*, or *chetuṃ*, *chetave*; *vibhattuṃ*, *vibhattave*; *bhettuṃ*, *bhettave*; *bhottuṃ*, *bhottave*, and so forth, where there is vowel strengthening (*ādivuddhi*) of the initial syllable.

In that grammatical context (tabbapaccaye), forms such as *chettabbaṃ*, *chettabbaṃ* (to be cut), *bhettabbaṃ* (to be split), *bhottabbaṃ* (to be eaten), and *vuccatīti vattabbaṃ* (it should be said "it is called") are used.
Thus ends the section on the group of similar conjunct consonants. Now follows the group of consonants from different classes.
Now the group of verbal roots ending in -u is stated:
kamu, kilamu, khanu, khamu, gamu, tanu, timu, damu, bhamu, manu, yamu, vamu, samu, hana.
(733) In these [roots], the final *n* becomes a nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*).

In roots ending in *m* or *n*, the *m* or *n* becomes a *niggahīta* (the nasal stop) when followed by a consonant other than *y*. According to the rule "at the end of a class [of consonants], the final of that class [is substituted]," the *niggahīta* is replaced by the final letter of its respective class.
From the root *kam* (to go): *pakkamittha* (he went forth) → *pakkanto*; *pādena akkamittha* (he stepped with his foot) → *akkanto*; *ukkanto*, *vikkanto*, *nikkhanto*;
in the case of *nito kamassā* ("gone from going"), the *k* is substituted for *ka*; *saṅkanto*, *okkanto*, *avakkanto*, *apakkanto*.
*Atikkanta*, *paṭikkanta*: whose two pairs [of opposites].
*Kilama* means weariness; one who has become weary is *kilanta*.
*Timu* means to moisten; one who has become moistened is *tinta*.
In the sense of taming (*damu*), one who has tamed is "tamed" (*danto*).
In the sense of wandering about (*bhamu*) or instability, one who wanders about is "wandering" (*bhanto*) or "distraught" (*vibbhanto*).
In the sense of knowing (*mana*), that which knows is "knowledge" (*manto*).
In the sense of vomiting (*vamana*), *vanta* means "one who has vomited.
In the sense of tranquility (*santi*), *santa* means "tranquil," "calmed," or "appeased.
In the sense of exhaustion (*kheda*), *santa* means "one who is exhausted" (*sammati khijjati*), and so forth.

In the *tipaccaya* suffix: *kāmanaṃ* is *kānti*, *nikāmanaṃ* is *nikanti*, *pakkamanaṃ* is *pakkanti*, *khamanaṃ* is *khanti*, *tananaṃ* is *tanti*, *damanaṃ* is *danti*, *bhamanaṃ* is *bhanti*, *vibbhanti*, *mananaṃ* is *manti*, *samanaṃ* is *santi*, and so forth.

In the *tupaccaya* suffix: one who goes forth (*pakkamati*) is *pakkantā*; one who digs (*khanati*) is *khantā*; one who endures (*khamati*) is *khantā*; one who goes (*gacchati*) is *gantā*; one who stretches (*tanoti*) is *tantā*; one who moistens (*temayati*) is *tintā*; one who tames (*damayati*) is *dantā*; one who wanders (*bhamati*) is *bhantā*; one who thinks (*manati*) is *mantā*.

In the case of the *ni* suffixes: one who restrains is a *niyantā* (restrainer); one who vomits is a *vantā* (vomiter); one who pacifies is a *santā* (pacifier); one who kills is a *hantā* (killer), and so forth. In the case of the *tvā*-type suffixes:

having gone is *gantvā*, *gantvāna*, or *gantuna*; having thought is *mantvā*, *mantvāna*, or *mantuna*; having killed is *hantvā*, *hantvāna*, or *hantuna*, and so forth. In the case of the infinitive suffixes *-tuṃ* and *-tave*:

departing is *pakkantuṃ* or *pakkantave*; digging is *khananaṃ* or *khantuṃ* or *khantave*; going is *gamanaṃ* or *gantuṃ* or *gantave*; thinking is *mananaṃ* or *mantuṃ* or *mantave*; killing is *hananaṃ* or *hantuṃ* or *hantave*, and so forth.

In these cases: *tabbamhi* means "it should be gone toward" (*abhikkantabba*); *paṭikkantabba*, "it should be gone back"; *khaññateti khantabbaṃ*, "because it is endured, it is endurable"; *gacchīyateti gantabbaṃ*, "because it is gone, it is to be gone to"; *maññateti mantabbaṃ*, "because it is thought, it is to be thought"; *vamīyateti vantabbaṃ*, "because it is vomited, it is to be vomited"; *haññateti hantabbaṃ*, "because it is slain, it is to be slain," and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the group of internal vowel changes. The section on the group of changes at the end of verbal roots is finished.
The Section on Conditional Modifications; The Section on *Kāda* Substitutions.
Now, the Section on Conditional Modifications is being stated.
After *pac*, the suffix *ta* is used for the past participle (*tavantūnaṃ*).
That which has been cooked is "cooked" (*pakko*), or "one who has cooked" (*pakkavā*).

Due to the governing rule of *bahula*, the suffix *ta* occurs even for the three times [past, present, and future]. Thus, one who has been able (*asakkhi*), is able (*sakkhati*), or will be able (*sakkhissati*) is called *sakka*.
By the great rule, the suffix *ta* becomes *ka*. [The root] *muc* [is used] in the sense of releasing. 735. *Mucā vā ka* (Pāṇini 3.1.140); Rūp 617; Nī 1186.
Now, for those who have finished [the recitation], what comes after that?
"Omuccittha" means "omukka," or "omukkavā"; likewise "paṭimukka" or "paṭimukkavā.
The term *susa* means drying.
736. *Susā* indeed, Ka. 583; Rū. 617; Nī. 1186.
*Susamhā ta*, for those who possess that, it indeed exists.
*Sussittha* means dried up, thus *sukkha* (dry). *Sukkhavā*.
737. *Go* is substituted for the suffixes *ta*, *tavantūnaṃ*, and *tassa* after roots such as *bhañj*.
Examples: *abhañjittha* becomes *bhaggo*; *bhaggavā*, *obhaggo*, *sambhaggo*, *palibhaggo*.
From *lagga-laggane*: that which has clung (*lagittha*) is *lagga*; one who clings (*laggavā*), *vilagga*, or *vilaggavā*.
From *muja-mujjane*: that which has sunk (*mujjittha*) is *mugga*; one who sinks (*muggavā*), *nimmugga*, or *ummugga*. From *vija* in the senses of fear and trembling:
that which has been agitated (*saṃvijittha*) is *saṃvigga*; one who is agitated (*saṃviggavā*), *ubbigga*, or *ubbiggavā*.
In *palujja-vināse*, [the word] *paluggo* means "fallen apart" (*palujittha*); likewise *paluggavā*, *oluggo*, *oluggavā*, *viluggo*, *viluggavā*, and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the substitution of *ka*. Now follows the section on the substitution of *ṭha*.
Isu, āsa, esa, kasa, kisa, kilisa, kusa, ghusa, jusa, tusa, disa, dusa, daṃsa,
nasa, pisa, pusa, puccha, phusa, bhassa, bhajja, maja, masa, musa, vassa, visa, saja,
sisa, silisa, hasa, hassa, haṃsa.
738. *Sānantarassa tassa ṭho* (Ka. 573; Rū. 626; Nī. 1176 [slightly different]).

The letter *ṭha* is substituted for the *ta* of a suffix that immediately follows verbal roots ending in *s*; the final sound of the root becomes its corresponding single substitute (*pararūpa*); and by the rule *“catutthadutiyesvesan”* (Kaccāyana 1.2.40), the first sound of the conjunct is retained.
Examples: from the root *is* (to wish), *icchā* (desire) and *kantī* (longing); that which is wished for (*iṭṭhyate*) is *iṭṭha* (desired), as in *pariyiṭṭha* (sought after).
In the sense of sitting and reclining; one who sits and reclines in a distorted manner is *vipallaṭṭha*.
In the sense of plowing, sowing, and scratching.
739. Regarding this *kasa*, there is also *ka*; see Ka 573; Rūp 626; Nī 1176 (slightly different).
After the letter *ta* of the word *paccaya*, there is *ṭha*; or, after the first vowel of the word *kassa*, there is *ima* or *va*.
From *kassittha* comes *kiṭṭha*—meaning grain—or *kaṭṭha*.
With the prefix *upa*, it means "near," as in *upakaṭṭha*.
*Vipubbo* [is used] in the sense of being away from home (*pavāse*); *vūpakaṭṭho*.
*Paṭikiṭṭho* means emaciated (*kisa-hānimhi*), having fallen away; the meaning is "degraded" (*nihīno*).
*Kilisa-* [is used] in the sense of affliction (*vibādhane*) and torment (*upatāpe*); that which is afflicted is *kiliṭṭho*, *saṃkiliṭṭho*, or *upakkiliṭṭho*.
*Akkuṭṭha*: from *akusa*, meaning "to revile"; one who has been reviled is *akkuṭṭha*. Reviled by way of [one's] birth (*jātivāda*).

*Ghuṭṭha*: from *ghusa*, meaning "sound"; that which has been sounded is *ghuṭṭha*, as in *saṅghuṭṭha*. "Resounding with a throng of celestial nymphs" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.46). Also *ugghuṭṭha*. *Juṭṭha*: from *jusa*, meaning "to enjoy" or "to serve";
that which has been enjoyed is *juṭṭha*.
In the sense of satisfaction (*tussa-pīti*): it was satisfied, thus *tuṭṭho*, meaning "well-satisfied.
In the sense of seeing (*disa-pekkhana*): it was seen, thus *diṭṭho*, meaning "seen" (*sandiṭṭho*).
In the sense of pointing out (*disī-kathana*): it was pointed out, thus *uddiṭṭho*; it was specifically pointed out, thus *niddiṭṭho*; it was referred to, thus *apadiṭṭho*.
*Dūsa* means to corrupt; that which has been corrupted (*dūsīyittha*) is *duṭṭha*.
*Daṃsa* means to bite; that which has been bitten (*daṃsīyittha*) is *daṭṭha*, with the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra).
*Nasa* means not to see; that which has perished (*nassittha*) is *naṭṭha*, as in *vinaṭṭha*.
From the root *pisa* (to grind), "pisīyittha" means "it was ground," hence *piṭṭha* (flour).
From the root *pusa* (to nourish), "posīyittha" means "it was nourished," hence *puṭṭha* (nourished), as in *parapuṭṭha*.
From the root *phusa* (to touch), "phusīyittha" means "it was touched," hence *phuṭṭha* (touched), as in *samphuṭṭha*.
In the sense of speaking and departing, *bhassittha* means "he spoke," hence *bhaṭṭho* and *ābhaṭṭho*.
In the sense of touching and piercing, *masīyittha* means "he touched," hence *maṭṭho*, *āmaṭṭho*, *omaṭṭho*, and *ummaṭṭho*; as in *sattiyā viya omaṭṭho* (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.21).
In the sense of perishing, *mussittha* means "he perished," hence *muṭṭho*, *pamuṭṭho*, and *sammuṭṭho*.

In *vassa-secane* (the sprinkling of rain): because it has rained (*vassittha*), it is "rained" (*vuṭṭha*); "it has been" (*assu*) is [the past participle] *utta*. In *visa-pavesane* (the entering of poison):
because it has entered (*pavisittha*), it is "entered" (*paviṭṭha*), "settled" (*niviṭṭha*), or "approached" (*upaviṭṭha*).
In *sisa-sese* (what remains on the head): because it has remained (*avasesittha*), it is "remaining" (*avasiṭṭha*).
The prefix *vi-* is used in the sense of distinction; that which is distinguished is *visiṭṭha*.
The root *siliṣ* means to adhere; that which has adhered is *siliṭṭha*.
The root *has* means to laugh; one who has laughed is *haṭṭha*, or *pahaṭṭha*.
The *haṃsa* and *haṃsadhātu* suffixes are exactly alike.

This is in the section on the interrogative pronoun (*puccha-pucchāyaṃ*). 740. From the interrogative pronoun (*puccha*) onwards, [the suffix] *ka* [applies]. (Pāṇini 5.3.71; Rūpasiddhi 626; Nyāsa 1176).
The letter *ṭha* replaces the conditional *ta*-suffix of another verb following roots such as *puccha*.
Thus, from *pucchīyittha*, we have *puṭṭho* (asked).
From *bhajja* in the sense of splitting, from *bhajjittha*, we have *bhaṭṭhaṃ* (split) as in *dhaññaṃ* (grain).
In *maja* (to cleanse), "well cleansed" is *sammaṭṭha*, as in a portion of ground;
in *saja* (to adhere) and so forth, "adhered to" is *saṃsaṭṭha*; likewise *visaṭṭha*, *nisaṭṭha*, and *osaṭṭha*.
In *yaja* (to worship).
741. *Yajassa yassa ṭi* (Kaṇḍa 610; Rūpasiddhi 627; Nyāsa 1215).
For the letter *y* of the root *yaj*, the substitutes *ṭi* and *yi* occur when followed by a suffix beginning with the consonant *k* (excluding *kā*), provided the suffix has the marker *t*.
Thus, from *yajittha*, we have *iṭṭho* and *yiṭṭho*.
In the case of the *tipaccaya* suffix, there is *pariyeṭṭhi*, meaning seeking or search.

In the sense of "this seeking," *esanaṃ* becomes *eṭṭhi*, *pariyeṭṭhi*. *Tussanaṃ* becomes *tuṭṭhi*, *santuṭṭhi*. *Dassanaṃ* becomes *diṭṭhi*, *sandiṭṭhi*. *Vassanaṃ* becomes *vuṭṭhi*; it is stated that [the word] is "assū. *Visajjanaṃ* becomes *visaṭṭhi*. In the case of *tvā* and so forth, regarding the root *dis* (to see):

by the rule “*disassa passa-dassadasādadakkhā*,” there is a substitution of *dasa* for *disa*; by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is the elision of the letter *v*, resulting in *daṭṭhā*, *daṭṭhāna*, and *daṭṭhuna*.
‘Tuṃyāna’: this is the substitution of *tuṃ* for the suffix *tvā*. In the verse at SuN 426, “nekkhamaṃ daṭṭhu khemato,” there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) by way of the metrical rule.
[Examples include: *tuṃ* and *tave* becoming *daṭṭhuṃ* and *daṭṭhave*; *pucchanaṃ* becoming *puṭṭhuṃ* and *puṭṭhave*. In the sense of the gerundive (*tabbamhi*):
*tussitabbaṃ* becomes *tuṭṭhabbaṃ* and *toṭṭhabbaṃ*; *passitabbaṃ* becomes *daṭṭhabbaṃ*; *pucchitabbaṃ* becomes *puṭṭhabbaṃ*; *phusitabbaṃ* becomes *phoṭṭhabbaṃ*.
Thus ends the section on the substitution of *ṭha*.
Section on the Substitution of *ḍha* (Ḍhādesarāsi): 742. *Daha* becomes *ḍha*; Ka. 576; Rū. 607; Nī. 1179.

After *dah* [the root], when followed by another immediately succeeding conditional *takāra*, *ḍha* is substituted; and when the subsequent form is applied, the first consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyoga*) becomes the third [consonant of its class].
*Daha* means "to burn"; from *dayhi* (aorist), we have *daḍḍho* ("burnt").
After *baham*, there is *ḍha* for the immediately following [suffix]; after the initial vowel of *baha*, *uma* also occurs.
In the case of the increment (*vuḍḍhi*) of *baha*: *abahī* becomes *buḍḍho*; *va* replaces *ba*, thus *vuḍḍho*.
There is an increment of *timhi* and *baha*.
744. *Lopo vaḍḍhā tissa ‘ttissa* (in many cases).
There is elision of the letter *t* of the suffix *ti* following *vaḍḍha*.
*Vaḍḍha* means increasing; *vaḍḍhana* is growth.
Thus ends the section on substitutes beginning with *ḍha*.
Now, the section on substitutes beginning with *ṇa*: *kira*, *khī*, *cara*, *jara*, *tara*, *thara*, *pūra*.
745. *Kirādīhi ṇo*.
After the roots beginning with *kiri*, the *ta* of the suffixes *tavantūnaṃ* becomes *ṇo*; there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpattaṃ*) for the final letter of the verbal root.
*Kiri* means scattering, mixing, and throwing. Thus: *kirittha* becomes *kiṇṇo*, *pakiṇṇo*, *ākiṇṇo*, *vikiṇṇo*, *saṃkiṇṇo*, *samākiṇṇo*.
*Pūra* means filling; that which has been filled is *puṇṇa*, *sampuṇṇa*, or *paripuṇṇa*.
*Khī* means destruction; that which has been destroyed is *khīṇa*. Thus there are those who have filled, those who have fulfilled, and those who have destroyed.
746. *Tarādīhi riṇṇo* (ka. 581; rū. 616; nī. 1184).

After the roots beginning with *tar*, the suffix *riṇṇo* is substituted for the letter *t* that immediately follows the forms *ta* and *tavantu*. By the rule “*rānubandhentasarādissā*,” there is elision of the consonant at the end of the verbal root and of the initial radical vowel.
From the root *car* (to move, to eat): *carittha*, *carīyittha*—thus it is called *ciṇṇo* (done), *āciṇṇo* (practiced), or *samāciṇṇo* (habitually practiced).
In the sense of decaying (*jara-jiraṇe*): it has decayed, thus "decayed" (*jiṇṇo*), "not yet decayed" (*anujiṇṇo*), and "completely decayed" (*parijiṇṇo*).

In the sense of crossing over (*tara-taraṇe*): it has crossed over, thus "crossed over" (*tiṇṇo*), "gone across" (*uttiṇṇo*), "gone beyond" (*nittiṇṇo*), "gone through" (*vitiṇṇo*), "gone down into" (*otiṇṇo*), and "fully gone across" (*samotiṇṇo*).
In the sense of spreading out (*thara-vitthāre*): it has spread out, thus "widely spread" (*vitthiṇṇo*).
Ciṇṇavā, jiṇṇavā, tiṇṇavā, vitthiṇṇavā. Thus ends the section on the substitution of *ṇ*.
The section on the substitution of *th*.
747. *Dhasto* and *utrasta*.
These two words ending in the suffix *tap* are established as *dhasta* and *utrasta*.
From the root *dhaṃs* (in the sense of destruction), that which destroys is *viddhaṃsta*, or it is *viddhaṃsita*.
*Tasa* (fear): *uttrasati* means "he is terrified," thus *utrasta*; or it means "he is frightened.

*Bhasa* (in the sense of reducing to ashes): *bhāsanti* means "they reduce to ashes by means of this," thus *bhastā* or *bhastrā*, meaning a blacksmith’s bellows; such terms as these are also to be understood here. 748.
*Sāsa vasa saṃsa haṃsā tho … saṃsa sasā tho* (in many texts).
By these [rules], the *tha* is substituted for the *ta* of another immediately following word.
[This applies] in the sense of "instruction" (*anuśiṣṭi*) in the word *sāsa*. 749. Regarding *sāsa*, there is the rule: "The *si* of *sāsa* [is optionally elided]" (as found in many texts).

In the case of the suffix *sās*, when followed by the conditional suffix (*paccaya*) *tā*—excluding those beginning with *tvā*—there is substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the final vowel of the root, and the first member [of the consonant cluster] remains for that which begins with a conjunct (*saṃyoga*).

Thus, from "it is caused to sit" (*sāsīyati*), we get *sittho*; from "it is instructed" (*anusāsīyati*), we get *anusiṭṭho*. In the *Mahāvaṃsa* (126), it says: "He was instructed by me" (*Anusiṭṭho so mayā*);

here, however, it is stated in the *Vutti* that the letter *tth* becomes *ṭṭh*. [The word *sāsana* is derived as follows: "That which instructs in this or that matter" (*taṃ taṃ atthaṃ sāsati ettha, etena*).
...or the science of weapons, the science of grammar, and the science of the Vedas.

Regarding the root *vas* in the sense of dwelling: it is stated that "he has dwelt" (*avasī*) means "he has lived" (*vuttho*), or "he was caused to dwell" (*vasīyittha*) means "he has lived" (*vuttho*); "he lived for the rains" (*vassaṃ vasittha*) means "one who has lived the rains" (*vassaṃvuttho*);

"it was caused to be dwelt in" (*āvasīyittha*) means "the Jeta Grove where one has dwelt" (*āvutthaṃ-jetavanaṃ*); "he dwelt" (*nivasittha*) means "one who has dwelt" (*nivuttho*); "he presided over" (*ajjhāvasittha*) means...
*ajjhāvuttho*. Due to the predominance of the *bahula*-rule, it is explained as "the deity residing in the tree" (*rukkhe adhivatthā devatā*).
Here, there is no [separate] *utta*-suffix. *Uposathaṃ upavasitthā* means *uposathaṃ-upavuttho*; or, having fasted (*upavasīyittha*), it is *upavuttho-uposatho*.
*Parivāsaṃ parivasitthā* means *parivāsaṃ-parivuttho*; or, having undergone the probation (*parivasīyittha*), it is *parivuttho-parivāso*.
In *saṃsa* (to praise) and *pasaṃsa* (to praise), that which has been praised is *pasattha*.
In *haṃsa* (to fly) and *pahaṃsa* (to fly up), that which has flown is *hattha*; here the *niggahīta* [anusvāra] is elided, resulting in *pahattha*.
In the suffix *-ti*, *anusāsanaṃ* becomes *anusitthi* or *anusiṭṭhi*, and *nivasanaṃ* becomes *nivutthi*.
In the sense of the *tupa* suffix: he instructs and guides the world together with its devas, thus he is the Teacher (*satthā*).
In the sense of the *tavantu* suffix: he has dwelt there, thus he is one who has dwelt (*nivutthavā*). In the sense of *tāvī*: one who has dwelt (*nivutthāvī*).
*Vattha* means to dwell; it is used in the sense of residing.
It should be dwelt upon at the foot of that tree, or it should be dwelt in the assembly hall. The root *vas* means to wear;

because of the rule regarding frequentative usage (*bahulādhikāra*), there is no prefix [required], thus *vatthaṃ* means "that which is to be worn. That which has been worn is *nivatthaṃ*; that which is to be worn is *vatthabbaṃ*, and that which is to be worn over [the other] is *nivatthabbaṃ*.
Thus ends the section on substitutes for nouns (*thādesarāsi*).

Now, the section on substitutes for verbal roots (*dhādesarāsi*): *idha*, *kudha*, *gidha*, *badha*, *budha*, *budhi*, *midha*, *yudha*, *rādha*, *rudha*, *vidha*, *sidha*, *sudha*, *thabhi*, *rabha*, *labha*, *lubha*, *sambhū*, *duha*, *naha*, *muha*.
750. *Dho* [is substituted] for *dha*, *bha*, and *ha*. (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī 576; Rūpasiddhi 607; Netti 1179; in many manuscripts: *dho dhahabhehi*).
After these [letters], the following *t* becomes *dh*.

In the word *idha-ijjhane*, the final letter of the verbal root (*dhā*) undergoes substitution with the subsequent vowel (*pararūpa*), and the first letter of the consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) becomes the third letter (*t*); thus, from *samijjhittha*, we have *samiddho*, meaning "one who has attained great wealth."
*Kudha* means anger; one who has become angry is *kuddho*, or *saṃkuddho*.
*Gidha* means greed; one who has craved is *giddho*, or *anugiddho*, or *abhigiddho*.
*Badha* means binding; one who has been bound is *baddho*, or *pabaddho*, *ābaddho*, or *nibaddho*.

In the sense of awakening (*budha*), knowledge (*ñāṇa*), waking (*jāgara*), and blossoming (*vikasana*): one who awakens and knows is a *buddha*, a *sambuddha*, or a *sammāsambuddha*; or, one who wakes up and is awake is *pabuddha* or *paṭibuddha*. In the sense of obstructing (*budhi-nivāraṇa*):
that which is obstructed is *palibuddha*, as in "obstructed by wind," "obstructed by bile," or "obstructed by phlegm. In the sense of sloth (*midha-mijjhana*):
that which is slothful is *middha*, as in *middha* (sloth) or *kapimiddha* (monkey-sloth).
In the sense of engaging in combat, *yuddha* means "to fight"; thus, there is wrestling, ram-fighting, elephant-fighting, and cock-fighting.
In the sense of propitiating or pleasing, *āraddha* means "propitiated" or "pleased," as in the phrase *ārādhayittha*.
With the prefix *vi-*, it signifies failure; thus, *viraddha* means "failed."

Regarding *rudha* with the prefix *ā*: it is "obstructed" (*ruddho*), "blocked" (*oruddho*), or "impeded" (*avaruddho*) because it was obstructed (*rundhīyittha*). With the prefix *ni*, it means "cessation":
it is "ceased" (*niruddho*) because it was ceased (*nirujjhittha*).
With the prefix *vi*, it means "opposition": it is "opposed" (*viruddho*) or "counter-opposed" (*paṭiviruddho*) because it was opposed (*virujjhittha*).
*Anuruddha*: from *anu* (following) and *ruddha* (shining);
thus, one who shines following [others]. *Viddha*: from *vidha* (piercing) and *vijjhati* (to pierce); thus, one who has been pierced, as in "pierced by an arrow" (*sallaviddha*).
*Siddha*: from *sidha* (accomplishment) and *sijjhati* (to be accomplished); thus, one who has attained accomplishment.
*Pa-*, preceded by *pubba-*, means "manifest"; thus, it is *pākaṭa* (manifest).
*Ni-*, preceded by *paṭi-*, means "obstructing"; thus, it is *nivārita* (obstructed) and *paṭisiddha* (prohibited).
*Sudh-*, meaning "to purify," [gives] *sujjhati* (it is purified); thus, it is *suddha* (pure), *visuddha* (purified), and *parisuddha* (completely purified).
In *thabhi-thambhane*: one who stiffens is *thaddho*—stiffened, thoroughly stiffened, or completely stiffened.
In *rabha-ārabhe*: one has begun is *āraddho*; or, having been undertaken (*ārabbhittha*), it is *āraddho*;

or, it is fully undertaken (*samāraddho*). In *labha-lābhe*: one has obtained is *laddho*; or, having been obtained (*labbhittha*), it is *laddho*; it is acquired (*paṭiladdho*) or apprehended (*upaladdho*).
In *lubha* (to be greedy), one who has become greedy is "greedy" (*luddho*), "overcome by greed" (*paluddho*), or "completely overcome by greed" (*viluddho*).
In *passambhati* (to become tranquil), one who has become tranquil is "tranquil" (*passaddho*).
In *duha* (to milk), a cow that has been milked is "milked" (*duddhā-gāvī*).
In the sense of binding (*naha-bandhane*): *sannaddho* means "bound," as in "girded" (*sannayhittha*), "covered" (*onaddho*), or "fastened" (*avanaddho*).
In the sense of delusion (*mūha-andhabhāve*): *muddho* means "deluded," as in "one who is deluded" (*muyhati*), thus a fool.
In the sense of the suffix *-tippaccaya*: *ijjhanaṃ* is *iddhi*; or alternatively, *iddhi* is that by which things succeed (*ijjhanti etāya*); *samijjhanaṃ* is *samiddhi*; *gijjhanaṃ* is [the same].
Giddhi is greed; mijjhana is sloth; abhirādhana is success; virujjhana is obstruction, as well as opposition;
sijjhana is accomplishment, as well as complete attainment and prohibition; sujjhana is purity, as well as purification and absolute purity;
labhana is gain, as well as acquisition; lubbhana is greediness; passambhana is tranquility; muyhana is delusion.
In the case of *tavant*, one should say *tāvīsu*—namely, *samiddhā*, *samiddhāvī*, and so forth.
In the case of *tvādi*: *rabha*-and-*ārabhe*, *āraddhā*, *āraddhāna*.
*Labha*-and-*lābhe*, *laddhā*, *laddhāna*, *paṭiladdhā*, *paṭiladdhāna*.

In the case of *tuṃ*, [the following forms are used]: *tavesu*, *budhañāṇe*, *buddhuṃ*, *buddhave*, *subuddhuṃ*, *subuddhave*, *boddhuṃ*, *boddhave*, *laddhuṃ*, *laddhave*, *paṭiladdhuṃ*, *paṭiladdhave*.
In the neuter (*tabbamhi*), [the forms are]: *boddhabbaṃ*, *laddhabbaṃ*, *paṭiladdhabbaṃ*. 751. Or [it is] *vaddha*.
Furthermore, when the suffix *vā* follows an augmented form (*vaddha*), the letter *t* of the conditional suffix (*paccaya*) is dropped, provided it is not one of those beginning with *tvā*.

Thus, from the root *vaddh*, we have *vuddho* (grown) or *vaddho*; *vuddhi* (growth) is the act of growing (*vaddhana*). According to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), the *u* is substituted. And there is the elision of that suffix *ti*. This concludes the section on substitutes for verbal roots.
In the *Visaṃyoganādesarāsi*:
*hā*, *i*, *ci*, *ji*, *ṭi*, *thī*, *dī*, *pī*, *mi*, *lī*, *thu*, *dū*, *dhū*, *pū*, *bhū*, *lū*, *vu*, *su*, *hu*, *āsa*, *katha*, *kupa*, *pala*, *mala*, *supa*, *paḷa*.
(752) After roots beginning with *bhid* [the suffix] *kta* and *ktavantu* take the augment *no*.
After roots beginning with *bhid*, the *t* of the suffixes *kta* and *ktavantu* becomes *n*.

In the case of the root *hā* (to abandon): *hīyittha* [becomes] *hīno*, *pahīno*, *nihīno*, *ohīno*. Here, having applied the substitute *no*, the augment *ī* is subsequently added by the rule “*ūbyañjanassa*,” and in some instances this [augment] is shortened. It is the same in other cases. With the prefix *adhi* in the sense of dependence:
that which goes beyond (*adhicca eti*) is *adhino*.
One who accumulates (*cinoti*) or has accumulated (*cayittha*) is a *cino* or an *ācino*.
One who conquers (*jināti*) the five enemies is a *jino*.
In the sense of motion (*ḍi-gati*), one who moves (*ḍeti*) is a *ḍino*.
*Thī* means to congeal; that which congeals is *thina* (sloth).
*Dī* means to diminish; that which gradually diminishes or wastes away is *dina*, meaning a day.
*Pī* means to fill; that which is filled is *pīna* (fat).
*Mi* means to measure; thus, one who measures is a *mino*. *Lī* means to dissolve;

one who has dissolved is *līno*, and one who has clung is *allīno*. One who has settled down is *nilīno*; one who has withdrawn is *paṭilīno*; a monk who practices withdrawal is *paṭilīnacaro*; one who has secluded himself is *paṭisallīno*.
*Thu* means to snort; one who snorts is *nitthuno*.
*Dū* means to be distressed; one who is distressed is *dūna*. *Dhū* means to shake off;
one who shakes off unwholesome states (*dhama*) is *dhuna*, thus "one possessing the wisdom of the shaker" (*dhonapaññavā*).
*Pū* means to purify; one who purifies is *puna*. That by which they purify what has been tamed is *dantapoṇa*; here, the *ṇa* replaces the *na*.
In the sense of growth (*bhū-vuddhi*), that which becomes or increases is *bhūno* (the root *bhū*).
In the sense of cutting (*lū-chedane*), that which cuts is *luno*.
In the sense of covering (*vu-saṃvaraṇe*), that which covers is *āvuṇo*.
*Susavane*: from *suṇāti* (he hears), *suno*; *soṇo*, where *na* becomes *ṇa*. Or, in the sense of "good procreation":
from *pasavati* (it brings forth/grows), *sunaṃ*—meaning swollen (*uddhumātaṃ*).
*Hu* means worship or giving; that which is to be offered is *āhunaṃ*; that which is to be brought as an offering is *pāhunaṃ*—an object to be given.
*Āsa-upavesane*: one who sits is *āsīno*; one who sits silently is *tuṇhīmāsīno*.
*Katha-thaddhe theriye ca*: it is called *kathina* because it speaks (*kathati*). *Kupa-kope*:
it is called *hirīkopinaṃ* because shame (*hirī*) is agitated (*kuppati*) by it.
In *pala-gatiyaṃ*, one who moves away (*paleti*) is "one who has departed" (*palino*).
In *mala-malinabhāve*, one who soils (*malati*) is "soiled" (*malino*), as in a soiled cloth (*malinaṃ-vatthaṃ*).
In *supa-soppane*, one who sleeps (*supati*) is "a dream" (*supino*).

In the *paḷa*-group: that which moves (*paḷeti*) is "one who moves" (*paḷino*); by means of the one who moves, [he crossed] to the further shore of Jambudīpa. Eight. 1. The Discourse on the Third Council.
Thus ends the collection of nouns with disjoined vowels.
The collection of nouns with conjoined vowels.
*Khida*, *chida*, *tuda*, *dā*, *nuda*, *pata*, *pada*, *bhida*, *vida*, *sada*.

By the rule “*bhidādito no ktaktavantūnam*” (after *bhid* and the others, *no* is substituted for the suffixes *kta* and *ktavantu*), the final vowel of the root undergoes *pararūpa* (single-substitute) sandhi. Thus: *khijjittha* becomes *khinno*; *chijjittha* becomes *chinno* and *sañchinno*; *tudittha* becomes *tunno*, *patunno*, and *nitunno*;
from the root *nuda* (to push), *nudittha* becomes *nunno* and *panunno*.

*Pat* means "to fall"; thus, one who has fallen is *panna*. *Pannadhaja* (one whose banner has fallen) refers to the leaf (*panna*) of a tree, which is derived from the root *pann*, or it means a wing (*patta*).
*Pad* means "to go"; thus, one who has gone is *panna*. [Other forms include: *āpanna*, *uppanna*, *nipanna*, *vipanna*, *sampanna*, *upapanna*, *samupapanna*, and *pariyāpanna*.
*Bhid* means "to split"; thus, that which has been split is *bhinna*. [Other forms include: *pabhinna*, *sambhinna*, *paribhinna*, and *vibhinna*.
In *vida-tuṭṭhiyaṃ*, one who has become weary (*nibbindati*) is *nibbinna*.

In *sada visaraṇa*, [the suffix] *-ta* occurs at the end of a verb root, a motion, or a state; thus, one who has sat down is *sanna* (or *osanna*), one who has become confident is *pasanna* (or *abhippasanna*), and one who has sat down is *nisinna*.

In *sannisinna*, the suffix *-ima* is applied according to the rule "after *sa*, *da*, *ja*, and *na*, [there is] *īma*," and there is shortening in a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoge rasso*). Thus: *khinnavā*, *chinnavā*, *sañchinnavā*, *tunnavā*, *patunnavā*, *panunnavā*, *pannavā*, *āpannavā*, *bhinnavā*, *sambhinnavā*, *sannavā*, *pasannavā*, *nisinnavā*.
After the root *dā*, the suffix *inno* is substituted for the past participial suffixes *ta* and *tavantūna*. Thus: *dīyittha* becomes *dinno*;
likewise *padinno*, *ādinno*, *samādinno*, *upādinno*, *pariyādinno*. When the *n* of *inno* is changed to *ṇ*, it becomes *upādiṇṇo*.
Thus ends the section on the substitution of *sa* with *ya*.
The section on the substitution of *ha* consists of: *ūha*, *gāha*, *guha*, *baha*, *bāha*, *buha*, *muha*, *ruha*, *vaha*.
754. *Ruhādīhi ho ḷo ca ka.* (Pāṇini 8.2.33; Rūpasiddhi 621; Nyāsa 1192; ‘...ḷa ca’ [in many manuscripts]).

After *ruh* and other such roots, the *t* of the suffix *ta* that follows immediately becomes *h*, and the final letter of the verbal root becomes *ḷ*. In the sense of “accumulation,” from *ūha* (to accumulate):
because it was accumulated (*byūhittha*), it is *byūḷho*; *viyūḷho*, *paribyūḷho*; “the battle between the gods and asuras was fully arrayed” (*samupabyūḷho ahosi*)—Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249.

In the sense of grasping (*gāhu*) and tossing about (*bhusattha*), as well as in the sense of agitation (*vilolana*), [the suffix] *ka* is applied after the words *mā*, *gāḷha*, and *parideva*. One intends for what is deep (*āgāḷhāya ceteti*). *Gāhittha* means "deep" (*gāḷho*); there are eight types: *pagāḷho*, *āgāḷho*, *ogāḷho*, *ajjhogāḷho*, and *pārā*.

1.1. In the sense of much increase (*bahu-vuddhi*). 755. After the words *muha*, *baha*, and *buhu*, the letter *ka* is applied when followed by the suffix *te*. (Moggallāna 5.1.7; Rūpasiddhi 488; Nyāsa 1105; cf. "muhabahānañca... in many manuscripts.)

When a suffix beginning with *k* and having a mute consonant (*kanubandha*) follows, and when a suffix containing the letter *t* follows, there is lengthening of the vowels in *muh*, *bah*, *buh*, and *guh*.
By the rule “*ruhādīhi ho lō cā*,” the final *l* of the root is substituted, and the suffix *ta* becomes *ho*. Thus, *abahī* means "intensely.
In *buh*-uddharaṇa (the act of pulling out), from *abuhittha*, we have *būḷho*; likewise *abbūḷho* and *abūḷhasallo* (one whose arrow has been pulled out). (Saddanīti 785)
In the case of *muha-andha-bhāve*. 756. Or *muhā*.
After *muhā*, the letter *t* of a following word becomes *h*, and the final *ḷ* of the verbal root optionally becomes *h*.
*Muyhittha* means "deluded" (*mūḷho*) or "foolish" (*muddho*).
Regarding the roots *ruha* (to grow) and *gati* (motion): from *ruhittha* come *rūḷho*, *parūḷho*, *ārūḷho*, *orūḷho*, *virūḷho*, and *nirūḷho*.
Regarding the root *vaha* (to carry away): from *vahittha* comes *vūḷho*; it is stated that this means "tears."
In the case of the *tipaccaya* suffix, "growing" is *rūḷhi*, "growing out" is *nirūḷhi*, and "growing forth" is *virūḷhi*.
Regarding the suffixes beginning with *tvā*: 757. *Pyo* optionally replaces *tvā* when it occurs in a compound (*samāsa*).

In the place of a compound (*samāsa*), the suffix *tva* may optionally have the augment *pā* as its prefix. The augment *pā* is for the purpose of distinguishing it [from other suffixes] by the rule "the suffix *ya* preceded by *pā* is called *sissa*.

There is a substitution of *ha* for *ya*, which is a reversal of the suffix *yana*. Thus: *byuyha*, *paribyuyha*; or *byūhitvā*, *viyūhitvā*; *vigāyha*, *vigāhitvā*; *ogāyha*, *ogāhitvā*; *ajjhogāyha*, *ajjhogāhitvā*.
Due to the force of the general rule (*bahulādhikāra*), the suffix *pya* occurs even outside of compounds: *guyha*, *gūhitvā*; *niguyha*, *nigūhitvā*; *oguyha*, *ogūhitvā*.
*Naha* in the sense of binding: *sannayha*, having bound.
*Bāha* in the sense of warding off: long vowel [form], *bāyha*, having warded off; *paṭibāyha*, having repelled.
*Buha* in the sense of uprooting, preceded by *pa*: *pabbuyha*. Having completely uprooted craving, root and all (*samūlaṃ taṇhaṃ pabbuyha*), Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.159 (taṇhamabbumha).
*Āpubba-abbuyha*, as in “*abbuhe sallamattano*” and so forth; *pamuyha*, *pamuyhitvā*; *vimuyha*, *vimuyhitvā*; *sammuyha*, *sammuyhitvā*; *āruyha*, *āruhitvā*, *ārohitvā*; *oruyha*, *orohitvā*;
*saha* in the sense of enduring, as in *pasayha*, *pasahitvā*.
Thus ends the section on the substitution of *h*.
The Group of Substitutes for *tv-* and so forth:
Now, the substitutes for *tvā*, *tvāna*, and *tunānaṃ* are stated:
*i*, *kara*, and *hana*.
758. *Ito* and *cco*.
After the word *itthā*, the suffix *cco* optionally occurs before another word.
Examples: *pecca*, *samecca*, *abhisamecca*, *avecca*, *anvecca*, *apecca*, *upecca*, *samupecca*, *adhicca*, *aticca*, *paṭicca*.
What does it mean [to say] *vāti*? It means having approached, having fully approached, and having studied.
759. *Sādhikarā raccariccā* (Ka. 598; Rū. 643; Nī. 1203; in many texts: *sāsādhikarā cacariccā*).
When *karamhā* follows *santa* and *adhiparā*, the forms *racca* and *riccā* optionally occur; here, the analysis provided in the Sutta is applicable.
*Sakkacca*: the augment *bind* is added to *sakka*, meaning "having performed a service" (*adhikicca*).
What about [the form] *vā*? It means *sakkatvā*, *sakkaritvā*, or *adhikaritvā*.
[Examples from the Suttavibhaṅga: "The fool, having disregarded his own welfare, pursues what is pleasant" (Suttavibhaṅga 2.21.461); "having prepared the food" (*abhisaṅkhacca*).
760. *Hanā* [the suffix] *racca* [is applied] after the root *han*. (Bahūsu: *sāsādhikarā cacariccā*).
After *han*, the suffix *tvā* becomes *assa* when in a compound (*samāsa*). It also occurs after *har* by means of the *sutta*-analysis.
Examples: *āhacca*, *uhacca*, *vihacca*, *saṃhacca*, *upahacca*.
What does it blow? Having struck, having raised up, having scattered, having gathered together.
"Haramhi-sā no āhacca poseti jā" (2.22.2334) means "having struck. Then, "udakamāhacca" (having struck the water). It is used in the sense of looking toward the directions.
761. *Disā vā na vā sa ca* (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī 599; Rūpasiddhi 644; Niddesa-aṭṭhakathā 1204; ‘...sa ca’ in many manuscripts).
From the word *disa*, there is either *vāna* or *vā*; and for the word *disa*, *sa* is substituted for *ssa*. This is a negation of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*).
[Examples: *disvāna*, *disvā*.
What [is the suffix] *vāti*? It is *passitvā*.
[The roots] *khā*, *ñā*, *dā*, *dhā*, *hā*, *ki*, *khi*, *ci*, *ji*, *nī*, *lī*, *si*, and *bhū* [are included].
By the rule “*pyo vā tvāssa samāse*,” the *tvā* becomes *pyo*; by the optional application of the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is sometimes the elision of *ya*, as in *saṃpubbo*.
In *khā-ñāṇe*, *saṅkhāya*, *saṅkhā*, *paṭisaṅkhāya*, *paṭisaṅkhā*, *aññāya*, *aññā*, *abhiññāya*, *abhiññā*, *pariññāya*, and *pariññā*.
What is excluded from the compound? *Ñatvā*.
Why is *vā* used? [To include] *ājānitvā*, *abhijānitvā*, and *parijānitvā*.
*Adhiṭṭhāya*, *adhiṭṭhā*; *patiṭṭhāya*, *patiṭṭhā*. What is compounded? *Ṭhatvā*.
Why [is the suffix] *-tvā* used? [In the examples:
*adhiṭṭhahitvā*, *patiṭṭhahitvā*. By the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is also *-ittam*: *upaṭṭhitvā*.
*Ādāya*, *upādāya*, *upādā*. What is the compound (*samāsa*)?
*Datvā*. Why is there the particle *vā*?

[Because it is] *ādiyitvā*, *samādiyitvā*. By the rule “*ū byañjanassā*” (*ū* is the augment after a consonant), there is the insertion of *ī*; and by the rule “*dāssiyaṅa*,” when a vowel follows in a compound, there is the substitution of *iy*.
762. *Tuṃyānā*.
In some compounds, both *tvam* and *yānam* occur as *tuṃ*.

Due to the rule of frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*), even in non-compounds they appear in this verse: *nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato* (Sn. 426) and *kimabbhutaṃ daṭṭhu marū pamoditā*, where the nasal drop (*bindulopa*) has occurred.

One may invite [another] to accept what has been brought (*abhihattuṃ pavāreyya*). There is also a reading *abhihaṭuṃ*, where the initial consonant cluster is elided and the *ṭ* is substituted for *t*. Some recite it as *abhihaṭṭuṃ*; however, this does not agree with the phonetic rules (*byañjanaṃ na sameti*).

[Examples of forms with the suffix -ya: *ādiyāna*, *upādiyāna*; *vidhāya*, *nidhāya*, *sandhāya*, *odhāya*, *samodhāya*; *vidahitvā*, *nidahitvā*, *odahitvā*, *samodahitvā*; *pahāya*, *vihāya*, *ohāya*, *hitvā*, *jahitvā*.
In cases involving the vowels *i* and *u*, there is doubling of the following consonant (*pyassa dvittaṃ*): *vikkiyya*, *vikkiṇitvā*.

“Having examined, a gift should be given,” etc. (Va. 329). Regarding “having exerted” (*ūlasse*): this is the form *etta*. [The following are examples: having investigated (*vicinitvā*), having removed (*vineyya*), having led away (*vinetvā*), having disciplined (*vinayitvā*), having approached (*allīya*), having approached (*allīyitvā*), having retired for seclusion (*paṭisallīya*), having retired for seclusion (*paṭisallīyitvā*).
There is the augment *yā*. 763. Regarding *pye*, the suffix *sissa* becomes *ka* (Ka. 517; Rū. 488; Nī. 1105). Regarding *pye pare*, the suffix *sissa* becomes *ā* (Ka. 517; Rū. 488; Nī. 1105).
*Nissāya*, *upanissāya*, *apassāya*, *apassayitvā*, *avassāya*, *avassayitvā*.
What [is the example] for *vā*? *Adhisetvā*, *adhisayitvā*.
For the sense of existence (*sattā*) of the root *bhū*: *rassattaṃ*, *sambhuyya*, *vibhuyya*, *anubhuyya*, *adhibhuyya*, *paribhuyya*, *abhibhuyya*.

What is compounded (*samāsa*)? [The following examples: *bhutvā* (having eaten); in the case of roots ending in *e* or *o*, by the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), *e* becomes *ā*: *nijjhāya* (having reflected), *upanijjhāya* (having closely reflected), *abhijjhāya* (having coveted).

In the case of verbal roots (*dhātu*) ending in consonants, by the rule "after the *vaggas* and *la*, *te*," there is the substitution of the *ca-vagga* for the *ta-vagga*, and the substitution of the *pa-vagga* for the *pa-vagga*; after *s*-sounds, there is the single-substitution (*pubbarūpatta*) of *y*.

In the case of the *ta-vagga*, by the rule "for the *ta-vagga* and the labials (*varaṇa*), the *ca-vagga* and the labials (*bayañā*) respectively," the *ta-vagga* is replaced by the *ca-vagga*, and thereafter there is the single-substitution of *y*.
*vipacca*, *paripacca*, *vimucca*, *adhimucca*.
By the rule of the Great Recitation (*Mahāvutti*), there is elision of *ya* and lengthening of the vowel: *āpucchā*, *anāpucchā*, *vibhajja*, *saṃvibhajja*, *visajja*, *nisajja*, *paṭinisajja*.
In the case of the root *ujjha* with the suffix *-visagga*, there is elision of *ya*: *ujjha*, *ujjhiya*, *ujjitvā*.
*Kati* in the sense of cutting: *kacca*, *vikacca*, having cut (*kantitvā*), having cut apart (*vikantitvā*).
*Nikara* in the sense of deceiving: *nikacca*, as in the case of a gambler (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.35).
*Pata* in the sense of going: *pacca*, *nipacca*, having fallen (*patitvā*), having fallen down (*nipatitvā*).
In the sense of conversing, [the forms] are *sākaccha*.
In the sense of going on foot, [there are]: *pajja*, *āpajja*, *nipajja*, *vipajja*, *sampajja*, *upasampajja*, *paṭipajja*.

Regarding the rule “*ū byañjanassā*” (an augment *ū* is added after a consonant), when the augment *ī* is applied according to the rule “*padādīnaṃ yuka*,” there is the substitution of the preceding form (*pubbarūpa*). Thus: *pajjiya*, *pajjiyāna*; *āpajjiya*, *āpajjiyāna*; *nipajjiya*, *vipajjiya*, *sampajjiya*, *paṭipajjiya*.
The root *sad* (with prefix *ā*) means "to strike. Thus it is said: "Having struck the Tathāgata," as in the verse:

"Like a crow striking a rock. [Root *chid*: *chejja*, *bhijja*, *chindiya*, *acchijja*, *acchindiya*, *vicchijja*, *vicchindiya*, *paricchijja*, *paricchindiya*, *bhejja*, *bhijja*, *sambhijja*, *paṭisambhijja*, *bhindiya*, *sambhindiya*.

In *budha* (to know), there are the forms *bujjha*, *sambujjha*, *abhisambujjha*, *bujjhiya*, *bujjiyāna*; and from the Pāḷi phrase *“marīcikūpamaṃ abhisambuddhāno”*, by applying the substitution of *ot* for *da*, the form is established as in *“anupādiyāno”*.
In *vadha* (killing), there are *vajjha* and *vajjhiya*.
In *vidha* (beating), there are *vijjha* and *vijjhiya*.
In *khana-vilekhane*, there is the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* in *khañña*, *khaṇiya*, and *nāssa*.
In the group of *pavaggas*: *khippa*, *nikhippa*, *saṃkhippa*, *khipiya*, *saṃkhipiya*.
In *labi-avasaṃsane* (to hang down), there is the elision of *y*: *ālamba*, *vilamba*, *avalamba*.
In *lubi-santhambhane* (to support), as in *daṇḍamolumba tiṭṭhati* (he stands supported by a staff) and *jhānamolumba vattati* (he proceeds supported by meditation).

With the prefix *ut*, in the sense of lifting up—as in the *Mahāvagga*: *“ullumpatu maṃ bhante saṅgho”* (May the Saṅgha lift me up)—as seen in *ullumpatu* and so forth; [the forms] *ullumba*, *ārabbha*, *samārabbha*, *labbhā*, *upalabbhā* have a long vowel.
Pakkamma, akkamma, vikkamma, nikkhamma, okkamma, abhikkamma, atikkamma, paṭikkamma, āgamma, saṅgamma. [These are used] in the sense of "having reflected" (*samanupadhāraṇe*).
A king, O Lord of the Earth, should act with reflection; he should not act without reflection, O Ruler of Men. (1.4.128: *nisamma* for a Kṣatriya).
*Samu* is used in the sense of "peace" (*santi*) and "exhaustion" (*kheda*): *upasamma*, *vūpasamma*, *vissamma*.
In the sense of dragging away: *apakassa*.
In the sense of looking toward a direction: *ādissa*, *uddissa*, *odissa*, *apadissa*.
In the sense of touching: *phussa samphasse*. "Having touched again and again, he brings it to an end" (A. IV 195).
*Vasa* means dwelling. Furthermore, *upavassaṃ* [is used] with reference to the full moon of the month of Kattika (Kattikapuṇṇamaṃ); here, there is the insertion of the vowel *i*.
*Visa* means entering; [examples include] *pavissa*, *nivissa*, *abhinivissa*, and so forth.
Thus ends the section on modifications beginning with *iti*.
The Section on Conditions and Transformations is finished.
The Section on Natural Form and the Section on the "Such-like" Condition.
Now, the collection of basic verbal roots (*pakatirūparāsi*) is stated:
*ta*, *ti*, *tu*, *tavantu*, *tāvī*, *tvā*, *tvāna*, *tuna*, *tuṃ*, *tave*, *tāye*, *tabba*.
*Dā*, *khyā*, *gā*, *ghā*, *ṭā*, *ṭhā*, *tā*, *thā*, *dā*, *dhā*, *pā*, *phā*, *bhā*, *mā*, *yā*, *lā*, *vā*, *sā*, *hā*.
Akkhāta (declared), svākkhāta (well-declared), ākhyāta (proclaimed), vikhyāta (renowned).
In the case of *ūbyañjanassa*, there is sometimes the augment *ī* and the shortening of the vowel; thus: saṅgāyita (recited), ghāyita (smelled), ñāta (known).
From *jñā* etc., with the suffix *knā*, the suffix *na* is applied; thus: jānita (made known).

*Kārita* means caused to be made; *ñāpita*, caused to be known; *ñāpayita*, caused to be made known. One who protects (*tāti*) and guards his son is called *tāta*—that is, father (*pitā*). *Datta* [is formed from] *dvitta* with the shortening of the vowel. *Devadatta*, *Brahmadatta*, *Yaññadatta*; also *dāpita*, caused to be given; *dāpayita*, caused to be caused to be given.
According to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*): see *passa*, drink *piva*, drunk *pivita*.
*Phā* occurs in the sense of increase (*vuddhi*); *phita*, the night has become bright (*pabhātā*).
*Mā*: māna, mita, sammita, upamita, nimmita, yāta, lāta, vāta.

Or, according to the *Mahāvutti*, the sutta [is applied] as follows: *nibbuto*, *parinibbuto*, *nibbāpito*, *parinibbāpito*, *osito*, *pariyosito*, *osāpito*, *pariyosāpito*, *pahito*, *pajahito*, *hāpito*.
In the locative (*timhi*): *ñatti*, *datti*, *pāti*, *phāti*, *nibbuti*, *parinibbuti*.

"You" (tumhe) means those who know all phenomena (jānanti). "Proclaimers" (akkhātāro) refers to the Tathāgatas. They will be "knowers" (aññātāro), "informers" (ñāpetā), and "causers of knowing" (ñāpayitā). "The one who exerts himself finds wealth" (uṭṭhātā vindate dhanaṃ).

In some instances, the form *lasse* is a substitution of *īssa* for *ettaṃ*; thus there are forms such as *uṭṭhāpetā*, *samuṭṭhāpetā*, "protector from evil" (*aghassa tātā*), "protector" (*tāyitā*), "giver" (*dātā*), "causer of giving" (*dāpetā*), "connector" (*sandhātā*), "causer of connecting" (*sandhāpetā*), "builder" (*māpitā*), "causer of building" (*māpayitā*), "extinguisher" (*nibbāpetā*), "causer of extinguishing" (*nibbāpayitā*), "diminisher" (*hāpetā*), and "causer of diminishing" (*hāpayitā*).
Examples include *tavantu*, *tāvīsu*, "proclaimer" (*akkhatā*), and "one who has proclaimed" (*akkhātāvī*), and so forth.
Having understood, having known, having made known, having caused to be known, having stood—there is shortening in conjunction with *tvādīsu*.
From the root *ṭhā*, there is the substitution of *ṭha*; having stood firmly, having established oneself.
In the causative (*kārita*), there is shortening in some instances: having placed, having set forth, having established; having given, having taken up, having undertaken, having caused to give.
In *dada-dāne*, *tvā* becomes *pyo*; in *yamhi*, *dassa* becomes *jo*; for that which has a long vowel as its prior form, [the following applies]:
*dajjā*, *dāpetvā*. From the beginning [of the root], it is short: *samādapetvā*.

In *dhā-dhāraṇe*, there is doubling (*dvittaṃ*), the third letter of the prior [consonant] becomes short, and for the subsequent *dhā*, *ho* is substituted; thus: *padahitvā*, *vidahitvā*, *nidahitvā*, *saddahitvā*, *odahitvā*, *pidahitvā*, *paridahitvā*.

Having caused to be made, having had it measured out, having had it stored, having drunk, having caused to drink, having caused to drink, having fashioned, having caused to fashion, having caused to finish, having caused to complete, having abandoned, having relinquished, having let go, having caused to relinquish.
In the forms *tuṃ* and *tave*: to tell, to be told; to count, to be counted; to know, to be known; to cause to know, to be caused to know;
to cause to know, to be caused to know; to stand, to be stood; to stand firmly, to be stood firmly.
to settle, to cause to settle; to place, to cause to place; to establish, to cause to establish; to give, to cause to give; to bestow, to cause to bestow;
to take, to cause to take; to give (with *dajj-*), to cause to give (*dajjitave*); to cause to give, to cause to cause to give;
to encourage, to cause to encourage; to reconcile, to cause to reconcile; to have faith, to cause to have faith.
To deposit, to cause to be deposited, to preserve, to cause to be preserved; to drink, to cause to drink, for drinking, to be drunk;
to measure, to mete out, to compare, to liken; to go, to cause to go, for going; to conclude, to cause to conclude, to bring to a final end;
to abandon, to relinquish, to leave behind the realm of Māra; to give up, to completely abandon, to cause to abandon, to cause to relinquish, to cause to completely relinquish.
In that regard, it is to be declared, reckoned, enumerated, sung, known, understood, made known,
caused to be understood, stood, established, given, taken up, undertaken,
caused to be given, caused to be undertaken, arranged, disposed, drunk, sipped, and measured.
It should be understood, it should be gone to, it should be taken, it should be abandoned.
In words beginning with *ivaṇṇa* (i, ī), when preceded by *vi*, the sense is "gone": *vīto*, *vītadoso*, *vītamoho* (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249);
*udito*, *samudito*, with the augment *d*. *Samito*, *sameto*, *samaveto*, *apeto*, *upeto*, *samupeto*, *abhito*, *kīto*, *kayito*, *kiṇito*, *cito*.
*cinito*, *ācito*, *upacito*, *sañcito*, *jito*, *parājito*, *ḍito*, *oḍḍito*, *nīto*, *ānīto*, *vinīto*, *oṇīto*, *paṇīto*;
the substitution of *ṇa* for *na*.
*pīto*, *bhīto*, *mito*, *sito*, *nissito*, *pahito*.
*Timhi*: *samiti*, *viciti*, *nīti*, *dvitte*, *ādivuddhi*, *netti*, *saddhammanetti*, *bhīti*.
*Tumhi*: *sametā*, *abhisametā*, *vicetā*, *jetā*, *netā*, *vinetā*, *ninnetā*.
*Tavantu*: *tāvīsu-sametavā*, *sametāvī*, *abhisametavā*, *abhisametāvī*, and so forth.

Having approached you, having gone to you, having bought, having searched, having conquered, having completely conquered, having won, having completely won, having defeated, having led, having brought, having guided, having led away, having brought back, having disciplined, having clung, having retired for solitude, having lain down.
In the forms ending in *tum* and *tave*: to approach, to go to, to approach together, to approach together; to buy, to buy; to buy; to search, to investigate;
to conquer, to completely conquer; to lead, to bring, to guide, to lead, to bring back, to discipline, to lead away, to lead back.
To bring, to discipline, to lead.
*Tabbamhi-sametabbaṃ*, *ketabbaṃ*, *kiṇitabbaṃ*, and so forth.
Among those with *uvaṇṇa*: *cuto*, *cavito*.
*Kārite* (in the sense of causing to do) there is *cāvito*. *Juto*, *javito*, *thuto*, *abhitthuto*, *abhitthavito*. With a prefix, *dhu* means "dear":
*sandhuto* means "a dear friend. There is also a textual reading: *“asaṇṭhutaṃ cirasaṇṭhutenā”* ("not having long been acquainted with one who has long been acquainted").
In *du-gati* and *hiṃsā*, [the prefix] *dud-* means "afflicted" (*upadduta*).
In *dhū-kampane*, *dhuta-* means "shaken off" (*niddhuta*).
In *bhū*, *sambhūta-* means "arisen."
*Kārita* means caused to be done; *bhāvita* means cultivated; *sambhāvita* means esteemed; *vibhāvita* means analyzed; *paribhāvita* means thoroughly cultivated. *Yu* in the sense of mixing:
*saṃyuta* means joined. *Ru* in the sense of sound: *ruta*, *luta*, *vuta*, *saṃvuta*, *susaṃvuta*, *suta*, *vissuta*.
In *hu-pūjāyaṃ*, [the suffix] *huta* occurs.
In *timhi*: *cavanaṃ* (falling), *cuti*; *thavanaṃ* (praising), *thuti*, *bhūti*, *vibhūti*;
*savanaṃ* (hearing), *suti*. In *tumhi*: *cavitā*, *cāvetā*; *javitā*; *thavitā*, *santhavitā*; *sotā*, *sāvetā*.
In the *tavant* suffixes: *cutavā*, *cutāvī*, *cāvetavā*, *cāvetāvī*, and so forth.
In the *tvādī* suffixes: *cavitvā*, *cavitvāna*, *cavituna*; *javitvā*; *abhitthavitvā*; *bhutvā*; *anubhavitvā*; *bhāvetvā*; *bhāvayitvā*;
*sutvā*; *suṇitvā*; *sāvetvā*; *sāvayitvā*. In the infinitive suffixes *tuṃ* and *tave*: *cavituṃ*, *cāvetuṃ*; *bhotuṃ*, *bhavituṃ*; *anubhavituṃ*; *bhāvetuṃ*; *bhāvayituṃ*; *sotuṃ*; *sāvetuṃ*.

*Hū-sattāyaṃ*, [meaning] "to be. "Whatever man should wish to be, O lady, he is not unable to be," thus says the *Buddhavamsa* (2.9). In the *pāḷi*, it appears as *hotuye*. From that [root], there should be:
*cavitabbaṃ*, *bhavitabbaṃ*, *anubhavitabbaṃ*, *bhāvetabbaṃ*, *sotabbaṃ*. In the double forms (*dvitte*), there are *sottabbaṃ* and *sāvetabbaṃ*.

Among those ending in *-e* and *-anta*, according to the "Great Rule" (*mahāvutti*), the vowel *e* sometimes becomes *i*: *gāyito*, *apacāyito*, or *apacito*; *ujjhāyito*, *nijjhāyito*, *abhijjhāyito*.
Gāyanaṃ is singing; apacāyanaṃ is honoring.
[The agentive forms are] tumhi-gāyitā, apacāyitā, ujjhāyitā.
[The past participles are] tavantu, tāvīsu, gāyitavā, gāyitāvī, and so forth.
Having sung, having meditated, having envied.
To sing, to sing for the sake of, to honor, to honor for the sake of, to meditate, to meditate for the sake of, to envy, to envy for the sake of.
That which should be sung, that which should be honored, that which should be censured.
Thus ends the collection of base forms for monosyllabic roots.

Regarding the polysyllabic roots of the *bhūvādi* class and others, their base forms should be expanded in detail by dividing them according to the method of classification found in the *Tyādikanda*, following the seven groups of roots beginning with *bhūvādi*, as well as the *kārita* suffixes, root suffixes (*dhātuppaccaya*), and other applicable suffixes.
Herein, this is the demonstration of the method:
*āsa*, *isa*, *gamu*, *disa*.

In the case of *āsa* [meaning] "to sit," there is no substitution of *ccha* for the *ta*-suffix because of the addition of the rule "in *māna*, *tyādi*, etc. in the *Cchādesa-sutta*; thus, one has "waited upon" (*upāsito*) or "honored" (*payirupāsito*) the teacher.
*Tumhi*: *upāsitā*, *upāsetā*, *upāsitavā*, *upāsitāvī*, *upāsitvā*, *upāsitvāna*, *upāsituna*.
With the substitution of *pya* according to the rule “*pyo vā tvāssa samāse*”: *upāsiya*, *payirupāsiya*, *upasiyāna*, *upāsituṃ*, *upāsitave*, *upāsitabbo*.
*Isu*: *icchā*, *kantīsu*. Due to the general rule (*bahulādhikārā*), there is the substitution of *chā*; thus: *icchito*, *icchitā*, *icchitavā*, *icchitāvī*, *icchituṃ*, *icchitave*, *icchitabbaṃ*.
*Kārite*: caused to be desired, caused to be wished for; *icchāpitā*, *icchāpitāvī*, having caused to be desired, in order to cause to be desired, to be caused to be desired.

Regarding the root *es* (to seek): *esito*, sought after, searched for; *esitā*, *pariyesitā*, one who has sought, one who has searched for; *esitavā*, *pariyesitavā*, having sought, having searched for;
*esitvā*, *pariyesitvā*, *esitvāna*, *pariyesitvāna*, having sought, having searched for; *esituṃ*, *pariyesituṃ*, in order to seek, in order to search for; *esitave*, *pariyesitave*.
It should be sought, it should be pursued.
In the sense of going: *gamu*, *gatimhi*, *gamito*, *gamitā*, *gamitavā*, *gamitāvī*, *gamitvā*, *gamitvāna*, *gamituna*, *gamituṃ*, *gamitave*, *gamitabbaṃ*.
In the causative: *gamāpito*, *gamāpetā*, and so forth.
In the sense of looking at the directions: *passito*, *passitā*, *passetā* (one who has looked), *passitvā*, *passitvāna*, *passituna*, *passituṃ*, *passitave*, *passitabbaṃ*.

In the causative sense: *dassito*, *dassayito*, *dassitā*, *dassetā*, *dassayitā*, *dassitavā*, *dassitāvī*, *dassetvā*, *dassayitvā*, *dassetvāna*, *dassayitvāna*, *dassetuṃ*, *dassayituṃ*, *dassetabbaṃ*.

*Dakkhādese* (in the sense of showing): *dakkhito*, *dakkhitā*, *dakkhitavā*, *dakkhitāvī*, *dakkhitvā*, *dakkhituṃ*, *dakkhitave*. The Pāli text at *Dīghanikāya Aṭṭhakathā* 2.332 reads: *“dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅghaṃ”* (to show the unconquered Saṅgha). [The gerundive form is] *dakkhitabbaṃ*. [In the case of] *dusa* (the prefix *du-*) in the sense of destruction, with the causative suffix *ṇi*:
764. In the presence of *ṇi*, there is lengthening of the vowel of *dus*;
*ka* is substituted for *dus*. (Kaccāyana 486; Rūpasiddhi 543; Niddesa 977).
When the suffix *ṇa* follows, there is a long vowel for the word *dussa*.
Examples: *dūsito*, *dūsitā*, *dūsetā*, *dūsitavā*, *dūsitāvī*, *dūsetvā*, *dūsetvāna*, *dūsituna*, *dūsetuṃ*, *dūsetave*.
Why "when *ṇa* follows"? [Example: *duṭṭho*.
Thus ends the *bhū* class (*bhūvādigaṇa*).
The *rudh* class (*rudhādigaṇa*): *bhuja*, *yuja*, *chida*, *bhida*, *rudha*.
765. *Maṃ vā rudhādīnaṃ* (Ka. 446; Rū. 509; Nī. 926).
After the roots beginning with *rudh*, the augment *m* (niggahīta) optionally occurs before the suffixes beginning with a vowel (*ma*). Thus:
*bhuñjito*, *bhuñjitā*, *bhuñjitavā*, *bhuñjitāvī*, *bhuñjitvā*, *bhuñjitvāna*, *bhuñjituna*, *bhuñjituṃ*, *bhuñjitave*, *bhuñjitabbaṃ*.

*Kārite-bhojito*, *bhojitā*, or *bhojetā*; *bhojitavā*, *bhojitāvī*; *bhojetvā*, *bhojayitvā*; *bhojetuṃ*, *bhojetave*, *bhojetabbaṃ*. Similarly for the root *bhuj*: *yuñjito*, *anuyuñjito*. For *chind* (to cut):
*chindito*, *chinditā*, or *chindetā*; *chinditavā*, *chinditāvī*; *chinditvā*, *chinditvāna*, *chindituna*. Regarding the substitution of *py* for *p*:
*lataṃ dantehi chindiya gavesitabbaṃ* (the creeper is to be sought after having been cut with the teeth), *chindiyāna*, *sañchindiya*.
"Having completely cut off" (*sañchindiyāna*), [the object] "to be cut off" (*chinditabba*).
In the causative: "caused to be cut" (*chindāpito*), "one who causes to cut" (*chindāpetā*), and so forth.
"Broken" (*bhindito*), "one who has broken" (*bhinditā*), or "one who breaks" (*bhindetā*)—these are similar to the verbal root *chid*.
Rundhito, rundhitā, rundhetā, rundhitavā, rundhitāvī, rundhitvā, rundhitvāna, rundhituṃ, rundhitave, rundhitabbaṃ. In the causative:
rundhāpito, rundhāpayito, and so forth. Thus ends the *rudh* class (the seventh class).
Divādigaṇa:
*pada*, *budha*, *tusa*, *divu*. 766. In some instances, [the suffix] is added after *pada* and the others.

In certain cases, the augment *y* occurs after roots beginning with *pa*, etc.; there is the insertion of *y*. By the rule “for the *tavagga* and *varaṇa* [consonants], the *cavagga* and *bayañña* [substitutes]” (*tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā*), the *cavagga* substitution takes place;

by the rule “after *vaggas* and *lasas*, those [preceding sounds]” (*vaggalasehi te*), the preceding form (*pubbarūpa*) is applied to the *y*. *pajjito*, *āpajjito*, *paṭipajjito*, *paṭipajjitā*, *paṭipajjitavā*, *paṭipajjitāvī*, *paṭipajjitvā*, *paṭipajjitvāna*, *paṭipajjituna*, *paṭipajjituṃ*, *paṭipajjitave*, *paṭipajjitabbaṃ*.
In the causative (*kārita*): *āpādito*, *uppādito*, *nipphādito*, *sampādito*, *paṭipādito*; *āpāditā*, *āpādetā*, *uppāditā*.

The one who causes the unarisen path to arise; the producer, the accomplisher, the one who brings about, the one who causes to be brought about, the one who causes to be practiced, the one who causes to be caused to be practiced;

having caused to be brought about, having caused to arise, having accomplished, having brought about, having caused to be brought about, having caused to be practiced, having caused to be caused to be practiced;

in order to cause to be brought about, in order to cause to arise, in order to accomplish, in order to bring about, in order to cause to be brought about, in order to cause to be practiced; that which is to be caused to be brought about.
It is to be produced, brought to completion, accomplished, and practiced;

he has awakened to, or has awakened to the truths—thus he is "Buddha," the Great One. (192) [The forms derived from the root *budh* are: *bujjhitavā*, *bujjhitāvī*, *bujjhitvā*, *bujjhitvāna*, *bujjhituna*, *bujjhituṃ*, *bujjhitave*, *bujjhitabbaṃ*.
From the causative form *bodheti*: "He who awakens the world" is called a Buddha, O Great One.
(192) [Derivatives: *bodhetavā*, *bodhetāvī*, *bodhayitvā*, *bodhayitvāna*, *bodhetuṃ*, *bodhetave*, *bodhetabbaṃ*;
*tussito*, *santussito*, *tussitā*, *tussitavā*, *tussitāvī*, *tussitvā*, *tussituṃ*, *tussitabbaṃ*.

*Kārite*: *tosito*, *tositā*, *tosesā* (or *tosesā*), *tositavā*, *tositāvī*, *tosesitvā*, *tosesituṃ*, *tosesitabbaṃ*; *dibbito*, *dibbitā*, *dibbitavā*, *dibbitāvī*, *dibbitvā*, *dibbituṃ*, *dibbitabbaṃ*.
Thus ends the *divādi-gaṇa*.
The *svādi-gaṇa*.
Suta, sutaṃ, suto, sutā, soto vā, sutavā, sutāvī, sutvā, sotuṃ, sotabbaṃ. In the causative (kārita):
sāvitā, sāvetā, sāvetavā, sāvetāvī, sāvetvā, sāvetuṃ, sāvetabbaṃ; saṃvutā.
strung, having strung, having wound together, to wind together, that which is to be wound together; attained, mastered, one who has attained,
one who has mastered, one who has attained, one who has mastered, one who has attained mastery, one who has mastered mastery, having attained, having mastered,
to attain, to master, that which is to be attained, that which is to be mastered.
*Kārite-pāpito*, *pāpitā*, *pāpetā* or *pāpetā*, *pāpetvā*, *pāpetuṃ*, and so forth.
Thus ends the *svādi-gaṇa*.
The *kiyādi-gaṇa* has been stated only among those [roots] with a single consonant.

The *tan-ādi* group [of roots] beginning with *kṛ*: *tana*. Regarding *karoti*, [the forms are]: *kassa*, *kho*; *abhisaṅkhato*, *abhisaṅkhārito*; *abhisaṅkhārako*, *abhisaṅkhārako*; *abhisaṅkhāritavā*, *abhisaṅkhāritavā*; *abhisaṅkhāritāvī*, *abhisaṅkhāritāvī*.
Having done, having done, having performed, having performed, to perform, that which is to be performed.

Caused to be done—caused to be done, caused to be made, one who has caused to be done, one who causes to be done, one who has caused to be made, one who causes to be made, one who has caused to do, one who has caused to do, having caused to do, having caused to make, to cause to do, to cause to make, that which is to be caused to do, that which is to be caused to make.
Stretched, having stretched, to stretch, and so forth.
Thus ends the *tanādi* group.
The *curādi* group consists of *kappa*, *cinta*, *cura*, and *vida*.

In the sense of imagining or conceiving: *kappita*, *saṅkappita*, *kappayita*, *saṅkappetā*, *saṅkappayitā*, *kappetavā*, *kappetāvī*, *kappetvā*, *kappayitvā*, *kappetuṃ*, *kappayituṃ*, *kappetabbaṃ*, *kappayitabbaṃ*.
In the causative: *kappāpita*, and so forth.

In the sense of thinking or reflecting: *cintita*, *cintayita*, *cintetā*, *cintayitā*, *cintitavā*, *cintitāvī*, *cintetvā*, *cintayitvā*, *cintituṃ*, *cintetuṃ*, *cintayituṃ*, *cintitabbaṃ*, *cintetabbaṃ*.
*Kārito*, *cintāpito*, and so forth;
*corito*, *corayito*, *coretā*, *corayitā*, and so forth;
*vedito*, *vedayito*, *vedetā*, *vedayitā*, and so forth.
Thus ends the curādigaṇa (the group beginning with *cur*). [Roots such as] *titikkha*, *vīmaṃsa*, *bubhukkha*, and *pabbatāya*.
[Derivatives: *titikkhito*, *titikkhitā*, *titikkhitavā*, *titikkhitāvī*, *titikkhitvā*, *titikkhituṃ*, *titikkhitabbo*.
*Kārite*: *titikkhāpito*, etc.
*Vīmaṃsito*, *vīmaṃsetā*, *vīmaṃsitavā*, *vīmaṃsitāvī*, *vīmaṃsitvā*, *vīmaṃsituṃ*, *vīmaṃsitabbaṃ*.
*Kārite*: *vīmaṃsāpito*, etc.
Bubhukkhito, bubhukkhitā, bubhukkhita-vā, bubhukkhita-āvī, bubhukkhitvā, bubhukkhituṃ, bubhukkhita-bbaṃ.
In the causative: bubhukkhāpito, etc.
Pabbatāyito, pabbatāyitā, pabbatāyita-vā, pabbatāyita-āvī, pabbatāyitvā, pabbatāyituṃ, pabbatāyitabbo.
"Kārite-pabbatāyāpito," and so forth.

In the same way, *kukkuccāyito*, *kukkuccāyitā*, *kukkuccāyitavā*, *kukkuccāyitāvī*, *kukkuccāyitvā*, *kukkuccāyituṃ*, *kukkuccāyitabbaṃ*, *piyāyito*, *piyāyitvā*, *piyāyituṃ*, and so on, should be applied.
Now, the specific group (*visesarāsi*) is stated.
767. *Kattari cārambhe* (Ka. 556–7; Rū. 606, 622; Nī. 1143–4). "Ārambha" means the initial action—the very first commencement.
When expressing the commencement of an action, the suffix *kta* occurs after both the agent (*kattari*) and the object (*kammasu*).
By this rule, even with respect to a present continuity of action, [the suffix denotes] a past object by way of its initial commencement.
The *tap* affix is prescribed: how so? As in "one who has eaten" (*bhuttāvī*) or "one who has been invited" (*pavārito*), [the suffix] *pāci* is used.
238. A man made a mat (*kaṭaṃ pakato*); by the man, the mat was made (*purisena kaṭo pakato*). 768.
[The suffix] *ka* is applied after the roots *ṭhā*, *vasa*, *sila*, *sis*, *ruha*, *raja*, and *nī*. 556; Rūpasiddhi 606, 622; Nāmamālā 1143–4.
After the suffixes *ṭha* and so forth, the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent, the abstract state (*bhāva*), and the object (*karman*).
In the case of *ṭhā*: the teacher was attended upon by the pupil; the teacher was attended upon by the pupil.
In the case of *ās*: the teacher was waited upon by the pupil; the teacher was waited upon by the pupil.
The teacher dwells in dependence upon the pupil; the pupil dwells in dependence upon the teacher.
In the sense of embracing, the son is embraced by the father; the father is embraced by the son.
The pot is placed upon the fire by people; the pot is placed upon the fire by the people—the meaning is that it has been set on the hearth.
A person has climbed upon a tree; the tree has been climbed by a person.

Devadatta has surpassed a low-born woman in old age; the low-born woman has been surpassed by Devadatta. A young man has been born after a young woman; the young woman has been born after the young man. 769.
[The suffix *ka* occurs] after verbs meaning "going," after intransitive verbs, and after words denoting the locus (*adhāra*). (Kaccāyana 556–7; Rūpasiddhi 606, 622; Nyāsa 1143–4).

The suffix *kta* occurs after roots meaning "going" (*gamanattha*) and after intransitive roots (*akammaka-dhātu*), expressing the locus (*ādhāra*), the agent (*kattar*), the abstract state (*bhāva*), and the object (*kamma*).

*Yātaṃ*: that to which they have gone is "yātaṃ"; this is their "yātaṃ. *Padakkantaṃ*: that upon which one steps is "padakkantaṃ"; this is their "padakkantaṃ. Examples with the locus: "They have gone here" (*iha te yātā*); "this path has been traversed by them" (*ayaṃ tehi yāto maggo*);

"here [is] what has been traversed by them" (*iha tehi yātaṃ*). Examples with the intransitive: "This is the place where they have sat" (*idaṃ tesaṃ āsitaṃ ṭhānaṃ*); "they have sat here" (*iha te āsitā*); "this is the place where they have sat" (*idaṃ tehi āsitaṃ ṭhānaṃ*); "here [is] what has been sat by them" (*idha tehi āsitaṃ*).
770. Regarding the sense of food (*āhārattha*): according to *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* 556–7; *Rūpasiddhi* 606, 622;

and *Niruttidīpanī* 1143–4, from the verbal root meaning "to swallow" (*ajjhoharaṇa*), the suffix *-ta* (the past participle) occurs in the sense of the agent, the action itself, the object, and the locus.
Examples: "These were eaten by them," "eaten," "drunk," "chewed," "tasted. "These things were eaten by them," "eaten," "drunk," etc.
Chewed, tasted. Herein, for them there is what has been eaten, drunk, consumed, chewed, and tasted.
This is their place of eating, their place of consuming, their place of drinking, their place of chewing, and their place of tasting.
Thus is the group of conditions beginning with "thus" (tādi).

The group of suffixes beginning with *anīya*: regarding the verbal roots *bhū* and *kṛ*, [the suffix] *anīya* is applied according to the rule "after *bhū* and *kṛ*, [the suffix] *anīya*. That which is experienced is "to-be-experienced" (*anubhavanīya*).

Among those ending in long vowels, there is mutual elision; in some cases, there is the augment *y*. Thus: "to-be-presented" (*upaṭṭhānīya*), "to-be-given" (*dānīya*); and one who exerts himself is a "striver" (*padhānīya*)—namely, the practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*).

It is to be drunk, thus it is *pānīya* (drinkable); it is worthy of being tasted, thus it is *sāyanīya* (palatable), *paṭisāyanīya* (re-savorable), *pahānīya* (to be abandoned), or *abhitthavanīya* (to be praised);

it is to be heard, thus it is *savanīya* (audible); it is to be offered, thus it is *havanīya* (sacrificial); it is worthy of being attended upon, thus it is *upāsanīya*; it is to be approached, thus it is *abhikkamanīya* (approachable); it causes passion, thus it is *rajjanīya* (arousing passion);
it is to be gone to, thus it is *gamanīya* (accessible); it is spoken, thus it is *vacanīya* (to be said).
Kara, tara, thara, dhara, sara, hara. 771. *Rā nassa ṇo ka*.
(Aṭṭhakathā 549; Rūpasiddhi 550; Niddesa 1135).
After a verbal root ending in the letter *r*, the *n* of a following suffix becomes *ṇ*.

That which is to be done is *karaṇīya*; that which is to be crossed is *taraṇīya*; that which is to be spread is *attharaṇīya*; that which is to be borne is *dhāraṇīya*; that which is to be remembered is *sāraṇīya*; that which is to be carried is *haraṇīya*, and so forth.
That which is to be obstructed is *rundhanīya*; that which is to be eaten is *bhuñjanīya* or *bhojanīya* or *paribhojanīya*;
that which is to be joined is *yojanīya*; that which is to be played with is *dibbanīya*; that which is to be understood is *bujjhanīya*; that which is to be reached...
That which is to be led away is *pāpanīya*; that which is to be made known is *ñāpanīya*; that which is to be thought about is *cintanīya*; that which is to be avoided is *vajjanīya*;
that which is to be endured is *titikkhanīya*; that which is to be investigated is *vīmaṃsanīya*, and so forth.
Thus ends the group of suffixes beginning with *-anīya*.
Now, the group of *māna* suffixes:
next, the *māna* suffixes are being explained. 772.
*Nta* [is used] for the agent (*kattari*) in the present tense (*vattamāne*). (Ka. 565; Rū. 646; Nī. 1157).
That which is occurring is called "present" (*paccuppanna*). In the present tense, after a verbal root meaning "to do," the suffix *-nto* occurs for the agent (*kattari*).

The root *bhū* signifies existence (*sattāyaṃ*). By the rule “*kattari lo*,” the primary suffix (*apaccaya*) *-lo* is applied; by the rule “*yuvaṇṇānameopaccaye*,” the vowel *u* is replaced by *o*. Thus, *bhavatī* becomes *bhonto*—as in *bhonto puriso* (the venerable man), *bhontaṃ kulaṃ* (the venerable family), and *bhontī itthī* (the venerable woman).

Again, by the rule “*eonamayavā sare*,” the *o* is replaced by *ava*. Thus, one says *bhavaṃ puriso* (the venerable man), *bhavantaṃ kulaṃ* (the venerable family), *bhavantī* (the venerable woman), *bhavatī*, or *bhotī* (the venerable woman).
773. *Māno* (the suffix -māna). [Kaccāyana 565; Rūpasiddhi 646; Nyāsa 1157].
When the action is currently taking place, the suffix *māna* follows a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) to denote the agent (*kattari*).
Examples: *bhavamāno puriso* (the man being), *bhavamānaṃ kulaṃ* (the family being), *bhavamānā itthī* (the woman being).
774. Regarding the suffix *ka* in the sense of state (*bhāva*) and object (*kamma*): Kaccāyana 565; Rūpasiddhi 646; Nyāsa 1157.
When the time is present, the suffix *māna* occurs after verbal roots to express state and object. [The rule] “*kyo bhāvakammesū...*” prescribes the suffix *ya*. Thus:
*anubhūyamāno bhogo purisena* (wealth being experienced by a person), *anubhūyamānā sampatti* (prosperity being experienced), *anubhūyamānaṃ sukhaṃ* (happiness being experienced).
775. Regarding "yassa dvittaṃ, anubhuyyamāno":

when the future tense (*anāgata*) is to be expressed, the suffixes *t* and *nta* preceded by the particle *ssu* take the form of the *māna* suffixes (i.e., *sant*, *santa*). Thus, *te* becomes *ssapubbā*. When the future time is to be stated, those [suffixes] *t* and *nta* become *ssapubbā* (preceded by *ssu*).

"Bhavissati" means "one who will be," [forming] *bhavissanto*. The rules for nominal forms (*rūpavidhi*) should be consulted at the end of rule 403—namely: *puriso* (a man), *bhavissantaṃ kulaṃ* (a family that will be), *bhavissantī vibhatti* (the case-ending that will be), or *bhavissatī* (will be), *bhavissamāno* (one who will be), *bhavissamānaṃ* (that which will be), *bhavissamānā* (she who will be). In the passive voice (*kamme*):
*anubhūyissamāno* (one who will be experienced).
776. For the suffix *-māna*, there is *-ma*.
In some instances, there is the elision of the *m* of the suffix *māna*.
For example: *nisinno vā sayāno vā* (Khu. pā. 9.9), *sato sampajāno* (Dī. ni. 1.217); here the *n* is always elided.
[Examples include] *paññāyanto*, *paññāyamāno*.
In the passive voice: being made known;
in the causative: causing to know, making known, causing to be known; in the passive causative:
being caused to be known.

In the passive sense (*kamme*): *jānāpīyamāno*.
Standing, standing, standing; halting, halting, halting.
In the passive sense: being established.
In the causative sense: establishing, establishing, establishing.
Being established in action;
giving, bestowing, granting, undertaking, bestowing, bestowing, undertaking;
being given, being bestowed in action.

In the sense of the object: *dāpīyamāno*, *samādāpīyamāno*.
In the sense of placing down: *nidhento*, *nidahanto*, *nidahamāno*, *nidhīyyamāno*, *nidhāpento*, *nidhāpayanto*, *nidhāpayamāno*.
Being caused to be laid down, going forth; those who go forth are followed by the people. The great king, while going forth, saw [him] sitting on a mountain in the midst of the forest.

Accumulating, accumulating; conquering, conquering; giving, giving; leading, leading; guiding, guiding; leading, leading; disciplining, disciplining;

*javanto*, *javamāno*, *abhitthavanto*, *abhitthavamāno*, *abhitthavīyamāno*, *sandhavanto*, *sandhavamāno*,
*dhunanto*, *niddhunanto*, *dhunamāno*, *niddhunamāno*, *punanto*, *ravanto*, *lunanto*, *āvuṇanto*, *pasavanto*, *vissavanto*.

Hū-sattāyaṃ, honto. Edantesu-ento.
When the sun has gone to its setting (atthaṃ entamhi sūriye), there is jā.
2.2.2.187 (atthaṅgatamhi): samanto, abhisamento, khāyanto, khāyamāno, gāyanto, gāyamāno, gāyīyamāno, gāyāpento, gāyāpayanto, apacāyanto.
Honoring the Dhamma: *jhāyanto*, *jhāyamāno*, *pajjhāyanto*, *ujjhāyanto*, *nijjhāyanto*, *abhijjhāyanto*.
In the causative: *jhāpento*, *ujjhāpento* (with the elision of *ya*).
*Bhāyanto*, *bhāyamāno*. *Sāliṃ lāyanto*, *lāyamāno*. *Cīvaraṃ vāyanto*, *vāyamāno*.
In *kile-kīḷā* (sport) and *peme* (love), *kelāyanto* and *kelāyamāno* mean "causing to sport" or "cherishing," or alternatively, "moving" or "loving.

In *pale-gatiyaṃ*, it means "fleeing";
in *mile-hāniyaṃ*, it means "withering";
in *saṅkase-nivāse*, it means "doubting," and so forth.
In the case of multiple suffixes (*anekabyañjana*) ending in *a* or *bhu*, according to the rule "there is elision of the initial [vowel] of *nta*,

*māna*, *anta*, *ti*, *yi*, and *yuṃ*," there is elision of the initial [vowel] in *nta* and *māna*: *santo*, *samāno*, *upāsanto*, *upāsamāno*, *upāsīyamāno*, *icchanto*, *icchamāno*, *icchīyamāno*, *gacchanto*, *gacchamāno*, *gacchīyamāno*.

When a root ending in *r* or *l* is followed by a suffix beginning with *s*, such as in the future tense (*ssapubbo*), according to the rule “*labha vasa chida gama bhida rudānaṃ cchaṅa*,” the final consonant of the root is replaced by *cch*. Thus:
*gacchanto*, *gamissanto*, *gacchamāno*, *gamissamāno*; *jiranto*, *jiramāno*, *jiyyanto*, *jiyyamāno*; *dahanto*, *dahamāno*.
From *dah* (to burn): *dassa*, *ḍo*; *ḍahanto*, *ḍahamāno*.
In the passive sense (*kamme*):
*ḍayhamāno*. From *dis* (to see): *pekkhane*; *passanto*, *passamāno*, *passīyamāno*.
In the passive sense: kārite—dassento, dassayanto, dassayamāno;
labhanto, labhamāno.

Dying, in the process of dying, passing away, in the process of passing away.

*Vacanto* means speaking; *vaccamāno* means being spoken to.
Regarding the object (*kamma*), it is stated as *assu*, meaning "being spoken to.
