In the passive voice (*kamme-vācī*), when [the suffix] *ya* is added: for the future tense, by the rule “*vaca bhuja muca visānaṃ kkhaṅa*,” there is the substitution of *kkha* for the final consonant of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Thus: *vakkhanto*, *vakkhamāno*, *vadanto*, *vadamāno*, *ovadanto*, *ovadamāno*, *vajjanto*, *vajjamāno*.
In the passive voice: *vadīyamāno*, *ovadīyamāno*, *ovañjīyamāno*.
Causing the drum to be sounded means having it beaten;
"dwelling" means staying.
"In the act" refers to the preliminary stage, as in "raining down."
Dwelling, causing to dwell.
About to go, about to dwell, going, dwelling.
Entering, entering.
In the *kamme* (accusative) case:
*pavisīyamāno*. In the *anāgate* (future) tense: *pavekkhanto*, *pavisissanto*, *pavekkhamāno*, *pavisissamāno*, and so forth.
In the *rudhādi* (root class beginning with *rudh*) group: *rundhanto*, *rundhamāno*.
Being obstructed by karma;
being obstructed while in the state of the prior form;
obstructing, obstructing oneself, and being obstructed.
Cutting, cutting, being caused to cut, being cut, causing to cut, causing to cause to cut.
In the future: will cut, will be cutting, is about to cut, will be about to cut.
Breaking, breaking, being caused to break, being broken, intending to break, will break, is about to break, will be about to break.
While eating, while being eaten;
in the sense of an object—being eaten;
in the state of prior form—being eaten.
Feeding, causing to feed, making one feed, being made to feed.
In the future: about to eat, intending to eat, eating, intending to eat.
Releasing, releasing, being released, being released.
*Anāgate-mokkhanto*, *muñcissanto*, *mokkhamāno*, *muñcissamāno*, and so forth.
In the case of the present tense (*divādimhi*), the pure agent form and the pure object form are identical to those in the future tense; for example: *dibbanto*, *dibbamāno*, *dibbīyamāno*.
When in the state of the future tense, it is *dibbamāno*.
Being cut, being cut down, causing [another] to be cut, causing [another] to cause [another] to be cut.
Awakening, awakening, being awakened, causing [another] to awaken, causing [another] to cause [another] to awaken, causing [another] to cause [another] to cause [another] to awaken.

Being liberated, being liberated, causing [another] to liberate, causing [another] to cause [another] to liberate, causing [another] to cause [another] to cause [another] to liberate, being caused to be liberated.
*Yujjanto*, *yujjamāno*, and so forth.
In the sense of the agent (*svādī*): *suṇanto*, *suṇamāno*. In the sense of the object (*kamme*): *suyyamāno*.
In the causative: causing to hear, making hear, making hear;
reaching, mastering the Dhamma, mastering, being reached, being mastered. In the causative:
causing to reach, causing to master, causing to master.
*Pari*, preceded by *sam*: *parisamāpento*, *parisamāpayanto*, *parisamāpayamāno*, *parisamāpīyamāno*.
*Sak*: *sakkuṇanto*, *āvuṇanto*, and so forth.
Regarding roots beginning with *ki*: *kiṇanto*, *kiṇāpento*, *vikkayanto*, and so forth.
In the sense of beginning: *tanonto*, *karonto*, *kubbanto*, *kubbamāno*, *krubbanto*, *krubbamāno*, *kurumāno*, *kayiranto*, *kayiramāno*. In the passive sense (*kamme*):

*karīyamāno*, *kayyamāno*—here the substitution of *y* for the final of the root occurs according to the rule: “For the *tavagga* and *varaṇa* [consonants], there are the *cavagga* and *bayañña* [vowels] respectively.
Also: *saṅkharonto*, *abhisaṅkharonto*.
*Kārite*: *kārento*, *kārayanto*, *kārayamāno*, *kārīyamāno*.
*Sakkonto* and so forth.
In the *curādi* [class]: *corento*, *corayanto*, *corayamāno*, *thenento*, *thenayanto*, *thenayamāno*, *cintento*.
*cintayanto*, *cintayamāno*, *cintīyamāno*, *cintāpento*, *cintāpayanto*, *cintāpayamāno*, *cintāpīyamāno*, and so forth.
*Titikkhanto*, *titikkhamāno*, *titikkhīyamāno*, *titikkhāpento*, *titikkhāpayanto*, *titikkhāpayamāno*. *Vīmaṃsanto*, *tikicchanto*, *cikicchanto*, *vicikicchanto*.
One who desires to eat is *bubhukkhanto*; one who desires to consume is *jighacchanto*; [one who desires] to drink or to enjoy...
"One who desires" means one who is thirsty; "one who desires to guard" means one who feels disgust; "one who desires to take away or seek out" means one who wishes to steal (*jigīsanto*);
"one who desires to conquer" means one who wishes to triumph (*vijigīsanto*).
"One who moves about like a mountain" is *pabbatāyanto*; thus, forms such as *pabbatāyamāno*, *piyāyanto*, and *mettāyanto* should also be construed accordingly.
Thus ends the section on the group of suffixes beginning with *māna*.
Now follows the group of suffixes beginning with *ṇya*: those ending in the suffixes *ṇya*, *ya*, and *yak* are now being explained.
777. Ghyana.

After verbal roots (bhāva), when followed by the suffix *gha*, the suffix *ṇa* becomes the substitute for *ya*. The suffix *gha* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) serves as a qualifier in rules such as “*kagācajānaṃ ghānubandhe*” and so forth. The suffix *ṇa* as an indicatory letter serves to indicate vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*).

This applies everywhere in this manner. That which is to be experienced is "the experience" (*anubhāviya*); thus, enjoyment is experienced by a person, pleasure is experienced, and prosperity is experienced.
778. *Āsse ca*.
In the case of roots ending in *ā*, *ā* becomes *e* before the suffix *ghyaṇ*. By the word "and" (*ca*), there is also the substitution of *e* for the augment *ī* in roots ending in *i*.
That which is to be told or spoken is "to be told" (*akkheyya*).
That which is to be counted is "countable" (*saṅkhyeyya*); that which cannot be counted is "innumerable" (*asaṅkhyeyya*).

That which is to be sung is "chant" (*geyya*), namely a discourse accompanied by verses (*sagāthaka-sutta*). That which is worthy of being smelled is "fragrant" (*gheyya*) or "to be smelled. That which is worthy of being honored is "venerable" (*apaceyya*).
That which is worthy of being known is "knowable" (*ñeyya*); that which is worthy of being fully understood is "to be realized" (*aññeyya*) or "to be discerned" (*viññeyya*).
To be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).
With the addition of *ī*: to be cognized (*jāniya*), to be discerned (*vijāniya*);

the *ī* becomes short: to be known (*jāneyya*), to be discerned (*vijāneyya*). That which is to be resolved is "to be resolved" (*adhiṭṭheyya*, *adhiṭṭhaheyya*); that which is to be given is "to be given" (*deyya*).
"Ādātabbaṃ" means that which is to be taken up; "saddaheyyaṃ" means it is worthy to be believed; "vidheyyaṃ" means it is worthy to be determined;
"avidheyyaṃ" (not to be determined) refers to the characteristic of non-self; "māradheyyaṃ" means that wherein Māra’s command burns;
"maccudheyyaṃ" (the realm of death); "sannidheyyaṃ" means that which is to be stored; "abhidheyyaṃ" means that which is to be designated or spoken of.

*Pidahitabbaṃ* means that which should be covered (*pidheyyaṃ*), or *alopa*, or *apidheyyaṃ*. *Pātabbaṃ* means that which should be drunk (*peyyaṃ*). *Minetabbaṃ* means that which should be measured (*meyyaṃ*).

*Pametabbaṃ* means that which should be measured (*pameyyaṃ*). That which is worthy of being approached and measured is *upameyyaṃ*. *Hātabbaṃ* means that which should be abandoned (*heyyaṃ*), *paheyyaṃ*, or *pajaheyyaṃ*.

Among those with the vowel *i*: *ajjhāyitabbaṃ* means that which should be studied (*ajjheyyaṃ*) or *adhiyeyyaṃ*. *Upetabbaṃ* means that which should be approached (*upeyyaṃ*). *Vikkiṇitabbaṃ* means that which should be sold... [text ends]
*vikkeyyaṃ*, *vikkāyiyaṃ*, *vikkāyeyyaṃ*, or *vikkiṇeyyaṃ* means "to be sold"; *viceyyaṃ*, *vicineyyaṃ* means "to be investigated" (*vicinitabba*);
*jeyyaṃ*, *vijeyyaṃ* means "to be conquered" (*jetabba*); *neyyaṃ*, *vineyyaṃ* means "to be led" (*netabba*); *adhiseyyaṃ* means "to be laid upon" (*adhisayitabba*);
*pāheyyaṃ*, *pahiṇeyyaṃ* means "to be sent" (*pahitabba*).
In the case of *u-vaṇṇa* vowels, there is the substitution of *vuddhi*. Regarding the word *ku*, because it is said "it is made" (*kuyyati*), it is *kāveyyaṃ*.
In the absence of *ī*, *va* becomes *ba* and is shortened, thus *kabyaṃ*. When the preceding form is applied, it is *kabbaṃ*.

That which is to be moved away is *cāveyyaṃ*; that which is to be run is *javeyyaṃ*; that which is to be praised is *abhitthaveyyaṃ*. That which is worthy of becoming is *bhabbaṃ*. That which is to be offered is *habyaṃ*—namely, clarified butter (*sappi*).
From the roots *apacāyati*, *apaceyyaṃ* (that which is to be honored) and *apacāyiyaṃ* [are derived].
From the root *ve* (to weave), in the sense of weaving threads, *vetabbaṃ* (that which is to be woven) becomes *veyyaṃ*.
The suffix *ghyaṇ* is applied after roots such as *vac*, *bhaj*, *bhuja*, and *yuj*.
779. *Kagā ca jānaṃ ghānubandhe* (Ka. 623; Rū. 554; Nī. 1229).
When a suffix with *gh* as its consonantal ligature (*anubandha*) follows, *k* and *g* are substituted for the final letters of the roots *ca*, *jāna*, *dhā*, and *vaca*.
Thus: *vattabbaṃ* (to be spoken), *vākkaṃ* (speech), *vāccaṃ* (to be spoken), or *vāceyyaṃ* (should be spoken).
*Bhājya* means that which is to be served; *bhāgya* means that which is to be enjoyed; *bhogya* means that which is to be used; *bhogga* means that which is to be employed;
*yogya* means that which is to be joined. (Rule 780: *Vadādīhi yo ka*. Kaccāyana 541; Rūpasiddhi 552; Niddesa 1126.
After roots such as *vad*, the suffix *ya* frequently occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an object (*kamma*).

That which is to be eaten is *bhojja*; that which is to be chewed is *khajja*; that which is to be bitten is *vitujja*; that which is to be pushed away is *panujja*; that which is to be drunk is *pajja*; that by which one intoxicates is *majja*.
In the sense of joy and laughter, that by which one rejoices is *pāmojja*; that which is spoken of is *vajja*.

In the sense of killing and harming, that which is to be killed is *vajjha*; that which is to be pierced is *vijjha*; that by which beings purify themselves and become clean is *puñña* (the addition of the letter *n* is an augment).
*Vihaññate* becomes *vihaññaṃ*; *vapiyate* becomes *vappaṃ*; *supanaṃ* becomes *soppaṃ*; that which is to be obtained is *labbhaṃ*; that which is to be gone to is *gammaṃ*;
that which deserves to be tamed is *dammaṃ*; that which is to be delighted in is *rammaṃ*, as in *abhirammaṃ*; that which is observed is *nisammaṃ*; that which is measured out is *visammaṃ*;
that which is touched is *phasso*; *ussa* is the suffix *-attaṃ*.
*Sāsitabbo* means a pupil (*sisso*); it is called *sissa* because he is to be taught (*sāsassa sisā*).
[The suffix] *ka* is applied after roots such as *gaha*, *guha*, *garaha*, *duha*, *vaha*, and *saha*.
(Pāṇini 3.1.140; Rūpasiddhi 552; Nyāsa 1126).
O Venerable Sir, when the suffix *yaka* frequently occurs after these verbal roots, there is a substitution of *ha*.
That which is to be grasped is *gayha*; that which is to be hidden is *guyha*. The root *garah* means censure;
that which is to be censured is *gārayha*. The root *duh* means to carry; that which is to be carried is *duyha*. The root *vah* means to carry; that which is to be carried is *vayha*.
*Saha-sāhase*: *Sahitabbaṃ* means "to be endured," hence *sayhaṃ* and *pasayhaṃ*.
782. Regarding *kicca*, *ghacca*, *bhacca*, *gabba*, and *lyā*: the word *babbaleyyā* occurs in many [texts].

These words are formed with the suffix *ya*; having applied this suffix *ya*, they are established by forming *kicca* from *karassa*, *ghacca* from *hanassa*, *bhacca* from *bharassa*, *gabba* from *gussa*, and *lyatta* from *lissa*.

*Karīyati* means "that which is to be done" (*kicca*), or "the state of being to be done" (*kiccaya*). *Haññati* means "that which is to be slain" (*ghacca*), or "the state of being to be slain" (*hacca*).

*Bharīyati* means "that which is to be carried" (*bhacca*). In the case of *gudabbē*: it is concealed (*guyate*) as a *gabba*; one retreats into solitude (*paṭisallīyate*) as *paṭisalya*. This is the specific rule of formation (*visesavidhāna*).
*Bhara* means "to support"; *bhāriyaṃ* means "that which is to be supported"; *hāriyaṃ* means "that which is to be taken away";
*bhājiyaṃ* means "that which is to be distributed"; *bhājeyyaṃ* [is derived similarly]; *upāsiyaṃ* means "that which is to be attended upon"; *iccheyyaṃ* means "that which is to be desired";
*adhigameyyaṃ* means "that which is to be attained," and so forth. *Rundheyyaṃ* means "that which is to be obstructed"; *chindeyyaṃ* means "that which is to be cut"; *chejjaṃ* and so forth.

*Dibbitabbaṃ* means "it should be seen" (*dibbeyyaṃ*), "I should see" (*dibbaṃ*), "it should be understood" (*bujjhitabbaṃ*), "I should understand" (*bujjheyyaṃ*), "I should cause to understand" (*bodheyyaṃ*), "it should be awakened" (*bojjhaṃ*), and so forth.

*Sotabbaṃ* means "it should be heard" (*suṇeyyaṃ*); *pāpuṇitabbaṃ* means "it should be reached" (*pāpuṇeyyaṃ*); *sakkuṇitabbaṃ* means "it should be possible" (*sakkuṇeyyaṃ*); *na sakkuṇeyyaṃ* is *asakkuṇeyyaṃ*, and so forth.
*Tanitabbaṃ* means "it should be extended" (*tāneyyaṃ*) or "it should be stretched" (*taññaṃ*); *kātabbaṃ* means "it should be done" (*kāriyaṃ*) or "it should be made" (*kayyaṃ*).

*Coretabbaṃ* means "to be stolen" (*coreyyaṃ*); *thenīyate* means "theft" (*theyyaṃ*); *nassa* means "the state of another's form" (*pararūpattaṃ*). *Cintetabbaṃ* means "to be thought" (*cinteyyaṃ*); *na cinteyyaṃ* means "not to be thought," i.e., *acinteyyaṃ*, *acintiyaṃ*. *Manteyyaṃ*, *mantiyaṃ*, *vediyaṃ*, *vedeyyaṃ*, and so forth.
*Titikkheyyaṃ*, *vīmaṃseyyaṃ*, and so forth should also be applied accordingly. Thus ends the group of suffixes beginning with *ṇya*.
The Group of Primary Suffixes (*Ādipaccayarāsi*).
Now, those ending in *a*, *aṇa*, *ghaka*, and *ghana* suffixes are being stated. 783.

Regarding the rule "for the state and the agent, *aghaṇa* and *ghaka*" (*bhāvakārakesvaghaṇaghakā*), [the reading] "for the state and the agent, *aghaṇa* and *ghakā*" (*bhāvakārakesvaghaṇaghakā*) is found in many manuscripts.

In the case of abstract nouns (*bhāva*) and the six factors of action (*kāraka*), the suffixes *a*, *ghaṇ*, and *ghaka* occur after verbal roots (*kriyāttha*), whether the root has an object (*sakamma*) or is intransitive (*akamma*).
784. *Kvacaṇa*.
In some instances, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root that has an object as its subordinate word (*upapada*), provided it refers specifically to the agent (*kartṛ*).
A, aṇa, ghaka, ghaṇa.

I am [thus]: one who knows the beginning is an *aggañña* (one who knows the origin); one who knows the lineage is a *vaṃsañña* (one who knows the lineage); one who stands on the path is a *maggaṭṭha* person, a *maggaṭṭhā* woman, or *maggaṭṭha* knowledge. Likewise, there are those standing on the fruit (*phalaṭṭha*), on dry land (*thalaṭṭha*), in water (*jalaṭṭha*), on a mountain (*pabbataṭṭha*), or on the ground (*bhūmaṭṭha*).
"Go" is said to mean knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and sound (*sadda*). That which protects (*tāyati*) and guards (*rakkhati*) cattle (*gavaṃ*) is *gotta*.

That which protects and guards against fear on all sides (*parito*) is *paritta*. One who gives food (*anna*) is an *annada*. Likewise, a *vatthada* (clothing-giver), *vaṇṇada* (complexion-giver), *yānada* (vehicle-giver), *sukhada* (happiness-giver), *dīpada* (lamp-giver), and *cakkhuda* (eye-giver).
One who takes his share from an inheritance (*dāyaṃ*) is an *dāyāda* (heir). That which allows one to go to the further shore (*pāraṃ gantuṃ*) is *pārada-rasa* (the elixir of immortality).
One who gives food is an *annada*; the doubling of the consonant and the shortening of the preceding vowel [apply here].
One who gives first is *purindada*; according to the *Mahāvutti*, the word *pura* becomes *puri* and the nasal bindu (*m*) is added.
One who gives everything is a *sabbada*. One who upholds truth is a *saccasandha*; one who upholds people is a *janasandha*.

*Kaku* is said to mean a heap of virtues; because he protects (*sandheti*) that *kaku*, he is Kakusandha. A man who protects cows is a cowherd (*gopa*); the wife of a cowherd is a cowherdess (*gopī*). *Kassaṃ* is said to mean a field;
because he protects (*pāti*) the field, he is Kassapa. *Bhū* is said to mean the earth;
because he protects the earth, he is a lord of the earth (*bhūpa*). In the same way, one is a lord of the ground (*bhūmipa*).

It is called a *pādapa* because it drinks the essence of the earth and the essence of water by means of its root, which serves as its foot (*pāda*). It is called *subha* because it shines or appears beautiful (*subhati*).

It is called *amama* because it does not claim ownership (*mamāyati*). It is called *bāla* because it takes or grasps two kinds of harm (*anattha*). It is called *bahula* because it takes or grasps much.
It is called *rāhula* because it takes or grasps like Rāhu. [This applies to] the beginning [of the names].

"It blows suffering" or "it binds [suffering]"—this is *ādīnava* (disadvantage); "it blows toward another mass of water" or "it binds [toward another mass of water]"—this is *aṇṇava* (ocean), and so forth.

When a suffix (*paccaya*) that lacks the markers *ṇ* or *v* follows, the augment *yuk* is inserted at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in *ā*; this is the meaning of "with *yāgama*. That which is to be known or understood is a *ñāya*—a method (*yutti*);
that by which the deathless state (*amata-pada*) is known is a *ñāya*—the Noble Path (*ariya-magga*). That which stands depending [on something] is a *patiṭṭhāya*.
That which is to be given is a *dāya*—a gift of material things (*āmisa-dāya*) or a gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāya*). One who drinks milk is a *khīrapāya*.
One who measures grain is a *dhaññamāya*; one who blows or moves is *vāyo*, and so forth.
Among words containing the vowel *i* (*ivaṇṇa*), first those ending in *-aya*:
that which comes or proceeds is *āya*; that which comes together is *samaya*; that which goes away or perishes is *vaya* (as in *mandādi*); likewise, *vigamana* means "departure" or "perishing."
The breaking up of age is *vaya-bhaṅga*; rising up is *udaya*, and rising up together is *samudaya*; or else, it is *samudaya* because the fruit arises (*samudeti*) by means of it;
transcending and proceeding is *accaya*; that from which the fruit comes forth dependently is *paccaya*; buying is *kaya*; selling is *vikkaya*;
wasting away is *khaya*, or it is *khaya* because things waste away (*khīyanti*) therein; the wasting away of lust is *rāgakkhaya*.

Piling up (*caya*) is accumulation (*caya*), heaping up (*ācaya*), piling high (*uccaya*), gathering together (*samuccaya*), and building up (*upacaya*). It is "investigation of phenomena" (*dhammavicaya*) because by means of it one investigates phenomena (*dhamma*).
Conquering (*jaya*) is victory (*jaya*), triumph (*vijaya*), or defeat (*parājaya*). It is "method" (*naya*) because by means of it one is led out (*niyyati*);

or it is "discipline" (*vinaya*) because one is disciplined (*vineti*) therein or by means of it; it is a "good method" (*sunaya*) because it can be led or known with ease; and it is a "bad method" (*dunnaya*) because it can be led or known with difficulty.

*Pātabbo* means milk, water, and curd. *Niraya*: from the root *ri*, meaning "to shake"; it is called *niraya* because suffering beings constantly (*niccaṃ*) tremble (*rayanti*) and quiver (*phandanti*) therein. *Ālaya* is a place of clinging; *nilaya* is a place of hiding; *saya* is a place of lying down; *āsaya* is where they lie down intensely (*bhuso senti*); likewise *ajjhāsaya*. *Visaya* means "that wherein one feels"; *nissaya* means "that depending upon which one lies or proceeds therein"; *upanissaya*; and *anusaya* means "it lies latent therein," and so forth.
Regarding *aṇa*: *āya* is increase or growth; *apāya* is that which is devoid of *āya*; *upāya* is that which is endowed with *āya*; and *samudāya* is "that wherein things arise together."
*Samavāyo* is that which comes together (*samaveti*) here; *pariyāyo* is a synonym; *vipariyāyo* is a reversal; *nāyo* or *ñāyo* is that which is to be led;
or alternatively, *nāyo* is that by which one is led; *bhūmisāyo* is that which lies on the ground, and so forth.
Regarding the *uvaṇṇa* [vowels] ending in *-am*, first:
*Cavanaṃ* is falling away (*cavo*), *javanaṃ* is speed (*javo*), and *abhitthavanaṃ* is exultation (*abhitthavo*). That which violently (*bhusaṃ*) runs toward or harms is an affliction (*upaddavo*).
*Sandhavanaṃ* is meeting (*sandhavo*); meeting by way of friendship is "friend-meeting" (*mittasandhavo*). That which comes to be is a state (*bhāvo*).

*Vibhavanaṃ* is dissolution (*vibhavo*). *Sambhavanaṃ* is origination (*sambhavo*); or else, that from which something originates is an origin (*sambhavo*). *Adhibhavanaṃ* is overcoming (*adhibhavo*).
*Abhibhava* is overcoming; *paribhava* is humiliation; *parābhavanaṃ* is destruction; *parābhavo* is ruin. It "sounds," thus it is *ravo*, meaning sound.

*Lavanaṃ* is cutting, thus *lavo*. It "produces," thus *passāvo* (urine). It "flows out," thus *āsavo* (taint). Flowing toward [the object], thus *paṭissavo* (reply), and so forth. In the case of the suffix *-aṇ*:

*Bhāva* is the act of becoming (*bhavana*). It is called *bhāva* because sounds and cognitions arise (*bhavanti*) by means of it; for example, "one reaps rice" is *sālilāva*, and "it flows or trickles badly" is *kasāva*, and so forth. Regarding words ending in *-e* and *-anta* with the suffix *-aṇ*:

according to the Great Rule (*Mahāvutti*), the *e* becomes *āya*; thus, one who studies the *manta* is a *mantajjhāya*, and one who dwells upon what is blameworthy and blameless is an *upajjhāya* (Thera), while the female counterpart is an *upajjhāyinī* (Therī).
In *de-pālane* (to protect): it protects—that is, it nurtures—what is nestled within itself, thus *dāya*; *migadāya* (deer-park); *tantaṃ vāyati* (weaves the thread), thus *tantavāya* (weaver).

In *vhe-avhāne* (to call): it is called, thus *vhaya*, which is a name; [here] there is shortening [of the vowel], as in *āvahayo* and so forth. Regarding roots with multiple consonants ending in *am*:
