*Kamana* means desire. *Kama* refers to advancing, retreating, approaching, or withdrawing. That wherein one walks is a *caṅkama*. One who performs what is beneficial (*hita*) is a *hitakara*.
That which must be done with difficulty is a *dukkara*—this is the meaning; thus there is a "difficult practice" (*dukkarā-paṭipadā*) and a "difficult deed" (*dukkaraṃ-kamma*).

That which can be done with ease is a *sukara*. That which can be done with little effort is an *īsakkara*. One who makes an island (*dīpa*) is a *Dīpaṅkara*; this is a compound where elision (*alutta-samāsa*) has not occurred.
It comes, thus it is an *āgama*; or else, coming is *āgama*. Meeting together is *saṅgama*, a coming together (*samāgama*). Grasping up is *paggaha*; gathering together is *saṅgaha*;
or else, that in which things are gathered, or by means of which they are gathered, is *saṅgaha*.

Favoring is *anuggaha*; receiving is *paṭiggaha*. Cattle graze there, thus it is a *gocara* (pasture). It moves within sense pleasures, thus it is *kāmāvacara*. It covers the chest, thus it is *uracchada*.
It is called *jarā* because one ages by means of it; *Vessantara* because he crosses over the state of a commoner (*vessa*), this being an elided compound (*aluttasamāsa*).
He spreads out on a chariot, thus a *rathatthara*; likewise, an *assatthara*. He tames the enemy, thus *arindama*. He tears asunder or breaks fortune, thus *bhagandara*.
He bears the pair of the sun and moon, which are like a yoke, thus *yugandhara*. He upholds the Dhamma, thus...
One who upholds the Dhamma is a *dhammadhara*. "Pajjate" is a word; training itself is the word, thus it is a *sikkhāpada* (training rule).
That which can be maintained with ease is *subhara*; that which can be maintained with difficulty is *dubbhara*. One who does not die is an *amaradeva* (immortal god).
Restraining is *niyama*; fully restraining is *saṃyama*. That which grows on the head is *siroruha* (hair). That which is obtained with ease is *sulabha*; [that which is obtained] with difficulty...

*Labbhati* means "is difficult to obtain," hence *dullabha*; *saṃvaritabbo* means "should be restrained," hence *saṃvara*; *vuccati* means "is spoken," hence *subbacca* ("easily spoken to") and *dubbacca* ("difficult to speak to");

*vāriṃ vahati* means "carries water," hence *vārivaha*; *sarati gacchati* means "moves or flows," hence *sara*; *manaṃ harati* means "captivates the mind," hence *manohara*, and so forth. In the case of the suffix *-aṇ*: [examples follow].

*Kamu-icchā*, desire; *kantīsu*, in desires; it is called *kāma* because one desires (*kāmeti*), or it is called *kāma* because it is desired (*kāmīyati*). One who desires welfare is "one who desires welfare" (*atthakāma*).

The suffix *-kāra* denotes an instrument, as in: *pakāra*, *ākāra*, *vikāra*, *upakāra*, *apakāra*. One who makes a pot is a "potter" (*kumbhakāra*); likewise, a "chariot-maker" (*rathakāra*), a "garland-maker" (*mālakāra*).
*Saṅkhāra* means the act of constructing (*saṅkharana*); or it is called *saṅkhāra* because it is constructed (*saṅkharīyati*), or because one constructs (*saṅkharoti*).
Or: volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*), requisite (*parikkhāra*), precedence (*purakkhāra*); that wherein sensual desires go forth and proceed is a village (*gāma*);

it grasps, thus it is a grasp (*gāha*); he grasps the bowl, thus it is the bowl-grasp (*pattagāha*); he grasps the reins, thus it is the rein-grasp (*rasmigāha*); wandering about is investigation (*vicāra*);
one moves having approached, thus it is the vicinity (*upacāra*); moving having approached the village is the village-vicinity (*gāmūpacāra*); it ages, shame is broken by this—thus [it is *hiri*].

*Jāra*: a lover; *kantāra*: a wilderness, because it must be crossed with difficulty (*kicchena taritabbo*); [the suffix] *ka* is added to *kiccha* by way of a great grammatical rule (*mahāvuttinā*), and there is the addition of the vowel *i* (*bindāgamo*).
*Vāḷakantāra* (wild-beast wilderness) and *yakkhakantāra* (yakṣa wilderness). *Atthāra*: spreading out; *kathinatthāra*: the spreading out of the *kathina* cloth. *Dāra*:

one by whom people split (*darati*), break (*bhindati*), or go through (*kulavibhāgaṃ gacchati*) their family divisions; *kudāra*: that which splits the earth (*kuṃ pathaviṃ dāreti*); the *r* becomes *l*, thus *kudāla* (a pickaxe).
It is called an *ādhāra* because it holds (*dhāreti*) what has been done (*kriyaṃ*); a bowl-rest is a *pattādhāra*. It is a *paṭisandhāra* because it provides support (*paṭisandhāraṇaṃ*).
It is a *pāda* because one goes by means of it (*pajjati etena*). It is an *uppāda* because of arising (*uppajjanaṃ*); it is *paṭiccasamuppāda* because of dependent arising (*paṭicca samuppajjanaṃ*).

It is a *bhāra* because it must be borne or carried (*bharitabbo vahitabbo*). It is a *sambhāra* because it is accumulated and gathered together (*sambharīyati sannicīyati*), such as the equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) or the equipment of materials (*dabbasambhāra*).

He kills, thus he is Māra; [namely] the Māra of defilements (kilesamāra), the Māra of the aggregates (khandhamāra), and the Māra of death (maccumāra). He determines, thus it is a determination (niyāma);

[namely] the determination of phenomena (dhammaniyāma) and the determination of kamma (kammaniyāma). He ascends, thus it is an ascent (āroha); [as in] ascending a tree (rukkhāroha), ascending an elephant (hatthāroha), ascending a horse (assāroha), or ascending a chariot (rathāroha).
It is obtained, thus it is gain (lābha); [namely] acquisition (paṭilābha). It obstructs, thus it is an obstruction (nivāra); it surrounds, thus it is a retinue (parivāra).
That which carries is *vāha*; *āvāha* (bringing near) and *vivāha* (marrying). That which moves along a path or proceeds is *sāra*.
*Vippaṭisāra* is resorting to what is disagreeable or repeated reflection. *Pahāra* is striking. *Āhāra*, *nīhāra*, *vihāra*, *abhihāra*, and *parihāra*. 786.
For the root *han*, [the suffix] *ghāta* occurs when followed by a consonant (*ṇānubandhe*); Kaccāyana 591; Rūpasiddhi 544; Niddesa 1195.
When a suffix marked with the *ṇ* anubandha follows, *han* becomes *ghā*.
Killing is *ghāta*; afflicting is *vighāta*; harming is *upaghāta*; striking back is *paṭighāta*. There is no vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*) in the case of the suffix *gha*;
by the rule "the nasal of *man* becomes *niggahīta*," even the *n* of the verbal root's anubandha becomes *niggahīta*.
And by the rule “*vagganta ca kagā ca jānaṃ ghānubandhe*,” when a suffix having *gh* as its marker follows, the letters *ka* and *ga* become *gha* and *ha* respectively at the end of verbal roots;
thus, from the root *nipajjati*, one is called *nipako*. The root *bhañja* means breaking or dividing.

*Bhañjanaṃ* is "breaking," and *vibhajjanaṃ* is "dividing. It is called *vibhaṅgo* because phenomena (*dhammā*) are analyzed therein, or by means of it; for example, the *Khandhavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Aggregates) and the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Elements).

*Raṅga*: from the root *rañj* (to color/delight), *rañjanaṃ* is *raṅgo*; it is called *raṅgo* because beings delight (*rañjanti*) therein. *Saṅga*: from the root *sanj* (to cling), *sañjanaṃ* is *saṅgo*;
*pasaṅgo* is clinging or attachment (*lagganaṃ*, i.e., *saṅganaṃ*). *Āsaṅgo* means that which one clings to (*āsajjati*). *Uttarāsaṅgo* is the upper robe (*uttari-āsaṅgo*). *Sagga*:
from the root *saj* (to hang/attach), *atisajjanaṃ* is the act of hanging up or fixing (*atisaggo*). The doubling of the *g* [in *sagga*] is due to the doubling of the consonant after the vowel.
*Nissajjana* is relinquishing (*nissagga*), renunciation (*paṭinissagga*); *vissajjana* is giving away (*vissagga*);
*saṃsajjana* is mixing together (*saṃsagga*). That which is joined here is a *yuga*: the Kali-yuga, a cart-yoke, a grandfather’s generation.
*Nitudana* is a thrusting (*nituda*); *panudana* is a driving away (*panuda*). That which breaks upward is an *ubbhida*; that which knows skillfully is a *kovida*. In this manner...

"He gets angry" (*kujjhati*) thus he is "wrathful" (*pakudha*); "he awakens" (*bujjhati*) thus he is "awakened" (*budha*), i.e., wise; "he is deluded" (*muyhati*) thus he is "confused" (*momūha*); "he is greedy" (*loluppati*) thus he is "greedy" (*loluppa*);

"that which has been cooked" (*otta*) and "that which is being cooked" (*āditta*), and so forth. In the sense of the *ghañ*-suffix: "cooking" (*pacana*) is "cookedness" (*pāka*); or, "it is cooked" (*paccati*) thus it is "cookedness" (*pāka*); "ripening" (*vipācana*) is "ripening" (*vipāka*); "separating" (*viviccana*) is "separation" (*viveka*); "sprinkling" (*siñcana*)...

Seko (sprinkling), abhiseko (consecration); socanaṃ (lamenting) is soko (sorrow); cajanaṃ (giving up) is cāgo (renunciation); bhajanaṃ (sharing) is bhāgo (portion); bhuñjanaṃ (eating) is bhogo (enjoyment);
saha bhogo is sambhogo (communal enjoyment); paribhogo (consumption); ābhujanaṃ is ābhogo (mental application); obhujanaṃ is obhogo (bending). In the sense of sacrifice and worship:
yajanaṃ is yāgo (offering); āmisayāgo (material offering); dhammayāgo (Dharma offering); yujjanaṃ is yogo (yoking/application); payogo (employment); āyogo (exertion).
*Viyoga* means separation; *anuyoga* means application; *upayujjitabbo* means that which is to be employed, hence *upayoga*; *lujjati* means it breaks down, hence *loka*;
by the great grammatical rule (*mahāvutti*), the *g* is substituted for the *k*, thus *kāmaloka*, *rūpaloka*; *saṃvijjanaṃ* means agitation, hence *saṃvega*, and so forth. 787.
[The suffix] *ḷoka* occurs after [roots ending in] *a*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *s*, and *pa*. (Kaccāyana 614; Rūpasiddhi 581; Nyāsa 1219).
Ā: In the case of the causal suffixes (ghana-paccaya), when *pari* precedes *dah*, *ḷo* becomes *ana*.
*Paridahanam* is *pariḷāho*; by the alternative rule (*vikappa*) stating that *da* becomes *ḍa* after *pari*, there is the substitution of *ḍa*. *Dayhanam* is *ḍāho* or *dāho*.
Thus ends the section on the group of suffixes beginning with *a*.
The Group of Suffixes Ending in -a.
Now those ending in the suffix -a will be stated.

The suffix *an* occurs after verbal roots in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and in the sense of the six grammatical factors (*kāraka*). There is elision of the preceding and following vowels (*parassaralopa*) when [the suffix] is present;
when there is no elision, there is the augment *y*. It is called *akkhānaṃ* because it is proclaimed (*akkhāyate*), or alternatively, it is *akkhānaṃ* because one proclaims by means of it.

"The proclamation of the Dhamma" is *dhammakkhānaṃ*. It is *paṭisaṅkhānaṃ* because one reflects upon or understands by means of it. *Saṅgāyanaṃ* is singing together (*saha gāyanaṃ*); they sing together (*saha gāyanti*).

Alternatively, it is called *saṅgāyana* because they recite there (*sajjhāyanti ettha*). It is *ñāṇa* because knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is known (*ñāyate*), or because one knows (*jānāti*), or because one knows by means of it (*jānantī etena*).
It is *paññāṇa* because it is made manifest (*paññāyati*). It is *viññāṇa* because one discerns (*vijānāti*). [In the case of] *saññāṇa*, the suffix *-ṇa* replaces *-na*.
In the causative (*kārita*), there are *ñāpana*, *paññāpana*, *viññāpana*, and *saññāpana*.
Knowing, full understanding, discerning, perceiving—here there is the elision of the preceding vowel. That which is stood upon is a *ṭhāna*; or, that wherein one stands is a *ṭhāna*.
In the causative sense, it means establishing or re-establishing.
That which protects and guards is a *tāṇa*, a refuge; here the change of *na* to *ṇa* has occurred.

It is called *avatthāna* because one stands (*avatiṭṭhati*) therein; it is called *dāna* because giving (*diyyati*) is bestowed (*diyati*) by means of it; it is called *sampadāna* because something is properly given (*sammā padīyati*) to it; it is called *apādāna* because one takes away (*ādadāti*) depending upon (*apecca*) it. In the causative form, they are *dāpana* and *samādapana*.
It is called *padhāna* because one exerts oneself (*padahīyate*) or because one exerts oneself by means of it; likewise, there are *ādhāna*, *vidhāna*, *nidhāna*, and *sannidhāna*.
The substitution of *sannidhāpana* occurs when [the suffix] *ita* is applied. Regarding the words *pāna*, *paṭibhāna*, *māṇa*, *pamāṇa*, *upamāṇa*, and *parimāṇa*:

the change of *na* to *ṇa* occurs. That by which one goes is *yāna*; *uyyāna* (pleasure garden), *niyyāna* (departure). That by which they blow, that is, go from existence to existence, is *vāna*. There is no blowing (*vāna*) here, thus it is *nibbāna*; or, they extinguish (*nibbāyanti*) here, thus it is *nibbāna*.
Causing to be made; extinguishing.
The end, the conclusion, the termination, the abandoning, the falling away.
Causing to be made; causing to fall away, causing to perish.
In the case of roots beginning with *ivaṇṇa* (the vowel *i*), there are: *ayanaṃ*, *vikkayanaṃ*, *vikkiṇanaṃ*, *khayanaṃ*, *khiyanaṃ*, *khiyyanaṃ*;
the substitution of *iya* and *iyya*; *cayanaṃ*, *cinanaṃ*, *ācinanaṃ*, *vicinanaṃ*; *jayanaṃ*, *vijayanaṃ*; and *leṇaṃ*—meaning "they lie down here"—where *ṇa* is substituted for *na*.
*Paṭisallānaṃ* means "they retire here," where *issa* is replaced by *ātta*. *Senaṃ* means "they lie here," and [it is also] *sayanaṃ*.
In the *kārita* (causative) forms:

*sayāpanaṃ* (having someone lie down), and so forth. In those with *uvaṇṇa* suffixes: *cavanaṃ* (falling away), *javanaṃ* (speeding), *abhitthavanaṃ* (praising), *dhunanaṃ* (shaking), *viddhunanaṃ* (shaking off), *niddhunanaṃ* (shaking out), *bhavanaṃ* (becoming), *abhibhavanaṃ* (overpowering), *lavanaṃ* (mowing), *lunanaṃ* (cutting), *savanaṃ* (flowing), *pasavanaṃ* (procreating), and so forth. In those ending in *-eda*: *ajjhenaṃ* (studying), *ajjhāyanaṃ* (reciting), *apacāyanaṃ* (honoring);
*jhānaṃ* is that which is meditated upon (*jhāyate*), or it is called *jhānaṃ* because one meditates by means of it (*jhāyati etena*).
First jhāna, second jhāna, *ujjhāna*, *nijjhāna*, *abhijjhāna*, *sālilāyana*, *cīvaravāyana*, and “he is ill” (*gilāyati*) thus he is “ill” (*gilāna*), and so forth.

By the rule “*rā nassa ṇo*,” after the letter *r*, the following *n* becomes *ṇ*; thus: *kāraṇaṃ*. That wherein something is performed (*adhikarīyati*) is *adhikaraṇaṃ*; [also] *saṅkharaṇaṃ* and *abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ*.
*Kārite* means causing to do.

*Ākiraṇaṃ*, *vikkiraṇaṃ*, *caraṇaṃ*, *jiraṇaṃ*, *taraṇaṃ*, *kaṅkhāvitaraṇaṃ*, *attharaṇaṃ*. A *susānaṃ* (cremation ground) is so called because dead bodies are brought (*āgantvā*) and burned (*dahanti*) there;

for the letter *da*, there is *ḷo*. That which is seen is *passanaṃ*, *dassanaṃ*. One who sees well is King Sudassana; that which is to be seen well is Sudassana, the city of the gods. *Sandassanaṃ*, *nidassanaṃ*, *dhāraṇaṃ*, *uddhāraṇaṃ*, *niddhāraṇaṃ*; [in these cases] the initial vowel is long.
Filling, completely filling, pervading, spreading forth; in the causative sense:
causing to kill.
Obstructing, going for refuge, escaping, taking away, bringing, carrying out, and so forth.

Because of the rule for common [suffixes], the suffix *-ana* occurs after the roots *ruca-* (to shine), *juta-* (to shine), and *vaḍḍha-* (to increase), etc., in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tassīla*) and so forth.
Thus: one who shouts by habit is *ghosano*; one who shouts according to the Dhamma is *ghosano*;
one who shouts with approval is *ghosano*. Likewise: *kodhano*, *dūsano*, *padūsano*, *kopano*, *calano*, *phandano*, *kampano*.

Maṇḍana (adorning), bhūsana (adorned), vibhūsana (beautifying), rocana (shining), virocana (radiating light), verocana (splendidly shining), jotana (illuminating), ujjotana (brightening), vaḍḍhana (increasing).
One who acts by means of virtue is a *karaṇa*. "Lust is a maker of signs, hatred is a maker of signs, delusion is a maker of signs" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.349), and so forth.
789. *Kara-ṇana*.
After the root *kara*, the suffix *ṇa* with the augment *an* becomes *ana* when expressing the agent.
That which brings about its own fruit is called a *kāraṇa* (cause).
790. *Hā* in the sense of "at the time of rice.
When the sense is "at the time of rice," the suffix *ṇa*, which has no *anubandha*, is substituted for the root *hā* in the agentive case.
Thus, from *hāpeti*, we have *hāyana*, meaning both a specific variety of rice and a year. In the phrase "an elephant sixty *hāyana*s old," it is the year that is called *hāyana*.
Thus ends the section on suffixes that do not require a prefix.
Now, the section on suffixes that do not require a prefix (akapaccaya) is being stated.
791. *Āsīsāyama* means "one who possesses a wish" (*āsīsāmaka*;
this form occurs in many texts). A wish (*āsīsā*) is called an aspiration (*patthanā*). When a wish is being expressed, the suffix *-aka* is applied to the agent.
For example: "May he live" is *jīvako*; "may he rejoice" is *nandako*. [Examples include: Jinabuddhi, Dhanabhūti, Bhūta, and Dhammadinna.
The words "vaḍḍhamāno" and so forth are formed differently: "jinabuddhi" means "one by whom the Victor is awakened";

"dhanabhūti" means "his wealth becomes or increases"; "bhūto" means "it becomes or increases"; "dhammadinno" means "given by Dhamma," just as in the cases of Devadatta and Brahmadatta; and "vaḍḍhamāno" means "he is increasing."

In the word *kattari ltuṇakā*, the suffix *ṇaka* occurs; and because it is prescribed as a general rule, it is applicable in the sense of one who is worthy (*arahā*), capable (*satti*), virtuous (*sīla*), righteous (*dhamma*), or one who performs well (*sādhukāra*).
In the word *akkhāyako*, there is the augment *y* according to the rule "āssāṇāpimhi yuka"; thus, he is one who is worthy to declare, or is able to declare.
His nature (*sīla*) or his duty (*dhamma*) is to declare; the meaning is that he performs the act of declaring with diligence. This applies to all three times.
"It succeeds" means that he has declared it in the past, he declares it today, and he will declare it in the future.
In this way, it should be understood as appropriate for the remaining general grammatical rules.

Regarding the feminine gender: by the rule "adhātussa ke... (Pāṇini 7.3.50), the substitution of *it* for *ak* occurs; thus, *akkhāyikā* (one who tells) is a woman, *akkhāyakaṃ* (that which tells) is a family, and *saṅgāyako* (one who recites together). One who knows is a "knower" (*jānako*).
When the augment *nā* follows a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), the suffix is shortened: *jānanako*, *ājānanako*, *vijānanako*, *sañjānanako*. In the causative (*kārita*):
he causes to know is *ñāpako*, *viññāpako*, *saññāpako*.
When the augment *nā* is present: *ñāpanako*, *viññāpanako*, *saññāpanako*. He resolves is *adhiṭṭhāyako*; he causes to resolve is *adhiṭṭhāpako*. He gives is *dāyako*; he causes to give is *dāpako*.

In *ṇāpi*, there is no augment (*āgama*); thus, one who causes to undertake is a "prompter" (*samādapaka*), with shortening in both instances. One who arranges is an "arranger" (*vidhāyaka*); one who abandons is an "abandoner" (*pajahāyaka*); one who is left behind is a "left-behind" (*ohiyaka*)—such as in *āssa ittaṃ*.
Among those with *ivaṇṇa*: one who studies is a "reciter" (*ajjhāyaka*); one who studies a mantra is a "mantra-reciter" (*mantajjhāyaka*);

one who buys is a "buyer" (*kāyaka*); one who causes to buy is a "causer-to-buy" (*kāyāpaka*); one who gathers is a "gatherer" (*ācinaka*); a "discriminator" (*vicinaka*); one who is defeated is a "defeated-one" (*pārājika*), with elision (*alopa*); a "person" (*puggala*); one who defeats is a "defeater" (*parājetīti*).

*Pārājika*: one who has committed a defeat; *alopa* and *kāritalopa*: one who causes to cut off. *Dhamma*: the teaching. *Bhāyāpeti* means "he causes to fear," hence *bhayānaka*: terrifying. [The suffix -aka] is added after the root *bhī*, and the initial vowel is shortened.
*Bhūmisāyaka*: one who lies on the ground; *sayāpaka*: one who causes to lie down; *pahiṇaka*: one who sends—thus it begins. Regarding the *uvaṇṇa* (u, ū) vowels:

*punāti* means "he purifies," hence *pāvaka*: fire; *bhavati* means "he becomes," hence *bhāvaka*: a meditator; *vibhāveti* means "he makes manifest," hence *vibhāvaka*: a revealer; *lunāti* means "he cuts," hence *lāvaka*: a reaper; *suṇāti* means "he hears," hence *sāvaka*: a male disciple (*purisa*), *sāvikā*: a female disciple (*itthī*); *juhoti* means "he offers," hence *hāvaka*: an offerer—thus it begins.

One who attains evil is an evildoer (*pāpaka*); one who causes [another] to attain it is an instigator (*sampāpaka*). One who sits near is a lay follower (*upāsaka*)—a man; a female lay follower (*upāsikā*)—a woman; a family of lay followers (*upāsaka-kula*).
One who does is a doer (*kāraka*), a female doer (*kārikā*), a male doer (*kārakaṃ*); one who helps is a benefactor (*upakāraka*). One who causes to do is a causer (*kārāpaka*).

One who constructs is a constructor (*saṅkhāraka*), a thorough constructor (*abhisaṅkhāraka*). One who throws is a thrower (*khipaka*), a remover (*ukkhipaka*), a depositor (*nikkhipaka*), a scatterer (*khepaka*), or a lifter-up (*ukkhepaka*).
One who places down is a *nikkhepaka*; one who does not cause [something] to come quickly is a *nāgamekhipanaka*.

One who takes is a *gāhaka*; one who causes to take is a *gāhāpaka*. Likewise, a *gopaka* (protector). One who moves at the foot is a *pādacāraka*; one who plucks flowers is a *ocināyaka*—the verbal root ends in *-e*. One who cuts is a *chedaka* or *chindaka*;

one who causes to cut is a *chedāpaka* or *chindāpaka*. One who produces is a *janaka*: a man is a *purisa-janaka*, a mother is a *mātā-janikā*, and karma is a *kamma-janaka*; here there is the elision of the causative suffix (*kārita-lopa*).
In the sense of burning (*jhāpa*), one who burns is a burner (*jhāpaka*).
In the sense of making known (*ñapa-paññāpana*), one who makes known is a maker known (*paññāpaka*).
In the sense of placing (*ṭhāpa-ṭhāna*), one who establishes is an establisher (*patiṭṭhāpaka*).

*Ṇāpa* [is used] in the sense of commanding: one who commands is a *āṇāpaka*; one who strikes is a *tudaka*; one who is satisfied is a *santussaka*; one who sees with distinction is a *vipassaka*; one who shows is a *sandassaka*; one who defiles is a *dūsaka*, with the initial vowel lengthened. One who cooks is a *pācaka*; one who causes to cook is a *pācāpaka*;

one who brings about is an *āpādaka*, as well as a *nipphādaka*, a *sampādaka*, a *paṭipajjaka*, and a *paṭipādaka*. One who fills is a *pūraka*; there is no lengthening of the vowel due to the heaviness of the final syllable (*garupanta*).
One who touches is a *phusaka*; there is no lengthening because it belongs to the *tudādi* group.

One who distributes is a distributor (*bhājaka*); one who splits is a splitter (*bhindaka*), a divider (*bhedaka*), or a maker of divisions (*kārabhedaka*); one who eats is an eater (*bhuñjaka*), a feeder (*bhojaka*), or a village-feeder (*gāmabhojaka*);

one who awakens is an awakener (*bujjhaka*) or an enlightener (*bodhaka*); one who dies is a dead man (*miyyaka*); one who kills is a killer (*māraka*); one who releases is a releaser (*muñcaka*) or a liberator (*mocaka*);
one who begs is a beggar (*yācaka*); one who sacrifices is a sacrificer (*yājaka*); one who yokes is a yokker (*yuñjaka*), an attendant (*anuyuñjaka*).

One who joins is a *yojaka*; one who causes to join is a *payojaka*; "he joins" (*yujjhati*) thus he is a *yujjhaka*; one who fights is a *yodhaka*; "he obstructs" (*rundhati*) thus he is a *rundhaka*;

one who blocks is an *avarodhaka*; "he speaks" (*vacati*) thus he is a *vācaka*; one who advises is an *ovādaka*; one who exhorts is an *ovajjaka*; "he plays the lute" (*vīṇaṃ vādeti*) thus he is a *vīṇāvādaka*; one who plays the drum is a *bherivādaka*;
"he pays homage to the teacher" (*garuṃ abhivādeti*) thus he is an *abhivādaka*; "he knows" (*vidati*) thus he is a *vedaka*; "he finds" (*vindati*) in the sense of obtaining is a *vindaka*.
One who investigates and examines is an *anuvijjaka*; one who experiences is a *paṭisaṃvedaka*; one who pierces is a *vedhaka*;
one who pierces bone is an *aṭṭhivedhaka*; one who pierces a leaf is a *pattavedhaka*.

Due to the force of frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*), it is also seen in the sense of "action": that which is worn between [the layers] is an *antaravāsaka* (undergarment); that which is pleased is...
One who is confident, or one who inspires confidence; one who clarifies a lamp, or one who clarifies water; one who sews is a *sibbaka*; one who serves is a *sevaka*;
one who kills is a *ghātaka*; one who kills cows is a *goghātaka*; the killing of killing (*hanassa ghāto*).
One who carries away is a *hāraka*. Regarding the object (*kamma*): it is stated in the *Vutti*—“one who is struck with the feet is a *pādapahāraka*. One who endures is a *titikkhaka*.
One who treats is a *tikicchaka*; one who investigates is a *vīmaṃsaka*; one who desires to eat is a *bubhukkhaka*; one who stretches out like a mountain is a *pabbatāyaka*, and so forth.
Thus ends the group of suffixes ending in *aka*. Now follows the group of suffixes ending in *ivaṇṇa* and *uvarṇa*.
Now, the forms containing the vowel *i* are stated.
792. *Dādhātvi ka*. (Rule 551; Form 598; Nīti 1138):
After the roots *dā* and *dhā*, the suffix *ip* occurs when expressing the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the agent (*kāraka*).

"First, it is taken up by the mind," and so forth. It is called *upādi* because it is grasped (*upādīyati*) by craving and views; thus there is the "grasping at aggregates" (*khandhupādi*) and the "grasping at defilements" (*kilesupādi*).

*Vidhi*: it is a disposition (*vidhāna*); it is a method (*vidhi*), for by means of this one is disposed (*vidhiyyati*). *Nidhi*: it is stored away (*nidhiyyati*). *Sandhi*: it is joined together (*sandhiyate*).

Thus there is "junction" (*sandhi*), "re-union" (*abhisandhi*), and "re-linking" (*paṭisandhi*). *Sannidhi*: it is the act of storing (*sannidahana*). *Samādhi*: it is composure (*samādhāna*); it is so called because by means of this they are composed (*samādahanti*).
*Samādhi* means concentration. *Paṇidhi* is derived from *paṇidahana*, meaning aspiration. *Odhi* means limit; *avadhi* and *upanidhi* are similar. *Paṭinidhi* means a counterpart.
*Udadhi* is so called because water (*udaka*) stays (*tiṭṭhati*) within it. A great ocean is a *mahodadhi*. *Vāladhi* is so called because hairs (*vāla*) stay (*tiṭṭhanti*) at its end.
793. *Iki-ti* [is used] in the sense of identity. (Ka. 669; Rū. 679; Nī. 1315).

When verbal roots (*dhātu*) are to be expressed in their own forms as denoted by the term "hearing" (*suti*), the suffixes *i*, *ki*, and *ti* follow those that have the sense of action (*kriyāttha*).
[Examples] with *avaṇṇu* (the vowel *a*) preceding: *i*, *gami*, *paci*, etc.;
with *uvaṇṇu* (the vowels *u* or *o*) preceding: *ki*, *budhi*, *rudhi*, etc.
"Kehici," "karoti-ssa," "atthi-ssa," and so forth. 794.
Regarding *sīla*, *abhikkhañña*, and *avassaka*, the suffix *ṇī* is applied (Ka. 532, 636; Rū. 590, 659; Nī. 1114, 1245).

*Sīla* is said to be natural conduct (*pakaticariyā*). *Abhikkhañña* means that which is constant (*abhikkhaṇam eva*), referring to repeated action. *Avassaka* refers to that which will necessarily occur in the future (*āyatiṃ avassaṃbhāvī*).
Regarding the term *avassaka*: by the inclusion of "virtue" (*sīla*), the "Dhamma" (*dhamma*) is also comprised; thus, even the word "well done" (*sādhukāra*) is included.

When these specific actions, such as virtue and so forth, are understood [in context], the suffix *-ṇī* is applied to the agent. In the case of the roots beginning with *ādanta*, there is the augment *y* according to the rule "after *āsa* and *āp*, *y* is added.

It is called *akkhāyī* because it explains (*akkhāyati*); that is, one whose nature is to explain, whose quality is to explain, or one who is intent upon performing the act of explaining with thoroughness—this is the meaning. It is formed in all three tenses because the general rule applies.
But that which is inevitable (*avassaka*) has not yet come: a man who proclaims the Dhamma, a woman who proclaims the Dhamma, a family that proclaims the Dhamma;
one who sings songs frequently is a "song-singer" (*gītagāyī*); one who will certainly remain for an eon is an "eon-endurer" (*kappaṭṭhāyī*);
one who will remain through an incalculable period while the world is dissolving is a "dissolution-endurer" (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*). Likewise for the "evolution-endurer" (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).

One who takes what is not given by habit is an *adinnādāyī*. Likewise, one who takes only what is given is a *dinnādāyī*; one who gives food by habit is an *annadāyī* (according to the rule *dā-suppanne*).
One whose habit is sleeping is a *niddāyī*; one whose habit is drinking intoxicants is a *majjapāyī*, meaning one who drinks intoxicants frequently is a *majjapāyī*;
one whose habit is traveling quickly is a *sīghayāyī*; and one who will certainly attain final nibbāna through effort and application is [an *ussakki-parinibbāyī*].
One who attains final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*). Likewise, one who attains final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*);

one who will necessarily attain final nibbāna in the middle of the lifespan—that is, within the duration of the life-span—is called "one who attains final nibbāna in the interval" (*antarā-parinibbāyī*); one who will necessarily attain final nibbāna having reached the end of the lifespan—that is, at its conclusion—is called "one who attains final nibbāna after reaching [the end]" (*upahacca-parinibbāyī*), and so forth.
One who constantly recites a mantra is a *mantajjhāyī*; one who constantly sells grain is a *dhaññavikkāyī*;
one whose nature is to fear is a *bhāyī*; one whose nature is to sleep on the ground, or who constantly sleeps on the ground, is a *bhūmisāyī*;
and one whose nature is to recline on thorns is a *kaṇṭakāpassayī*, and so forth.
The following terms should also be explained here: one whose nature is to grow upward is *udāyī*; one whose nature is to show reverence toward elders is *vuddhāpacāyī*.
Likewise, one who shows reverence toward seniors is *jeṭṭhāpacāyī*. One whose nature is to meditate, whose dharma is meditation, or who is engaged in the careful practice of meditation, is a *jhāyī*;
or, one who meditates at all times is a *jhāyī*. [Likewise: a *pajjhāyī*, an *ujjhāyī*, a *nijjhāyī*, an *abhijjhāyī*, and one whose nature is to fear (*bhāyanasīlo*).
One who mows grass frequently is a *tiṇalāyī*; one who weaves thread at all times is a *tantavāyī*; one whose nature is to flee is a *palāyī*;
one who does not flee is an *apalāyī*, and so forth. Regarding words with the suffix *-u*:

a person whose nature is to discern the meaning as it truly is is a *vibhāvī* man; a woman whose nature is to discern is a *vibhāvinī* woman; that which will certainly come to be in the future is a *bhāvī*; one whose nature is to reap rice is a *sālilāvī*, and so forth.

One whose nature is to bear ill will is *byāpī*; one who desires or wishes by nature is *kāmī*, such as one who desires the Dhamma (*dhammakāmī*) or one who desires welfare (*atthakāmī*); one whose nature is to do is *kārī*, such as a doer of evil (*pāpakārī*) or a doer of merit (*puññakārī*). One who will certainly come is *āgāmī*.
When shortened, it becomes *āgaminī*, as in *āgaminī-ratti* (the coming night) or *āgaminī-puṇṇamāsī* (the coming full moon).
One who goes toward accumulation and the cycle of existence by nature is *ācayagāmī*; one who goes toward diminution and the turning away from the cycle by nature is *apacayagāmī*. Once...
One who will certainly come [only once more] is a *sakadāgāmī* (once-returner). One who will not come [again] in such a way is an *anāgāmī* (non-returner). "Adhāna" means firm persistence;

one whose nature is to grasp by making such a firm persistence is an *ādhānagāhī*, meaning one who grasps firmly. One who practices the Dhamma through virtue is a *dhammacārī*. One who practices the sublime (*brahma*)—that is, the best—through virtue is a *brahmacārī*.
Furthermore, in this context, "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of family custom; having grasped firmly, "I practice that Dhamma," until...
One who abandons [unwholesome states] and practices the Dhamma by way of non-transgression is called a "Dhamma-practitioner" (*dhammacārī*).

Practicing in that manner, when there is an occasion for a matter that might lead to transgression, one who maintains that Dhamma without falling away from it is called a "Dhamma-practitioner" by way of restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*).
And while maintaining that Dhamma in such a way, [one refrains from] self-exaltation...

One who practices the Dhamma by means of acting skillfully—purifying it in the sense of cleansing it from evil qualities such as disparaging others, while making it thoroughly bright through peaceful qualities such as fewness of desires—is called a "Dhammacārī" (one who walks in the Dhamma).
Furthermore, "Brahma" refers to the training precepts which are even more excellent than that; one who, having taken them up, does not abandon them in the interim...
One who, having taken it up, maintains it without letting it fall away, and keeps it unstained and perfectly purified, is called a "brahmacārī" (one living the holy life) in three senses;
it is appropriate to analyze this by way of undertaking, attainment, and abandonment through eradication.
However, one who takes it up but does not maintain it thus, or who maintains it but stains it, is [a brahmacārī] only in a partial sense.
One is called a "brahmacārī" by virtue of the meaning.
However, for one who is devoid of that meaning in its threefold sense and only occasionally practices that Dhamma, his act of practicing is not an act of virtue;
he is not called a "dhammacārī. By this same method, [the same applies] to the remaining [terms], whether they refer to evil or to what is beautiful.
The analysis of the meaning of these terms regarding moral conduct (*sīla*) should be understood as follows:

A woman who lives in celibacy is a *brahmacāriṇī*. One whose nature is especially characterized by seeing is *Vipassī*; likewise, one who sees the goal (*attha*) is *Atthadassī*, one who sees the Dhamma is *Dhammadassī*, one who sees what is dear is *Piyadassī*, and one who sees clearly is *Sudassī*.

One whose nature is to see badly is *Dussanasīlo* or *Dussīmāro*. One whose nature is to hold or maintain is *Dhārī*; specifically, one who holds a debt is *Iṇadhārī*, one who holds a parasol is *Chattadhārī*, and one who holds chaff is *Bhusadhārī*.
One who has the habit of harboring resentment is *upanāhī*. Because it is a portion of the conditions that have been finalized, it will necessarily arise in the future;
thus, it is *uppādī* (arising). Phenomena that are arising (*uppādino dhammā*)...

[Dhammasaṅgaṇī Tikamātikā 17]. *Bhṛ* means to carry or support. One who carries a garland (*māla*) at all times is a *mālabhārī*. One whose habit is to bear [burdens] is a *bhājī*. One whose habit is to eat hot food is [a *uṇhabhojī*].

One who eats hot food is a "hot-eater. One who considers oneself possessed of virtue is "one who fancies oneself" (*attamānī*). One who considers oneself wise is "one who fancies oneself wise" (*paṇḍitamānī*). One whose nature is to obtain is "one who gains" (*lābhī*); one whose nature is to speak is "one who speaks" (*vācī*).

Likewise: one who speaks thus; one who speaks on the goal (*atthavādī*); one who speaks on the Dhamma (*dhammavādī*); one who speaks what is logical (*yuttavādī*); one who speaks what is liberated (*muttavādī*); one who speaks by way of analysis (*vibhajjavādī*).

One who dwells constantly is a "resident" (*vāsī*); specifically, a village-resident (*gāmavāsī*) or a town-resident (*nagaravāsī*). One whose nature is to bear a burden is "one who bears the burden" (*bhāravāhī*).
One who carries the burden is a *bhāravāhī*. One who follows and pursues the Dhamma and wisdom is a *dhammānusārī*. Likewise for a *saddhānusārī*.
One who frequently remembers and thinks about the unsightly side of evil is a *vippaṭisārī*. One who kills living beings by way of his character is a *pāṇaghātī*;
it is the killing (*ghāta*) of one who kills (*hanassa*).
"Because one carries away everything that ought to be carried away by means of virtue, he is a *hārahārī*," and so forth.
According to the rule of grammatical analysis, "kagā ca jānam," even when not followed by the vowel *a*, there is a substitution of *ka* and *ga* for *ca* and *ja*;
thus, "that which digests equally" is *samavepākī* (the digestive fire), *samavepākinī* (the stomach), and "that in which the substrate (*upadhi*) ripens as its fruit" is *upadhivepākinī*.

One who is habitually sorrowful is "sorrowful" (*sokī*); one whose offspring are sorrowful is "one with sorrowing offspring" (*sokinī-pajā*). One who, having become liberated, is habitually generous is "liberally giving" (*muttacāgī*). One who is habitually sharing is "sharing" (*saṃvibhāgī*).

One who is habitually enjoying sensual pleasure is "enjoying sensual pleasures" (*kāmabhogī*). One who is habitually enjoying wealth that is not divided separately is "one who enjoys undivided wealth" (*apaṭivibhattabhogī*).
One who is habitually applying himself [to yoga] is "a practitioner of yoga" (*yogī*), and so forth.
795. *Āvī* (Kaccāyana 532; Rūpasiddhi 590; Nyāsa 1114).
The suffix *āvī* occurs after a verbal root (*kattari*).
One who has the habit of seeing fear is "one who sees fear" (*bhayadassāvī*).
Thus ends the section on the group of forms containing the vowel *i*.
Now, the group of forms containing the vowel *u*: 796. *Bhaṅgu*, *bhīrū*, *bhāsu*, *assavā*.
These words are declined with the suffix *nipacca* after "sīla" and other bases according to the Great Grammarian (*Mahāvutti*).
The root *bhanj* means destruction; that which has the nature of being destroyed is "pabhaṅgu," referring to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*).
The root *bhī* means fear; one who has the nature of fearing is "bhīru."
*Bhā-dittiyaṃ*: one whose nature is to illuminate is *bhāsu*, meaning radiance. One who listens with reverence according to his character is called *assava*-putta (an obedient son);
[likewise] *assavā*-bhariyā (an obedient wife). 797. *Vidā kū ka*. 535; *rū*. 593; *nī*. 1119.
After the word *vid*, *kū* becomes *ka* in the agentive case.
One who knows by means of virtue is a *vidū* (wise person); [specifically] a knower of the world (*lokavidū*) or a knower of others' minds (*paracittavidū*). In the feminine, it is *paracittavidunī*.

[Note on the suffix -ū: From the root *vit-* (known), after the prefix *vi-*, the suffix *-ū* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). This is established in the Kaśikā 535, Rūpasiddhi 593, and Niddesa 1119.
One whose nature is to cognize is "viññū" (wise).
799. *Kammā ka* 535; *rū* 593; *nī* 1119. When preceded by an object (*kamma*), the suffix *kū* occurs after the verb *jñā* (to know) in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

One who knows everything by virtue of his moral conduct is *sabbaññū* (omniscient). He is one who knows the past (*rattaññū*), knows the meaning (*atthaññū*), knows the Dhamma (*dhammaññū*), knows the proper time (*kālaññū*), and knows the occasion (*samayaññū*).
[Grammatical rule: After the word *gama*, when followed by a karmopapada, the suffix *rū* occurs in the sense of the agent.
By the rule "when followed by *rā* as an anubandha, there is elision of all vowels following the final consonant of the verbal root," there is elision of the final vowel of the root.

One who goes to the further shore by means of virtue is a *pāragū*; "veda" refers to the knowledge of the supreme path, and one who goes to that *veda* is a *vedagū*; one who goes along the course is an *addhagū*.
Thus ends the collection of forms with inserted vowels (*uvaṇṇantarūparāsi*). This concludes the collection of feminine-gendered forms (*itthiliṅgarūparāsi*).
Now, the feminine gender suffixes are stated. 801.

In the feminine gender, when expressing a state (*bhāva*) or an agent (*kāraka*), the suffixes *a*, *ṇa*, *ti*, *ka*, *yaka*, *ya*, and also *ana* occur. (Note: *...kti...* appears in many manuscripts.
When it is intended to express the feminine gender, the suffixes *a*, *ṇa*, *ti*, *ka*, *yaka*, *ya*, and *ana* are applied to denote either a state or an agent.
The suffix *itthiyam* (denoting the feminine) occurs after [stems ending in] *ka*, *a*, *ṇa*, *yaka*, *ya*, and *ana*.
For example: that in which one sits by oneself (*attani*) and conceals or restrains [faults] is a *guhā* (cave); she who defiles herself or another is a *dūsī* (a corrupt woman).

From *muda* (joy) and *hāsa* (laughter): *modanaṃ* is *mudā*; *pamudā* (exultation). That by which one is purified is *sudhā* (lime/plaster). She who bears wealth (*vasu*), that is, treasure, is *vasudhā* (the earth), and so forth.
It is called *saṅkhā* because one reckons by means of it; likewise, it is *saṅkhyā*. It is *paññā* because one understands (*pajānāti*); it is *aññā* because one fully knows (*ājānāti*);
it is *saññā* because one perceives (*sañjānāti*), or else it is *saññā* because one perceives by means of it, or *saññā* as the act of perceiving.

It is *abhiññā* because of higher knowing; it is *paṭiññā* because of acknowledging; it is *pariññā* because of knowing by way of delimitation. It is *patiṭṭhā* because one stands firmly established therein (*patiṭṭhati*).
It stands in its own place; it remains as a limit, thus it is *avatthā*. It is grasped, thus it is *upādā-paññatti*.
It is designated as *upanidhā-paññatti* because it is held by approaching and relying upon one another. *Saddhā* is the act of believing; or, it is *saddhā* because they believe by means of it.
It is *vidhā-māno* because by means of it they distinguish themselves and hold themselves. It shines, it is divine, thus it is *bhāti dibbati*.
*Bhā* is a lunar mansion; *pabhā*, *ābhā*, and *nibhā* are its radiance. *Upamā* is so called because it is compared (*upamīyate*).
*Jhi* means to think; *pajjhāyanaṃ* is *pajjhā*. One who contemplates what is blameworthy and what is blameless is an *upajjhā*; thus, *upajjhā*. *Abhijjhā* is meditation directed toward something.
*Āsa* is in the sense of wishing; *āsīsanaṃ* is *āsā*. *Paccāsīsanaṃ* is *paccāsā*.
In the sense of sitting down, *acchana* is *acchā*.
In the senses of seeing and marking, *apekkhana* is *apekkhā*, *upekkhana* is *upekkhā*, *upaparikkhana* is *upaparikkhā*, *icchana* is *icchā*, and the desire to pervade is *vicchā*.
In the sense of envy and jealousy, *issana* is *issā*.
In the sense of striving (*īha*), *īhana* is "striving" (*īhā*).
In the sense of cutting (*ucchi*), *ucchana* is "cutting" (*ucchā*).
In the sense of shaking (*ela*), that which shakes is "the fault of *elā*" (*elā-dosa*).

It is *ojā* because it supports (*oja-thambhane*) and invigorates (*te jane*) beings and formations (*saṅkhāra*) endowed with it, or because it sustains (*samupatthambheti*) and inspires (*samuttejeti*).

It is *kalā* because it reckons (*kala-saṅkhyāne*) or is reckoned; *khamā* is forbearance (*khamana*); it is *gadā* because they roar by means of it; it is *girā* or *vācā* because it is uttered (*girīyati*) or spoken;
it is *ghaṭā* or *yūtha* because they are joined (*ghaṭīyati*) or assembled therein; it is [called] such because it causes to move intensely (*bhuso cāreti*) or moves about.
*Accharā* means a goddess. *Mahāvutti* means his great livelihood. It is called *jaṭā* because it entangles; as stated in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 1.23:

"Internal entanglement, external entanglement. It is *jarā* because one ages by means of it, or *jarā* is the state of aging. One falls into or incurs [misfortune] through it, thus it is *āpadā*. The act of succeeding is *sampadā*.
It is *upasampadā* because by means of it one thoroughly reaches or attains a superior state. The act of proceeding is *paṭipadā*.

Alternatively, it is called *paṭipadā* because by means of it they proceed toward higher distinction; thus there is the pleasant practice (*sukhappaṭipadā*) and the painful practice (*dukkhappaṭipadā*).

It is called *paṭisambhidā* because by means of them they discern—that is, they attain the differentiation of knowledge—regarding the meaning and so forth; thus there are the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
In the sense of begging for alms (*bhikkha-yācana*), it is called *bhikkhā* because one begs for alms (*bhikkhīyati*).

In the sense of training and striving (*sikkha-ghaṭana*), it is *sikkhā* because of training; or it is *sikkhā* because learners (*sekkhā*) train and strive therein—namely, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*), the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*), and so forth.

It is *titikkhā* because of enduring (*titikkhana*); it is *vīmaṃsā* because of investigating (*vīmaṃsana*); it is *tikicchā* because of healing (*tikicchana*); and it is that in which healing has departed (*vigatā tikicchā etissā*).
Doubt (*vicikicchā*); the desire to eat, hunger (*bubhukkhā*), or *bubhokkhā*; the desire to consume, appetite (*jighacchā*);
the desire to drink or enjoy, thirst (*pipāsā*); the desire to seize, the wish to take away (*jigīsā*); the desire to conquer, the wish to overcome (*vijigīsā*);
the desire to kill, the wish to slay (*jighaṃsā*), and so forth.

In the sense of the suffix *ṇamhi* and the root *ara* (to go): it goes swiftly while piercing, thus it is an *ārāvedhaka* (an awl); they perform various acts here, thus it is a *kārā-addu* (a prison);
one ages by means of this, thus it is *jārā* (old age); it crosses over, going very swiftly, thus it is *tārā* (a star); they speak by means of this, thus it is *bhāsā* (speech);
it carries swiftly, thus it is *dhārā* (a stream)—such as the edge of a sword (*khaggadhārā*) or a stream of rain (*vuṭṭhidhārā*); it transforms into various forms, thus it is *mayati*.

It goes by means of this, thus it is *māyā* (illusion); it is written, thus it is *lekhā* (writing); it is spoken, thus it is *vācā* (speech); it carries away what is delightful and sets it in motion, thus it is *hārā*—as in *muttāvali* (a string of pearls), and so forth.

In the *yak*-suffix: speaking together is *sākacchā* (conversation); cutting in that manner is *tacchā* (carpentry); lying down is *nipajjā*; he finds or knows by means of this, thus it is *vijjā* (knowledge); or, they find or know by means of this, thus it is *vijjā*; the opposite of knowledge is *avijjā* (ignorance); sitting down is *nisajjā*.
In the sense of "shining here," *samijjhana* becomes *samijjhā*.
In the sense of "accomplishment" (*nipphatti*), *sijjhana* becomes *sijjhā*, and so forth.

In the sense of "thoroughly sweeping" (*saṃsuddhi*) that which is to be swept (*yamhi-maja*), *sammajjana* becomes *sammajjā*. "Going forth" (*apecca vajana*) or "departure" (*gamana*) is *pabbajjā*; "wandering" (*caraṇa*) is *cariyā*; "attending upon" (*paricaraṇa*) is *pāricariyā*. [In these cases], by the rule "after a vowel" (*ūbyañjanassa*), there is the augment *ī* and the shortening of the vowel.
*Jāgara-niddakkhaye*: "The exhaustion of wakefulness and sleep. *Jāgaraṇaṃ* is "wakefulness"; *seyyā* is that wherein one lies down (the word is a feminine noun).
*Saṅgāyanā*: they sing together or recite the scriptures there; it is a compound. *Paṭṭhānaṃ*: it is established or firmly fixed therein; *pāpanā*:
it is brought to completion, fully accomplished, or brought to a conclusion; *upāsanā*: it is attended upon or honored; *payirūpāsanā*; it is sought after.
Seeking (*esanā*), searching (*pariyesanā*); seeking for sensual pleasures (*kāmesanā*), seeking for existence (*bhavesanā*), seeking for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*);
performing actions such as cutting and breaking, which constitutes "inflicting punishment" (*kammakāraṇā*); initial growth; the thirty-two types of inflicting punishment.
It is called volition (*cetanā*) because it thinks (*cetati*) and because associated states think by means of it. It is thought (*cintanā*), and it is established (*ṭhapīyate*).
*Ṭhapanā* (establishing); *dīpanā* (illuminating), from *dīpiyate*; *vipassanā* (insight), from "they see clearly by means of this"; *sandassanā* (pointing out), from *sandassīyate*;

*desanā* (teaching), from *desīyate*, or alternatively, *desanā* from "it is taught by means of this"; *patthanā* (aspiration), from *patthīyate*; *pharaṇā* (pervading), from *pharīyate*; *phusanā* (touching), from *phusīyate*;
*bhāvanā* (cultivation), from *bhāvīyate*; *vibhāvanā* (clearing away); *sambhāvanā* (conceiving); *mantanā* (counseling), from *mantīyate*; *nimantanā* (invitation).
*Āmantanā* means addressing. *Anumodanā* means that by this they rejoice again and again. *Yācanā* means that which is requested; *āyācanā* is a request made with reverence.
*Yojanā* means that which is joined. The root *rac-* signifies arrangement: *racanā*, *āracanā*, and *viracanā*.
The root *vaṭṭ-* signifies turning: *āvaṭṭanā* and *vivaṭṭanā*. *Vedanā* means that which is felt (*vedīyate*).

In *vara-icchā*, it is desired (*icchiyate*), thus it is *icchā*; it is invited (*pavāriyate*), thus it is *pavāraṇā*. It is perfumed (*vāsīyate*), thus it is *vāsanā*. It is wished for (*āsīsīyate*), thus it is *āsīsanā*. It is harmed (*hiṃsīyate*), thus it is *hiṃsanā*, and so forth.

Because of the rule regarding the abundance of the suffix *-ti*, there is also the feminine form; thus: singing is *gāyanaṃ* or *gīti*. Singing together is *saṅgīti*. Bad singing is *duggīti*. Following after singing is *anugīti*. One is known as "a relative" (*ñāti*) because it is known that "this one is among our own.

Knowing is *ñatti*. [The suffix *-ti*] becomes double (*dvitta*); standing is *ṭhānaṃ* or *ṭhiti*. From the root *dā* in the sense of cutting, it is given by this, thus it is *datti*; [the suffix *-ti*] becomes double. She holds, thus she is a *dhāti*; holding is *dhāraṇaṃ* or *akampanaṃ* (steadfastness).
*Dhīti*: from *samādahana*, it is *samādhi*; by the rule of *mahāvutti*, the *ā* becomes *ī*, and by the rule for doubling (*dvitte*), *dh* becomes *dd* with shortening of the vowel;

thus, *dīdhiti* means "ray. *Nibbāyana* is *nibbuti*; the *ā* becomes *u*. *Samiti*: that which goes together (*saha ayanaṃ*). *Īti*: that which comes (*eti*) or arrives; thus, *īti* refers to calamity or affliction.

*Viciti*: the act of discerning. *Vijiti*: the act of conquering. *Nīti*: that by which one is led (*nīyati*) or known (*ñāyati*); thus, *nīti* refers to worldly policy (*lokanīti*) or the policy of the Dhamma (*dhammanīti*).
*Saddanīti*: it leads to existence, thus *bhavanetti*; increase and doubling; the guidance of the True Dhamma (*saddhammanetti*).
It gladdens, thus *pīti*; the state of fearing is *bhīti*; falling away is *cuti*; impelling is *juti*; praising is *thuti* or *abhitthuti*;
blowing is *pūti*; becoming is *bhūti*; it becomes well, thus *subhūti*; disintegration is *vibhūti*; and excellent reflection.
Binding is *sammuti*; hearing is *suti*, or *suti* because it is heard; *pasuti*, *upasuti*; it is called *huti* because it is offered (*hūyati*);

it is called *āhuti* because it is to be offered after being brought; honoring is *cāyana*, *pūjana*, and *citi*; from the doubling [of the consonant] comes *citti*, *apaciti*; *essa* means one's own self; and contemplation is *nijjhāyana*, which is *nijjhatti*.
According to the *Mahāvutti*, the substitution of *ku* for *ka* occurs before *ta*: *kriyā-kutti*, *sara-kutti*, *itthi-kuttaṃ*, *purisa-kuttaṃ*.
*Janetti*: she who gives birth (*janeti*); here, *ī* is substituted for *ī* by rule. *Bandhati*: that which is bound (*bandhīyate*); *patti*: that which reaches (*pajjati*) or a foot (*padāti*);
here, *ā* is substituted for *ī* by rule. *Vasati-gehaṃ*: a dwelling where they reside (*vasanti ettha*); or "residing" (*vasanaṃ*), as in "he resides" (*vasati*), and so forth.
802. *Jāhāhi ni*: by these [rules], *ni* becomes [the suffix].

In the case of *jā-hāni*, there is *jiyyate* (he is worn out/decays), *jāni* (loss); *dhanajāni* (loss of wealth), *bhogajāni* (loss of enjoyments). One who has great loss is *mahājāniyo*. *Hiyyate* (he is lost/decreased) is *hāni*; *vaṇṇahāni* (loss of beauty), *balahāni* (loss of strength), *āyuhāni* (loss of life-span), *avahāni* (deprivation), *parihāni* (decline).
803. *Karā ririyo* (Ka. 554; Rū. 601; Nī. 1141).
The suffix *ririya* occurs after the root *kṛ*.
From *kṛ*, [the form] *kiriyā* is derived; by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the form *kriyā* is established.
Thus ends the section on the mass of feminine gender forms.
804. The Section on the Mass of Nouns beginning with *rīrikkha* (the sky):

The suffixes *ka*, *kām*, *kāni*, etc., are used after nouns denoting direction (*disā*) when they function as the object (*kamma*), provided they are similar or different from the subject (*samānaññabhavanta*). *rīrikkha-kā*: [rīrikkha + kā] = 642; [rūpa: 588]; [nīti: 1269].

When the words *samāna*, *añña*, *bhavanta*, and *yādi*—acting as the bases of comparison (*upamānabhūta*)—are followed by the conditions *para*, *disa*, *mha*, *kammerī*, *rikka*, *kho*, and *ca*, the suffixes *rī* and *rikka* are applied.

In the forms *disa-rī* and *disa-rikka*, the vowels following the final consonant of *disa* are elided by the rule “*rānubandhentasarādissa*” (the elision of vowels following the final consonant when *r* is the suffix).
The letter *kā* attached as a suffix serves no purpose other than to prevent vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). This is established by the compound rules such as “*rīrikkakesu*.”
The form of the preceding words must be established:
*ya*, *ta*, *eta*, *ima*, *kiṃ*, *tumha*, *amha*, *bhavanta*, *samāna*, *añña*.
"That which is seen like *ya*" is *yādi*; [one who is] *yādikkha*, *yādisa*. "Those whom they see like *ya*" is *yādi*; "those who are seen like *ye*" is...
That which is seen as "like *yā*" is *yādinī*, *yādikkhā*, *yādikkhī*, *yādisā*, *yādisī*;
those which are seen as "like *yā*" are *yādiniyo*, *yādikkhāyo*, *yādikkhiyo*, *yādisāyo*, *yādisiyo*. The same applies to the remaining [forms].
That which is seen as "like *so*" is *tādī*, *tādikkho*, *tādiso*.
"Appearing like this" is *edī*, *edikkho*, *ediso*, *etādī*, *etādikkho*, or *etādiso*.
"Appearing like this one" is *īdī*, *īdikkho*, or *īdiso*.
"Appearing like what? is *kīdī*, *kīdikkho*, or *kīdiso*.
"One who appears like you" is *tādī*, *tādikkho*, or *tādiso*.
"One who appears like me" is *mādī*, *mādikkho*, or *mādiso*.
In the plural, however, "those who appear like you" are *tumhādī*, *tumhādikkho*, or *tumhādiso*.
"Seen as like us" means *amhādī*, *amhādikkho*, or *amhādiso*.
"Seen as like your honor" means *bhavādī*, *bhavādikkho*, or *bhavādiso*.
"Seen as like oneself" means *sadī*, *sadikkho*, or *sadiso*.
"Aññādī" means "appearing as something else," "resembling something else," or "of another kind. Regarding the feminine:
"yā viya dissati" means "a woman who appears like this," thus *yādisā-itthī* or *yādisī-itthī*. Similarly, *tādisā-itthī* or *tādisī-itthī*, and so forth. 805.
After *vama* and other such words, the suffix *thu* is added. (Kaccāyana 644; Rūpasiddhi 661; Nyāsa 1271–3; 'vamādīhyathu' [found in many manuscripts]).
The suffix *thu* occurs after roots such as *vam* when they function as causative agents (*bhāvakāraka*).
For example: *vamīyate* becomes *vamathu* ("vomiting"), and *davīyate* becomes *davathu* ("fever"), and so forth. (Kaccāyana 530; Rūpasiddhi 584; Nyāsa 1112).
The suffix *kvip* occurs after verbal roots (*bhāvakāraka*).
807. The elision of *kvip* occurs. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.67; Rūpamālā 585; Nyāsa 1266).
The elision of *kvip* takes place.
Regarding the *ivaṇṇa* vowels first: it "accumulates" (*cayati*) or "increases" (*vaḍḍhati*) abundantly, thus *acci*; there is the doubling of the consonant and the shortening of the vowel.

It "accumulates" or "increases" in various ways, thus *vīci*. It "conquers" (*jināti*) the five Māras, thus *māraji*. It "conquers" what is auspicious (*bhadda*), thus *bhaddaji*. Likewise, *puṇṇaji*.
It leads (*neti*) the village (*gāma*) or the multitude, thus *gāmaṇī*; here, the *na* becomes *ṇa*. It leads the army (*sena*), thus *senānī*, and so forth.

He kills and causes [beings] to fall away from their states, thus he is *maccu*; by the rule of the Great Grammarians (*Mahāvutti*), there is the substitution of the short vowel for the following form.
It moves swiftly and spreads in various ways, thus it is *vijju*. That wherein beings (*bhava*) exist is *bhū*, meaning "ground" (*bhūmi*).
He originates and exercises sovereignty, thus he is *pabhū*. Dissolution is *vibhū*. He overcomes, thus he is *abhibhū*. He exists by himself, thus he is *sayambhū*. He overcomes lineage, thus...
*gottabhū*, *gotrabhū*, and so forth. Regarding the elision of final consonants: 808.
*Kvimhi lopontabyañjanassa ka* (Ka 615; Rū 586; Nī 1220). [In the presence of the suffix] *kvim*, there is the elision of the final consonant.
There is elision of the final consonant of verbal roots before the suffix *kvip*.

One who brings an end is "an end-maker" (*antaka*); one who causes joy is "a bringer of joy" (*nandaka*); one who gives life is "a giver of life" (*jīvaka*); one who makes the mind variegated is "one who makes the mind variegated" (*cittaka*).
That which is to be endured with ease is "ease" (*sukha*); that which is to be endured with difficulty is "suffering" (*dukkha*). Around...
It is called *parikkhā* because it is worn away (*khaññati*). It is called *saṅkho* because it digs itself up (*saṃ khanati*). It is called *ago* or *nago* because it does not go (*na gacchati*).
It is called *sīsūpago* because it goes toward the head (*sīsaṃ upagacchati*). Likewise, *gīvūpago*. It is called *ninnagā* or a river because it goes to a low place (*ninnaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati*).
It is called *turaṅgo* because it goes swiftly and quickly (*turaṃ sīghaṃ gacchati*), with the addition of the syllable *-bind-* in the middle.

It is called a *bhujaga* because it moves with its curved body; an *uraga* because it moves on its belly; a *khaga* because it moves through the sky (*kha*); a *vihaga* because it moves through the air (*vehāsa*). In the Great Rule (*mahāvutti*), there is a substitution of *viha* for *vehāsa*.

Furthermore, in cases such as "the bull goes" (*go gacchati*) or "the cows go" (*gāvo gacchanti*), and in terms like *gocara*, *godhana*, *gotta*, and *gotrabhū*, when the suffix *kvim* is applied, after the elision of the final consonant and the elision of the *k*, the Great Rule effects the substitution of *otta* for the *upanta* (the penultimate vowel), resulting in the form *go*.
The natural form (*pakatirūpa*) is to be understood. That in which strength is counted is *balagga*; that in which food is taken is *bhattagga*.
Likewise, there are *salākagga* (voting by lots) and *uposathagga* (the assembly for the Uposatha).
That which is produced by action is *kammaja*. Likewise, there are *cittaja* (mind-born), *utuja* (heat-born), and *atrāja* (born of oneself); *pubbaja* (born previously).
"Born after" is *anuja* (younger brother); "born together" is *sahaja* (congenital); "born on dry land" is *thalaja*. Likewise, *dakaja*, *vārija*, and *ambuja*.
"Born from an egg" is *aṇḍaja*; "born twice" is *dvija*; "they speak together here" is *sabhā*;
"he delights in a bower" is *kuñjara*, and so forth.
809. *Kvimhi gho paripaccāsamohi ka.* (Ka. 538; Rū. 595; Nī. 1123; ‘...pacca... in many texts).
Before these suffixes—*pari*, *pati*, *ā*, *sañ*, and *o*—the substitution of *gha* occurs for the following root *han*. In *parihaññati* (“is obstructed”), it becomes *paligho*;
here, the short vowel *a* is replaced by *l*. In *patihanati* (“strikes back”), it becomes *paṭigho*; here, the short vowel *a* is replaced by *ṭ*. [In *bhuso hanati* (“he strikes violently”)]...
It is called *agha* because it oppresses (*bādhati*), meaning suffering and evil; it is called *vyaggha* because it specifically and intensely strikes down (*visesena bhuso hanati*);

it is called *saṅgha* because it is gathered together (*saṃhata*) through commonality of virtue, referring to a community such as the community of deities, the community of Brahmas, or a herd of deer;
and it is called *ogha* because it carries away (*ohanati*) by casting one down, referring to the flood of defilements, the flood of saṃsāra, or a flood of water.
In the *Suttavibhaṅga*, the suffix *gha* occurs even from other [roots]: *mātaraṃ hanati* (he kills his mother) becomes *mātugha*;
likewise *pitugha*, and so forth. 810. *Ṇvādayo* (Ka. 650; Rū. 651; Nī. 1288).

The suffixes beginning with *ṇu* occur after verbal roots (*kriyattha*) when expressing the action itself (*bhāva*) or the agent (*kāraka*). All the subsequent section on *ṇvādi* suffixes that will be stated hereafter constitutes an exposition (*niddesa*) of this rule; therefore, only a small portion is stated here.

One who *karoti* (makes) is a craftsman (*kāru-sippī*); one who *ayati* or *vaḍḍhati* (goes or increases) is *āyu*; or else, that by which beings (*sattā*) *ayanti* or *vaḍḍhanti* (go or increase) is *āyu-jīvitaṃ* (life-span).

They abandon (*rahanti*) or leave behind (*jahanti*) a special splendor (*sobhā-visesaṃ*) because of him, thus he is Rāhu, the lord of the asuras (*asurindo*). One who accomplishes (*sādheti*) welfare and happiness is a good person (*sādhu-sappuriso*).
It blows (*vāyati*), thus it is wind (*vāyu-vāto*), and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the group of conditions such as *rī* and *rikkha*. The section on the natural forms is concluded.
Thus ends [this work] called the Moggallānadīpanī, which is an elucidation of grammatical terminology.
The section called "The Chapter on That" is concluded.
